papers.abstract: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.
authors: Derong Jin, Xiyi Chen, Ming C. Lin, Ruohan Gao
bullets: Introduces Video-to-4DAVScene, a task for generating time-varying audio-visual scenes from a single video.
Reconstructs a 360° static background and explicit motion trajectories for dynamic, sound-emitting objects.
Uses dual-space audio diffusion synchronization to synthesize physically grounded, multi-source sound fields.
Supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial-audio rendering.
Real-world evaluations and a user study indicate perceptually realistic audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SONOWORLD4D. Given a monocular video, we extract depth maps, camera poses, foreground masks, and VLM-derived audio prompts. For visual scene generation (Sec. 4.2), the framework reconstructs per-object dynamic Gaussians, lifts an outpainted 360◦ panorama into background Gaussians, and aligns them into a common world frame via scale correction and local displacement correction. For dynamic sound field generation (Sec. 4.3), static sources are synthesized via text-to-audio and anchored to the background. Dynamic sources are generated via dual-space diffusion synchronization: at each sampling step, forward rendering (Ri) maps object-space predictions to camera space, while source separation and inverse rendering (Qi) map camera-space mixtures back to individual object spaces. The resulting scene enables real-time novel-pose visual and spatial audio rendering (Sec. 4.4).

Figure 4: STFT visualization of spatial audio rendered at a novel-listener position. The top two rows show input video frames and our novel-view renderings on a shared timeline. Highlighted intervals (a) and (b) indicate when the airplane is closest to the input camera and the novel listener, respectively. Correct spatialization should concentrate energy near (b) with a downward frequency shift due to the Doppler effect. Sonic4D retains strong energy near (a). Ours (V2A) responds near both (a) and (b). Ours (T2A) responds near (b) but lacks clear spectral structure. Our full method produces a dominant response with a visible Doppler shift around (b), correctly adapting both amplitude and frequency to the novel-listener position.

Figure 3: Time-azimuth RMS visualization of ambisonics. Top: mid-frame panoramas of each video rendered by our method at microphone poses in SONOSCENE4D with faces blurred to protect privacy. Remaining rows compare the reference FOA recordings with baselines and ours. Each map shows the peak-normalized directional RMS response over time and azimuth after spherical-areaweighted aggregation over elevation. Our method more closely follows the reference azimuthal trajectories and temporal structure, while the baselines exhibit directional mismatches or reduced spatiotemporal variation.

Figure 6: Motion-type-specific instantiations for dynamic foreground generation. Each branch combines object motion estimation with canonical Gaussian generation and a local deformation model: identity for rigid objects, linear blend skinning (Magnenat-Thalmann et al., 1989) for humans, and learned per-Gaussian center offsets (Litman et al., 2026) for non-rigid objects.

Figure 7: Qualitative ablation on visual components. Top: Ablation of displacement correction in foreground-background alignment. Both variants include global scale alignment; adding local displacement corrections reduces foreground interpenetration with the ground. Bottom: Both panorama-to-3D backbones produce usable scenes, but Marble yields fewer visible reconstruction artifacts in the illustrated example.
Figure 5: Pairwise user preferences. Bars show mean per-participant preference rates, and error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 8: VLM prompt for video-based scene understanding. Condensed presentation of the instructions used to obtain scene descriptions, sound-source attributes, and generation and separation prompts. Examples and repeated validation instructions are omitted for brevity.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison on SONOSCENE4D for video-to-4D audio-visual scene generation. We compare our full method against baselines and two ablated variants: Ours (T2A) and Ours (V2A), which use text-to-audio and video-to-audio generation for dynamic-source signals, respectively. Angular errors are in degrees. ↓/↑ indicate whether lower/higher is better.

papers.title: SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
papers.tldr: SonoWorld4D converts a monocular video into an explorable 4D scene with synchronized novel-view visuals and spatial audio.

papers.abstract: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck
authors: Yuze He, Yixiang Wei, Wang Zhao, Chuhao Chen, Yanning Zhou, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Targets game- and avatar-ready stylized hair represented as artist-placed hair-card primitives.
Models each card as a token and jointly denoises the unordered card set with a diffusion transformer.
Also generates spring-bone chains and exports assets in downstream-ready formats.
On CHARM’s test set, reduces Chamfer distance by 44%, more than halves orientation error, and runs 33× faster.
Outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines, and strand-based methods from single images.

Figure 3. Network design. Top: the card VAE. The encoder reads the control points of one card with their arc-length fractions ui, plus a learned summary token [CLS], whose output alone gives the mean and log-variance of the 32-d latent z. papers.title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image

papers.abstract: Cross-modal scene and instance retrieval aims to retrieve a corresponding 3D environment or object given query 2D images, serving as a foundational mechanism for spatial reasoning in robotics and AR/VR. Existing methods achieve this by learning alignment only at the level of whole scenes or objects, which provides no supervision for the fine-grained local structure within them. In this work, we show that supervision on a set of sparse 2D-3D correspondences, without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives, is sufficient to train a single model for both scene- and instance-level retrieval. Specifically, we propose $\textbf{CrossWeave}$, a novel framework for cross-modal retrieval that learns sparse patch-point alignment, which alone outperforms existing methods. An optimal transport-based aggregator over the aligned features gives further gains by clustering structurally redundant regions, freeing descriptor capacity for semantically distinct local features. CrossWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance on both scene- and instance-level retrieval on ScanNet and 3RScan with a $\textit{single model}$, whereas existing methods require separate models for each task. Our results suggest that whole-scene encoding is unnecessary for cross-modal retrieval and that sparse local correspondence supervision is a more effective and flexible alternative.
authors: Aadith Warrier, Gnana Prakash Punnavajhala, Siddharth Tourani, Muhammad Haris Khan, Avinash Sharma, Madhava Krishna
bullets: Targets cross-modal retrieval of 3D scenes or objects from 2D image queries for robotics and AR/VR.
Learns fine-grained sparse patch–point alignment without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives.
Aggregates aligned features with optimal transport to cluster redundant regions and preserve capacity for distinct local features.
Reports state-of-the-art scene- and instance-level retrieval on ScanNet and 3RScan using a single model.
Suggests sparse local correspondence supervision can replace whole-scene encoding, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CrossWeave. CrossWeave learns cross-modal retrieval representations from sparse image patch-3D point correspondences rather than scene- or instance-level labels. Scene Sampling: Given calibrated RGB-D observations and a reconstructed 3D map, visible patchpoint pairs are obtained by projecting 3D points into the image plane, filtering occluded points using rendered depth, quantizing valid pixels into DINOv2 patch tokens, and selecting a compact semantically diverse subset using feature-space farthest point sampling. Feature Extraction: Frozen encoders extract local patch and point features, which are projected by learnable projection matrices W patch and W point into a shared embedding space. Feature Aggregation: A shared SALAD aggregator then maps variable-sized sets of local features into fixed-dimensional descriptors. Training combines a local patch-point Lp2p contrastive loss with an aggregated image-point-cloud contrastive loss Li2pc, preserving fine-grained alignment while organizing local evidence into retrieval-ready descriptors. At inference, the same encoders and projection heads serve both tasks: SALAD descriptors are used for scene retrieval and mean-pooled local features for instance retrieval.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison of cross-modal scene retrieval on ScanNet. Given a set of query RGB images, each model retrieves the most similar 3D scenes from the database. The groundtruth scene is shown on the left, and retrieved scenes are ordered by similarity from left to right. CrossOver and CrossOver (Updated) fail to retrieve the correct scene within the top five results, while CrossWeave retrieves it at rank 1. The remaining retrieved scenes are also semantically consistent, indicating that CrossWeave learns descriptors that capture both local cross-modal correspondences and global scene context.

Figure 7: Comparisons of Top-5 retrievals on a ScanNet room scene. Retrievals are ordered from most to least similar moving left to right, with correct matches highlighted in green. CrossWeave successfully retrieves the correct scene at rank 1, while CrossOver (Updated) retrieves it at rank 2, and the base model of CrossOver fails within the top 5.

Figure 9: Qualitative results on a 3RScan dining area scene. CrossWeave successfully retrieves the ground truth point cloud as its top match, while CrossOver (Updated) ranks it fourth and the base CrossOver model fails to retrieve it within the top 5.

Figure 10: Retrieval results on a 3RScan kitchen and dining scene. CrossWeave demonstrates superior discriminative ability by retrieving the exact scene at rank 1 from highly localized query images, whereas both baseline models completely fail to place the correct match within their top 5 retrievals.

Figure 3: Qualitative instance retrieval on ScanNet. For each query view with its instance mask (left), CrossWeave ranks the instances of the same scene (middle) by cosine similarity. The Top-3 retrievals are shown with their similarity scores, and the correct match is outlined in green.

Figure 13: Failure case on a 3RScan living room scene. All three models miss the ground-truth scene in the top 5, as the retrieved scenes are visually and structurally similar to the query (a brown sectional sofa with a wooden coffee table). CrossWeave’s top matches still share the furniture arrangement (sofas and central coffee tables), whereas CrossOver (Updated) retrieves structurally different scenes.

Figure 6: Visualizations for the effect of FPS sampling. Images with red dots denote random sampling. Images with blue dots denote FPS sampled points. It can clearly be observed that FPS enables us to avoid over-sampling on the often visually dominant but geometrically uninformative areas in the images such as walls, floors and other flat surfaces, thereby boosting feature diversity within each training batch. Note: We have visualized a large number of pixel-point pairs in these images; in our training framework we only use 32 patch-point pairs. Refer to Section 3.1 for more details.

Figure 8: Additional qualitative results on a ScanNet office scene. CrossWeave retrieves the ground truth point cloud as its top match, whereas both CrossOver (Updated) and CrossOver only identify the correct scene at rank 5.

Figure 11: Additional results on a 3RScan kitchen scene. CrossWeave correctly identifies the target environment at rank 1, outperforming CrossOver, which places the match at rank 4, and CrossOver (Updated), which misses it entirely.

Figure 12: Qualitative instance retrieval on 3RScan. For each query view with its instance mask (left), CrossWeave ranks the instances of the same scene (middle) by cosine similarity. The Top-3 retrievals are shown with their similarity scores, and the correct match is outlined in green.

Figure 14: Instance retrieval failures on ScanNet and 3RScan. In both cases the query is a chair and the Top-1 retrieval (red) is another chair of the same type in the same scene, while the correct instance (green) is ranked second with a similar score.

Figure 4: Scene retrieval performance (Top-1 recall) on ScanNet and 3RScan as a function of training data volume. Performance is stable across data regimes, with even 10% of the full training set sufficient to outperform the previous state of the art.
Figure 5: Scene retrieval performance (Top-1 recall) as a function of the number of query camera views. The main results use 10 views.

Table 2: Comparison of within-scene instance retrieval performance on ScanNet and 3RScan. †
Table 3: Scene retrieval on 3RScan against SceneGraphLoc and CrossOver. Each query image is ranked against N candidate scenes; Top-k: percentage of queries with the correct scene in the top k.

papers.title: CrossWeave: Cross-Modal Scene and Instance Retrieval from Sparse 2D-3D Alignment
papers.tldr: CrossWeave uses sparse 2D–3D patch-point correspondences and optimal-transport aggregation to jointly retrieve scenes and instances with one model.

papers.abstract: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.
authors: Oliver Hahn, Rodrigo Marcuzzi, Sangeetha Grama Srinivasan, Alessandro Burzio, Sherwin Bahmani, Jiahui Huang, Stefan Roth, Shengyu Huang, Qunjie Zhou, Laura Leal-Taix\'e
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually realistic generative 3D reconstruction and the semantic, instance-level understanding needed for robotics and physical AI.
Jointly predicts 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues from video latents.
Requires neither captured multi-view data, manual 3D annotations, nor per-scene optimization.
Supports novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, object grouping, and extension to structured dynamic scenes from monocular video.
Outperforms combined reconstruction and 3DGS-segmentation baselines on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks while preserving reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Infant pose and shape estimation is essential for applications in childcare, developmental monitoring, and medical diagnosis. However, existing methods and datasets are largely designed for adults, and direct transfer to infants fails due to substantial differences in body proportions, articulation limits, and frequent self-occlusion. To address this gap, we introduce InfantNet, the largest real-image infant dataset to date, comprising 108,902 RGB images of infants aged 6-18 months. Each image is annotated with 2D keypoints, and a curated subset of 11,642 images additionally includes 3D pose and shape annotations with full SMIL parameters, verified through multi-view rendering and reprojection-error filtering. We use an iterative annotation pipeline to ensure high fidelity across both 2D and 3D labels. InfantNet establishes a large-scale, comprehensive benchmark for infant 2D keypoint detection and 3D pose-and-shape recovery. Baseline experiments demonstrate that state-of-the-art adult pose estimators do not generalize well to infants, whereas fine-tuning on InfantNet yields a consistent improvement. The gains are even more pronounced for 3D pose and shape estimation, where SMIL-based estimation demonstrates robust performance with accuracy comparable to results reported for SMPL-based models. By releasing the InfantNet dataset and benchmark, we provide a vital resource for advancing infant pose analysis and related healthcare applications.

papers.abstract: Aerial imagery provides complementary spatial context for autonomous driving by exposing road structure beyond the immediate perception range of onboard sensors. Yet map construction from aerial imagery, aerial-assisted online HD mapping, and cross-view localization are typically studied on separate data and benchmarks. We introduce KITScenes Aerial, an extension of the KITScenes Multimodal dataset that augments synchronized onboard sensor data, vehicle poses, and rich Lanelet2 map annotations with spatially associated aerial imagery and higher-resolution neural representations, providing a common basis for a variety of research tasks. Our mapping evaluation focuses on all 53 KITScenes map classes across different model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions, while retaining compatibility with the widely used three-class setting. Representative baselines show that aerial context is particularly beneficial for fine-grained and extended-range mapping, more than doubling 53-class mAP at the larger mapping extent. Higher-resolution aerial imagery yields a further 4.3 mAP (+24 %) improvement, with gains extending to challenging map elements such as traffic lights. We additionally evaluate cross-view localization under geographically disjoint conditions, where an adapted fine-grained feature-matching baseline achieves a mean translation error of 5.13 m. KITScenes Aerial thus enables unified study of aerial and ground-level information across complementary mapping and localization tasks. Project page: https://kitscenes.com/aerial

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. papers.abstract: Generating interactive 3D assets from a single image requires realistic appearance, fidelity to the depicted object, and plausible physical behavior. Yet detailed geometry alone does not determine how an object should move or deform. We introduce PhysAg3D, which couples 3D generative models with agentic reasoning and tool use. A vision-language agent first infers semantic parts, candidate interactions, and physical priors from the image; a 3D generator then produces a textured whole-object mesh from the same image. A hierarchical interaction representation links these revisable priors to mechanisms and the generated surfaces they control, organizing interaction construction and refinement. Guided by this representation and observations of the mesh, the agent uses geometric and physical tools to construct parts, joints, deformable regions, and surface bindings while retaining useful generated geometry and materials. Rendered interactions and execution measurements guide targeted revisions within a fixed budget. The framework accommodates both rigid articulation and compliant deformation. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks demonstrate detailed, image-aligned assets with plausible interactions. Ablations support bounded refinement and source-surface preservation. Project Page: supra-3d.github.io/PhysAg3D.

papers.abstract: Iterative refinement models have significantly improved stereo matching accuracy, but their rigid, fixed update schedules incur heavy computational costs and a strict trade-off between speed and accuracy. This challenge is magnified in video streams, where traditional online methods resort to reducing feature channels or relying on expensive temporal warping. To address this, we propose \textbf{DEQ-Stereo}, a novel video stereo matching framework based on the Deep Equilibrium (DEQ) paradigm. Instead of unrolling a fixed number of iterations, DEQ-Stereo reformulates the refinement as an implicit fixed-point problem, adaptively terminating once convergence is met. To ensure fast and stable intra-frame convergence, we introduce the \textbf{Convolutional Simplified Gated Unit (ConvSGU)}, which eliminates unnecessary non-linearities by modeling the latent state as a gated, element-wise sum of inputs. Furthermore, to exploit cross-frame temporal coherence, we propose \textbf{Temporal State Transfer (TST)}, a warm-start strategy that propagates the converged hidden state to the next frame without requiring explicit pose or warping priors. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that DEQ-Stereo delivers state-of-the-art performance with a superior accuracy-to-latency trade-off.
authors: Kiljoon Han, Kyumin Hwang, Wonheok Choi, Jeonghoon Kim, Sunghoom Im
bullets: Targets the high computational cost and fixed speed–accuracy trade-off of iterative stereo refinement, especially for video.

Introduces ConvSGU for faster, more stable intra-frame convergence through gated element-wise state updates.
Uses Temporal State Transfer to warm-start each frame from the previous frame’s converged state without explicit pose or warping priors.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance with a superior accuracy-to-latency trade-off.

We denote the frame index as t, the DEQ iteration step as k, and the converged state as ∗. (b) Standard ConvGRU structure. papers.abstract: Generating editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from text requires selecting operations that produce the intended changes to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can compromise subsequent steps, making reliable multi-step generation challenging. Existing methods based on large language models (LLMs) primarily learn to predict commands, without explicit supervision of the geometric states those commands should produce. Inspired by world-action models, we introduce CAD-WAM, which couples geometry-conditioned action generation with next-state prediction. We define complete modeling operations as actions in a CAD domain-specific language (DSL) and encode surface point clouds of intermediate solids into compact latent states using a pretrained variational autoencoder. An LLM backbone generates the next action from the target description and current geometric state, while an auxiliary head on the same backbone predicts the next state to provide geometric supervision during training. We construct step-wise training trajectories from parametric CAD models in the DeepCAD dataset, pairing each trajectory with an expert-level textual description. At inference, each generated action is executed by a CAD kernel, and the resulting solid is re-encoded to inform the next decision. On the DeepCAD test set, CAD-WAM outperforms the task-specific baselines in geometric accuracy and output validity, with larger gains on models requiring more operations, and produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Ablations further show that next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2\% relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions. Code is available at https://github.com/Lzy-1037/CAD-WAM.

papers.abstract: We develop a fast method for the rigid alignment of voxelized three-dimensional density functions over $\mathsf{SO}(3)$ using sliced optimal transport. Our approach efficiently transforms each density map into a tensor of one-dimensional quantile functions, taken from central slices over the unit sphere, such that the Euclidean distance of the transformed volumes approximates the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance. Our formulation is therefore compatible with existing, fast, voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms. We provide theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrating that the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance is a robust metric for comparing three-dimensional shapes and for computing their rigid alignment.
authors: Oscar Mickelin, Yunpeng Shi, Amit Singer, Eric J. Verbeke
bullets: Targets rigid rotational alignment of voxelized 3-D density functions over SO(3).
Transforms each volume into tensors of one-dimensional quantile functions from central spherical slices.
Enables use of existing fast voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms.
Provides theoretical analysis and numerical experiments supporting sliced 2-Wasserstein distance for robust 3-D shape comparison and alignment.

(Top) Example alignment of the first 11 models from the chair category. The reference model is shown in purple and the aligned models are shown in gold. (Bottom) Summary of alignment results for 10 different categories. Each dataset contains n ≈ 100 models, and the plots show the number of correctly aligned models as a function of increasing radians under the geodesic distance in eq. (24).

Each metric is normalized by its maximum value for visualization.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is increasingly explored as an input representation for 3D perception. Yet it remains unclear how current 3D architectures exploit heterogeneous Gaussian attributes. This ambiguity makes accuracy hard to interpret and limits principled architecture design for 3DGS perception. However, existing object-level 3DGS datasets lack the appearance variation or artifact control needed for systematic attribute-level analysis. We introduce COGS, a large-scale 3DGS dataset with 15,675 artifact-filtered and appearance-rich objects across 40 categories. Built on COGS, we establish COGS-Bench for object classification and attribute-usage diagnosis, complemented by external validation. Our benchmark shows that Gaussian attributes are not uniformly beneficial: selected subsets can outperform the full attribute set, and the effects of appearance, opacity, and covariance-related attribute combinations vary substantially across architectures. We further study this finding with HALO, a reference model that preserves attribute-specific evidence before hierarchical aggregation. Experiments on COGS-Bench and external 3DGS datasets demonstrate that COGS supports systematic diagnosis of 3DGS attribute usage, while HALO highlights the value of role-preserving attribute organization. Our dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/XiaoZhengCV/COGS.
authors: Zheng Xiao, Yifan Liu, Weijian Deng, Jiashu Li, Ziqin Liu, Zhenjun Han, Jianbin Jiao
bullets: Introduces 15,675 artifact-filtered, appearance-rich 3DGS objects spanning 40 categories.
Provides COGS-Bench for object classification and attribute-usage diagnosis, with external validation.
Finds that using all Gaussian attributes is not always optimal; selected subsets can perform better, with effects varying by architecture.
Presents HALO, a reference model that preserves attribute-specific evidence during hierarchical aggregation.
Experiments show COGS enables systematic attribute analysis and that role-preserving attribute organization is useful.

papers.abstract: Aligning a partial, real-world 3D face scan to a canonical representation requires solving two coupled problems at once: estimating the rigid pose that brings the scan into a common frame, and completing the facial shape in regions the scan never observed. Existing pipelines typically decouple these steps, running a generic point-cloud registration front end followed by a separate non-rigid fitting or deformation stage. Building on the GeoTransformer superpoint-matching architecture, we propose a single network that predicts both a rigid pose and a shape-complete point cloud in one forward pass: a cross-attention regressor, conditioned on transformer point features and predicted coarse correspondences, maps a partial scan to per-patch coefficients of a 3D morphable face model learned offline from a corpus of 8,000 identities. The resulting morphed template is then used, in the same forward pass, as the target for fine-grained Sinkhorn matching and rigid pose estimation, supervised purely by geometric alignment to ground-truth morphed geometry, so no hand-labeled coefficients are required. Against six classical and learned non-rigid registration baselines on held-out identities, our method leads the strongest ones by 3-4 times on per-vertex error and baselines that collapse the head onto the visible region by more than an order of magnitude, and is simultaneously the most accurate and fastest method on ground-truth-free scans from two independent real-scan datasets, NoW and NPHM. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Eli A. Underwood, Nicolas Rondan, Angel V. Peterchev, J. Matias Di Martino
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of rigid pose estimation and completion of missing face regions in partial scans.
Builds on GeoTransformer features and coarse correspondences, then predicts local 3D morphable-model coefficients via cross-attention.
Uses the reconstructed morphed template for fine-grained Sinkhorn matching and pose estimation in one forward pass.
Trains using geometric alignment to ground-truth morphed geometry, without hand-labeled morphable-model coefficients.
Outperforms six classical and learned baselines by 3–4× or more in per-vertex error and is fastest and most accurate on NoW and NPHM real scans.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline overview. A shared KPConv (Kernel Point Convolution) backbone and GeoTransformer produce coarse superpoint correspondences between the mean-face template and a partial scan; a cross-attention regressor predicts per-patch morphable-basis coefficients z (conditioned on post-transformer features, pre-transformer backbone features, and the coarse correspondences), which are decoded into a morphed template that updates the reference positions used by Sinkhorn optimal-transport (OT) fine matching and local-to-global registration (LGR) to produce the estimated pose (R̂, t̂). Bottom: detail of the coefficient regressor, showing its various input feature sources and the per-patch decoding into z.

Figure 3. Accuracy (1-way CD, partial scan→deformed-template, median) vs. wall-clock time (log scale, includes rigid-ICP prealignment for every baseline that requires it) across each method’s own iteration/step budget, NoW benchmark test split. Baselines: NRICP [1], CPD [11], NSFP [10], GraphSCNet [16], ClusterReg [25], OAReg [26].

Figure 1. Mean-face template and partial validation scan (top), with the morphed references produced by three representative nonrigid registration baselines—OAReg [26], ClusterReg [25], and CPD [11]—and our method (bottom). The baselines collapse the head onto the visible region, whereas our method recovers a plausible full head from the same partial input.

Figure 4. Qualitative results on Val (left), NoW (middle), and NPHM (right) examples. Rows: Self-Occlusion / Face-Cut crops (Val) and two representative scans each for NoW and NPHM. Columns: the partial input scan; our morphed reference alone, viewed from the side to show its departure from the fixed template (dark blue); and the same morphed reference (light blue) overlaid with the input scan (orange) to show surface-fit quality.

Table 3. NoW benchmark test split, no ground truth: 1-way CD (partial scan→deformed-template) and end-to-end wall-clock time, median ± std over the test scans, all methods timed on the same cluster hardware. CD uses each scan’s own recovered scale factor rather than a fixed dataset-wide constant (Sec. 4.3). Ours leads on both CD and time.

Table 4. NPHM head dataset [7], face-only crops (full-head scans include hair, incompatible with our hairless template, so not usable as shape-completion ground truth): 1-way CD (partial scan→deformed-template) and end-to-end wall-clock time, median ± std over 271 scans, all methods timed on the same cluster hardware (a different cluster from Tabs. 2 and 3, so timings are comparable within this table but not across tables).

Table 2. Val set (250 identities × 2 views = 500 pairs: 266 Self-Occlusion / 234 Face-Cut pairs), GT vertex error and 1-way CD (partial scan→deformed-template, visible region only, same definition as Tab. 3), median ± std over pairs, all methods timed on the same hardware. Ours leads every column. Four of six baselines (NRICP, CPD, ClusterReg, OAReg) have GT error an order of magnitude worse than Ours despite ClusterReg posting some of the best CD in the table alongside 38–47mm GT error: CD’s blind spot to implausible completions, visible in single rows (Sec. 4.3).

papers.title: Joint Rigid Alignment and Morphable Reconstruction from Partial 3D Face Scans
papers.tldr: A single transformer-based network jointly aligns partial 3D face scans and reconstructs unseen facial geometry, achieving substantially lower errors and faster inference than existing registration pipelines.

papers.abstract: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.
authors: Peter D. Sharpe, Corey Adams, Negin Sobhani, Sanjay Choudhry
bullets: Processes batched meshes on GPUs within PyTorch autograd, with semantic fields on points, cells, and whole meshes.
Stores complete PDE specifications, including boundary conditions and prescribed values, while preserving field ranks and named boundaries.
Enables preprocessing at model-use time, reducing dependence on costly, one-time dataset curation and supporting multiple workflows from one dataset.
On a GB200, mesh operations are 6.2–1,068× faster than 72-thread VTK, and complete-case loading is 8.0–88× faster than reading VTK files.
Per-boundary conditions reduced heat-conduction error from 87% to 6–9% when shapes and wall conditions varied.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Only the per-boundary conditions keep the error low as the wall conditions vary. Each panel is one architecture. Markers are medians over eight training seeds of the mean relative L2 error on 200 unseen geometries, and bars span the seeds. The gray curve is the lowest expected error that any model seeing only the geometry can reach (zero at σ = 0).

Figure 5: Two orders of the same four stages. A conventional pipeline preprocesses on the CPU and then stores model-specific arrays. With a stored DomainMesh, the mesh is stored first and each model’s features are computed on the GPU at training time, so the stored dataset does not depend on the model.

Figure 6: One stored case, three models. (a) The DomainMesh the recipe’s pipeline builds from one stored DrivAerML case: the interior, the named boundary mesh, and the reference freestream conditions in global_data. (b) The forward_kwargs blocks of the three surface-model configurations in the PhysicsNeMo unified external-aerodynamics recipe (two long paths are wrapped for display). Each entry extracts a field from the DomainMesh in (a), so all three models share a single DrivAerML dataset. GLOBE’s reference_lengths are constants, in units of the scaled positions, that set the length scales of its multiscale kernels: a reference length L_ref and a turbulent boundary-layer thickness delta_turb.

Figure 8: Three unseen geometries at σ = 1 (rows), with Transolver predictions (seed 0). Teal walls have a fixed temperature (Dirichlet), and gold walls a prescribed heat flux (Neumann). Without the conditions, the model returns one field per geometry, whatever the wall conditions are: a faded copy of the nominal pattern that the conditions vary around. Under relative error, which weighs small fields more, that faded copy scores better on average than the nominal pattern itself (Appendix B.3). The global vector of five wall summaries recovers the broad pattern in the first two rows but not in the third, and the per-boundary conditions recover the field in all three. Each row has its own color scale. The rows are the test geometries at the 20th, 50th, and 80th percentiles of the shape deformation, chosen before training.

Figure 3: The GPU is faster on every operation except field transfer with a reused locator (0.96×), with a median speedup of 198× on the DrivAerML car surface. Bars show the speedup of one GB200 GPU over a 72-thread Grace CPU baseline (the fastest batch VTK filter, or NumPy/pyacvd where VTK lacks an equivalent) across all operations in Table 3.
Figure 2: An AirfRANS case [Bonnet et al., 2022] as a DomainMesh: the interior mesh, the named airfoil and freestream boundaries, and the freestream velocity U∞ in global_data.

Figure 1: One Mesh class for all four manifold dimensions, so each operation is written once: points (Mesh[0, 3]), line segments (Mesh[1, 3]), triangles (Mesh[2, 3]), and tetrahedra (Mesh[3, 3]). Each holds points, simplicial cells, and named fields.

Figure 4: Overlap hides most of the preprocessing for the 127ms step (2.1% cost through the DataLoader) and none for the launch-bound 23ms step (35%), because kernel launches saturate the host thread (Section 4.4). Bars show the throughput reduction of configurations B–D relative to configuration A for both model sizes (Table 5).
Figure 10: One flagged rotate call is a change of frame; the angle of attack is unchanged. The airfoil, the velocity field, and U∞ in global_data turn together by 0.1 rad.

Figure 9: Flattening named fields into one array of columns. The Mesh keeps each field’s name and trailing shape, so scalars and vectors stay distinct; in the flat array, only the column order says which columns form a vector.
Table 1: Matching PyVista and PhysicsNeMo-Mesh calls, with GB200 speedups over VTK’s 72- thread backend on Grace CPUs. b: different by design; d: VTK and NumPy; warm: locator reused.

Table 5: Training throughput of a surface Transolver with per-step preprocessing on one GB200 (median of three repetitions; cost relative to configuration A, which does no augmentation). The larger model is the recipe’s surface model; the smaller is a reduced 1.7M-parameter model (four layers, width 192). Preprocessing alone takes 9.9ms per sample, including the host-to-device copy.

For DrivAerML and SHIFT-SUV, VTK reads whole files while the copies keep only the physics fields. †: VTK reads only the physics fields (full files: 136.0 s). ‡: with 13 s of cleaning (Appendix A.2).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PhysicsNeMo-Mesh, a GPU-native library for mesh processing and physics simulation. The technical contribution of efficient, differentiable mesh handling is transferable to 3D vision and embodied AI simulation.
papers.title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
papers.tldr: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh enables fast, GPU-native, differentiable mesh processing and complete simulation-case representation for flexible physics-AI workflows.

papers.abstract: Recent generation methods produce 3D assets with detailed geometry and rich textures. However, these assets are non-emissive: they reflect light but emit none. We study a new task, emission generation: predicting spatially varying RGB emission over a 3D asset's surface from its geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view. To support this task, we introduce LightGenBench. Our benchmark makes three contributions. First, we curate a dataset of 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view form. Second, we establish baselines across four method families: UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based generation. Third, we design an evaluation protocol that measures where an asset emits and how, complemented by user-study comparisons on renderings with varying emission strength. Across the four families, the sparse-voxel baseline TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best because generating emission natively in 3D avoids the failure modes of the other representations, such as the fracturing artifacts of UV space and the occluded emitters that multi-view generation cannot see. However, TRELLIS.2-Emission only reaches an IoU of 0.271, leaving the task far from solved. We hope LightGenBench establishes emission generation as a benchmarkable problem for 3D generation.
authors: Dongchen Yang, Xingguang Yan, Manolis Savva
bullets: Targets emission generation from geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view.
Provides 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view formats.
Benchmarks four method families: UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based methods.
Uses spatial emission evaluation plus user studies across varying emission strengths.
TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best at IoU 0.271, while exposing representation-specific failures such as UV fracturing and unseen occluded emitters.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the four emission-generation methods in our benchmark. Each method takes the non-emissive materials M, the geometry g, and a rendered image I , and generates the emission Le in its own representation: an emission map on the input UV atlas (top), per-voxel emission on the o-voxel grid (middle), or multi-view emission images that are back-projected onto the mesh (bottom). TRELLIS.2-Emission and SegviGen-Emission share the same pipeline and differ in the target: continuous emission e, or a mask M that is thresholded and multiplied by the albedo (M ⊙ a); their initialization and decoders are detailed in Secs. 4.3 and 4.5.

Figure 3. Overview of our data filtering pipeline. (1) Metadata filtering (1st row) keeps assets with an emissive texture or a nonzero emission factor (left) and drops the rest (right). (2) Heuristic filtering (2nd row) removes any asset whose emission map is entirely black (left) or identical to its albedo map (middle), or that duplicates another asset (right). (3) VLM filtering (3rd row) rejects non-emissive assets and assets with other defects, e.g., the multi-object asset is rejected. It agrees with human annotations on 87% of 404 held-out shapes.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of the baselines. Each object is rendered in a dark room and lit only by its predicted emission; the leftmost column is the input image, and GT is rendered with ground truth emission. TRELLIS.2-Emission stays closest to the ground truth on all three assets, but still mislocates emissive surfaces or assigns inaccurate color (the ring’s emissive region is misplaced and it should glow yellow). The other baselines show their characteristic failures: TEXGen-Emission scatters emission across UV islands (spilled color on the helmet) and fails to keep non-emissive regions at exact zero (speckles on the helmet, faint glowing noise over the ring); Hunyuan3DEmission shifts the emission color (the red beam turns white) and lights up regions that should stay dark (the saber handle and the ring band); and SegviGen-Emission over-extends or misses emissive regions (the ring’s whole band glows, while the helmet’s stripes stay unlit).

Figure 2. Samples from our curated dataset. Each pair shows an object under standard lighting (top) and the same object rendered in a dark room, lit only by its own emission (bottom). Apart from illuminating the object’s surroundings (the lamps, the lit house), emission also decorates (the glowing cracks, the blade, the tree’s lights) and informs (the screen’s content).

Figure 5. User study. Each asset is rendered in a dark room with each baseline’s predicted emission (Pred 1 to Pred n) ramping from 0 to 8. Participants rank the baselines by plausibility, with the ground-truth emission video and a well-lit rendering as reference (Ref).
Table 3. User study results. 14 participants each ranked the outputs of all four baselines on 53 objects. We report the mean rank and the fraction of rankings in which a method was placed first.
Table 1. Dataset statistics. The statistics of our curated dataset. Per-shape emissive ratio denotes the percentage of UV-occupied texels with non-zero emission.
Table 2. Quantitative evaluation on the test set. We report the mean over five sampling seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and baselines for 3D emission generation, directly fitting 3D scene/asset generation.
papers.title: LightGenBench: A Benchmark for 3D Emission Generation
papers.tldr: LightGenBench introduces a benchmark for generating spatially varying RGB emission on 3D assets, showing that the task remains challenging despite the strongest baseline’s advantages.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces the number of acquired projections, but conventional sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference. Here, we investigate optimal task-aware projection selection for directly predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography (CTA) measurements. Using computational fluid dynamics simulations of intracranial aneurysms, we generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections and train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) to predict two targets: the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. The FNO was coupled with optimal input selection for simultaneous optimal sampling and training. Our goal was to investigate if agentic AI could discover optimal sampling strategies that outperform current methods. We compared fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling with three task-aware optimal selection strategies: Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method, and an agentic AI selector. The methods were compared at different view selection budgets. A detailed analysis of the AI agent was performed to understand its reasoning and performance. For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors (Agentic performs slightly better) and substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimized selection becomes important at extremely sparse acquisitions. Analysis of the selected masks reveals multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions. Moreover, masks optimized for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions, showing that task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition. This work suggests the possibility of designing sparse acquisitions directly around downstream physical quantities.
authors: Mahmoud Elhadidy, Roshan M. D'Souza, Amirhossein Arzani
bullets: The study targets prediction of spatially resolved and spatially averaged time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) from sparse-view CT angiography.
Synthetic intracranial aneurysm projections were generated from computational fluid dynamics simulations and processed with a Fourier neural operator.
Sampling and prediction were jointly optimized using Gumbel-Softmax, Soft top-K, and an agentic AI selector, alongside uniform and golden-angle baselines.
For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieved the lowest mean errors, with Agentic slightly better and notably stronger than fixed sampling under extreme sparsity.
Task-optimized projection masks focused on informative regions and differed fundamentally from masks optimized for image reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the study. (a) Data generation: an idealized aneurysm geometry gives a pulsatile velocity field, which drives an advection–diffusion simulation of contrast concentration. The concentration field is voxelized and fan-beam sinograms are synthetically generated. The training dataset contained distinct geometry and flow rates. (b) Prediction from a fixed sparse view set: the predictor fθ : RNd×Nv → RM maps the sparse-view sinogram directly to the projected time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) on the vessel wall, where M is the number of predicted outputs as introduced in Sec. 2.3. (c) Prediction with learned view selection: the acquired subset S of the Nv candidate views is optimized together with the predictor model fθ, guided by the task loss.

Figure 3: Prediction of spatially resolved TAWSS at different view budgets K. (a) Test Rel-L2 error across five runs. Boxes span the mean ±1 standard deviation, center lines indicate the mean, and whiskers span the mean ±2 standard deviations. Stars mark the lowest mean error at each budget. papers.abstract: In procedural videogame level design, many existing techniques combine hand-authored level chunks. Some existing analysis techniques also rely on a higher-level graph structure which abstracts the level design. In this paper, we explore techniques for computing both of these things automatically from an existing design. We introduce the concept of perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax. We use this perceptual distance to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering. We compare with past work on StarCraft analysis, show results on rooms from Super Metroid, and also demonstrate a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on this segmentation method.
bullets: Addresses automatic extraction of reusable level chunks and higher-level graph structures from existing videogame levels.
Defines perceptual distance to measure relationships within level layouts.
Applies hierarchical clustering to segment levels into structural regions.
Compares the approach with prior StarCraft analysis and evaluates it on Super Metroid rooms.
Demonstrates proof-of-concept level generation using the resulting segments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The pipeline for computing the Perceptual Distance Segmentation shown on “Bubble Mountain” from Super Metroid. We begin by computing the probability of observing (angular area of) each visible surface (orange) from each point. The figure shows an example for a single point. Second, we use the Jensen-Shannon divergence of these probabilities to compute an approximate rate of change at each interior point (perceptual flux). We then find the minima of this field, and cluster the minima hierarchically based on the perceptual distance. Finally, the non-minima points are assigned to the cluster that they are closest to (in terms of perceptual distance).

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts a scene from a few images, but our predictor is less accurate than its own Gaussians optimized per scene on those images. This gap lies mostly in the shape of the Gaussians, their scale and rotation, since optimizing the shape alone recovers almost all of it and opacity and color recover less. Gradient steps on the input views correct this shape, and the model holds these views at inference. Log-anisotropy correction changes the axis ratios of each Gaussian in log space at constant volume, and in-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views and applies the gradient of the photometric loss with a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to the shape. GradSplat is a feed-forward model that refines its own Gaussians by learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, with no target view. On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, it has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods and keeps its accuracy from $6$ to $42$ input views. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++. The code will be released at https://github.com/Jingong-Chen/GradSplat/.
authors: Jingong Chen, Linlian Jiang, Guangyuan Li, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Kwanghee Won

Requires no target view and preserves accuracy across 6–42 input views.
Reports best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods on complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, and strong zero-shot results on DL3DV and ScanNet++.

papers.abstract: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is not merely long-sequence modeling. Once the volume is packed, sequence order no longer encodes the geometry of the sample---so a positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can learn the memory layout rather than the object. This is a general failure mode for attention over packed geometric data. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and indexes every query-key interaction with axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates rather than packed positions. Because the rotation is applied before a block is summarized, the query-to-summary logit remains a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements; compressed global context therefore stays spatially interpretable after packing, instead of collapsing to anonymous pooled content. We measure the failure mode directly. On a controlled synthetic task---train on one packing, change only the memory order of the tokens, hold the physical labeling rule fixed---learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE solve the training layout perfectly yet collapse under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact throughout. The same coordinate system carries to real data: on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, with controls isolating the coordinate system, not encoder capacity, as the source of the gain. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while supplying the long-range context windowing cannot---so the operator is not only correct but trainable at scale.
authors: Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath
bullets: Packed sequence positions can encode memory layout rather than physical object geometry.
PACK3D combines exact local attention with compressed summaries of distant 3D blocks.
Axial RoPE uses true token-grid coordinates, keeping query-to-summary relationships spatially interpretable.
On a controlled repacking task, packed-position methods fail after reordering, while grid-coordinate RoPE remains exact.
On hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over matched 3D U-Net and learned-position baselines; a fused implementation scales to 65k tokens with windowed-attention latency.

papers.abstract: Multi-source millimeter-wave (mmWave) observations offer an opportunity to learn human representations reusable across sensing tasks. However, sparse detections and multipath effects make these observations unstable, challenging existing point cloud pretraining methods. We propose PT$^3$, a prototype-guided self-supervised pretraining framework for mmWave human point clouds. PT$^3$ represents local states in spatial regions as sparse compositions of shared prototypes and learns their temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction. Observation consistency further stabilizes representations under radar perturbations. After pretraining on unlabeled sequences from multiple sources, the same frozen encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction on datasets not used for pretraining. Across these tasks, PT$^3$ outperforms the compared pretraining baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance to task-specific models.
authors: Ziyang Liu, Kieren Yu, Xiao Yang, Xin Yang, Kaishun Wu
bullets: Addresses sparse detections and multipath effects that destabilize mmWave point-cloud representations.
Represents local spatial states as sparse combinations of shared prototypes.
Learns temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction and improves stability with observation consistency.
A frozen pretrained encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction across unseen datasets.
Outperforms compared pretraining baselines and is competitive with or better than task-specific models.

papers.abstract: Robotic grasping relies on large manually annotated datasets, which are costly to create. We introduce a straight-skeleton-based algorithm for generating two-finger grasp keypoints and identifying regions suitable for stable, feasible grasps. Our automated pipeline produces consistent grasp annotations without human intervention. We also propose the Skeleton-based Generative Grasp Convolutional Neural Network (SkelGG-CNN), a 4-DoF architecture that learns geometric grasp features from skeleton-based guidance. To extend auto-labeling to 6-DoF grasping, we develop a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization algorithm that operates directly on point clouds. Using automatically generated 4-DoF labels, SkelGG-CNN achieves accuracies of 95.42%, 96.55%, and 97.1% on Jacquard V1, Jacquard V2, and Cornell, respectively. On the GraspNet novel split, 6-DoF auto-labeling achieves an average precision of 18.33, comparable to state-of-the-art model-based approaches. In simulation, the 6-DoF method achieves success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!. Real-world experiments with a Delta parallel robot show success rates of 97.4% on single household objects and 95.0% in cluttered scenes, outperforming state-of-the-art methods without domain adaptation. The 4-DoF pipeline adapts across environments and produces annotations approaching human-level precision, enabling efficient training of lightweight models on small datasets. The generalized 6-DoF method provides scalable, geometry-aware annotations for cluttered 3D scenes.
authors: Ali Sabzejou, Farbod Azimmohseni, Mehdi Tale Masouleh, Ahmad Kalhor
bullets: Generates two-finger grasp keypoints and stable, feasible grasp regions using straight-skeleton geometry.
Introduces SkelGG-CNN, a skeleton-guided 4-DoF model, and a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization method for point-cloud-based 6-DoF labeling.
Reports 4-DoF accuracies of 95.42%–97.1% across Jacquard and Cornell, and 6-DoF average precision of 18.33 on the GraspNet novel split.
Achieves simulated 6-DoF success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!, with real-robot success rates of 97.4% on single objects and 95.0% in clutter.
The approach supports small-dataset training and cluttered 3D scenes, with scope demonstrated on the reported benchmarks and a Delta robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed method. The pipeline begins with the simulation environment, where RGB-D images are captured from a set of 3D meshes sourced from the Dex-Net dataset. The subsequent stages show the details process of the straight skeleton-based grasp pose estimation algorithm. After this process, the generated grasp poses are used to create the SkelGG-CNN model labels. The skeleton heatmap is generated during the polygon offsetting phase of the algorithm, adding geometric features to the model.

Figure 8. Overview of the generalized 6-DoF skeleton-based auto-labeling pipeline. (Left) The input object point cloud is partitioned into overlapping horizontal cross-sections (80% overlap) orthogonal to the z-axis. (Center — upper path: 3D skeletonization) Each slice is processed with a Laplacian contraction skeletonization; skeleton points within a slice are connected using a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) and then linked to nearest neighbors in adjacent slices to produce a compact 3D skeleton graph that captures the object’s volumetric structure. (Center — lower path: 2D polygon approximation and initial centers) Each cross-section is projected to 2D and approximated with an alpha-shape polygon; a straight skeleton computed on this polygon yields initial central grasp centers. (Right) Candidate skeleton-node pairs are sampled and refined by traversing the 3D skeleton (depth-first search) from these initial centers; at each candidate pair a local plane is fitted to neighboring skeleton edges and the antipodality of the planes is evaluated as the grasp quality measure. (Far right) Top-scoring pairs are selected and visualized as final 6-DoF gripper poses superimposed on the original point cloud.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography is widely used for fast, low-dose volumetric imaging and lesion localization in dentistry and image-guided interventions, but it introduces severe artifacts. Feed-forward Gaussian methods transfer the reconstruction cost to training and decode each coordinate from projection-aligned features and neighboring anchors. However, information from the whole scan is written only when the field is constructed and cannot be retrieved during coordinate decoding, leaving the volume inconsistent within the scan. This is a common limitation of such methods: once the field is fixed, decoding uses only local features and reconstruction quality drops substantially. We propose SparseTokenGS, a Gaussian-based method for sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography reconstruction via a reusable token pool. Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention query this shared pool at the anchors and at the query coordinates, respectively. The local Gaussian prior is retained, and the volume is reconstructed in one forward pass, without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss. On three public chest and dental datasets, SparseTokenGS achieves the highest reconstruction performance among the compared methods. On clinical dental scans, reconstruction from only six projections reaches 29.51 decibels in peak signal-to-noise ratio and a structural similarity of 0.842 against the full-view reference, and off-the-shelf tooth-and-pulp segmentation keeps these structures separable for root-canal localization. Experiments on volcanic rock and chicken show performance after same-object adaptation. A reusable token pool gives feed-forward reconstruction a mechanism that keeps scan-wide context available through decoding and can benefit future rapid clinical lesion localization and analysis. The code is available at: https://github.com/FrankDengAI/SparseTokenGS.
authors: Zihan Deng, Zhenzhen Gong, Yujie Liu, Jiaxin Gong, Dingkun Liu, Kexian Xie, Yixing Huang, Peng Jin, Tianye Niu, Zhisheng Wang, Fenglin Liu, Hongming Shan, Lequan Yu
bullets: Targets severe artifacts in fast, low-dose sparse-view CBCT, where local-only decoding can produce inconsistent volumes.
Uses a reusable token pool queried by Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention, while retaining a local Gaussian prior.
Reconstructs volumes in one forward pass without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss.
Achieves the best reconstruction performance among compared methods on three public chest and dental datasets.
With six projections on clinical dental scans, reaches 29.51 dB PSNR and 0.842 SSIM; tooth and pulp remain separable for root-canal localization.

In (b), each anchor queries the token pool and a zero-initialized residual is added to its local feature. In (c), a coordinate network embeds the query, and the view feature, the neighboring Gaussian feature, and the point-token feature are concatenated and mapped to one intensity.

papers.abstract: 3D reconstruction from single-view sports broadcast is a pivotal capability for automated analytics and immersive AR/VR replays, yet notoriously ill-posed due to difficult-to-calibrate moving cameras and depth ambiguity. Unlike widely studied racket sports, team sports such as volleyball feature unpredictable multi-contact sequences and high altitude jumps. These dynamics categorically invalidate the standard planar projection assumptions relied upon by existing methods. To resolve these limitations without 3D training supervision, we propose a complete, physics-grounded pipeline tailored to monocular broadcast volleyball. First, we include a correction module to the perspective drift induced by ground-plane projection by coupling temporal jump spotting with Newtonian interpolation for 3D player placement. Second, for 3D ball trajectory estimation, we design a dedicated sub-trajectory segmentation architecture alongside a collision-matching algorithm. By anchoring physical equations to reconstructed 3D hand vertices, we lift noisy ball 2D detections into a spatiotemporally coherent 3D scene. Evaluations on multi-camera benchmarks demonstrate our approach significantly reduces 3D spatial drift compared to 2D-reprojection baselines.
authors: No\^am Boussouf, Adrien Maglo, Mohamed Chaouch, Hideo Saito
bullets: Addresses camera-motion calibration, depth ambiguity, and non-planar volleyball dynamics in single-view broadcasts.
Uses temporal jump spotting and Newtonian interpolation to correct ground-plane projection drift and place players in 3D.
Segments ball sub-trajectories and matches collisions, anchoring physical equations to reconstructed 3D hand vertices.
Evaluations on multi-camera benchmarks show reduced 3D spatial drift versus 2D-reprojection baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our proposed two-stage monocular 3D reconstruction pipeline. In the first stage, we extract and position the athletes in 3D world-space, combining smoothed homographic projections with a pose-based jump spotting module to handle aerial phases. In the second stage, we segment 2D ball tracks and explicitly anchor them to the reconstructed athletes, using the predicted 3D collision points to physically constrain the final 3D ballistic trajectory. The blue modules highlight the contributions introduced in this paper.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of 3D trajectory reconstruction on a short rally from Volliq [37]. Our drag model (green, err: 0.19 m, 12.7 px) accurately follows the ground truth (red) compared to MonoTrack [21] (purple, err: 1.69 m, 4.32 px).

While temporal filtering (blue dashed line) stabilizes ground locomotion, it fails during airborne phases (yellow zones). Our physicsinformed interpolation (solid red line) overrides the ground-plane.
