papers.abstract: While single-view novel view synthesis methods have been dramatically enhanced recently, how to quantify their performance has yet to be standardized. In this work, we demonstrate that an important factor lies in how each method's own reference frame is aligned with the so-called ground-truth pose. Existing methods often rely on test-time optimization of target poses for this alignment, which inherently is ill-posed due to the complexity of the optimization landscape of camera poses vs render accuracy, leading to methods being evaluated at an arbitrary local optimum. Some recognize this limitation and thus rely on 3D reconstructions of entire scenes using training and test views to align poses, which may be infeasible. In this work, instead, we propose to use traditional 2D-to-2D and 2D-to-3D image matching techniques to align 3D reconstructions. We also evaluate only within co-visible regions, between different views, which is the only place where a `correct' ground truth can be defined. Our evaluations show that with proper coordinate alignment, novel-view synthesis methods that use explicit 3D Gaussians achieve the state of the art, despite being previously reported in the literature to be outperformed by pure image-based 2D methods. We further provide a simple baseline that directly utilizes an off-the-shelf video generator and a feed-forward geometry estimator. Our simple baseline is already comparable to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for novel-view synthesis, without any task-specific training.
authors: Yang-Che Tseng, Erqun Dong, Jeong-gi Kwak, Gopal Sharma, Shakiba Kheradmand, Stephan Garbin, Hossam Isack, Kwang Moo Yi
bullets: Current evaluations can be unreliable because aligning predicted and ground-truth camera frames via test-time pose optimization is ill-posed.
The work aligns reconstructions using traditional 2D-to-2D and 2D-to-3D image matching instead of difficult pose optimization or full-scene reconstruction.
It evaluates only co-visible regions, where a valid ground truth can be defined across views.
Under this protocol, explicit 3D Gaussian methods achieve state-of-the-art results, contrary to some prior reports favoring image-based 2D methods.
A video-generator and feed-forward geometry-estimator baseline is competitive with task-specific methods without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative results – We show qualitative examples for each dataset under both evaluation resolutions, with the ground-truth target view (co-visibility overlay in blue) on the left. Middle: native-resolution methods, Flash3D [38], ViewCrafter [51], Lyra [3], SHARP [32], and our own baseline (Tab. 1). Right: methods that support the 256 × 256 centre-crop setting, LVSM [18], PF3plat [14], and our baseline (Tab. 2). Both halves show the same scene and held-out target view for each dataset, listed above each row. All methods are shown with our conservative co-visibility overlay. With our enhanced alignment protocol, the actual qualitative performances of Flash3D [38], ViewCrafter [51], and our baseline align well with the quantifications in Tab. 1. Our suggested baseline, while simple, performs on par with Flash3D [38].

Figure 3. Examples of misalignment leading to inaccurate evaluation – We show examples with Flash3D [38] for RealEstate10K (scene 01a5cc, fr. 50) and DTU (scan103, fr. 12), with test-time optimization only, and our proposed protocol. As shown, optimization alone leaves a large pose offset. Combined with the fact that many methods do not mask via co-visibility [5, 6, 18, 48, 51], the PSNR values can be very low, up to a level where it effectively is at a level where two random images are being compared (< 10 dB). With our image-matching-based pre-alignment, on the other hand, images are better aligned, and reasonable PSNR values are extracted. The yellow tint marks the non-co-visible region that our protocol excludes from computing the metrics.

Figure 6. Qualitative effect of generated views – For each scene we show the ground truth and the full init×train factorial of Tab. 3: rows vary the initialization (input view only vs. all generated views) and columns the training supervision. Training on generated views smears fine geometry (top scene) and hallucinates floaters in disocclusions (bottom scene); using them only for initialization stays sharpest. The teal overlay marks pixels outside the co-visible region, excluded from the metric.

Figure 2. Extracting co-visible regions – We show example covisible regions extracted by our protocol. We extract by projecting each pixel back and forth via DUSt3R [44] and checking their relative depths. We make a conservative estimate of co-visible regions to not disadvantage methods that do not extrapolate pixels outside the input view.

Figure 7. ViewCrafter [51] point-cloud conditioning vs. diffusion output. ViewCrafter [51] rasterizes its single-image point cloud from the (canonical) target pose to form the conditioning frame (middle), then a video-diffusion model synthesizes the final view (right). The raster is geometrically and photometrically faithful wherever the single view provides coverage (the speckled regions are sparse splatting where coverage thins); the diffusion model fills the remainder but can hallucinate geometry and drift in color as the viewpoint rotates away from the input. Rows: RealEstate10K (SV), RealEstate10K (VC), DL3DV-10K, DTU, Tanks & Temples (VC), on the same scenes as Fig. 4.

Figure 1. – Evaluation can be misleading due to inaccurate test-time pose alignment – We visualize the error map with the conventional test-time optimization and our proposed protocol (red is higher error, blue is lower). With the same 3D scene reconstructed from the reference view, conventional test-time optimization can leave residual misalignment between the rendered and ground-truth views, leading to large quantitative error. In contrast, our evaluation protocol provides a more robust alignment strategy, enabling more reliable performance measurement.
Figure 5. Example views generated by video models – We show example views generated by video models.

Table 1. Quantitative results – We summarize the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Metric (SSIM) [45], and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [52] for each method on our benchmark datasets, with the mean over all datasets reported on the right. Within each group, best results are in bold and second best are underlined. Using test-time optimization only reports wildly different results compared to when our evaluation protocol is used: Flash3D [38] is among the worst performing methods with a naive evaluation but, with better alignment, performs better than DepthSplat, while SHARP [32] leads the test-time-optimization-only group on average—its Gaussians are regressed directly in the input-camera frame, so it needs little alignment to begin with.

Table 2. Quantitative results (256×256 square evaluation) – PSNR, SSIM [45], and LPIPS [52] for the methods that support the square (256×256 centre-crop) setting, under both test-time-optimization-only and our evaluation protocol, with the mean over all datasets reported on the right. Flash3D [38] and ViewCrafter [51] are omitted as they cannot produce a comparable 256×256 cell. PF3plat [14] is evaluated with its RealEstate10K checkpoint on every dataset, as are MVSplat [6] and NoPoSplat [49]. Within each group, best results are in bold and second best are underlined.

Table 3. Ablation on using generated views – We ablate when to use generated views for training our 3D Gaussians. Including generated views for initialization only and training Gaussians only with the real input view gives best results.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising alternative to per-scene optimization, enabling fast novel view synthesis by predicting Gaussian primitives directly from input images. However, it quickly faces a bottleneck of rendering efficiency while scaling from sparse to dense multi-view inputs, which offer more geometric constraints but produce a rapidly growing set of candidate Gaussians. Existing solutions cannot reliably distinguish redundant primitives, leading to many redundant primitives from repeatedly observed regions and increased rendering cost without much gain in visual quality. We propose BudSplat, a compact feed-forward 3DGS framework that learns to keep the most valuable Gaussians under a limited primitive count. BudSplat has two novel designs. The first is a detail-aware importance score that is extracted from multi-level visual tokens, providing an explicit cue for regions where pruning is likely to harm perceptual quality. The score can be injected into voxel fusion to preserve high-value local contributors during multi-view aggregation. The second is quality-aware Gaussian pruning that selects a compact set of primitives by jointly considering rendering contribution and detail importance. The quality-aware pruning enables local quota redistribution that helps avoid over-allocating primitives to large redundant regions. Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show that BudSplat achieves a favorable trade-off among rendering quality and efficiency.
authors: Muyu Xu, Fangneng Zhan, Yu Wei, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses the rapid growth of redundant Gaussian primitives as the number of input views increases.
Uses multi-level visual tokens to estimate detail-aware importance and preserve regions where pruning could hurt quality.
Introduces quality-aware pruning that jointly considers rendering contribution and visual detail.
Redistributes local primitive quotas to avoid wasting capacity on large, redundant regions.
Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show a favorable quality–efficiency trade-off.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BudSplat. With dense geometry, confidence maps, and multi-layer tokens as predicted from multi-view RGB images by VGGT, the detail-aware decomposition first extracts residual token cues and predicts patch-level detail scores. The predicted scores are then propagated to the importance-preserving voxel fusion together with confidence and voxel support, retaining important local contributors during aggregation. Finally, the quality-aware pruning ranks the fused Gaussians by opacity, detail importance, and support-aware redundancy correction, followed by patch-level quota redistribution to select a compact set of retained Gaussian for rendering.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on challenging low-overlap target views. Red boxes highlight regions where baselines suffer from incomplete Gaussian coverage, blurred local structures, or uneven rendering quality. Our method allocates Gaussian budget more effectively, producing stable renderings and preserving perceptually important details with fewer Gaussians.

Figure 3: Target-view visualization of Gaussian density allocation and RGB rendering before and after pruning. Top row: projected Gaussian density before pruning, after pruning, removed density, and retention ratio. Bottom row: normal RGB rendering before pruning, after pruning, absolute difference, and reference image. The density diagnostic shows that pruning mainly removes redundant Gaussian support from low-frequency and highly overlapped regions, while preserving more support around high-frequency structures. The RGB difference map further shows that the remaining rendering changes are concentrated around edges, boundaries, and fine details rather than smooth regions.

Table 1: Main quantitative comparison under increasing input views. We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and the number of rendered Gaussians (#GS). For our method, Oursρ denotes retaining a ρ-fraction of fused Gaussians after pruning. Pink and orange cells indicate the best and second-best results under each dataset and view setting, following the metric direction indicated by the arrows. OOM denotes out-of-memory during inference.

Table 3: Additional main quantitative comparison 20, 24, 48 input views. We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and the number of rendered Gaussians (#GS). For our method, Oursρ denotes retaining a ρ-fraction of fused Gaussians after pruning. Pink and orange cells indicate the best and second-best results under each dataset and view setting, following the metric direction indicated by the arrows. OOM denotes out-of-memory during inference.

Table 2: Ablation of the main design modules under the same Gaussian budget. DT denotes detail-token importance estimation. IVF denotes importance-preserving voxel fusion. QAP denotes quality-aware pruning. PQ denotes patch-level quota redistribution.

papers.selection_reason: Presents BudSplat, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that optimizes rendering efficiency under a budget by pruning redundant primitives, contributing to 3D scene generation and representation.
papers.title: BudSplat: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting under a Rendering Budget
papers.tldr: BudSplat makes feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting more efficient by retaining the most visually valuable Gaussians under a fixed rendering budget.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulator robots rarely reposition their base during manipulation, because doing so requires real-time knowledge of how well the arm can reach its surroundings among obstacles. Reachability maps (RMs) encode this knowledge, but existing methods are slow, coarse (typically 5 cm), or ignore real obstacles. This article asks whether a neural network can predict an obstacle-aware RM at 2 cm resolution from a live depth camera, on embedded hardware, fast enough for online use. We present HERON, a 3D U-Net trained on RMs computed with the GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics of cuRobo, first on synthetic scenes and then on real depth data, and deployed on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT and INT8 quantization. HERON predicts the RM of a 2.56 m cube around the arm in 115 ms on average, for a measured system rate of 8.57 Hz, close to the 10 Hz update rate of the obstacle map, whereas computing the same map with cuRobo takes about 90 min. Against the cuRobo ground truth, 95% of the voxels lie within 1 class out of 51 with the FP32 model and within 3 classes with the INT8 model, with a Pearson correlation of 0.99 and a quadratic weighted kappa above 0.9. Accuracy degrades mainly at the workspace boundaries.
authors: G. Dupoiron, F. Michaud, J. P. Roberge
bullets: Targets the need for base repositioning during manipulation by estimating arm reachability around obstacles.
Predicts a 2 cm-resolution map over a 2.56 m cube from live depth data.
Trained on cuRobo-generated maps from synthetic and real scenes, then optimized with TensorRT and INT8 quantization on a Jetson AGX Orin.
Runs in 115 ms on average (8.57 Hz), compared with about 90 minutes for direct cuRobo computation.
Matches cuRobo closely: Pearson correlation is 0.99; accuracy mainly degrades near workspace boundaries.

figures.caption: Fig. 3 HERON’s architecture, a 3D U-Net. A 1283 obstacle map is downsampled by four maxpooling stages (16 to 256 feature maps), then upsampled by transposed convolutions to an RM of the same size. Skip connections (green) preserve fine spatial detail; each block applies convolution, normalization, and activation (purple arrows).

Fig. 5 Fraction of voxels whose predicted class lies within ±k classes of the ground truth, for the global, reachable and ridge regions (FP32 model). The dashed line marks 95%; dotted lines mark the tolerance at which each region reaches it.

Fig. 1 Experimental setup. HERON runs on a Jetson AGX Orin onboard an MM composed of a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base, a Doosan M1013 arm, and an Azure Kinect depth camera. A vertical slice of the generated RM is overlaid on the photograph, aligned with an ARTag marker.

Fig. 4 Visualization of the evaluation regions on an example generated with cuRobo: input obstacle map (top-left), ground-truth RM (top-right), reachable region (bottom-left, Ri ≥ 1 50 ), and ridge region (bottom-right, top 1% of voxels by gradient magnitude).

Fig. 2 Ground-truth RMs of four arms computed with cuRobo, without obstacles, on a 1523 grid at 2 cm resolution (vertical slice in the plane x = 0). From left to right: Doosan M1013, UR5e, Jaco7 and iiwa. Color gives the reachability score Ri, from 0 (no reachable orientation) to 1 (all 50 orientations reachable).

papers.abstract: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
authors: Binjie Wang, Xinran Zhao, Shoubin Yu, Xiang Li, Silong Yong, Chenyang Yang, Tianyu Chen, Ruofei Du, He He, Chen Zhao, Tongshuang Wu
bullets: Introduces 2,592 editing tasks across 108 Blender programs, covering parameter and structural edits, style redesign, and scene composition.
Evaluates 17 models using rendered outputs and human-reviewed checklists rather than code similarity alone.
Average success is 37%; even the strongest models solve fewer than 60% of structural and style edits.
As models improve, failures increasingly involve geometric foresight: executable code that produces the wrong shape.

Reviewer-model feedback describing render discrepancies helps more than additional reasoning effort or an agent harness, enabling a 27B model to exceed a 2.8T-parameter model’s single-shot performance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Progress in 3D program editing on the analysis subset (312 tasks). (a) All-pass rate of 44 models; lines join releases within four families, and the dashed line is the best rate so far. (b) Best rate per edit type among models released before April 2026 and among all models.
Figure 7: Twenty-four of the 108 source programs: 3DCodeBench objects (grey) and reconstructed designs (coloured).

Figure 2: Construction of 3DCodeEdit. papers.abstract: Recent advances in monocular depth estimation have demonstrated highly accurate 3D reconstructions within in-distribution terrestrial domains. This study investigates the efficacy of several state-of-the-art approaches to reconstruct out-of-distribution lunar environments using the NASA Ames Polar Optical Lunar Analog Reconstruction (POLAR) stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery. By leveraging these datasets, we establish a robust analog-to-field validation pipeline that evaluates quantitative performance against ground-truth physical analogs and qualitative performance against historical field data. Our results indicate that select state-of-the-art techniques can successfully generalize to produce high-fidelity relative 3D reconstructions of the unstructured lunar surface.

bullets: Evaluates monocular depth estimation under a challenging out-of-distribution lunar setting.
Uses the NASA Ames POLAR stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery.
Introduces an analog-to-field validation pipeline combining quantitative and qualitative evaluation.
Finds that selected methods successfully reconstruct unstructured lunar terrain in relative 3D.
The study focuses on efficacy in lunar environments rather than terrestrial in-distribution performance.

papers.abstract: Traditional computed tomography (CT) can capture paired 3D face and skull geometry, but it remains costly, fixed in location, and exposes patients to radiation. For applications such as remote diagnostics, digital healthcare, forensic identification, missing-person investigation, and archaeological analysis, there is an urgent need for a portable, safe, and accessible solution to capture 3D skull geometry. In this work, we introduce Vision Tomography (VT), a concept and framework capable of reconstructing paired 3D face-skull geometry from various visual modalities, and also enabling joint manipulation of 3D facial and skull geometry. To achieve this, we first construct a dataset of over 200 samples, where each case includes a CT-based skull, a CT-based face, and a high-fidelity textured face scan. Secondly, we propose a novel dense ray matching registration method that ensures topological consistency across face, skull, and their tissue correspondences. Building on this registration, we introduce the 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model (BFSM) as the foundation of Vision Tomography, which enables shape inference between the face and skull through a shared coefficient space, while also modeling tissue thickness variation to support one-to-many facial reconstructions from the same skull, reflecting individual facial changes such as age or body fat. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Vision Tomography across various forensic and medical applications, including paired 3D face-skull reconstruction from images or sketches and predicting surgical outcomes with joint face-skull editing. Extensive experiments confirm the robustness and accuracy of our method. Vision Tomography is available at https://github.com/wang-zidu/BFSM
authors: Zidu Wang, Meng Xu, Miao Xu, Hengyuan Ma, Jiankuo Zhao, Xutao Li, Zhen Lei, Xiangyu Zhu

Builds a Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model with a shared coefficient space and variable tissue thickness, enabling one-to-many face reconstructions from a skull.

papers.abstract: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360{\deg} cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180{\deg} and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180{\deg}, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200{\deg} FIORD and 205{\deg} FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT regress cameras and geometry in a single forward pass, but they report no uncertainty for the camera poses they predict: an incorrect relative pose looks no different from a correct one. We ask whether the frozen model nonetheless knows when its pose is wrong. On HardMatch, a benchmark of 1,000 deliberately difficult image pairs on which VGGT fails on 35% of pairs, a linear probe on VGGT's frozen features predicts pose failure on held-out categories with ROC-AUC 93.5%, compared with 79.7% for VGGT's own point-map confidence and 77.7% for a classifier trained on all of VGGT's outputs. The probe catches failures VGGT is confident about, lets a downstream system abstain on the pairs it distrusts, and transfers without retraining to rotation failures on PhotoTourism and ScanNet-1500, beyond what co-visibility explains. This knowledge is absent from the per-image encoder: it is computed partway through the layers that fuse the two views, and the same holds for a second model, $π^3$. In essence, we find that VGGT knows more about its own failures than it reports.
bullets: VGGT fails on 35% of difficult HardMatch image pairs, but its frozen features reveal these failures.

This signal emerges during two-view feature fusion, not in the per-image encoder, and also appears in π³.

papers.abstract: Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. While they can produce high quality images, they tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the input views (scene extrapolation). We propose to address this challenge for outdoor scenes by using satellite images as an additional information source to condition the multi-view generative model. We introduce a new satellite-conditioned multi-view diffusion model that combines conditioning from a satellite image and street-level input images when generating novel-views. Our cross-attention based conditioning allows us to retain pretrained multi-view diffusion priors to generate seamless, realistic, novel views from a handful of source views, while also adhering to the scene layout as seen from satellite images. Our model does not use 3D scene reconstruction, and only relies on posed street and satellite views. Our experiments on outdoor datasets show that our model is better than both satellite-conditioned or street-view conditioned baselines on novel-view synthesis, especially on challenging cases where target views have very little overlap with source views. Project page: https://nianticspatial.github.io/groundcontrol
authors: Akshay Krishnan, Matias Turkulainen, Jamie Wynn, Zawar Qureshi, Mohamed Sayed, Guillermo Garcia-Hernando, Sara Vicente, James Hays, Michael Firman, Daniyar Turmukhambetov
bullets: Addresses unrealistic spatial layouts when generating views far outside the input viewpoints.
Uses cross-attention to combine posed street images with satellite-image conditioning while retaining pretrained diffusion priors.
Generates seamless novel views from only a handful of source views and no explicit 3D reconstruction.
Outperforms satellite-conditioned and street-view-conditioned baselines on outdoor datasets, particularly for targets with little source-view overlap.

papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) gives the electronic structure of materials, but its cost limits large-supercell calculations and materials screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonians bypass the self-consistent cycle but are usually system-specific; universal ones could cover new compositions and disordered solids. Such models must generalize across chemistry and keep downstream properties physical, while staying inexpensive for large cells. Here we introduce UniTB, a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian representation framework that integrates physical priors rooted in density-functional tight-binding theory with deep learning. UniTB's network, which corrects a prior Hamiltonian, generalizes across chemistry through a mixture of experts routed by that prior and a charge-equilibration head as in self-consistent-charge tight binding. A projection bounds band shifts from the prior, suppressing spurious states and keeping downstream properties physical. We provide the fastest SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network. The variant UniTB-Flash assembles its prior from two-center tables at $O(N)$ cost for $N$ atoms, against $O(N\log N)$ on a grid. Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB reaches a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements. Without amorphous training data, both models agree with DFT optics and conductivity of amorphous Ge-Sb-Te. UniTB-Flash ranks candidates with no significant difference from UniTB, whose property values are more accurate; together they screen 16,195 crystals for five application domains of industrial relevance.
authors: Mingkang Liu, Zhanghao Zhouyin, Guanghui Wang, Daye Zheng, Lei Shen, Qiangqiang Gu
bullets: Addresses the high cost of DFT and the limited chemical scope of conventional machine-learned Hamiltonians.
Combines a density-functional tight-binding prior with a mixture-of-experts neural correction and charge equilibration.
Constrains band shifts to suppress spurious states and improve physicality of predicted properties.
Trained on 29,242 crystals, it achieves 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements.

UniTB-Flash enables linear-cost prior assembly and, with UniTB, screens 16,195 crystals across five industrial application domains; amorphous-material tests also agree with DFT without amorphous training data.

papers.abstract: 4D novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to render dynamic scenes across viewpoints and timestamps, which requires jointly inferring 3D structure and temporal dynamics. Existing monocular feed-forward methods often rely on explicit 4D Gaussian representations, which are prone to temporal inconsistency and severe rendering artifacts. We present FL4N, the first feed-forward latent 4D NVS model. Instead of relying on explicit 4D primitives, FL4N encodes a 4D scene prior into a unified latent representation across space and time. Our core insight is that learning temporal dynamics as residuals on top of a pretrained static latent prior enables effective 4D modeling with limited dynamic training data. To this end, we introduce a lightweight dynamic encoder that leverages static scene features to disentangle object motion from camera-induced parallax. Trained solely with an image synthesis objective, FL4N achieves state-of-the-art 4D NVS quality while rendering in real time. Its learned latent representation generalizes to real-world videos and disentangles viewpoint from time.
bullets: Targets dynamic-scene rendering across viewpoints and timestamps from monocular input.
Builds on a pretrained static latent prior and learns temporal dynamics as residuals, reducing dependence on dynamic training data.
Uses a lightweight dynamic encoder to separate object motion from camera-induced parallax.
Trained with an image-synthesis objective; reports state-of-the-art 4D NVS quality and real-time rendering.
Generalizes to real-world videos and disentangles viewpoint from time.

papers.abstract: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.
bullets: Addresses reduced MRI acquisition resolution, especially along the slice axis, without requiring a separate model for each geometry or scale.
Combines anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes, scale-conditioned frequency encoding, and exact measurement-consistency projection.
Uses one checkpoint per MRI contrast and supports arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic reconstruction resolutions.
Outperforms geometry-specific specialists at isotropic 2× and on perceptual metrics across geometries, though specialists achieve higher PSNR for anisotropic reconstruction.
Preserves downstream performance across segmentation, metastasis detection, and brain parcellation tasks, with reconstruction taking about 6 seconds per volume.

papers.abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) assisting human divers must continuously track not only the diver's 3D position but also their full-body orientation. However, vision-based perception is unreliable underwater, and forward-looking sonar -- despite being widely used -- discards the elevation information needed for orientation estimation, posing a fundamental limitation. Recently commercialized 3D sonar preserves elevation but produces sparse, noisy returns, and existing detectors are built for dense LiDAR data and for targets that remain upright and rotate only about the yaw axis (e.g., vehicles, pedestrians), making them unable to represent a freely pitching and rolling diver. To address this gap, we present two contributions. First, SonarVoxNet adapts a voxel-based encoder and an anchor-free center-based detection head to 3D sonar data, replacing the conventional yaw-only rotation representation with a continuous 6D rotation parameterization to predict full 9-DoF oriented bounding boxes -- to our knowledge, the first 3D sonar diver detector to do so. Second, Diver3D is the first public 3D sonar dataset with full 3D orientation labels for divers in diverse, non-upright poses, collected at a natural cave-diving site. Through controlled ablations over the backbone and detection head, we show that the dominant factor behind accurate 3D sonar-based diver detection is the transition from yaw-only rotation to full-SO(3) rotation. This transition substantially improves detection accuracy and reduces orientation error. These results demonstrate that full-body diver orientation is recoverable from 3D sonar alone, laying the groundwork for future work on diver pose estimation and diver-robot interaction.
bullets: Targets AUV diver tracking when vision is unreliable and conventional sonar lacks elevation.
Adapts voxel encoding with an anchor-free, center-based detection head for 3D sonar.
Uses continuous 6D rotations to predict full 9-DoF oriented bounding boxes, including pitch and roll.
Introduces Diver3D, a public cave-diving dataset with full 3D orientation labels.
Ablations show that replacing yaw-only rotation with full SO(3) rotation is the main driver of improved accuracy and lower orientation error.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.
authors: Prakhar Kaushik, Soumava Paul, Alan Yuille
bullets: Addresses the memory and compute costs of radiance-field and splatting methods in resource-constrained settings.
Represents scenes and images with larger, locally planar hexagonal elements and first-order spatial color fields.

Delivers 2.31× faster FPS and up to 4.74 dB higher per-primitive quality than 2DGS in ablations.
Reduces reconstruction error by 28.9% on 15 DTU scans and achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods on 6 Tanks and Temples scenes.

papers.abstract: Existing evaluations of text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation largely emphasize semantic fidelity and physical validity at rest, leaving interaction-time physical reliability insufficiently assessed. To address this gap, we introduce ScIntBench, a unified benchmark centered on interaction readiness: it executes prescribed manipulation actions (e.g., pushing, opening, and surface probing) in physics simulation and measures task success, capability and progress, post-interaction integrity, and dynamic plausibility. Multi-view semantic and static physical evaluations complement these metrics and help explain interaction outcomes. We systematically evaluate 12 state-of-the-art scene generation systems across 10 room types. Our results reveal that strong semantic and static physical performance does not necessarily translate into interaction readiness: a system with near-perfect static plausibility completes only 11.54% of interactions, 7 of the 12 systems produce scenes that cannot support any interaction, and even the best system succeeds in only 36.92% of prescribed tasks. These findings highlight two fundamental challenges in generating interaction-ready scenes: providing the necessary physical interaction capabilities and ensuring reliable physical behavior under active manipulation.

Shows that strong semantic and static physical quality does not guarantee reliable interaction, highlighting missing capabilities and unstable behavior under manipulation.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses noise from feeding large numbers of task-irrelevant 3D object tokens to LLMs.
Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction represents scene geometry and semantics in a unified voxel grid, enabling recognition beyond predefined categories. One approach reconstructs scenes with 3D Gaussians and converts them into voxel occupancy. However, Gaussian scale inflation and excessive overlap can distort voxel occupancy predictions, while semantic mixing can arise within Gaussians spanning multiple categories and during 3D--2D semantic feature alignment. We propose GCSR-OCC, which combines geometry calibration and multi-mode query-conditioned semantic routing for indoor occupancy prediction from a single RGB image. The Evidence-Conserving Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator (EC-G2O) uses kernel mass normalization, $p$-norm aggregation, and a learnable gain to suppress scale inflation and excessive local evidence accumulation while calibrating occupancy responses. Multi-mode Query-First Gaussian Semantic Routing (MM-QGSR) matches multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and aggregates query-specific evidence into voxels through a learnable text-conditioned router. Fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation further refine voxel-level predictions. Without 3D semantic annotations, GCSR-OCC achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary occupancy prediction on Occ-ScanNet, with 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU. It also reduces geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Bohua Wang, Congyang Zhao, Tianxiong Lv, Chenxu Zhao, He Zheng, Hangqi Fan, Leigang Luo, Zhihao Liao, Yihong Guo, Yang Cai

Uses MM-QGSR to match multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and route query-specific evidence into voxels.
Adds fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation for more precise voxel semantics.
Achieves 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU on Occ-ScanNet, while reducing geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms without 3D semantic annotations.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence panoramic reconstruction requires detailed scene geometry and globally consistent camera poses across distant revisits. Panoramic SLAM and incremental SfM rely on feature correspondences, but repeated, similar structures and small partial overlap make reliable long-range connections difficult to establish, leaving accumulated drift unresolved. Feed-forward models offer detailed local geometry, but their high computational costs limit inference window size, necessitating additional constraints for global consistency. This motivates combining continuous feature-based tracking and sparse mapping with rapid, high-quality local reconstruction from feed-forward models to achieve accurate localization and globally consistent dense mapping over long sequences. We therefore propose a panoramic reconstruction framework that couples an ORB-based sparse panoramic mapping frontend with a fine-tuned feed-forward model. Our key insight is that predicted local geometry enables 3D verification of feature matches across distant revisits, yielding long-range camera constraints even between regions. We calibrate predicted depths with sparse landmarks and use verified connections to optimize the global pose graph, updating dense geometry with the corrected camera poses. We also introduce PanoRecon, a seven-scene benchmark with repetitive architecture, large and small loops, and reference camera poses and LiDAR geometry for evaluating global consistency. Our method achieves the lowest mean absolute trajectory error and high F-1 Score among the evaluated methods. Project Page:https://zhuoxiaoli.github.io/HoloRecon_page/

papers.abstract: Achieving high-quality reconstruction and responsive camera tracking remains challenging for monocular RGB Gaussian splatting SLAM under a limited optimization budget. We present an online system that addresses this challenge by combining learned geometric priors with explicit geometric camera tracking, which can substantially outperform learned camera prediction in terms of tracking accuracy. A frozen streaming 3D foundation model serves as a virtual RGB-D sensor, providing depth estimation from monocular video. An explicit geometric solver then estimates camera motion through feature reprojection, and a streaming Gaussian mapper integrates the resulting observations into a dense scene representation. We further show that geometric tracking improves camera pose accuracy across representative streaming geometry backbones, demonstrating the broader applicability of our approach. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets show that our method significantly improves reconstruction quality over existing approaches, achieving about 7 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and delivering 2-3 times the throughput of the evaluated prior SLAM systems.
authors: Da Li, Yihan Zang, Ivan Viola, Zeyu Wang, Dominik Engel
bullets: Targets the joint challenge of accurate camera tracking and quality reconstruction under limited optimization budgets.
Uses a frozen streaming 3D foundation model as a virtual RGB-D sensor for monocular depth estimation.
Estimates camera motion with feature reprojection and integrates observations using a streaming Gaussian mapper.
Improves reconstruction quality and camera pose accuracy across indoor/outdoor settings and multiple geometry backbones.
Runs at about 7 FPS on one RTX 4090, with 2–3× the throughput of evaluated prior SLAM systems.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian Splatting enables efficient novel view synthesis, but pixel-aligned prediction makes the primitive count grow with image resolution and view count, leading to substantial redundancy and increased computational cost. Non-pixel-aligned methods address this limitation by predicting a fixed number of Gaussians. Without explicit ray and depth constraints, these methods yield misplaced Gaussian centers, causing rendering artifacts under large viewpoint changes. To address this issue, we introduce GeoGSplat, a geometry-grounded feed-forward model that explicitly incorporates geometric priors into the non-pixel-aligned framework. A dual-branch encoder constructs Anchors and Triplane to capture coarse 3D structure and fine-grained scene features, respectively. Subsequently, a hierarchical decoder progressively decodes dense 3D points and Gaussian primitives, enabling 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. GeoGSplat surpasses both state-of-the-art pixel-aligned and non-pixel-aligned Gaussian Splatting methods on DTU and NRGBD in terms of novel view synthesis and reconstruction. The advantage of our geometry-grounded paradigm further increases as target viewpoints move farther from the input cameras, demonstrating stronger generalization to large viewpoint changes. authors: Jiale Wang, Chen Zhao, Haoyang Zhang, Yanhao Wu, Fei He, Yanhu Shan, Rui Wu, Wei Ke, Tong Zhang
bullets: Non-pixel-aligned methods reduce redundancy but can misplace Gaussian centers without ray and depth constraints.

A hierarchical decoder progressively reconstructs dense 3D points and Gaussian primitives.
The method outperforms pixel-aligned and non-pixel-aligned baselines on DTU and NRGBD for reconstruction and novel view synthesis.
Its advantage grows as target viewpoints move farther from input cameras, indicating stronger large-viewpoint generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Pipeline of GeoGSplat. Image features are encoded in parallel into Anchors and Triplane. Anchor-to-Point Decoding (blue) gathers Triplane features within each Anchor region to predict offsets and recover dense 3D points; Point-to-Gaussian Decoding (orange) re-queries the Triplane at these points to predict the corresponding Gaussian primitives.

papers.abstract: Deformable image registration relies on accurate anatomical correspondences. However, explicitly coupling local matching reliability with spatial context selection and deformation update strength remains insufficiently explored in learning-based registration. This challenge is particularly pronounced in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions, where ambiguous matches may induce erroneous deformation updates. We propose ReliMorph, a reliability-routed symmetric framework for 3D deformable registration that couples correspondence assessment with spatial context selection and update strength.Local correlation distributions characterize correspondence ambiguity using shared anatomical features with modality-specific adaptation. These reliability cues guide spatial expert fusion and gate residual velocities during coarse-to-fine refinement. Updated inverse-inconsistency feedback guides routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. To our knowledge, ReliMorph is the first 3D deformable registration framework to jointly condition spatial expert routing and residual velocity gating on correspondence reliability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReliMorph consistently outperforms competing methods in anatomical overlap, highlighting its effectiveness across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.
authors: Chenyu Guo, Wenjie Dai, Yiqian Chang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Yunfan Wei, Shuhan Qi

Estimates correspondence reliability from local correlation distributions using shared features with modality-specific adaptation.

Incorporates inverse-inconsistency feedback to refine routing and gating at finer pyramid levels.
Experiments report consistently better anatomical overlap across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.

papers.abstract: Point cloud registration is an essential task for scene reconstruction, requiring the alignment of partially overlapping point clouds. Under low-overlap conditions, this task remains challenging because existing geometry-only methods cannot distinguish geometrically similar but semantically distinct structures (e.g., TV corners vs. desk corners and chair legs vs. table legs), resulting in incorrect correspondences. To address this geometric ambiguity, we present Semantic-Augmented Geometric Experts (SAGE), which integrates frozen pre-trained point cloud semantic representations into the registration pipeline without requiring additional sensors or fine-tuning the semantic encoder. To effectively leverage these semantic distinctions, SAGE employs a Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts (SG-MoE) architecture. Through semantic-aware routing, SG-MoE enables each expert to specialize in distinct semantic-geometric patterns, reducing mismatches that confound geometry-only methods. With a structure-aware estimator, SAGE achieves the highest registration recall on 3DLoMatch while remaining competitive on 3DMatch. When evaluated with the same number of refinement iterations, SAGE further achieves the highest inlier ratio and registration recall on both benchmarks. These results indicate that frozen semantic representations provide effective cues for resolving geometric ambiguity in low-overlap registration.
authors: Tomoyasu Shimada, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Shoichiro Takeda, Shogo Sato, Riku Inoue, Toshihiko Nishimura, Ryuichi Tanida
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity between visually similar but semantically different structures.
Uses frozen pre-trained point cloud semantic features without additional sensors or semantic-encoder fine-tuning.
Introduces a Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts to specialize in semantic-geometric patterns.
Combines SG-MoE with a structure-aware estimator for registration.
Reports highest recall on 3DLoMatch and strong inlier ratio and recall on both 3DLoMatch and 3DMatch under equal refinement iterations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overall pipeline of SAGE. Given two input point clouds, the Two-Stage Feature Extraction (Sec. 3.2) first applies a frozen Sonata encoder to extract point-level semantic features from each point cloud, and then feeds these semantic features together with the raw point coordinates into the KPConv encoder to produce semantic-geometric features. The Spatial Feature Aggregation (Sec. 3.3) then maps both the semantic and semantic-geometric features to the superpoint level via nearest-neighbor search and average pooling. The aggregated features are refined through N alternating iterations of Geometric Transformer layers (red box, self-attention) and Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts (Sec. 3.4) layers (blue box, cross-attention), where semantic features guide expert routing to enable semantic-aware specialization. Finally, the framework adopts GeoTransformer’s coarse-to-fine matching for correspondence estimation and registration.

Figure 3. Comparison of MoE architectures. (a) Standard MoE feeds the fused semantic-geometric features into both the router and the experts. (b) Our SG-MoE decouples the inputs, feeding pure semantic features to the router and semantic-geometric features to the experts. These processes apply symmetrically with P and Q swapped.

Top: GeoTransformer’s registration with correspondences (red for outliers, green for inliers). Bottom: SAGE’s registration and correspondences. SAGE effectively leverages semantic guidance to correctly identify inliers, even in low-overlap scenarios.

Figure 5. Expert activation patterns. Top: Standard MoE produces fragmented expert assignments primarily driven by local geometry. Bottom: SG-MoE consistently assigns semantically similar regions, such as the furniture highlighted by red circles, to the same expert, demonstrating semantic-guided specialization.

papers.abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.
authors: Yonglong Zhang, Zongwu Xie, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses uneven keypoint errors in sparse event data and their impact on pose recovery.

Optimizes time-aligned observation scales from heatmap, reprojection, and geometric-conditioning descriptors.
Scores 0.0474 on the official SPADES test set; ablations show progressive improvement from 0.0772 to 0.0514, with quality weighting improving 0.0549 to 0.0514.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution, offering a complementary signal that is largely immune to these artifacts, but whether this modality can be incorporated into existing RGB based 4D reconstruction pipelines without a full architectural redesign remains an open question. In this preliminary study, we investigate a minimal extension: we augment Monst3R, an existing RGB-only 4D reconstruction model, with an additional event-camera input branch, leaving the rest of the architecture unchanged. Across 3 benchmark datasets, this simple RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average relative to the RGB-only Monst3R baseline, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the improvement grows with the magnitude of camera and object motion, with the largest gains observed under high object motion conditions where RGB-only reconstruction degrades most. These early results suggest that even a lightweight, non-invasive fusion of event data can meaningfully improve 4D reconstruction robustness, motivating a more thorough architectural investigation in future work.
authors: Dulanga Weerakoon, Darshana Rathnayake, Van Minh Do, Hemanth Sabbella, Kaichen Zhou, Fangneng Zhan, Alok Prakash, Sanjay E. Sarma, Archan Misra, Paul Pu Liang

Improvements increase with motion magnitude and are largest under high object motion.
The preliminary results motivate deeper investigation of event-RGB fusion architectures.

papers.abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.
authors: Suozhi Huang, Kelsey Fu, Binxu Li, Luna Lyu, Kaize Wu, Wenbo Lu, David Smerkous, Jiahan Li, Siqi Zhu, Zhizhou Sha, Jiacheng Guo, Zhixuan Liang, Shilong Liu, Le Cong, Mengdi Wang

Evaluated on real pipetting and vortexing videos, achieving Mask IoU of 0.501 and Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638.
Event-conditioned reconstruction increased satisfied modeled physical constraints from 14.3% to 100% across five pipetting videos.

papers.abstract: We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. Prior methods typically extract 3D targets by applying heuristic thresholding or top-ratio filtering to dense primitive-level relevance scores. However, these scores often vary substantially across scenes and prompts, making such heuristics sensitive and leading to unstable targeting. ClusterSplat addresses this by reframing 3D target selection as cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates. The method first learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms feature-aware seed voxels, and merges neighboring seed voxels when a description-length criterion decreases, producing a scene-specific set of cluster candidates. Given a referring expression, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the cluster candidates with a lightweight MLP, and the selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target while its cluster score is rendered for the 2D mask. On ScanRefer, ClusterSplat achieves the best rendered 2D segmentation and explicit 3D target metrics among the compared 3DGS baselines. It also obtains the best average Ref-LERF scores, supporting the same trend under fine-grained referring descriptions. On ScanNet v2 class name queries, ClusterSplat achieves the strongest rendered 2D results and the highest 3D matching accuracy, while maintaining competitive 3D IoU. Our project page is available at https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/ .
authors: Jaesung Lee, Hyeontaek Hwang, Gabriel Manalu, Daeyoung Kim
bullets: Targets referring expressions as both rendered 2D masks and explicit sets of 3D Gaussians.
Learns instance-aware features, builds feature-aware seed voxels, and merges them using a description-length criterion.
Uses a query-conditioned lightweight MLP to rank cluster candidates and select the 3D target.
Reports the best results among compared 3DGS baselines on multiple 2D and 3D grounding metrics across ScanRefer and ScanNet v2.
Scope: performance is evaluated on referring descriptions and class-name queries in indoor 3D scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ClusterSplat overview. The pipeline first performs Instance-Aware Gaussian Feature Learning and Scene-Adaptive Clustering: it learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms featureaware seed voxels, and merges them into scene-adaptive cluster candidates. It then performs QueryConditioned Cluster Scoring: the referring expression conditions the cluster tokens, and the MLP scorer ranks the candidates to select the Top-1 cluster as the explicit 3D target. Finally, Cluster-Level Mask Rendering assigns the selected cluster scores to Gaussians and renders a 2D mask supervised by the mask loss.

Figure 3: Qualitative examples on ScanRefer. Each row shows a referring expression with rendered masks and top-down 3D selections. ClusterSplat localizes the referred object more coherently and reduces distractor support compared with score-discretized baselines.

Figure 4: Illustration of how we prompt GPT-4.1 to obtain five diverse pseudo-captions for a trainingframe instance mask. The specific view shows two tables, and the mask/bounding-box cue enables GPT-4.1 to generate captions that are descriptive and localized to the selected instance.

Figure 5: Sensitivity of primitive-level target extraction to the top-ratio hyperparameter. We evaluate the 3D targeting performance (mIoU) of OpenGaussian [6] and Dr.Splat [10] across 10 ScanNet v2 scenes by sweeping the selection ratio ρ ∈ [0.01, 0.10]. The optimal ratio is highly scenedependent, and the performance often drops sharply away from the peak, indicating that primitivelevel score discretization requires careful calibration for robust open-vocabulary 3D targeting. This motivates cluster-level Top-1 (argmax) selection, which relies on relative cluster ranking rather than absolute score thresholds.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) remains unreliable under weak observations caused by long camera-to-person distances, occlusion, and motion blur. In challenging scenarios such as sports, these factors make the problem highly ambiguous, as different 3D poses may yield similar 2D projections. This ambiguity is especially severe for one-stage HMR, which recovers all meshes directly from the full image without person crops or external 2D cues. To handle this ambiguity, we present UT-HMR ( Uncertainty-guided Temporal HMR), to our knowledge the first one-stage HMR framework to capture correlated pose uncertainty across joints. Each person query predicts a Gaussian distribution over the full SMPL pose with a compact low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance, which is converted into joint-wise precision weights for heteroscedastic supervision while keeping inference deterministic. Temporal early fusion further injects neighboring-frame evidence before pose decoding, supplying the visual evidence needed to resolve the ambiguity that the uncertainty captures. With a lightweight ViT-B backbone, UT-HMR achieves state-of-the-art results on VIP-HockeyPose-v2 (ice hockey) and WorldPose (soccer), reducing MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, and PVE by up to 4.7%, 3.8%, and 5.6%, and remains competitive on 3DPW against methods with larger backbones and higher input resolutions.
authors: Zhibo Wang, Sirisha Rambhatla, Yuhao Chen, Maria Koshkina, David Clausi
bullets: Addresses unreliable monocular HMR under long-distance views, occlusion, motion blur, and fast sports motion.
Predicts a Gaussian distribution over the full SMPL pose using compact low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance.
Converts uncertainty into joint-wise precision weights for heteroscedastic supervision while retaining deterministic inference.
Uses temporal early fusion to provide neighboring-frame evidence before pose decoding.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on VIP-HockeyPose-v2 and WorldPose, with reported metric reductions of up to 4.7% MPJPE, 3.8% PA-MPJPE, and 5.6% PVE; remains competitive on 3DPW.

The predicted covariance is supervised by the distribution loss and converted into joint-wise precision weights for the heteroscedastic joint loss.

papers.tldr: UT-HMR improves robust one-stage 3D human mesh recovery by modeling correlated pose uncertainty and using neighboring video frames to resolve ambiguous poses.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly become the preferred representation for high-fidelity novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, the learned representation encodes sensitive visual information including human faces, license plates, documents, and computer screens, raising significant privacy concerns when trained splats are shared or deployed. In this work, we address the underexplored problem of privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting by proposing a representation-level anonymization framework that directly anonymizes a trained splat. Given a trained splat and a user-provided reference view identifying sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding regions in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them, ensuring that the sensitive information is absent from all subsequently rendered novel views while preserving the overall scene geometry and visual fidelity. We achieve this post-training anonymization in less than 1 second. Furthermore, we extend our framework with a privacy-by-design training strategy that prevents sensitive content from being embedded into the representation during optimization, enabling the generation of privacy-preserving splats directly from training images. Our method achieves a remarkably low Face Similarity Measure (FSM) of 9.79% at a retained Face Detection Rate (FDR) of 39.47% and makes sensitive text completely unreadable with an OCR Character Error Rate of 1.00. Our work aims to serve as the primary stepping stone towards privacy-aware 3D representations and motivates further research along these directions.
authors: Gaurav Behera, Abhinav Raundhal, Archisha Panda, Saumya Balina, Gargi Shroff, Ponnurangam Kumaraguru
bullets: Addresses privacy risks from faces, license plates, documents, and screens encoded in trained Gaussian splats.
Localizes sensitive regions from a user-provided reference view and anonymizes them at the representation level.

Also introduces privacy-by-design training to prevent sensitive content from being embedded during optimization.
Reports 9.79% Face Similarity Measure, 39.47% retained Face Detection Rate, and 1.00 OCR Character Error Rate for sensitive text.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/
authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Youming Deng, Chulwoo Pack, Olaf Wysocki, Boris Jutzi, Kwanghee Won, Kyle Gao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of geometry foundation models that assume pinhole cameras and lens-dependent image-position representations.
Conditions positional encoding and supervision on dense per-pixel ray fields rather than lens parameters or fixed fields of view.
Uses angular rotary encoding and solid-angle-weighted point loss to make features and geometry training camera-type independent.
Evaluated across 13 central cameras and three datasets, Any3R is reported as the most consistently accurate method while predicting camera poses itself.
Supports heterogeneous imagery collections, including crowdsourced and archival images from diverse cameras.

papers.abstract: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.
authors: Rui Yang, Yanwei Li, Sili Chen, Jingjia Huang, Yi Lin, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Studies how visual generation can support spatial understanding through training-time geometric supervision and inference-time geometric evidence.
Introduces GeoUG, which combines spatial understanding with depth and multi-view generation using a multi-scale depth codec.
Presents 3DCueBench to test geometric difficulty while controlling 2D visual cues.
Finds generated depth particularly helps fine-grained geometric reasoning.
Uses reinforcement-learned adaptive interleaved reasoning to decide when to generate evidence; reports 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% circular accuracy on three benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a unified model for geometric understanding and generation, explicitly targeting 'Spatial Intelligence' and improving 3D scene understanding through generative supervision.

papers.tldr: GeoUG improves spatial reasoning by generating geometric evidence only when it is useful, achieving strong accuracy with fewer generation calls than always generating.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

papers.abstract: Object-wise reconstruction increasingly inserts generated meshes into captured scenes as editable proxies for observed objects. This use creates a requirement absent from isolated-asset scores and pose estimates: at the captured metric state, the proxy should reproduce calibrated observations of the same instance. We present ObjectTwin, a scan-grounded measurement protocol that freezes the instance, cameras, scan-projected support and recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator, then replaces only the object representation. The resulting asset correspondence gap measures lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry without treating the scan as complete physical ground truth. Across two indoor RGB-D capture domains and two generation backends, visible, anchored generated assets lose 0.302-0.497 MaskIoU under this replacement. Every tested scene-level estimate is positive, while same-input generator preference reverses across capture domains. Coverage and overlap-depth analyses locate disagreement in both visible support and surface placement; the evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover it. These results establish capture correspondence as a separately measurable interface between generated-asset quality and stronger physical or task-level evaluation.
bullets: Addresses a gap in isolated-asset and pose metrics: editable proxies must match the same object instance in its captured metric state.
Freezes the instance, cameras, scan-derived support, recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator while replacing only the object representation.
Defines the asset correspondence gap as lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry, without assuming the scan is complete ground truth.
Across two indoor RGB-D domains and two generation backends, generated assets lose 0.302–0.497 MaskIoU; disagreement involves both visible support and surface placement.
The evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover the mismatch, and generator preferences reverse across capture domains.

papers.abstract: Multimodal medical AI requires a common visual interface for encoding heterogeneous imaging evidence for patient condition modeling. However, existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific dimension and imaging modality, forcing multimodal systems to rely on fragmented and poorly reusable representations. We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose visual tokenizer that maps 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges: preserving anatomical structure across dimensions and capturing clinical semantics across modalities. To this end, MedVTok introduces (i) slice differential regularization, which explicitly models inter-slice anatomical coherence missing in previous per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, and (ii) multi-expert representation alignment, which integrates knowledge from multiple medical expert encoders while retaining modality-specific complementary knowledge. Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes across 9 imaging modalities, MedVTok supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation through a single tokenizer. Across 24 benchmarks, MedVTok achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating a scalable token interface that unifies medical image dimension, modality, and task usage.
bullets: Addresses fragmented tokenizers that are limited to specific image dimensions or modalities.
Uses slice differential regularization to preserve anatomical coherence across 3D slices.
Applies multi-expert representation alignment to combine clinical knowledge while retaining modality-specific information.
Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes spanning 9 imaging modalities.
Supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and report generation, with state-of-the-art results across 24 benchmarks.
