papers.abstract: Medical image segmentation remains fragmented along two axes: segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality. Existing methods are typically developed separately for semantic, in-context, and interactive segmentation, and are further specialized to either native 2D images or 3D volumetric data. In clinical practice, however, segmentation workflows take many forms: a case may be initialized by semantic prediction, reference-guided segmentation, or user interaction. Regardless of how it begins, fine-grained refinement is naturally performed on 2D views; for volumetric scans, such 2D edits must propagate coherently to the rest of the volume. We present UniPro, a unified model that bridges segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality, using propagation to extend 2D segmentation to 3D volumes. Our key insight is that volumetric propagation and in-context segmentation share the same reference-conditioned prediction mechanism, differing only in whether the reference image-mask pairs come from other cases or from previously segmented neighboring slices. Building on this view, UniPro supports semantic, in-context, interactive, and propagation-based segmentation within a single slice-based framework, using class priors, reference exemplars, user clicks, and neighboring-slice predictions as mode-specific conditioning inputs. To improve propagation reliability, UniPro further incorporates bidirectional and 3D supervision to regularize slice-wise propagation beyond per-slice losses. Extensive experiments across diverse modalities and anatomies show that UniPro achieves strong performance across all segmentation settings, enabling annotation-efficient 3D segmentation from sparse 2D initialization and reducing slice-by-slice correction effort.
bullets: Addresses fragmented segmentation methods across paradigms and 2D/3D data.
Uses a shared slice-based framework conditioned on class priors, reference examples, user clicks, or neighboring-slice predictions.
Treats volumetric propagation as reference-conditioned prediction, analogous to in-context segmentation.
Adds bidirectional propagation and 3D supervision to improve consistency beyond independent slice losses.
Experiments across modalities and anatomies show strong performance and enable sparse-initialization 3D annotation with fewer slice corrections.

figures.caption: Figure 2: UniPro overview. (a) A unified slice-based segmentation pipeline for semantic, in-context, interactive, and propagation-based segmentation. UniPro uses a shared image encoder and decoder, with different settings instantiated through mode-specific conditioning inputs. Conditioning signals are converted into dense 2-D fusion features and sparse 1-D queries, which are jointly fed to the MoE Transformer decoder. Notably, propagation is formulated as in-context segmentation over neighboring slices, enabling coherent volumetric segmentation. (b) Two-stage training strategy. Stage 1 jointly pretrains semantic, in-context, and interactive segmentation with the shared backbone. Stage 2 further adapts the model to propagation with bidirectional and 3D consistency supervision.

Figure 1: Comparison of medical image segmentation paradigms. Existing task-specific, universal, and propagation-based models cover only part of the design space, with limitations in segmentation modes, data dimensionality, or propagation capability. UniPro unifies multi-mode segmentation, native 2D and 3D data, and volumetric propagation in a single slice-based framework.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on pancreas segmentation under the single-click propagation setting. Each row shows a different method propagating from a single positive click (⋆) on the seed slice (z = 34) to representative slices at z = 22, 28, 43, 48, with the resulting 3D reconstruction shown in the rightmost column. UniPro produces masks that closely follow the ground-truth pancreas boundary across the entire volume, while baselines exhibit boundary leakage (PAM, iSegFormer), partial coverage (nnInteractive, MedSAM2), or large over-segmentation toward neighboring organs (SAM2). Per-volume 3D Dice is reported next to each method name.
Figure 3: Ablation analysis of UniPro’s 3D propagation behavior.

Figure 6: Selected success and failure cases on LiTS, KiTS, and BraTS. Each row shows the seed slice (red border), four additional slices ordered by absolute distance from the seed, and 3D ground-truth and predicted surfaces. Green contours and orange overlays denote ground truth and predictions; 3D surfaces use the same colors. z is the slice index and ∆ the absolute index distance in the preprocessed volume.
Table 1: Propagation-based segmentation (3D Dice, %, ↑). All methods are initialized from a single positive click on one seed slice and propagated to the remaining slices.

Table 2: Semantic and in-context segmentation across internal and external datasets (Dice, %, ↑). All in-context models use one-shot inference; propagation is applied only to 3D volumes. nnU-Net (3D) is reported as a fully supervised upper bound. Best results in each block are in bold.
Table 3: Ablation studies on Stage-2 propagation training.

Table 7: Statistical analysis of propagation performance. (a) UniPro’s mean Dice (%), SD, and 95% CI. (b) Paired comparisons with MedSAM2, where ∆ denotes the Dice difference in percentage points. Bold p-values indicate significance at the unadjusted p < 0.05 level.

Table 5: Comparison between standard full-volume Dice (%) and target-containing-slice Dice. Results are averaged over organs within each dataset when applicable. ∆ denotes target-containing-slice Dice minus full-volume Dice, reported in percentage points.
Table 10: Training-stage ablation using only cardiac training data. All variants are evaluated on ACDC with the same ground-truth seed masks. Dice scores are percentages.
Table 9: Inference runtime and memory on AbdomenCT-1K using one NVIDIA Quadro RTX 8000 GPU and batch size 1. Time is the median per volume; memory is peak GPU memory during inference.

Table 6: Seed-position robustness on ACDC under ground-truth seed-mask initialization. GT-init removes seed-slice segmentation error and isolates the effect of seed location on propagation. All results are 3D Dice on target-containing slices.
Table 8: Liver propagation on AbdomenCT-1K with the same seed slice and ground-truth seed mask for all methods. Dice scores are percentages.

papers.title: UniPro: Unified Multi-Mode Medical Image Segmentation from 2D Images to 3D Volumes via Propagation
papers.tldr: UniPro unifies semantic, in-context, interactive, and 3D medical image segmentation by propagating conditioned 2D predictions across volumetric slices.

papers.abstract: Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation-ready indoor environments. Language-guided methods support semantic planning and object-level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held-out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.
authors: Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, Shenji Wan
bullets: Targets the challenge of converting visually plausible layouts into simulation-ready, spatially grounded 3D environments.
Uses hierarchical diffusion sampling to arrange furniture within functional room zones.
Compiles proposals by extracting spatial relations, fitting geometry, and locally correcting object poses.
Across five room types, it achieves the highest reported visual quality and physical stability, with no detected collisions or out-of-bounds objects.
Navigation policies trained in SceneBloom scenes outperform those trained on an equal number of real scans when evaluated on held-out real scans.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Framework overview. SceneBloom decouples visual layout sampling from 3D scene compilation. Given a room description and retrieved exemplars, a vision–language model (VLM) produces a zone plan with a prompt qj for each zone, and a diffusion model conditioned on qj and asset LoRAs Λj samples zone visual proposals Ij . 3D perception models lift the proposals into zone layouts Lj , and a VLM extracts relation contracts Cj from the proposal images. Guided by these relation contracts, the geometric compiler applies hierarchical layout fitting and relational refinement to produce the compiled furniture layout. Wall and surface objects are then added, yielding the simulation-ready scene shown in room and agent views.

Figure 1: Overview of SceneBloom. SceneBloom compiles visual proposals of functional zones into a simulation-ready 3D scene, and resampling the same prompt yields different layouts. Its scenes are more physically plausible than those of prior generators and train a better objectnavigation policy than an equal number of real scans.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. For each method and room type, we show the scene whose score is the median of its ten scenes. Enlarged regions illustrate functional organization and physical placement across methods, each retaining its native asset source. Aggregate results are in Table 1.

Figure 3: Effect of contract-guided compilation. All rows start from the same lifted scene, and each adds one step; the enlarged views show relation groups from the contract. Raw lifted layout: objects keep their lifted poses, and lifting errors break relations such as chairs facing their table. Geometry-only compilation: fitting assembles a collision-free room but leaves these relations broken. Contract-guided compilation: fitting under the contract, followed by relational refinement, restores these relations while the layout stays collision-free.
Figure 6: Training from scratch. SR (%) on the 36 real HM3D validation homes. Points average three training seeds. Shading marks our margin over the best other source.
Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparisons on offices and bathrooms.
Figure 5: Ablation of proposal source and contract guidance. Results on 50 furniture-only scenes with shared inventories, assets, and sizes. Appendix D lists the exact values.

Table 7: Generation wall clock per scene. Measured from each run’s own artifacts, one scene at a time, over the baseline pools of Table 1 and a 50-scene run of our pipeline. The span is layout generation for every system: rendering and physical settling are excluded. Each job generates one scene on one H100-class GPU, except SceneWeaver, which runs on 8 CPU cores. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 2: Policy fine-tuning and generalization. SR and SPL (%) on 100 seen-goal and 107 unseengoal held-out generated scenes and on the 36 scanned scenes of the HM3D-OVON subset. Finetuned rows average three training seeds. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.
Table 1: Comparison with scene generation methods. Coll. and Stab. are percentages, OOB counts objects per scene. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.
Table 3: Real-environment transfer with occluders. SR and SPL (%).
Table 9: Language-model usage and cost per scene. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 8: Our layout-generation time breakdown. Mean wall clock over a 50-scene production run with the same scene requests as Table 1. Components differ from the total by 0.2 seconds due to uninstrumented orchestration and rounding.

Table 12: Navigation-mesh connectivity. Our layouts and the two controls are measured on their fine-tuning pools of Section 4.2.2, the baselines on their pools of Table 1. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 15: Search difficulty of navigation episodes. Share of episodes (%) whose goal stays hidden after a full turn at the start position or is hidden at the start heading, measured with one camera for every set.
Table 14: Real-environment transfer on cleaned episodes. SR and SPL (%) on the 631 HM3D-OVON episodes without annotation errors.
Table 4: Relations a zone contract can hold. The VLM selects relations; the compiler checks them geometrically and performs all pose changes.

Table 5: Physical stability under the REST3D protocol (Ma et al., 2026). Stab. is the percentage of movable objects within the translation and rotation thresholds, and the last three columns measure motion severity. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 6: Layout alignment with Matterport3D under three kernels. LDD is the metric of Table 1; multi-scale LDD and Layout-KID replace its kernel as defined in Section B.1. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 11: Ablation of proposal source and contract guidance. Values plotted in Figure 5. Viol. is the percentage of relations in the extracted contract that the compiled layout violates. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 10: Retrieval ablation. Results on 50 scenes, ten per room type; LDD uses the 30 bedroom, dining-room, and living-room scenes. Zones is the mean number of functional zones per scene, and the visual quality of both rows is judged in a single run, so the with-retrieval row rescores the scenes of Table 1 and differs from it by at most 0.02. Bold marks the better value.

Table 13: Training from scratch. SR and SPL (%) on the 36 real HM3D validation homes for 40, 80, and 120 training houses. Trained rows average three training seeds. Bold/underline mark best/second-best at each house count.

papers.selection_reason: Generates realistic 3D indoor environments for embodied agent training; fits embodied learning and 3D scene generation.
papers.title: SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning
papers.tldr: SceneBloom generates realistic, diverse, and physically valid indoor 3D scenes by combining diffusion-based layout sampling with contract-guided geometric compilation.

papers.abstract: To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure-from-Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse-to-dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non-matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub-pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/flexglue .
authors: Philipp Lindenberger, Paul-Edouard Sarlin, Ondrej Miksik, Marc Pollefeys
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–robustness trade-off between sparse keypoint and dense pixel matching.
Takes image pairs and points from the first image, then predicts corresponding coordinates in the second image.
Searches a limited set of dense-pixel correspondences to provide dense-matching accuracy at sparse-matching speed.
Simultaneously rejects unrelated or visually ambiguous image pairs, improving correspondence reliability.
Experiments report improved Pareto performance for relative pose estimation and strong gains in SfM and visual localization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of FlexGlue. Each of the two images is encoded by a CNN backbone. The resulting dense tokens are fused by a Transformer that outputs context-augmented tokens. These tokens are decoded into overlap heatmaps and classify whether the image pair is unmatchable, in which case the inference stops. Otherwise, a query point in one image is turned into a sub-pixel coordinate in the other by interpolation of its feature, dense correlation, and match refinement.

Figure 3: Visual disambiguation examples. Left: Images overlaid with PCA of learned features. Center: Estimated correspondences pre-filtering. Right: We report the covisibility score after 3 and 9 layers in the top-left. Top: Our method correctly identifies a covisible pair. Bottom: We correctly identify challenging doppelgangers from various domains early and stop matching.

Figure 5: Run-time on different keypoint budgets and layer ablations. RoMav2’s (Edstedt et al., 2026) run time is independent of the number of keypoints, but has a large overhead. LoMa (Nordström et al., 2026) is very efficient but scales quadratically, while our method is fairly efficient and scales linearly (left). Our method learns strong matching and disambiguation early on, while the run time grows linearly with the number of layers (right, black line).

Figure 10: Scene clustering on IMC2025. Image graphs recovered by our method with visual disambiguation only. Colors denote the predicted clusters and edges the retained image pairs. Top: landmarks are separated into clean clusters. Bottom: a single wrong pair (red) passes our filter.

Figure 13: Visual disambiguation examples. We show some visual disambiguation examples from the test sets of DG (Cai et al., 2023), ViSym-F (Xiangli et al., 2025), and LaMAR-DG (Sarlin et al., 2022). Top left is the GT label, right our covisibility score. Our method effectively distinguishes hard covisible pairs, but sometimes mislabels under extreme appearance or viewpoint changes, or when context is missing (middle row failure, wrong facade).

Figure 9: PCA of the aggregated tokens. For each image pair, we show the two views and the first three principal components of their tokens at 9 layers as RGB. Our method learns structural priors such as horizontal and vertical lines, perspective, and planarity, and clearly highlights covisible areas.

Figure 14: Qualitative matches. Correspondences of LoMa-G, SP+RoMav2, and SP+Ours on two pairs per dataset, colored by their reprojection error. We report the number of matches N and the precision at 3 px. LoMa gets 2048 keypoints, and RoMav2 and our method get 1024 keypoints for fair comparison.

Figure 6: Detailed results on LaMAR-DG. AUROC and AP of FlexGlue and DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) per scene (a), difficulty (b), time (c), and device (d). Difficulty bins are tertiles of MegaLoc similarity per label, i.e., hard negatives are highly similar and hard positives dissimilar. FlexGlue remains robust on hard, cross-day, and cross-device pairs, where DG++ degrades strongly.

Figure 14: Qualitative matches (continued). Bottom: failure cases on TartanAir, Hypersim, and MegaDepth. All methods fail under extreme rotation of a repetitive ceiling (top) and on a strongly self-similar scene (middle). On the repetitive facade (bottom), our method matches the wrong instance of a repeated element, while RoMav2 succeeds.

Figure 12: Dense matching across layers. Unfiltered dense correspondences of FlexGlue after 3, 6, and 9 layers, colored by their error from green (<1 px) to red (≥5 px), with the PCK@1px per image. Despite being supervised only at sparse queries, FlexGlue yields fairly accurate dense correspondences. Deeper layers mostly refine matches and fix errors close to depth discontinuities.

Figure 11: Dense matching. Dense correspondences of FlexGlue, colored by their error from green (<1 px) to red (≥5 px), with the PCK@1px per image, from the coarse readout, with our refinement, and with the RoMav2 (Edstedt et al., 2026) refiner. The coarse matching has weaknesses near depth discontinuities, which the refiners address.

Figure 8: Comparison of matching modes. Left: Point-to-point correspondences estimated by our model, colored by epipolar error (green < 1 px). Center: Keypoints colored by being matchable sparse-to-sparse (green), and keypoints only matchable sparse-to-dense (blue), highlighting the repeatability issue. Right: Sparse-to-dense correspondences. Especially under large scale changes and on low-texture areas, sparse-to-dense matching yields many more, accurate correspondences.

Figure 4: Hard negatives of our LaMAR doppelganger benchmark. From left to right: different floors (CAB), indoor (HGE), outdoor (HGE), and cross-device (LIN) pairs. None of the pairs overlap, despite a high retrieval similarity (sim) from MegaLoc; ∆xy and ∆z denote the horizontal and vertical distance between the two cameras.

Figure 7: Corrected ViSym test labels. Each pair shows the original ViSym label (Orig.) and our label (New). The original labels miss covisible pairs under strong viewpoint changes and mark some pairs of distinct but similar facades as covisible.

Table 8: Doppelgangers ablation. AUROC on ViSym-F and LaMAR Disambiguation. Our model learns disambiguation early, and guidance from match supervision improves generalization. Even without labelled data our model achieves high accuracy. Training in-domain increases accuracy. Right: Qualitative examples with GT, DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) and our disambiguation score.
Table 2: Two-view matching in additional domains. FlexGlue exhibits the highest matching accuracy over multiple datasets from different domains. A higher resolution further improves results.
Table 11: Training datasets. Number of training scenes and relative sampling weight of each dataset. Doppelgangers is only mixed in during fine-tuning with negatives.

Table 4: Uncalibrated end-to-end SfM. On ETH3D, FlexGlue exhibits a higher matching accuracy than existing approaches, resulting in more accurate poses. Disambiguation further increases pose accuracy by preventing collapse of reconstructions.

Table 5: SfM with distractors. On IMC2025, FlexGlue yields better reconstructions thanks to its disambiguation. Using 10k keypoints instead of 4k further improves, but makes LoMa timeout on Kaggle (OOT).
Table 9: Keypoint detectors. FlexGlue works with any detector. RaCo yields the most accurate reconstructions, while all detectors perform similarly on two-view matching.
Table 10: ViSym test relabelling. We manually clean GPS-annotated labels of ViSym by hand. Most corrections turn negatives into positives. The last row counts the pairs kept in our balanced subset.

Table 3: Detection of Doppelgangers. We report AUROC and AP on DG (in-distribution), ViSym and LaMAR, as well as the matching time. FlexGlue achieves the highest disambiguation accuracy across all datasets when trained on the same labelled data (DG), especially +10 AUROC points on the LaMAR benchmark, at much higher throughput.

papers.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
papers.tldr: FlexGlue combines sparse-to-dense matching with pairwise disambiguation to achieve efficient, accurate, and reliable visual correspondence estimation.

papers.abstract: Real-world 3D reconstruction pipelines often rely on multi-view images degraded by lossy compression. While compression artifacts have been extensively studied in single-image or video restoration, their impact on multi-view geometry remains largely overlooked. In this work, we identify compression-induced cross-view geometric inconsistency as a critical failure mode, where view-dependent artifacts disrupt feature matching, dense correspondence, camera parameter estimation, and downstream 3D reconstruction tasks such as novel view synthesis. To address this problem, we propose CompMVR, a compression-aware multi-view diffusion restoration framework that jointly refines compressed views while preserving cross-view consistency, and construct compressed datasets for systematic evaluation. Unlike conventional restoration methods that optimize each image independently for 2D perceptual quality, CompMVR leverages learned compression priors and cross-view correspondence to recover visual details while improving geometric reliability across views. Experiments across diverse datasets, codecs, and compression levels demonstrate gains in restoration quality and downstream 3D tasks, including novel-view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and view matching. These results establish compressed multi-view restoration as a distinct problem and highlight its importance for 3D reconstruction under lossy compression. Code and data for this paper are available at https://mchaewon.github.io/CompMVR-project-page/.
authors: Dong-hwi Kim, Chaewon Moon, Hojun Song, Dongbeom Kim, Junyeong Jang, Aro Kim, Gahyeon Kim, Heejung Choi, Jehee Kim, Gianella Cravioto, Sohyun Lee, Gyeongjin Choi, EunHye Jeong, Soo Ye Kim, Jaehyup Lee, Sang-hyo Park
bullets: Lossy compression disrupts cross-view geometry, harming feature matching, correspondence, camera estimation, and novel-view synthesis.
CompMVR jointly restores compressed views while preserving geometric consistency across views.
The framework combines learned compression priors with cross-view correspondence rather than restoring images independently.
Compressed datasets enable evaluation across diverse datasets, codecs, and compression levels.
Experiments report improved restoration quality and downstream performance in novel-view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and view matching.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our proposed CompMVR. (a) In Stage 1, we learn a compression-aware latent representation by training a compression prior embedder. The latent is optimized through image reconstruction and supervision of coding parameters (codec type and QP). (b) In Stage 2, we perform multi-view restoration using a diffusion model conditioned on the learned compression prior. The latent is injected via cross-attention and fused with the UNet input, while a compression artifact estimator (CAE) predicts spatially varying residual maps for degradation-aware restoration. To enforce cross-view geometric consistency, we further apply a cross-view correspondence loss during training.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparison on the Free dataset. The top rows correspond to an indoor scene (Lab), and the bottom rows correspond to an outdoor scene (Sky). The Lab scene is compressed using HEVC with QP 42, while the Sky scene is compressed using AV1 with QP 42. Highlighted regions reveal that our method better preserves fine details and structures under severe compression.

Fig. 9. Qualitative novel-view synthesis results rendered at ground-truth target camera poses. The top two rows correspond to HEVC QP42, and the bottom two rows correspond to AVC QP42. We compare each method with the corresponding GT view using full-scene renderings and zoomed-in regions. Our method better preserves object structures, text regions, and high-frequency details, producing results closer to GT than diffusion-based restoration baselines. Red boxes indicate representative regions for comparison.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison of synthesized novel 3D views from restored multi-view inputs on the Free dataset. We evaluate global consistency using scene renderings synthesized from multiple viewpoints and local structural fidelity using zoomed-in regions. Views 1 and 2 correspond to HEVC QP42, and View 3 corresponds to AV1 QP42. Our method preserves sharper geometry-critical details and reduces blur and distortion compared with diffusion-based restoration baselines. Red boxes indicate representative regions for comparison.

Fig. 7. Visualization of estimated artifact maps on the Free dataset. The estimated artifact maps highlight compression-sensitive regions, such as edges and texture-rich structures, demonstrating that our CAE effectively captures spatially varying degradation cues.

Fig. 4. Failure cases of a video diffusion restoration model [Dehaghi et al. 2025] on multi-view images. Examples from the Free dataset (hydrant and pillar scenes, left to right) show that the model fails to maintain crossview consistency. Highlighted regions reveal inconsistent restoration and geometric misalignment caused by large viewpoint differences.

Fig. 3. Energy maps computed from uncompressed images and artifact maps compressed at identical QP settings, for low and high complexity scenes. Higher scene complexity yields larger compression residuals.

Fig. 5. t-SNE visualization of the Stage 1 latent representations learned by using Lcodec and LQP, and their combination, respectively. Color denotes codec type (AVC / HEVC / AV1 / VP9) and point size denotes QP level.

papers.abstract: Generating editable 3D urban scenes from a single image requires detailed building assets with a coherent spatial arrangement. Occlusion and perspective ambiguity make it difficult to infer complete building geometry together with consistent relative scales and positions. We present CityLift, a framework that generates individual textured building meshes from an urban image by coupling scene-level spatial modeling with building-level synthesis. CityLift first learns building shape and placement jointly through coupled scene and instance streams, producing coarse sparse structures in a common coordinate system. We then introduce generative spatial inheritance, which maps each building's coarse occupancy and scene-conditioned 3D feature field into a local volume to guide a flow model that generates finer structure. The same coordinate mapping places the generated meshes back into the scene, preserving their spatial relationship to the scaffold. To address the scarcity of urban data pairing scene images with individual 3D buildings, we construct CityLift-5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic scenes with instance masks, building meshes, and placement annotations. Experiments on CityLift-5K and scene blocks from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved building geometry and scene composition. The project page is available at https://ranhaogong.github.io/CityLift/.
authors: Haoran Gong, Jie Feng, Chenxu Wang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and perspective ambiguity in reconstructing complete buildings with consistent scales and positions.
Uses coupled scene- and instance-level streams to produce coarse building shapes and placements in a shared coordinate system.
Introduces generative spatial inheritance to guide flow-based refinement of detailed textured building meshes.
Builds CityLift-5K, a dataset of 4,997 synthetic scenes with masks, meshes, and placement annotations.
Experiments on CityLift-5K and UrbanScene3D scene blocks show improved building geometry and scene composition.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CityLift. Given a single urban image and building instance masks, CityLift generates individually editable building meshes in a shared scene frame. (a) A shared scene–instance generator predicts coarse occupancy in a common scene frame, implicitly modeling building placement, scale, and geometry. (b) A scaffold-derived coordinate map Ti deterministically resamples occupancy and contextual features Fi into each building’s local volume, forming the aligned condition Ai. (c) Conditioned on Ai and building image features ei, a local flow model regenerates finer sparse structures from noise. These structures guide mesh generation, and the resulting buildings are mapped back into the scene using the inherited transforms.
Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on blocks extracted from CityLift-5K testset. We slightly adjust the viewing angle to better showcase the generated scenes.
Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on blocks extracted from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding. We slightly adjust the viewing angle to better showcase the generated scenes.
Figure 5. Qualitative results of the ablation study.

Table 4. MLLM-as-a-judge visual evaluation on UrbanScene3D. ChatGPT 6 Astra scores the input image and four rendered views of each output. Results are averaged over all blocks shared by all six methods. All values are on a 0–100 scale, with higher values better. L, G, A, and M denote layout and completeness, shape and proportion, appearance and detail, and multi-view structural quality.
Table 1. Geometric evaluation on CityLift-5K. An em dash denotes unavailable building-level output.
Table 2. External evaluation on UrbanScene3D. Quantitative comparison on blocks extracted from a synthetic urban scene, assessing the geometric accuracy of individual buildings and assembled scenes.

Table 3. External evaluation on InstanceBuilding. Quantitative comparison on scene blocks from real-world reconstructed meshes, assessing the geometric accuracy of individual buildings and assembled scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for compositional 3D urban scene generation from a single image, addressing the scarcity of paired data. This contributes to 3D scene understanding and generation.
papers.title: CityLift: Compositional 3D Urban Generation from a Single Image
papers.tldr: CityLift generates editable 3D urban scenes from a single image by jointly modeling building geometry and spatial arrangement.

papers.abstract: We introduce SemGeo-Gen, an unsupervised method for generating approximate cross-instance semantic-geometric supervision from weakly aligned 3D object collections. Our goal is not to recover exact point-level correspondences, which are often ambiguous across different instances and would require expensive, impractical manual supervision at scale. Instead, we automatically produce approximate correspondences that are semantically meaningful, geometrically consistent, and diverse enough to train modern correspondence models. Given only coarse category-level rotation alignment, SemGeo-Gen lifts multi-view DINOv2 features to 3D, aligns object instances using continuous piecewise-affine registration, and prunes candidate matches using semantic consistency. The resulting 3D correspondences can be projected into rendered views, yielding scalable 3D-3D, 3D-2D, and 2D-2D supervision without manual annotation. We validate the generated correspondences against sparse human annotations from KeypointNet, obtaining 93% PCK@0.10 and 97% PCK@0.15. More importantly, we show that using the generated correspondences for synthetic pretraining improves recent state-of-the-art semantic correspondence models on SPair-71k after fine-tuning on real data, with gains of up to 5 PCK@0.10 points. Together, these results indicate that approximate semantic-geometric supervision generated from 3D assets can improve real-image correspondence learning and serve as a scalable alternative to costly manual annotation. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/SemGeo-Gen/.
authors: Roy Amoyal, Shira Ifergane, Oren Freifeld
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity and cost of exact point-level correspondence annotation across object instances.
Lifts multi-view DINOv2 features into 3D, aligns instances with continuous piecewise-affine registration, and filters matches by semantic consistency.
Projects the generated 3D matches into rendered views to produce 3D-3D, 3D-2D, and 2D-2D supervision.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed-set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real-world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed-set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real-world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open-set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround-view RGB cameras, a 128-beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real-world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in-distribution) and OOD (out-of-distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.
authors: Zhiran Yan, Savankumar Bhanderi, Sourabh Lolge, Rui Song, Girdharbhai Paneliya, Shiva Agrawal, Gordon Elger
bullets: Addresses the safety gap caused by closed-set 3D perception systems that cannot recognize previously unseen objects.
Provides 12,661 synchronized, annotated frames from six RGB cameras, 128-beam LiDAR, and GPS/IMU sensors.
Covers 52 driving scenes across clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions.
Separates known-class ID training scenes from OOD validation and test scenes containing annotated unknown objects.
Experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems; data, protocols, and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Real-time decoding of omnidirectional images is essential for immersive virtual reality (VR) experiences. Compared with conventional transform-based learned image compression (LIC), overfitted codecs offer lower decoding complexity by representing each image with a lightweight implicit neural representation (INR). However, existing approaches typically operate on the equirectangular projection (ERP), which introduces nonuniform spherical sampling and spatial distortion, leading to redundant sampling near the poles and latitude-dependent receptive fields. To address these limitations, we propose a spherical overfitted codec based on a multi-scale Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (HEALPix) representation, which enables equal-area sampling and efficient hierarchical modeling of spherical signals. Building on this representation, we develop a Spherical Inter-Scale Conditional entropy model that exploits spatial dependencies and cross-scale correlations among HEALPix latents to improve coding efficiency. We further introduce a Multi-Ring Spherical Convolution that aggregates neighboring pixels over a nearly uniform spherical receptive field across latitudes. Experiments on a public omnidirectional image dataset demonstrate BD-rate reductions of 16.3%, 26.5%, and 19.5% over VVC in terms of V-PSNR, V-MS-SSIM, and V-LPIPS, respectively. Our method also achieves a 13.1% BD-rate reduction over ERP-based Cool-Chic 5.0 in terms of V-PSNR, while providing 2.6-3.6x faster decoding than the evaluated learned autoencoder codecs.
authors: Yulong Cheng, Youneng Bao, Junfeng Zhou, Mu Li, Jie Wen
bullets: Addresses ERP distortion and redundant polar sampling in omnidirectional image compression.
Uses multi-scale HEALPix representation with a spherical inter-scale conditional entropy model.
Introduces multi-ring spherical convolution for nearly uniform receptive fields across latitudes.
Reduces BD-rate versus VVC by 16.3% (V-PSNR), 26.5% (V-MS-SSIM), and 19.5% (V-LPIPS).
Achieves 13.1% lower BD-rate than ERP-based Cool-Chic 5.0 in V-PSNR and 2.6–3.6× faster decoding than evaluated learned autoencoders.

papers.abstract: Developing multiple instance learning pipelines for the classification of whole-slide images involves many interdependent design decisions and expertise in both pathology and machine learning. We present AutoMIL, an open-source framework that applies principles from the field of automated machine learning to tackle this task by automating integral pipeline steps, such as preprocessing, training and evaluation. In a benchmark evaluation with default settings, AutoMIL reached ROC-AUC scores of 0.94 on UBC-OCEAN, 0.99 on PCam and 0.93-0.96 on a TCGA-NSCLC subset, comparable to specialised pipelines in related work. Ensembling mainly improved performance on imbalanced data, showing that an automated pipeline must adapt to dataset characteristics. AutoMIL thus provides an accessible baseline for whole-slide image classification without manual pipeline configuration.
authors: Jonas Waibel, Frank Kramer, Dominik M\"uller
bullets: Addresses the expertise and configuration burden of designing whole-slide image classification pipelines.
Automates preprocessing, training, and evaluation using automated machine learning principles.
Achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.94 on UBC-OCEAN, 0.99 on PCam, and 0.93–0.96 on a TCGA-NSCLC subset.
Ensembling primarily benefits imbalanced datasets, highlighting the need to adapt automation to dataset characteristics.
Provides an open-source baseline without manual pipeline configuration.

papers.abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse $\to$ ModelNet40; XYZRGB $\to$ XYZ-only), PFIR raises zero-shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated $2.6\times$ more on geometrically ambiguous samples---supporting part-level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir-3d.
authors: Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Pattern-matching 3D MLLMs struggle to distinguish geometrically similar objects, with accuracy dropping sharply on highly ambiguous samples.
The method reverses the usual information flow: geometry → function → identity, using part-level segmentation and functional chain-of-thought supervision.
PFIR trains on 507K functional QA pairs with a progressive curriculum and combines functional reasoning with descriptive grounding through dual-objective GRPO.
Under Objaverse→ModelNet40 and XYZRGB→XYZ-only zero-shot evaluation, accuracy improves from 60.5% to 66.7%.
Improvements are concentrated 2.6× more on geometrically ambiguous samples, supporting part-level functional reasoning for recognition.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PFIR framework. The part-level functional pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functionas-evidence reasoning chains. The three-stage curriculum progressively builds function-guided recognition: Stage 1 aligns part-aware representations, Stage 2 teaches the reasoning format via SFT, and Stage 3 trains two complementary RL experts (functional reasoning + descriptive grounding) composed via Task Arithmetic.

Figure 1: Motivation. Pattern matching collapses on geometrically ambiguous objects (a). A per-sample GCS reveals that the hardest 20% reach only 33.7% baseline accuracy. PFIR addresses this via part-level functional reasoning, with gains concentrated 2.6× more on the most confused quintile (b), by shifting from function-as-annotation to functionas-evidence (c).

papers.selection_reason: Part-level functional reasoning in 3D MLLMs to improve generalizable 3D recognition; relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D scene construction is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Recent methods such as SAM-3Dfy enable end-to-end reconstruction of 3D assets and their scene layouts, but still struggle with fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality. Meanwhile, specialized 3D object generators provide detailed object geometry, while 3D foundation models offer strong and generalizable spatial understanding. We propose Easy-3Dfy, a compositional workflow that decouples object generation from scene layout estimation, allowing specialized models to fully exploit their respective strengths. An RPF-based aligner then bridges these capabilities by establishing geometric correspondence between object-local meshes and partial scene pointmaps, recovering object layout for scene composition. Without requiring complete scene-level supervision, the proposed workflow consistently outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200. Our results demonstrate that explicit geometric composition can effectively combine high-quality object generation with strong spatial understanding, while enabling the workflow to benefit independently from advances in both 3D object generation and foundation models.
authors: Ziang Zhang, Wenyou Yi, Zehan Wang, Jiachen Xu, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Targets limitations in fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality in existing end-to-end methods such as SAM-3Dfy.
Uses specialized 3D object generators for object geometry and 3D foundation models for spatial understanding.
An RPF-based aligner matches object-local meshes with partial scene pointmaps to recover object layouts.
Requires no complete scene-level supervision and outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200.
Its modular design can independently benefit from advances in object generation and foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Easy-3Dfy. Given object masks, a spatial model predicts a scene pointmap. For each object, an image editor produces a completed object image and a replaceable image-to-3D provider generates a local mesh. The RPF-based aligner matches its anchor point cloud to the object-specific partial query extracted from the pointmap, predicts correspondence positions, and recovers a uniform-scale similarity transform via Umeyama fitting. Transforming all complete meshes assembles the final scene.

Figure 5: What direct alignment improves. Matched comparisons of MIDI, SceneGen, SAM-3Dfy, and Easy-3Dfy under a common rendering protocol. The multi-view results show that Easy-3Dfy reduces floating and interpenetrating objects while improving object ordering and placement.

Figure 4: How mesh quality affects visual and layout quality. Matched input–panorama–close-up comparisons. Each case consists of two columns, with the first showing the reconstructed full 3D scene and the second showing close-up views of the same asset regions.

Figure 3: Object-level data construction and RPF training. Aligned RGB–depth renders yield a monocular partial query and pixel-matched ground-truth correspondence positions. Independent anchor- and query-side geometric augmentations define the registration task, on which RPF learns the conditional velocity field.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.
Supports counterfactual simulation, such as predicting whether moving an object would block a path.
Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture, training recipe, and prompting interface. (A) Ψ-0.6 is a unified model across diverse modalities. Pretraining, mid-training, and post-training sample different sequence families; hollow tokens denote stochastically included sequence elements. Generic prompting interface: prompts specify the available information and requested inference pathway. Ψ-0.6 is interactive: it can generate a view based on a user-specified camera pose, then use that generated view as context for subsequent reasoning. (B) Fine-grained control: each patch is represented by a pointer token and content tokens. Pointers specify modality and spatial and temporal locations, enabling targeted conditioning and scene edits. Probabilistic prediction: Ψ-0.6 represents a distribution over compatible continuations, allowing the same prompt to yield alternative predictions through sampling.

Figure 6: Learning adaptive stream-of-thought reasoning. papers.abstract: We present PixGR, an efficient framework that integrates lightweight pixel-space generative modeling into feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction to model scene uncertainty. Context observations are encoded once into a scene latent representation, which conditions generative decoding from noisy target views to produce a shared 3D Gaussian representation. We formulate this process using pixel-space flow matching, enabling end-to-end optimization of 3D reconstruction with direct pixel-space generative supervision through differentiable rendering. This avoids VAE-based latent compression and error propagation inherent in previous two-stage pipelines. To preserve feed-forward efficiency, PixGR caches the scene representation and performs iterative inference using a lightweight DiT decoder. Experiments demonstrate that PixGR outperforms regression-based approaches in challenging sparse-view settings, particularly with widely spaced observations and view extrapolation. Meanwhile, it maintains sub-second inference and remains competitive with substantially heavier pretrained generative models. Our project page is available at https://ranrhuang.github.io/pixgr/.
authors: Ranran Huang, Wenjing Bian, Weixun Luo, Ye Mao, Krystian Mikolajczyk
bullets: Targets sparse-view 3D reconstruction, especially widely spaced observations and view extrapolation.
Encodes context views once into a scene latent that conditions generation from noisy target views.
Uses pixel-space flow matching and differentiable rendering for end-to-end reconstruction supervision.
Avoids VAE-based latent compression and associated error propagation in two-stage pipelines.
Achieves sub-second inference, outperforming regression methods while remaining competitive with heavier generative models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of feed-forward reconstruction and generative pipelines. (a) Deterministic reconstruction cannot model scene uncertainty. Existing generative approaches address this limitation through (b) generation then reconstruction or (c) reconstruction then generation, but suffer from error propagation between stages, VAE-based information loss, and high computational costs. (d) PixG3R instead integrates lightweight pixel-space generation directly into 3D Gaussian reconstruction, enabling end-to-end optimization with direct pixel-space generative supervision.

Figure 2: PixGR Overview. Multi-view posed context images are encoded once into a scene latent representation. Target viewpoints are sampled and encoded as ray maps, which are combined with noisy target images. A lightweight generative decoder processes the concatenated scene latent and target tokens to predict a shared set of pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians supporting both context and target views. The decoder adopts a DiT-style architecture with global self-attention, followed by a linear Gaussian prediction head. Differentiable rendering of the predicted Gaussians produces denoised target views, enabling direct supervision through pixel-space generative objectives.

papers.abstract: Generating physically stable 3D structures from visual specifications requires resolving geometric ambiguity while accounting for physical interactions among objects. We present StackGen3D, a framework for generating stable block assemblies conditioned on a given block inventory and three orthographic silhouettes. Our approach consists of two stages. First, we develop a physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) that models support relations between blocks and serves as a fast stability predictor for curating a diverse dataset of stable structures. Second, we train a conditional flow-matching model on this dataset to capture the multimodal distribution of block configurations consistent with the target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight geometric selection and refinement reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation. Preliminary experiments show that the PI-GNN generalizes from simple stacks to complex structures substantially better than a parameter-matched multilayer perceptron. For structure generation, Best-of-10 selection improves physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while achieving a silhouette IoU of 0.970. These results highlight the potential of combining relational physical reasoning, scalable data curation, and conditional generative modeling for creative 3D assembly. Project website: [https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/](https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/)
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang, Luzhe Sun, Yiqing Xu, Matthew R. Walter
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity and physical interactions in silhouette-conditioned 3D structure generation.
Uses a physics-informed graph neural network to model block support relations and curate stable training structures.
Trains a conditional flow-matching model to represent multiple valid block configurations.
Applies geometric selection and refinement to reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation.
Best-of-10 selection reaches 72.4% physical stability with 0.970 silhouette IoU; PI-GNN generalizes better than a parameter-matched MLP.

papers.abstract: Estimating a camera pose from 3D-2D correspondences - Perspective-n-Point - is one of the most fundamental problems in computer vision. Existing methods either solve a minimal problem or replace the objective with an easier one. Surprisingly, no scalable certifiable solver for the actual Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) exists. We propose PnP*, the first practical solver that guarantees efficient computation and returns a certifiable globally optimal solution. We prove that the underlying convex relaxation is exact under moderate noise, which to our knowledge is the first stability guarantee for any relaxation for the MLE of PnP. Furthermore, we reduce the relaxation by exploiting chordal sparsity pattern and quotient ring reduction such that the relaxation is tractable and scalable. The stability and scalability results are verified numerically, as PnP* returns a provably correct camera pose at over 10 Hz.
authors: Bang-Shien Chen, Caitrin E. Eaton, David M. Rosen
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable certifiable solvers for the true PnP maximum-likelihood objective.
Uses a convex relaxation with a proof of exactness under moderate noise.
Exploits chordal sparsity and quotient-ring reduction to make the relaxation tractable and scalable.
Numerical experiments verify stability and scalability, with certified solutions reported at over 10 Hz.

papers.abstract: Generating multiple videos of a dynamic scene from a single reference video requires synthesizing both observed and unobserved content consistently across viewpoints. Existing camera-control methods for video diffusion typically rely on architectural mechanisms, including camera embeddings, cross-view attention, and geometric conditioning. Although effective for static scene content, these approaches often struggle with the fine-grained, dynamic geometry that must remain coherent across views and over time. We synchronize the diffusion process itself by sampling the Gaussian noise prior in a canonical 3D space derived from the source video and rasterizing it into target cameras, rather than sampling independently in each 2D image plane. Our method, SyncVid, lifts a monocular video into a canonical 4D representation, associates noise with scene geometry and unseen space, and rasterizes the resulting structured noise into arbitrary views. Because rendering can introduce local correlations, we further propose a cross-view-consistent whitening procedure that decorrelates neighboring pixels while preserving correspondence across views. The structured noise serves as the diffusion prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model, requiring no architectural modifications. By enforcing spatiotemporal and cross-view coherence at the source of stochasticity, SyncVid generates synchronized videos and improves both perceptual quality and cross-view consistency in our experiments. Project page: https://qualcomm-ai-research.github.io/SyncVid-Webpage.
authors: Farhad G. Zanjani, Animesh Karnewar, Fatih Porikli, Amirhossein Habibian
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating temporally and cross-view coherent videos from a single reference video, especially for dynamic geometry.
Lifts the source video into a canonical 4D representation and rasterizes geometry-aware noise into target camera views.
Introduces cross-view-consistent whitening to reduce local correlations while preserving correspondence across views.
Uses the structured noise as the prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model without architectural modifications.
Experiments report improved perceptual quality and cross-view consistency, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SyncVid. Given a source video, SyncVid (1) lifts the observations into a canonical 4D point representation; (2) samples a Gaussian noise vector for each 3D primitive in the scene; and (3), after specifying novel camera trajectories, rasterizes and whitens the shared 3D noise into the corresponding views. These synchronized priors guide video diffusion to produce temporally and cross-view consistent videos from multiple cameras.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on a Multi-ViewBench example with an Arc-right trajectory.

Figure 2: View-consistent whitening Noise vectors z𝑖 are attached to 3D primitives and the cubemap; rasterization therefore provides cross-view correspondence, while overlapping footprints induce local correlation. We reduce this correlation with a per-pixel orthonormal transformation Q𝑝 derived from the rasterized canonical anchor position X𝑝 using random Fourier features and reduced QR (dashed box). Because Q𝑝 depends on X𝑝 rather than screen coordinates, pixels observing the same surface point share the transformation across views and over time. The resulting noise pattern (right) is approximately i.i.d. Gaussian within each frame while remaining cross-view synchronized.

papers.abstract: Existing 3D talking avatar methods mainly rely on parametric face models including 3DMM or FLAME, whose compact motion representations limit their ability to synthesize extreme expressions and to model accessories such as headwear. We introduce AudioLift, a two-stage framework that uses generated multi-view videos as the intermediate representation for audio-driven avatar generation without parametric face models or per-instance optimization. Our framework combines a synchronized multi-view video generation stage with an inconsistency-robust Gaussian reconstruction stage to recover coherent full-head geometry from a single portrait image. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AudioLift produces 3D talking avatars capable of capturing more extreme facial expressions than existing methods, with improved geometric completeness and strong multi-view consistency across the full $360^\circ$ viewing range.

papers.abstract: High-quality 3D reconstruction of lunar terrain from sparse rover images is indispensable for autonomous lunar exploration, but remains challenging because viewpoint overlap is insufficient, surface textures are weak, and data volume is limited. We propose MoonGS, the first feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework tailored to lunar scenes. Given only two input images, MoonGS predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass and renders photorealistic novel views without any per-scene optimization. MoonGS (i) adopts an adaptable backbone design that seamlessly integrates advanced vision foundation models to extract robust depth features; (ii) integrates semantic priors in two manners: merging semantic cues with visual features to refine Gaussian parameter estimation, and adopting a semantic ranking loss that regularizes background depth; and (iii) employs an entropy-guided heuristic resampling strategy to augment sparse observations by selecting the most informative distant viewpoints with negligible overhead. Experiments on the LuSNAR benchmark and our synthetic weak-texture MoonBlender dataset show that MoonGS surpasses state-of-the-art feed-forward NeRF/3DGS baselines by +4.9 dB PSNR, +0.29 SSIM, and 40\% lower LPIPS while maintaining sub-second inference. Furthermore, we validate the broad applicability of our framework by demonstrating that it effectively leverages state-of-the-art backbones, including VGGT, to significantly boost performance. Qualitative evaluations on Chang'e mission imagery also show the best visual quality among compared methods, indicating robustness on real lunar data. The source code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/InRobots/MoonBlender.
bullets: Addresses sparse-view lunar reconstruction challenges caused by low overlap, weak textures, and limited data.
Predicts pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian primitives in one forward pass, avoiding per-scene optimization.
Uses adaptable vision backbones, semantic feature fusion, semantic ranking loss, and entropy-guided viewpoint resampling.
Outperforms feed-forward NeRF/3DGS baselines on LuSNAR and MoonBlender, with sub-second inference and improved visual quality on Chang'e imagery.
Demonstrates compatibility with advanced backbones such as VGGT.

figures.caption: Fig. 12: Qualitative comparison on the LUSNAR dataset. We evaluate the effectiveness of integrating the VGGT foundation model within our proposed framework. In terms of visual quality, our method outperforms the baseline model.
Fig. 1: Novel view synthesis comparison. Compared to existing 3DGS-based methods, our approach provides higherfidelity novel view synthesis results.

Fig. 11: Qualitative comparison of depth maps on the MoonBlender dataset. This figure compares depth maps produced by several models on the MoonBlender dataset. Our proposed method (MoonGS) generates both accurate and smoothly varying depth maps. In contrast, MVSplat converges to erroneous depths, and although pixelSplat produces relatively accurate depths, it exhibits noticeable artifacts—such as non-smooth transitions (indicated by the arrows). These findings highlight the importance of robust depth estimation techniques for lunar scene reconstruction.

Fig. 13: Impact of ranking loss on depth estimation in weakly textured background areas. The results show the effect of ranking loss on improving depth estimation in regions with weak texture. In the absence of ranking loss, depth estimates in these areas are often imprecise due to the lack of texture. However, by introducing ranking loss, the model is able to refine the depth predictions in these challenging regions, leading to more reliable results. Moreover, integrating ranking loss with the pixelSplat model yields further improvements in depth accuracy. These results underscore the value of ranking loss in addressing depth estimation issues in weakly textured regions.

Fig. 9: Qualitative comparison of novel views on the LuSNAR (top) and MoonBlender (bottom) test sets. Compared to the baseline, our method is able to generate more accurate and perceptually attractive images, especially for lunar regolith close to the camera.

Fig. 10: Comparison of rendering results with and without heuristic resampling strategy. We present two groups of rendering results across four viewpoints: (a, c) with the heuristic resampling strategy, and (b, d) without the heuristic resampling strategy. The resampled region (Position2) is the selected resampling location. The results demonstrate that heuristic resampling effectively reduces artifacts and produces a more realistic textural appearance.

Fig. 5: Color distribution histograms for semantic categories. The color histograms demonstrate significant differences in color distribution between specific semantic categories, while the color distributions for the same semantic category show minimal variation. These patterns demonstrate that regions belonging to different semantic categories possess distinct color characteristics, whereas regions within the same semantic category exhibit high similarity. This property allows semantic information to serve as an effective feature for input. Semantic ranking loss. In extremely distant regions such as sky and lunar mountains, standard depth estimators often produce imprecise predictions and rarely refine them [51], [52]. Rather than imposing hard background priors like setting background splats to zero opacity or clamping depth to a fixed far plane, which can erase genuine far-range structure and introduce scale bias, we employ a semantic ranking loss inspired by DIW-style supervision [53], [54] to regularize lowtexture regions. Specifically, we sample from two categories c1 and c2 whose depth relationship is known. Assuming c1 is nearer than c2, two pairs of points [p1,c1 , p2,c2 ] and [p1,c2 , p2,c2 ] can be obtained. We treat the point closer to the camera as a reference depth point, while the more distant point is used for depth optimization.

Fig. 14: Visualization of features under different ablation settings. papers.abstract: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.
bullets: Addresses safe aerial navigation when accurate ground-truth obstacle data is unavailable.
Uses a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to encode detailed scene geometry.
Introduces a reachability-based planner exploiting quadrotor differential flatness.
Computes continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate vehicle occupancy.
Finds paths in 81.2% of challenging test cases, compared with 51.2% for the nearest baseline.

Fig. 1: AirSplan generates safe quadrotor trajectories in cluttered environments. The robot occupancy is tightly overapproximated using a reachable set (shown in pink) based on differential flatness. The scene is modeled as a Normalized 3D Gaussian Splat. A sampling-based planner jointly reasons over both representations to compute safe paths between waypoints (yellow) to the goal (red).

First, differential flatness is used to construct a tight sphere-based overapproximation of the robot volume along a trajectory. Second, the collision probability between each sphere and the normalized 3D Gaussian Splat is efficiently computed using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (visualized with gray wireframe boxes). Third, a GPU-parallel sampling-based optimizer evaluates many candidate trajectories to efficiently find safe paths through dense environments.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction is crucial for autonomous driving, but camera-based methods degrade in low-light conditions and LiDAR-based methods are sensitive to adverse weather. 4D radar is more robust, yet its sparsity and the high cost of radar tensor processing limit its use. We propose Radar Geometric-Semantic Occupancy Prediction (RadarGSOcc), an efficient framework that directly processes 4D radar tensors by separately extracting geometric and semantic features, including Doppler information, with a deformable attention-based geometric refinement module as its key component. We also introduce the K-Radar 3DSemOcc benchmark, the first large-scale benchmark for 3D semantic occupancy prediction using 4D radar tensors, built on the K-Radar dataset with refined LiDAR-based annotations. RadarGSOcc predicts 15 classes within a 51.2m range and achieves 38.2% IoU, 7.6% mIoU, and 25.5% weighted mIoU, outperforming RadarOcc by 17% relative (25.5 vs. 21.9) in weighted mIoU while using fewer parameters and lower computation. It substantially improves truck prediction while trading off car accuracy, outperforms camera-based approaches, and narrows the gap with LiDAR-based methods. To assess robustness without per-frame ground truth in adverse weather, we further propose a novel proxy metric, Environment-Based KL Divergence (EBKL), under which 4D radar proves a reliable and efficient modality for 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The dataset and code will be publicly available.
bullets: Addresses camera degradation in low light and LiDAR sensitivity to adverse weather, while tackling 4D radar sparsity and processing cost.
Separately extracts geometric and semantic features, including Doppler information, with deformable-attention geometric refinement.
Introduces K-Radar 3DSemOcc, a large-scale 4D-radar semantic occupancy benchmark with refined LiDAR annotations.
Predicts 15 classes within 51.2 m, reaching 38.2% IoU, 7.6% mIoU, and 25.5% weighted mIoU.
Outperforms RadarOcc in weighted mIoU with fewer parameters and lower computation; improves truck prediction but trades off car accuracy.

The extracted features are then passed to the occupancy head (bottom right), where the proposed geometric feature refinement module (Section III-B3) refines occupancy features using geometric representations. papers.abstract: Controllable 3D part generation is pivotal for digital asset creation, yet existing methods lack the flexibility to accommodate diverse user workflows requiring varying levels of control. In this paper, we introduce FlexPart, a unified image-to-3D part generation framework that supports variable-granularity geometric conditions within a single model. By seamlessly integrating heterogeneous inputs, ranging from sparse points to dense bounding boxes and masks, via gated adaptive modulation, FlexPart unlocks a powerful cross-modal synergy. We also propose an asymmetric geometric guidance mechanism that leverages strong spatial priors to align representations across granularities, improving geometric consistency and facilitating inter-task synergy. Under mask conditioning on PartVerseXL, FlexPart reduces Part CD by 16.6% relative to TripoSG + SAM3D and by 10.5% relative to OmniPart, while maintaining competitive whole-mesh quality. The code can be found at https://github.com/Gucci233/FlexPart
authors: Qiwen Gu, Xin Zhou, Xiwu Chen, Zhongyang Zhu, Zhuo Zhang, Junqiao Zhao
bullets: Addresses the need for flexible, variable-granularity control in 3D part generation.

Uses asymmetric geometric guidance to align representations across granularities and promote cross-task synergy.
On PartVerseXL with mask conditioning, reduces Part CD by 16.6% versus TripoSG + SAM3D and 10.5% versus OmniPart.
Maintains competitive whole-mesh quality.

papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/
authors: Ava Pun, Kevin Dai, Sally Chen, Maxwell Jones, Ruixuan Liu, Kangle Deng, Changliu Liu, Maneesh Agrawala, Deva Ramanan, Jun-Yan Zhu

The API halves inference cost compared with working directly in raw LDraw.
BrickWright-guided agents reached 100% validity on 512 prompts, versus 9–69% for baseline agents.
Improves prompt adherence for lightweight agents, maintains it for stronger agents, and outperforms specialized text-to-brick models.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D generation has achieved high fidelity on curated benchmarks, yet degrades sharply on real-world images with uneven illumination, blur, and occlusions. Purifying such inputs requires deciding when to intervene and preserving the visual cues needed for 3D generation, while leaving clean inputs unchanged. We introduce Gate3DGen, a selective pre-processing model that gates image inputs to existing 3D generators without retraining them. A degradation-aware router bypasses inputs classified as clean and extracts features to guide purification of the remaining inputs. Conditioned on these features, a 3D-oriented one-step purifier purifies degraded inputs with spatial losses that encourage preservation of object identity, contours, and textural cues. To provide paired supervision, we construct a synthetic data engine that renders clean views of 3D assets and synthesises composite degradations. On the synthetic benchmark, the purifier improves image fidelity and downstream 3D geometry in only 2.3s on average, reducing TRELLIS.2 mesh distance by 61.5% relative to degraded inputs. VLM evaluation and human preferences on real photographs further support identity preservation and degradation correction. More demos and code are available at https://supra-3d.github.io/gate3dgen.
authors: Xiaolin Li, Zihao Huang, Fanpeng Meng, Chen Yang, Guanjun Wu, Kai Zhang, Jiemin Fang, Qi Tian
bullets: Targets failures caused by uneven illumination, blur, and occlusions in real-world images.
Uses a degradation-aware router to decide whether to bypass or purify each input.
A one-step, 3D-oriented purifier preserves object identity, contours, and texture through spatial losses.
Synthetic paired data comes from rendered clean views combined with composite degradations.
On a synthetic benchmark, it reduces TRELLIS.2 mesh distance by 61.5% versus degraded inputs, with 2.3-second average processing; real-image evaluations support identity preservation.
