papers.abstract: Monocular models recover 3D geometry from a single image in one pass, but most assume a pinhole camera and produce distorted geometry on the wide-angle imagery produced by fisheye and panoramic lenses. Camera-aware models remove this assumption by predicting a per-pixel ray field. However, they represent different camera geometries using a single fixed basis to capture both the overall camera projection and its finer variations. We argue that camera geometry can be viewed as having a hierarchy of complexity for representing rays. We present OmniRay, a feed-forward model whose Ray Module is composed of three components: a monotone radial base that captures radially symmetric structure, a spherical-harmonic residual for smooth deviations from it, and a free-form residual for remaining local variation. These components are composed as successive rotations on the sphere, allowing the representation to accommodate diverse camera geometries. Given a single image, OmniRay predicts a ray direction and an up-to-scale radial distance for every pixel, from which a 3D point cloud is recovered without needing camera information at inference time. Extensive experiments across different camera configurations demonstrate that OmniRay establishes a new state-of-the-art in camera-agnostic monocular 3D reconstruction.
authors: Namitha Guruprasad, Abhay Yadav, Cheng Peng, Rama Chellappa, Anand Bhattad
bullets: Addresses distortions caused by applying pinhole-camera assumptions to fisheye and panoramic imagery.
Uses a hierarchical Ray Module with a monotone radial base, spherical-harmonic residual, and free-form residual.
Represents these components as successive rotations on the sphere to model both global camera geometry and local variation.
Predicts per-pixel ray directions and up-to-scale radial distances for 3D point-cloud recovery.
Experiments across varied camera configurations report state-of-the-art camera-agnostic monocular 3D reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 2: OmniRay Overview. Given a single image, a DINOv2 ViT-L/14 encoder produces global and dense features that drive two branches. The Ray Module progressively builds a camera-agnostic ray field from a monotone radial base, a spherical-harmonic residual, and a free-form residual. The Distance Module predicts a positive radial distance for each pixel. Combining the final ray d and distance ρ yields the local pointmap P = ρd, recovering 3D geometry up to scale without camera intrinsics or a camera-type label.

Figure 5: Ablation. (a) Held-out catadioptric camera: predicted ray field and point cloud for UniK3D, OmniRay trained without random-lens augmentation, and the full model, against the ground truth. (b) Panoramic image: the radial base alone covers only part of the sphere (orange) and leaves the reconstruction torn, while the spherical-harmonic and free-form residuals complete the field (blue) and close the geometry.

Figure 6: In-the-wild reconstructions. Qualitative reconstructions on photographs collected from the internet, shown in order as a panorama, a fisheye image, and a pinhole image. Although these camera families are represented during training, the images come from different camera instances with unknown intrinsics and lens parameters. OmniRay requires no camera metadata at inference.

Figure 3: Why combine the radial construction with the residual corrections? (a) The radial representation gives the same incidence angle to pixels that lie at the same radius in the base coordinates. (b) In the centered 2:1 equirectangular projection, point A is closer to the center of the image than point B, yet has a higher incidence angle. A monotone radial function cannot accommodate such ordering under fixed coordinate transformation and orientation. (c) The spherical-harmonic and free-form residuals improve upon the base direction via iterative correction on the unit sphere.

Figure 4: Qualitative reconstructions on unseen datasets. We compare OmniRay with Depth Anything 3 and UniK3D on PanoCity and CO3Dv2 across five camera configurations. Small visualizations show viewing-ray fields; larger renderings show the corresponding point clouds, with ground truth in the rightmost column. OmniRay better preserves scene structure in the panoramic and catadioptric examples without camera intrinsics or camera-type input.

Figure 8: Random-lens augmentation. Images rendered from a single panorama under cameras drawn from the sampling distribution of Sec. 4.2. A camera is a viewing direction, a monotone radial profile and an imaged sensor region, so one family spans narrow perspective crops, wideangle and fisheye views, off-center and anisotropic sensors, and annular domains. The projection varies continuously from sample to sample, so no fixed map from image position to ray direction fits more than one of them. Draws falling close to either held-out geometry are rejected and never enter training.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward models accurately estimate camera motion and 3D geometry from short video windows. However, computational and memory costs prevent direct inference on sequences containing thousands of frames. Long videos must therefore be processed as overlapping chunks. This division produces independent local reconstructions with inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate estimates of shared cameras. Achieving global consistency requires propagating constraints from adjacent overlaps and distant revisits across the sequence. This requirement naturally motivates pose graph optimization. However, the choice of graph level creates a trade-off. Chunk-level graphs efficiently resolve scale drift and close large loops. Yet, their rigid transformations cannot correct internal errors or conflicting frame predictions. Conversely, frame-level optimization offers local flexibility, but scaling it globally is computationally expensive and can break metric scale. HiP3R resolves this trade-off using a hierarchical pose graph. HiP3R first optimizes a robust chunk-level $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ graph to establish the global layout and scale. It then holds this layout fixed and estimates one shared $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ camera per frame, turning overlapping window predictions into a single trajectory. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP3R in improving camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction. Our method applies to both chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning. The codes are available at https://kkakkkka.github.io/HiP3R.
authors: Zunnan Xu, Shangchen Zhou, Yihang Luo, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Long sequences processed in overlapping chunks yield inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate camera estimates.
A robust chunk-level Sim(3) graph establishes global layout, scale, and loop consistency.
A subsequent frame-level SE(3) optimization produces one shared camera trajectory while preserving the global layout.
Experiments on multiple benchmarks improve camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction.
The method works with chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/.
authors: Jinyu Zhang, Haitao Lin, Jiashu Hou, Xiangyang Xue, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses ambiguity from intra-class variation, symmetries, and partial observations without instance CAD models or reference views.
Lifts frozen visual foundation features onto partial point clouds, models local geometry with DGCNN, and captures object structure using a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer.
Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion provide dense geometric supervision and metric consistency.
Reports state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE, with pose-only inference at 28 FPS; additional evaluations cover geometry, robustness, and real-object transfer.
Scope includes segmented RGB-D inputs and task-specific training on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data.

papers.abstract: Point cloud transformers aim to capture detailed local geometry and relationships across a scene at a manageable computational cost. Two common approaches are window attention and global attention. They differ in how they enable scene-wide interaction, which refers to information exchange among tokens across a scene. Window attention reduces computational cost by restricting self-attention to groups of tokens called windows; in serialized designs, each window contains a fixed number of consecutive tokens from a spatially ordered sequence. Because each block only directly connects tokens within the same window, information exchange across windows relies on changes in window membership across blocks and hierarchical pooling. Global attention, in contrast, directly connects all tokens within a scene, but computing attention over all token pairs can be costly when the number of tokens is large. To balance computational cost and scene-wide interaction, we introduce MixPT, a point transformer that uses a mix of window and global attention blocks in an interleaved schedule, while retaining a single fixed serialization pattern for its window blocks. For scenes with a large number of tokens, MixPT applies global attention to spatially pooled tokens and returns residual updates to the original-resolution stream. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, MixPT achieves competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window and global attention baselines. We further demonstrate the feasibility of scaling the attention stage in depth by repeating the interleaved pattern of window and global attention blocks.
authors: Minkyun Seo, Hyungtae Lim, Jaesik Park
bullets: Window attention lowers cost but limits direct communication across windows; global attention enables scene-wide interaction but is expensive for large token sets.
MixPT interleaves window and global attention blocks while keeping one fixed serialization pattern for window processing.
For large scenes, global attention operates on spatially pooled tokens and sends residual updates back to the original-resolution stream.
Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window- and global-attention baselines.
The interleaved attention pattern can be repeated to scale the attention stage in depth.

papers.abstract: Local feature matching is typically formulated for image pairs, although structure-from-motion and visual localization commonly match one reference image against many retrieved or covisible neighbours. Applying a pairwise matcher independently to these centre-neighbour edges duplicates reference-side computation and prevents the matcher from exploiting complementary multi-view geometric evidence from the remaining observations. To address these limitations, we introduce MVLoMa, a sparse star-graph matcher that extends LoMa from image pairs to multiple views. MVLoMa first uses a frozen multi-view geometry model to jointly describe all images in a star, then injects the resulting cross-view geometric context into local descriptors. It then matches the centre image to all neighbours in a single forward pass through per-view self-attention and bidirectional centre-neighbour cross-attention. For supervision, we derive positive correspondences only from depth-valid, mutually visible dense warps and explicitly penalize high-confidence matches that violate epipolar geometry. On 25-view star graphs from HyperSim, ScanNet++, Mip-NeRF 360, and Tanks and Temples, MVLoMa obtains the best macro-average relative-pose AUC among the compared methods at all three thresholds (58.65/85.41/90.99). Its matcher is 2.20 times faster than sequential evaluation of the 24 centre-neighbour edges. The same design supports four tested frozen geometry encoders -- DA3, $\pi^3$, VGGT, and VGGT-$\Omega$ -- with DA3-Giant performing best on all reported encoder-ablation metrics. Controlled ablations further isolate the effects of geometry-aware descriptors, visibility filtering, geometric negative supervision, and joint multi-view inference.
authors: Xinyang Lu, Shengzhe Wei, Sheng Tang, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
bullets: Addresses redundant reference-image computation and missed cross-view geometric evidence in pairwise matching.
Uses a frozen multi-view geometry model, geometry-aware local descriptors, and joint centre-to-neighbour attention.
Trains with depth-valid, mutually visible correspondences and penalties for epipolar-violating high-confidence matches.
On 25-view star graphs across four datasets, it achieves the best reported macro-average relative-pose AUC at all thresholds.
Runs 2.20× faster than sequentially matching the 24 centre-neighbour pairs; the design works with four frozen geometry encoders.

A trainable convolutional refiner fuses the two streams into descriptors sampled at 4096 keypoints per image. The multi-view star-graph matcher then jointly processes the centre and all neighbours and outputs sparse centre–neighbour correspondences for every edge. papers.abstract: 4D scene reconstruction requires robust handling of dynamic objects, yet existing streaming methods commonly assume static scenes, leading to pose drift and ghosting artifacts over long sequences. We introduce Stream4D, a training-free, motion-decoupled streaming reconstruction framework that can be directly integrated into causal Transformer backbones (e.g., StreamVGGT, Stream3R). Our key observation is that causal attention implicitly encodes rich temporal motion cues within the KV cache. We adaptively aggregate these cues from multiple attention layers and across temporal windows, and fuse them with depth priors to handle challenging cases such as occlusions and textureless regions, producing precise dynamic masks that decouple static and dynamic regions. We then apply a soft key masking scheme that leverages these dynamic masks to suppress interference from dynamic regions in causal attention, thereby improving camera pose estimation accuracy. Stream4D inherits the efficiency of causal attention and remains compatible with existing streaming architectures. On diverse dynamic-scene benchmarks, Stream4D significantly improves camera pose estimation and static-scene reconstruction quality, yields reliable dynamic masks, and effectively mitigates long-sequence ghosting.
authors: Wei Zhang, Ying Feng, Mengtong Wu, Shiqiang Gong, Huaqi Zhang, Qi Zhang
bullets: Addresses failures of static-scene assumptions in streaming reconstruction, especially long-sequence pose drift and ghosting.
Aggregates temporal motion cues from multiple causal-attention layers and windows, fusing them with depth priors to identify dynamic regions.
Uses soft key masking to suppress dynamic-region interference during camera pose estimation.
Integrates directly with causal Transformer backbones such as StreamVGGT and Stream3R while preserving streaming efficiency.
Improves camera poses, static-scene reconstruction, dynamic masks, and long-sequence ghosting on diverse dynamic-scene benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Streaming dynamic segmentation architecture. Left: standard causal streaming reconstruction with a KV Cache, where each frame attends only to past tokens. Right: our Stream4D augments the causal pipeline with motion-decoupled masking. Queries load cached keys/values to compute attention scores, aggregate temporal saliency across frames, and produce dynamic masks. These masks are then applied to modify the cached keys, effectively suppressing interference from dynamic regions during historical aggregation.

Figure 2: Streaming reconstruction overview. Each incoming frame is encoded into tokens and decoded with temporal causal attention that attends only to past frames via a KV Cache. The cache is incrementally updated with (K𝑡 ,V𝑡 ), enabling efficient online inference.

Figure 6: Ghosting suppression in streaming 4D reconstruction. Naïve causal streaming methods integrate geometry from all past frames, causing moving objects to be repeatedly fused into the scene and leaving stacked replicas along their trajectories (ghosting artifacts), which grow with sequence length and can eventually corrupt nearby static surfaces. In contrast, Stream4D derives training-free dynamic masks from causal attention cues and applies soft key masking to suppress dynamic regions in the KV cache, so that dynamic objects appear only in the current frame while the background remains clean and sharp even in long sequences.

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison of estimated camera trajectories on three DyCheck sequences (creeper, handwavy,mochi-highfive). We plot the predicted trajectory (solid blue) against the ground truth (dashed gray) in the 𝑥-𝑧 plane. Left: Stream3R exhibits noticeable drift and erratic deviations, particularly in sequences with large dynamic motion (handwavy, mochi-high-five), where moving objects corrupt the pose estimation. Right: our Stream4D produces trajectories that more closely follow the ground truth, demonstrating that motion-decoupled masking effectively mitigates the interference of dynamic regions on camera pose estimation.

Figure 5: Qualitative results on DAVIS dataset. Each panel shows the input frame, the Easi3R mask, and our Stream4D mask. Easi3R exhibits temporal jitter and boundary breaks under occlusions and non-rigid motions. Our streaming multi-level temporal aggregation with consistency constraints produces temporally smooth and spatially complete masks across slow motions (camel, goat, etc.) and fast motions (skateboarder, motorcyclist), demonstrating robust segmentation under causal KV-Cache attention.

Figure 8: Inference time comparison across different sequence lengths. While Easi3R exhibits exponential time growth and suffers from Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors between 100 and 200 frames, Stream4D maintains linear scalability, performing comparably to the efficient StreamVGGT baseline.

Figure 3: Temporal saliency aggregation and fusion visualization. We compare attention statistics across frames and layers: per-token mean and variance heatmaps revealing low-mean/high-variance patterns on dynamic objects; cross-frame attention maps highlighting temporal inconsistency; multi-scale attention fusion; and final fused saliency and binary masks.

papers.title: Stream4D: Streaming 4D Reconstruction with Training-free Motion Decoupling via Causal KV-Cache Attention
papers.tldr: Stream4D enables training-free streaming 4D reconstruction by extracting motion cues from causal KV caches to separate dynamic regions and reduce pose drift and ghosting.

papers.abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation is a fundamental component of 3D perception for autonomous driving and robotics. Projection-based methods map 3D point clouds into 2D representations for feature extraction using 2D networks. However, aggregating multiple points during projection can obscure geometric differences within each frustum, while local feature extraction limits the modeling of spatial relationships across scanning regions. Moreover, proximity in the projected representation does not necessarily imply proximity in 3D space, and interactions between point and projected features may mix features from different ranges, reducing semantic discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose the Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network (RaSFNet), which incorporates point cloud geometry and LiDAR scanning characteristics into projection-based semantic segmentation. Specifically, the Ray-Aligned Geometric Distribution Encoding (RAGDE) module characterizes point distributions within each frustum using a ray-aligned coordinate system. To model spatial context, a Scan-Topology-Aware Mamba (STAM) block organizes frustum features according to the LiDAR azimuth sampling pattern and captures long-range dependencies across scanning regions. In addition, a Range-Constrained Point-Frustum Fusion (RCPFF) mechanism uses shared range information to guide feature exchange between point and frustum representations while maintaining spatial correspondence. RaSFNet achieves mIoU scores of 70.2% and 77.7% on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes validation sets, respectively, indicating competitive segmentation performance compared with the evaluated methods.
bullets: Addresses geometric information loss within projected frustums and limited spatial-context modeling in 2D representations.
RAGDE encodes point distributions using a ray-aligned coordinate system.
STAM captures long-range dependencies according to LiDAR azimuth scanning patterns.
RCPFF uses shared range information to preserve correspondence during point–frustum feature fusion.
Reports 70.2% mIoU on SemanticKITTI and 77.7% on nuScenes validation sets, with competitive performance against evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.
authors: Wenhao Zheng, Xianggen Liu, Li Yue, Jiancheng Shi, Jiancheng Lv
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly modeling B-rep topology and precise spatial geometry.
Introduces EAG, a graph-based CAD representation designed for generative modeling.
Uses hybrid graph diffusion for discrete connectivity and continuous node attributes.
Renders node attributes as point sets and encodes them with an SE(3)-equivariant backbone for geometry-aware denoising.
Evaluations on the newly constructed EAGBench show strong geometric fidelity and distributional alignment, including models with over 50 faces.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the GraphCAD framework. Top: The generative pipeline. Themodel synthesizes CADmodels by iteratively denoising the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), our proposed topological representation of B-rep geometry. Bottom: The GeometryAware Denoising module. Unlike standard graph-based methods that treat node attributes as abstract vectors, our approach explicitly “renders” these attributes into spatial point sets through “Curve Sampling”. The sampled point sets are then processed by an SE(3)-equivariant Vector Neuron backbone to extract rotation-robust geometric embeddings.

papers.abstract: Neurosurgical navigation commonly presents magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as 2D slices, making it difficult to relate the anatomy in those slices to the cortical surface observed through the surgical microscope. We seek a common 3D visualization that combines a photorealistic reconstruction of the exposed cortex during tumor surgery with whole-brain MRI context and diffusion tractography pathways. This requires the reconstructed cortex to form a clear boundary around the brain anatomy rather than a diffuse volume that obscures internal structures. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reproduce observed views but, under limited surgical view coverage, may distribute opacity through a thick and geometrically ambiguous band. We introduce height-field 2D Gaussian Splatting (H-2DGS), a three-stage pipeline that concentrates a robust 3DGS reconstruction, fuses its depth into a shared truncated signed distance field (TSDF) surface, and represents that surface with curved, surface-oriented Gaussian primitives. Separate height, color, and opacity bases provide local geometry and appearance, while a neighbor-transition objective coordinates overlapping patches. The explicit surface further supports postoperative alignment: MRI-derived depth deforms the reconstruction, and tracked-color supervision with alternating optimization preserves its appearance. Across five real neurosurgical cases, H-2DGS gives low multi-view depth inconsistency, a compact 7.97MB representation, and interactive rendering at 29--42ms per frame. The resulting sharp, deformable surface integrates clearly with tractography and MRI anatomy, including a postoperative resection cavity.
authors: Zhang Zichuan, Bart Brouwers, Rembrandt Bakker, Maud Landers, Geert-Jan Rutten, Maxime Chamberland
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting, which can produce diffuse volumetric reconstructions of exposed cortex.
Uses a three-stage pipeline: robust 3DGS initialization, TSDF-based surface fusion, and curved surface-oriented Gaussian primitives.
Separates height, color, and opacity representations and uses neighbor-transition optimization to improve continuity across patches.
Supports postoperative deformation through MRI-derived depth and preserves appearance with tracked-color supervision.
Validated on five real neurosurgical cases, achieving low multi-view depth inconsistency, a 7.97MB representation, and interactive 29–42 ms rendering.

papers.abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. Across seven lifting methods and four datasets, the resulting query-time calibration consistently improves mean intersection over union in both multiclass and single-query segmentation. These gains require no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting, demonstrating the value of scene-conditioned comparison for making better use of existing lifted representations.
authors: Dominik Engel, Yousef Rajeh, Leon Sick, Ivan Viola
bullets: Addresses scene-specific directional concentration that makes raw CLIP cosine similarity unreliable for 3D segmentation.
Partially removes a shared scene direction and whitens text prototypes using a fixed vocabulary of generic terms.
Uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin for single-query prediction.
Improves class-relative feature separation across evaluated scenes and consistently raises mean IoU across seven lifting methods and four datasets.
Operates entirely at query time, requiring no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method Overview. Starting from a Gaussian scene with lifted CLIP features, we calibrate the scene and text query features using centering and text-whitening, based on a reference vocabulary. Instead of plain query-scene similarities, we further calibrate the similarity scores using soft clustering for multi-class and CSLS with a relevance margin for single-query. Our calibration results in increased class-relative separation, as visualized in the similarity maps on the bottom. Our final predictions achieve substantial improvements in segmentation mIoU for both multi-class (visualized in bar chart) and single class.

Figure 3: Score calibration. Starting from the Middle: First we use the reference vocabulary to determine the whitening statistics. Left: For multi-class queries (N > 1) we center and whiten all text queries and perform soft clustering of the primitive features, using fixed text-derived probabilities to guide assignments and weighted top-eight visual primitives to initialize the centers. After clustering, argmax decides the class of each primitive. Right: For a single-class query (N = 1) we center and whiten the query and the reference vocabulary, apply reduced CSLS and compute the margin between each primitive’s corrected query score and its highest corrected reference-bank score. To make a prediction we threshold this relevance margin using τ .
Figure 2: Scene centering maps blue input vectors z to teal calibrated vectors u by subtracting the orange mean direction µ and renormalizing.

papers.abstract: Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits are essential in applications such as portrait photography, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR). Despite recent progress, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains challenging due to the demands for photorealistic rendering, real-time performance, and generalization to unseen subjects. Existing works either rely on supervision from limited and expensive light stage captured data or produce suboptimal results. Moreover, many works are based on generative NeRFs, which suffer from poor 3D consistency and low real-time performance. We resort to recent progress on generative 3D Gaussians and design a lighting model based on a unified neural radiance transfer representation, which responds linearly to incident light. Using only in-the-wild images, our method achieves state-of-the-art relighting results and a significantly faster rendering speed ($\times12$) compared to previous 3D-aware portrait relighting research. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/GSHeadRelight/.
authors: Henglei Lv, Bailin Deng, Jianzhu Guo, Xiaoqiang Liu, Pengfei Wan, Di Zhang, Lin Gao
bullets: Targets 3D-aware portrait relighting and novel-view synthesis for VR, AR, and photography.
Uses generative 3D Gaussians instead of generative NeRFs to improve 3D consistency and real-time performance.
Introduces a unified neural radiance transfer lighting model with a linear response to incident light.
Requires only in-the-wild images, avoiding reliance on limited and expensive light-stage supervision.
Reports state-of-the-art relighting and 12× faster rendering than prior 3D-aware portrait-relighting methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. We incorporate a lighting model based on unified radiance transfer into a generative 3D Gaussian framework. The generator G takes in Gaussian noise and camera pose as condition and generates for each Gaussian an embedding x, which is then linearly transformed into the albedo 𝜌 and geometry attributes {g} including position, scale, rotation and opacity. A light-weight decoder conditioned on view direction transforms x into radiance transfer coefficients t, which are used to compute the unified light transport with the light condition. Color is obtained by multiplying the light transport component with the albedo. The image is then rendered by standard splatting and sent to the discriminator D, which takes both camera pose and light condition as input. Mapping modules are omitted for simplicity. Gaussian noise and camera pose are represented as icons, and light condition as a diffuse sphere.

papers.abstract: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.
authors: NVIDIA, :, S\'ergio Agostinho, Maximilian Apodaca, Emmanuel Attia, Guillem Braso, George Dong, Ilya Fedorov, Michele Fenzi, Gang Huang, Jiahui Huang, Shengyu Huang, Bingxin Ke, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Kuan-Ting Lee, Mingxuan Liu, Tian Liu, Tim Meinhardt, Aljo\v{s}a O\v{s}ep, Naveen Kumar Rai, Kefei Ren, Cristiano Saltori, Keqiang Wu, Ning Xu, Fei Xue, Jin-Bey Yu, Lei Zhang, Qunjie Zhou
bullets: Addresses geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction in one feed-forward model.
Uses a shared backbone with factorized spatiotemporal attention to fuse camera and temporal observations efficiently.
Refines camera trajectories with pose-graph optimization and assembles object tracks across video windows.
Introduces PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips.
Reports leading compared performance on Waymo depth, nuScenes detection, and OpenOccupancy occupancy; supports lidarless scene reconstruction for simulation.

papers.abstract: Generating an articulated object from a single image requires recovering both its appearance and the mechanism governing its parts. A compact encoding of joint attributes does not by itself ensure that reconstruction preserves the resulting motion. We present MoRE, Motion-Regularized Encoding for articulated 3D generation. MoRE represents coordinate-aligned joint lines with axis classification and two axis-orthogonal Pl\"ucker moment coefficients, removing the arbitrary choice of an origin along the axis. During representation learning, decoded joint hypotheses are used to move corresponding three-dimensional anchors, and their motions are compared with those of annotated joints. A differentiable expectation over joint types and axis directions couples attribute reconstruction to the motion it induces. An image-conditioned flow learns the resulting functional latents, while a multi-state-adapted Gaussian model supplies appearance. At inference, recovered part assignments and joints articulate a single set of rest-pose Gaussians without regenerating the object for each state. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility and ACD show stronger part-box agreement, articulated-state geometry and visual similarity than the compared baselines, while joint prediction reduces axis, origin and range errors relative to ArtiLatent. Controlled ablations support the joint-line encoding and show that motion supervision reduces anchor-motion error. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be released in the future.
bullets: Represents joints using axis classification and axis-orthogonal Plücker moment coefficients, avoiding arbitrary axis-origin choices.
Uses decoded joint hypotheses to move 3D anchors and matches those motions to annotated joints through differentiable motion supervision.
Combines image-conditioned functional latents with a multi-state Gaussian appearance model.
Articulates one set of rest-pose Gaussians across states instead of regenerating the object for each pose.

On PartNet-Mobility and ACD, improves part-box, articulated-state geometry, visual similarity, and joint-prediction errors over compared baselines; ablations support the encoding and motion supervision.

papers.abstract: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.
authors: Bangpu Chen, Yaxuan Li, Shirui Peng, Xiangtian Si, Liuxin Chu, Xitong Cao, Hongbo Jin, Jiayu Ding
bullets: Addresses temporal, multi-target, reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor referring expressions in dynamic 4D scenes.
Introduces R4D-Bench-QA with structured query annotations for evaluating referring segmentation.
ReferGaussian converts dynamic Gaussians into persistent language-addressable entities stored in an EntityBank.
MLLMs decompose queries into object phrases and referring constraints, enabling constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization.
Shows improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol.

papers.abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.69 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.
authors: Chao-Yeh Chen, Tiffany Chen, Lin Duan, Tianyi Hu, Yu-Hsiang Huang, Umar Iqbal, Jiefeng Li, Edy Lim, Yanchen Liu, Yihan Pang, Hang Qiu, Jun Saito, Shao Su, Qingsi Wang, Xiufeng Xie
bullets: Addresses accurate 3D hand reconstruction from challenging egocentric video.
Trains on a 14-million-image corpus combining synthetic, in-the-wild, and multi-camera motion-capture data.
Uses SOMA-Hand with a transformer encoder, camera cues, and an auxiliary 2D branch for geometric and image consistency.
Performs strongly on zero-shot HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O evaluations, with approximately 9.69 ms inference latency.
Model and source code are released under the OpenMDW license with free commercial use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: EgoHandmodel architecture. A DINOv3 encoder supports two branches. The 3D hand reconstruction branch uses a CLIFF-conditioned hand query to cross-attend to image features augmented with ray positional encoding, predicting SOMA-Hand pose, shape, and wrist translation. The 2D joint prediction branch uses separate learned joint queries to cross-attend to image features. Its predicted 2D joints, together with the SOMA-Hand 3D joints and camera intrinsics, refine lateral wrist translation while preserving the predicted depth, yielding hand geometry in camera coordinates.

Figure 3: Inference pipeline from egocentric video to world-coordinate hand motion, comprising hand detection, crop preparation, batched EgoHand inference, and transformation of predictions to world coordinates. Fisheye regions are resampled into virtual pinhole views; pinhole images use standard crops. Predictions are assembled in frame order, their hand parameters are smoothed in an adaptive window. A synchronized external camera trajectory supplies the camera-to-world rotations and translations that place the hands in a shared world frame. Benchmark annotations may supply hand boxes in place of detections. The EgoHand network is detailed in Section 3. Illustrations are schematic.

papers.abstract: A patient who has lost part of the skull vault needs an implant that fits the defect exactly, and such implants are still drawn by hand in CAD by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive. The task can be considered as a shape completion problem, so pretrained completion models, and now the first shape completion foundation models, look like a way to remove that manual step. We audited three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, two of them foundation models, applied zero-shot to 239 cranial defects, some carved from public skull datasets and some real post-craniectomy cases. Each output was compared with simply returning the patient's own remaining bone, and tested for whether the predicted material could be placed without intersecting the bone that is still there. On the 210 carved defects none of the three improved on doing nothing, and on the 29 real cases only one did so beyond chance. Yet not one output, from any model in any configuration, was implantable: none managed both to stay clear of the bone the patient still has and to place more material than doing nothing, where a task-specific volumetric model, trained for this task and selected on these cases, was implantable on all but one. The output that most convincingly resembles a skull is no more placeable than the rest, and at these point densities implant thickness cannot be read off the emitted points at all, which is a property of the output representation rather than of any one model. On this evidence the shape completion foundation models we could obtain cannot be trusted and, used as released, are not usable in clinical practice. Substantial research towards trustworthy foundation models for shape completion is still needed.
authors: Marek Wodzinski, Kamil Kwarciak, Daria Hemmerling, Mateusz Daniol
bullets: Evaluated three pretrained models on 239 cranial defects, including carved synthetic defects and real post-craniectomy cases.
None outperformed simply using the patient’s remaining bone on 210 carved defects; only one improved beyond chance on 29 real cases.
No model output was implantable because predictions failed to both avoid existing bone and add useful material.
A task-specific volumetric model was implantable on all but one case, indicating the limitation is not inherent to the task.
At the tested point densities, emitted points cannot reliably determine implant thickness, highlighting a representation-level limitation.

That 3 mm is a design target rather than a law, and the clinical data break it: 11 of the 29 real MUG500+ implants (38 %) are thinner than 3 mm, the 29 having median 3.05 mm and mean 3.30 ± 1.41 mm. Every synthetic result is significant at p < 10−24 under both. MUG500+ ships a manufactured implant, so its columns measure whether material went where the device goes.

papers.title: Plausible but Unimplantable: A Trustworthiness Audit of Shape Completion Foundation Models for Cranial Defect Reconstruction
papers.tldr: An audit finds that publicly released shape-completion foundation models produce plausible-looking but clinically unimplantable cranial reconstructions in zero-shot use.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
authors: Chenxu Zhou, Zhiyuan Yu, Yudong Jin, Yinji Shentu, Yu Zhang, Jiaming Sun, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Targets costly dense multi-view capture requirements and the limited resolution and 4D consistency of prior generative methods.
Builds auxiliary data from capture videos and combines latent representations with layout-aware positional embeddings.
Adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to model relationships across viewpoints and time.
Uses latent frequency-domain supervision to reduce the gap between generated videos and real captures.
Experiments on DNA-Rendering and the self-captured RealVV dataset show improved visual fidelity and 4D consistency over existing methods.

These auxiliary videos are fed into a high-resolution video diffusion model to produce enhanced videos, which are then used together with the input captures to optimize the 4DGS representation for volumetric video reconstruction. The detailed model architecture is illustrated in Fig. 3.

papers.abstract: Language 3D Gaussian Splatting enables open-vocabulary scene understanding by associating Gaussian primitives with language features. These semantic attributes increase model storage, while most existing 3DGS compression methods are designed mainly to preserve RGB rendering quality. One straightforward approach is to apply sparsification and quantization sequentially. However, pruning based only on rendering quality can remove Gaussians that have small RGB contributions but are important for semantic prediction. Once removed, their semantic information cannot be recovered by later quantization. We propose ClunoGS, a compact framework for Language 3DGS that combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in a unified constrained objective. Semantic supervision is used during sparsification, and the objective jointly considers rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness. We optimize the unified objective with alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates. We evaluate ClunoGS on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation using the LERF and ScanNet-10 benchmarks. Under aggressive compression, our unified, semantics-aware formulation substantially alleviates the degradation of semantic representations caused by sequential compression and semantics-agnostic Gaussian sparsification. Ablations further show that jointly coordinating sparsification and quantization better preserves semantic accuracy than applying them independently.
authors: Jian Xu, Yi Li, Ying Huang, Siyi Wu, Bingzhe Li, Yuede Ji, Miao Yin
bullets: Addresses the loss of important semantic information when RGB-focused Gaussian pruning is followed by quantization.
Combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in one constrained objective.
Balances rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness using alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates.
Evaluated on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation with LERF and ScanNet-10.
Under aggressive compression, better preserves semantic representations than sequential or independently applied compression.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$\Omega$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.
authors: Naru Suzuki, Satoshi Ikehata, Takehiko Ohkawa, Yoichi Sato, Shuhei Kurita
bullets: Addresses error propagation, monocular scale ambiguity, and ambiguous motion from occlusion or out-of-view hands.
Uses a single-stage model that jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system.
Combines VGGT-Ω scene geometry, metric-space supervision, and hand-specific articulation features.
Flow-matching generation outperforms direct regression in accuracy and temporal smoothness with two sampling steps.
Improves world-space accuracy on HOT3D and ARCTIC, estimates camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, and generalizes zero-shot across three datasets.

papers.abstract: Many robotic construction applications, such as progress tracking, require registering a sensor trajectory to a prior 2D floor plan. Visual capture is attractive for its low cost and availability, but aligning a visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) map to a floor plan is difficult; VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, the sparse point cloud is cross-modal to the symbolic floor plan, sites are only partially built during capture, and construction sites are visually repetitive, degrading map quality while removing distinctive features. Existing methods address at most two of these challenges. We thus introduce Reading the Room(RR), a global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous, sparse, semantic VSLAM maps to partially built floor plans. Our key idea is to define a single robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function that governs all stages of the pipeline. We develop two global initialization schemes, leveraging a single inaccurate user-provided correspondence if provided, or estimating the initialization globally using a cross-modal matching network. Both schemes are designed to find initial candidates with respect to the energy function, which is then directly optimized for local refinement. We evaluate RR on 33 sequences across three active construction sites against classical and learning-based baselines, achieving a 4.5x improvement in mean absolute trajectory error over the strongest baseline in the general unconstrained setting, which increases to 7.6x when an anchor is provided.
authors: Bjorn Stragier, Emilia Szyma\'nska, J. Micah Prendergast, Lukas Rosenberger Schmid
bullets: Addresses unknown scale, cross-modal map alignment, incomplete construction, and repetitive visual environments.
Uses a robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function throughout the pipeline.
Initializes registration either from one inaccurate user correspondence or via a cross-modal matching network.
Globally finds candidate alignments, then directly optimizes the energy for local refinement.
Evaluated on 33 sequences across three construction sites, improving mean absolute trajectory error by 4.5× over the strongest baseline generally and 7.6× with an anchor.

IV-A). A single energy function (Sec. IV-B) guides the remaining steps. If a known correspondence is provided it is leveraged to constrain global initialization, otherwise global initialization is performed using dense cross-modal feature matching (Sec. IV-C). Finally, the estimate is refined (Sec. IV-D) to minimize the energy function locally.

Fig. 3: Qualitative registration results for one representative sequence per site, increasing in difficulty from top to bottom. VSLAM BEV maps are rotated and scaled for visualization; this does not reflect their initial condition for registration. On Site A, all three methods recover visually similar trajectories, consistent with the small floor area, high coverage, and unique structural layout of the site. In Site B, the RoMa+MatchAnything collapses the entire map into several rooms. This yields a low cost as the outer walls align with the room walls, highlighting the challenge of scale-ambiguous registration. In Site C, both RoMa+MatchAnything and our approach fail due to the symmetry of the scene and align the sparse observations flipped. If a single noisy user-provided anchor is available, our method can leverage this to recover the right symmetry and achieve a good solution in spite of orientation and scale ambiguity.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward visual geometry models, exemplified by VGGT, have demonstrated strong multi-view reconstruction capabilities through dense global attention. However, the resulting all-to-all cross-view computation scales quadratically with the number of input views, making long-sequence inference particularly expensive due to substantial frame-level redundancy among highly overlapping observations. We uncover a topology-first, geometry-later evolution in VGGT camera tokens: shallow-layer tokens reliably capture local view neighborhoods, whereas deeper-layer tokens progressively encode globally organized inter-view geometry. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BlazeVGGT, a training-free framework for structure-aware frame-level key--value sparsification. At each global-attention block, BlazeVGGT constructs a view-level similarity kernel from camera-token relations and employs greedy determinantal point process inference to select a compact set of mutually complementary views. The selected views constitute the key--value context, while all input frames are retained as queries. This asymmetric attention design preserves dense per-frame predictions while eliminating redundant cross-view computation, allowing our method to be directly integrated into pretrained VGGT as a plug-and-play module without parameter updates. Its advantages become increasingly pronounced with sequence length: at 2,000 frames, BlazeVGGT achieves approximately 13$\times$ faster inference than VGGT while reducing the Chamfer Distance from 0.41 to 0.32. Extensive experiments demonstrate a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off in point-cloud reconstruction and camera-pose estimation, compatibility with existing VGGT accelerators such as FastVGGT and LiteVGGT, and transferability to VGGT-based models including StreamVGGT and PAGE-4D. Codes are publicly available at https://github.com/MagiciannnY/BlazeVGGT.git.
authors: Shujun Yao, Junhui Lin, Congying Han, Tiande Guo, Ziwen Liu, Bonan Li
bullets: VGGT’s all-to-all attention becomes costly for long, highly overlapping image sequences.

At 2,000 frames, inference is approximately 13× faster and Chamfer Distance decreases from 0.41 to 0.32.
The plug-and-play approach transfers to VGGT variants and supports point-cloud reconstruction and camera-pose estimation.

papers.abstract: Real-world physical sensing exhibits complex, heterogeneous noise patterns that deviate significantly from idealized simulation, posing a fundamental bottleneck for sim-to-real transfer. Existing sensor modelings typically treat depth noise as a monolithic black-box process, overlooking the distinct physical mechanisms that govern different error modalities. In this work, we introduce a physics-grounded paradigm that disentangles monolithic noise into two complementary modalities: \textbf{sensing invalidation} and \textbf{measurement inaccuracy}, enabling a tailored treatment of noise sources based on their physical origins. Building on this insight, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a tripartite framework that distills 3D Visual Foundation Model features as rich spatial-semantic priors for physics-based reasoning. To address the inherent sparsity and class imbalance of invalidation regions, we develop Hierarchical Positive-Prioritized Supervision, integrating multi-scale positive-weighted objectives with a positive-preserving dynamic hard mining strategy to enforce precise artifact delineation. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves state-of-the-art fidelity in noisy depth synthesis. Furthermore, downstream robotic experiments show that PRISM facilitates a \textbf{92.1\%} average success rate in the real world, marking a significant improvement over monolithic baselines. Our project page is available at: \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\href{https://shawnleung-sii.github.io/prism-icml2026/}{https://shawnleung-sii.github.io/prism-icml2026/}.}
authors: Xiujian Liang, Jiacheng Liu, Mingyang Sun, Qichen He, Anda Cheng, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
bullets: Addresses the sim-to-real gap caused by heterogeneous real-world depth-sensing noise.
Separates noise into sensing invalidation and measurement inaccuracy for tailored modeling.
Uses 3D Visual Foundation Model features as spatial-semantic priors in a tripartite framework.
Introduces Hierarchical Positive-Prioritized Supervision to detect sparse invalid regions and preserve hard positives.
Reports state-of-the-art noisy-depth fidelity and a 92.1% average real-world robotic success rate.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction estimates voxel-wise occupancy and semantic labels throughout a scene. Our experiments reveal that conventional sparse transposed-convolution upsampling yields poorly differentiated voxel responses and that successive decoder layers discard previously correct semantic predictions. To address these issues, we present Feature-Diverse Upsampling and Memory-Aware Decoding for 3D Occupancy Prediction (FM-Occ), comprising two components. First, 3D Sparse Subvoxel Shuffle (3S) mitigates feature homogenization by constructing candidate child features in the channel dimension, jointly transforming and normalizing them, and then rearranging them onto a finer sparse grid with explicit feature-coordinate correspondence. Second, Entropy-Regulated Layer-wise Memory (ER-LM) retains semantic information across decoder layers by maintaining a layer-wise memory for each query through gated recurrent updates and using prediction entropy to regulate the historical information propagated to the next layer. During training, a class-weighted entropy loss Lcwe provides label-guided regularization for matched semantic queries. On SemanticKITTI, 3S increases the spatial coefficient of variation of normalized voxel-wise root-mean-square (RMS) responses from 0.41% to 4.03%, while ER-LM reduces semantic degradation and improves error correction across decoder layers. The combined FM-Occ improves mIoU from 12.16% to 12.73% with negligible memory overhead. ER-LM further improves mIoU in the BEV-based DISC framework from 16.78% to 17.17%, supporting its applicability across 3D voxel-based and BEV-based architectures.
authors: Yujia Zhai (Great Bay University), Guoming Huang (Great Bay University), Zhuanghuai Wang (Great Bay University), Bangquan Xie (Great Bay University)
bullets: Addresses feature homogenization from sparse transposed-convolution upsampling and semantic degradation during decoding.

Introduces Entropy-Regulated Layer-wise Memory (ER-LM), using gated memory and prediction entropy to retain and regulate historical semantic information.
On SemanticKITTI, FM-Occ raises mIoU from 12.16% to 12.73% with negligible memory overhead; ER-LM also improves DISC from 16.78% to 17.17%.
Scope: evaluated across voxel-based and BEV-based 3D occupancy architectures.

papers.abstract: Robots deployed in human-centered environments need maps that support both geometric navigation and open-vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set. A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on manually annotated segmentation masks or closed-set semantic categories. Existing geometry-driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive by-product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on supervised semantic segmentation. We present AOV-GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration using frozen foundation models. During coarse exploration, AOV-GS re-ranks geometrically promising candidate views according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration toward semantically informative regions. Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language-aligned embeddings throughout mapping, while a lightweight scene-specific language field is fitted offline directly to the collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views. In a controlled comparison using the same SAM-CLIP perception stack, AOV-GS improves average language-field mIoU over geometry-only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica (34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes). With CorrCLIP, AOV-GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched Geometry-based + CorrCLIP baseline. Novel-view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry-only baseline on both datasets while depth L1 improves on Replica. Code is available at https://github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV-GS.

papers.abstract: As-built BIM reconstruction from point clouds demands semantic, volumetric, parametric, and editable building components, beyond 2D layouts or planar abstractions. Yet existing scan-to-BIM pipelines often rely on handcrafted rules, heuristic optimization, or manual correction, while learning-based methods fall short of recovering wall thickness, opening geometry, and component-level BIM structure. We introduce CRAB, a BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction framework that encodes walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with IFC-compatible semantics and parameters. CRAB bridges point clouds and editable BIM by combining ProposalNet, which predicts coarse component cuboids, with AssemblyNet, a relation-aware Flow Matching model that refines geometry, predicts structural relationships, and enables automatic structural correction and human-guided editing. To address limited cuboid-level supervision, we extend Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and construct cuboid-based procedural scenes. Experiments show CRAB surpasses floor plan and plane-based alternatives in component completeness, geometric accuracy, and generalization. For interior wall thickness estimation, CRAB achieves a mean error of 2.80 cm, with 79.50% of matched walls within 3 cm. The project page is available at https://vcc.tech/research/2026/CRAB.
authors: Haoran Xiong, Jing Wang, Shanshan Pan, Zihao Yan, Minglun Gong, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets scan-to-BIM limitations in recovering wall thickness, openings, and structured building components.
Represents walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with semantic and parametric information.
Combines ProposalNet for coarse cuboid prediction with AssemblyNet for relation-aware refinement, structural correction, and human-guided editing.
Extends Structured3D with cuboid annotations and creates procedural cuboid-based scenes to support training.
Reports a 2.80 cm mean error for interior wall thickness, with 79.50% of matched walls estimated within 3 cm.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of CRAB. Given a raw indoor point cloud, ProposalNet encodes the scan and autoregressively predicts an initial set of semantic cuboids for walls, doors, and windows. AssemblyNet represents each proposal with centerline-based cuboid tokens augmented by semantic, relation, and edit-control flags, and refines them through intra-cuboid, inter-cuboid, and cuboid–point attention. A velocity head performs relation-aware flow-matching refinement of cuboid geometry, while a relation head infers structural dependencies such as wall adjacency and door/window affiliation. The refined cuboids and relations are finally instantiated as editable BIM-ready components, converting unstructured scans into component-level architectural models.

Fig. 7. Qualitative comparison on Structured3D. Each column shows one scene, with rows showing the input point cloud, floor plan baselines, plane baselines, our cuboid reconstruction, and the ground truth. Compared with RoomFormer, CAGE, SceneScript, and SpatialLM, CRAB recovers more coherent wall structures and more accurate door and window geometry in ambiguous, non-Manhattan, and incomplete regions.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison on real-world scanned scenes. Each row shows one scene: input point cloud (left), SpatialLM (middle), and ours (right). CRAB better preserves wall continuity and opening geometry under practical noise and clutter.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison with a plane-based representation. Zoomed views compare the same local structures in GT, CRAB, and SpatialLM. CRAB’s volumetric cuboids better preserve wall thickness, component extent, and opening-wall consistency than the plane-based representation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.
authors: Junjie Wang, Zhihao Yuan, Yunhan Tang, Sheng Xu, Jiaqi Mao, Xiaoyu Ye, Yueru Luo, Xu Yan, Chun-Mei Feng, Zhen Li
bullets: Targets spatial hallucinations caused by occlusion, perspective changes, and sparse viewpoints.
Identifies task-critical objects, lifts their zero-shot masks into a shared 3D frame, and compresses geometry into structured text.
Uses hierarchical GRPO to teach the VLM when to trust geometric tools and when to rely on visual evidence.
Think-Capture-4B improves over its backbone by 21.5, 7.9, and 5.2 points on MindCube-Tiny, MMSI-Bench positional, and ViewSpatial, respectively.
The system remains robust to coordinate and mask perturbations, fits on one 24 GB GPU, and runs as an asynchronous reasoner on an Agibot G1.

papers.abstract: Recovering dynamic 3D scene geometry, appearance, and the physical motion states that govern scene evolution from multi-view videos is important yet challenging. A key difficulty is that appearance can be deceptive. Under rendering supervision alone, a model may fit the observed images by changing color or opacity to compensate for inaccurate deformation, rather than recovering the true evolving geometry and motion. This issue is especially severe in scenes with fast or locally complex motion, where inaccurate trajectories can still produce plausible images over the observed frames, but lead to unreliable reconstruction and discontinuous future prediction. In this paper, we propose PhyMo, a framework for learning evolving dynamics from multi-view videos. We introduce a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation that drives the model to recover accurate motion from deformation, rather than relying on appearance shortcuts to explain observed motion. On top of this, we propose a Continuous Motion Evolution module with bidirectional kinematic continuity constraint to promote temporally consistent evolution of displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Together, these designs yield geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation. Experiments on four dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Shangjia Liu, Jinxi Li, Siyuan Zhou, Bo Yang, Bing Wang
bullets: Addresses inaccurate geometry and motion recovery when rendering supervision lets appearance compensate for deformation errors.
Uses a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation to learn motion directly from deformation.
Adds Continuous Motion Evolution with bidirectional continuity constraints on displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
Produces geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across four dynamic-scene benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) synthesize photorealistic novel views from dense image collections, but degrade sharply when few views are available. We attribute a specific, measurable defect to the objective itself: the rendering loss is a sum over independent rays and contains no term comparing densities that different rays assign to the same region of space, so nearby 3D points can settle on contradictory densities while every training pixel is reproduced correctly. We make this quantity explicit by measuring cross-ray density disagreement directly during training, and show that it stays high in vanilla NeRF, falls only incidentally under frequency-based regularization, and moves together with held-out quality in the sparse regime. We then close the gap with DriftNeRF, a drop-in regularizer that instantiates the drifting-field template on density samples: a masked exponential kernel aggregates densities from nearby points on other rays into a stop-gradient consensus target, and the resulting drifting field penalizes unsupported disagreement while leaving agreed-upon boundaries intact. The regularizer reads only sampled positions, ray identifiers, and predicted densities, so it requires no pretrained model, external geometry, or additional images, and transfers across field parameterizations. On NeRF-Synthetic it reduces residual disagreement by an order of magnitude, and across NeRF-Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF it improves 3-view PSNR over the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline by 0.42-0.65 dB and remains competitive with sparse-view Gaussian pipelines under a matched protocol without their depth, flow, or covisibility preprocessing.
authors: Juntang Wang, Yihan Wang, Sheng'en Li, Hao Wu, Dongmian Zou, Shixin Xu
bullets: Identifies cross-ray density disagreement as a key sparse-view NeRF failure mode: independent ray losses can fit pixels while producing contradictory 3D densities.
Measures this disagreement during training and finds it remains high in vanilla NeRF and correlates with held-out quality.
Uses a drop-in masked-kernel regularizer that builds a stop-gradient consensus from nearby samples on other rays.
Requires only sampled positions, ray IDs, and predicted densities, with no extra images, pretrained models, or external geometry.
Reports order-of-magnitude lower residual disagreement and 0.42–0.65 dB higher 3-view PSNR than the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline across several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.
authors: Derong Yu, Qingsong Zhao, Yanbing Yue, Yikai Li, Zhi Zhang, Guoyan Zheng
bullets: Targets cross-modality one-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying or arbitrary FOVs.
Uses an end-to-end framework combining randomized synthesis of pseudo-data with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning.
Randomizes organ layouts, appearance, FOV, and pose to reduce domain-specific biases and improve robustness to contrast, resolution, and spatial-context changes.
Evaluated on adrenal-gland localization across three challenging datasets, where it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, especially across modalities.
Scope demonstrated on paired, small, irregular adrenal glands; source code is publicly available.

During training, patch quadruplets are randomly sampled to train the DD decoder via a Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss, while image pairs are randomly sampled to optimize the DS decoder via a Cross-domain Prototypical Semantic Contrastive (CPSC) loss.
