papers.abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images.
bullets: Addresses limited cross-domain generalization, privacy concerns, and the need for dataset-specific fine-tuning in abdominal organ segmentation.
Uses a two-stage framework: organ-agnostic synthetic pretraining of GSRNet, followed by organ-specific OESNet training initialized from the learned encoder.
Employs dedicated data engines to generate visually diverse synthetic images while preserving organ layouts and semantic structure.
Learns representations robust to anatomical, contrast, resolution, and spatial-context variations.
Evaluation across seven datasets and three imaging modalities shows consistent improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods without real training images.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A schematic overview of ReSeg. We leverage segmentation masks from the TotalSegmentator CT dataset (Wasserthal et al., 2023), excluding real images entirely. Two data engines, referred to as GenRep and GenSeg, are introduced to construct a Randomized Paired Image (RPI) database and an Anatomical Multi-view Image (AMI) database, respectively. ReSeg is a two-stage learning framework that is trained on these two databases. In particular, in stage I, the RPI database is used to train a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet), which learns organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic features with an Appearance-aware Semantic (AS) decoder and a Context-aware Semantic (CS) decoder. In stage II, an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet) is initialized with the pretrained encoder weights and then trained on the AMI database. OESNet is guided by semantic priors calculated by the well-trained GSRNet to enhance domain-invariant anatomical feature extraction within a Semanticsguided Segmentation (SS) decoder. We reduce the dimension of the embeddings to 3 using PCA and visualize them as RGB images. Embed.: embedding.

Figure 1: Illustration of the proposed two-stage retraining-free framework and the zeroshot segmentation performance. (a) We utilize organ shape templates to randomly sample images from a wide range of distributions and train the model on the synthetic images through two learning stages. Stage I learns organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic features that are robust to imaging variations, while stage II leverages these semantic priors to learn abdominal-organ-specific semantic features for image segmentation. In the inference stage, our model can segment real images from multiple domains without retraining or finetuning. (b) ReSeg achieves superior performance compared with existing state-ofthe-art (SOTA) methods on seven abdominal segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET. In particular, SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023) is trained only on synthetic data while ZeroShotSAM (Shaharabany and Wolf, 2024) leverages Segment Anything Model (SAM) (Kirillov et al., 2023) to perform minimally-guided zero-shot segmentation using foreground prompt points as the input. The solid line in the radar plot depicts the average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) on each dataset.

Figure 5: Framework for the organ-agnostic semantic representation learning stage. During training, a synthetic image pair is randomly sampled from the RPI database to train a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). This network consists of a shared CNN encoder with two distinct decoders: an Appearance-aware Semantic (AS) decoder optimized via a Dual-view Prototypical Contrastive (DPC) loss, and a Contextaware Semantic (CS) decoder trained by a Multi-patch Context-aware Contrastive (MCC) loss. During inference, an input image is fed into GSRNet to generate the AS embedding and the CS embedding from the AS decoder and the CS encoder, respectively. These embeddings are then concatenated to produce the generalizable semantic embedding. We reduce the dimension of the embeddings to 3 using PCA and visualize them as RGB images. Embed.: embedding.

Figure 6: Framework for the abdominal-organ-specific segmentation learning stage. During training, a synthetic image with its GT segmentation label is randomly sampled from the AMI database and then randomly cropped to get an image patch with its GT segmentation label patch. The synthetic image patch is fed into an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), which employs the pretrained weights to initialize the encoder, followed by a Semantics-guided Segmentation (SS) decoder. In the inference stage, OESNet can segment on real images from multiple domains without finetuning. We reduce the dimension of the embeddings to 3 using PCA and visualize them as RGB images. Embed.: embedding. CE: cross entropy.

Each SFE module takes the segmentation feature of the current layer f in d and the generalizable semantic embedding fs from the frozen GSRNet as inputs. Within the SFE module, fs is first aligned with f in d and then generates attention map to enhance the segmentation feature. After that, the feature undergoes multi-kernel processing and finally the output feature fout

Figure 3: Illustration of the Generalizable Appearance (GA) model. Given a label map L with L labels, GMMs are used to randomly sample intensities. For all label l ∈ {1, 2, · · · , L}, a lower bound aµ for the mean parameters are first drawn from a uniform distribution U(aLµ , a H µ ), where aLµ and aHµ are two fixed hyperparameters controlling respectively the lowest and the highest value for this dynamic lower bound. Then, for each label l in L, the intensity Il is sampled from a Gaussian distribution N (µl, σ 2 l ), where µl ∼ U(aµ, bµ), σl ∼ U(aσ, bσ), and bµ, aσ, and bσ are fixed hyperparameters. After GMMs, Perlin noise (Perlin, 1985) is applied, followed by random offline and online augmentations.

papers.abstract: True whole-body medical imaging captures a patient from head to toe and provides comprehensive anatomical and/or functional information. This coverage enables reconstruction of the external body surface, yielding patient body models. However, scanner geometry (e.g., bore diameter), patient characteristics, and positioning can leave body regions missing (e.g., lateral arms/torso, hands, forearms, elbows), producing incomplete patient body models. Such incompleteness limits downstream medical analyses, including derivation of body-habitus metrics (BHMs), such as body volume and surface area, for injected radiotracer activity regimens, cardiometabolic risk assessment, and computational anatomical modeling for medical imaging simulation and radiation dosimetry. We present the Medical Body model Optimization-based Estimator (MedBOE), an automated, training-free framework for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions. Our innovation is to leverage the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) template, a parametric body mesh representing a broad range of body shapes and poses, in medical imaging. MedBOE aligns the SMPL template to the incomplete patient body models via attribute-guided optimization and estimates missing body regions through geometrically and volumetrically constrained deformation. We evaluated MedBOE using two public datasets: AutoPET (91 whole-body PET-CT images) and Human Implicit Tissues (HIT; 40 whole-body segmentations from MRI images). MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.
authors: Hoijoon Jung, Yuhao Wei, Mingxiao Tu, Younhyun Jung, Michael Fulham, Jinman Kim
bullets: Addresses incomplete body models caused by scanner geometry, patient characteristics, and positioning.

papers.abstract: Accurate 6-DoF object pose tracking is essential for robotic interaction, yet conventional monocular pipelines frequently suffer from catastrophic divergence under rapid object motion. We present RoPT, a robust tracking framework engineered to overcome this limitation by unifying visual perception, temporal kinematics, and global re-localization into a tightly coupled closed loop. Unlike existing open-loop trackers, RoPT delivers three critical capabilities that fundamentally alter system resilience. First, the visual perception component tracks object masks to robustly handle partial and severe occlusions. Second, a kinematic factor graph regularizes frame-to-frame updates, forecasts forward pose predictions, and drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme to bypass local minima. Finally, an active re-localization module transforms the pipeline into a closed-loop system, making it failure-aware and capable of deterministic self-recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across challenging benchmarks alongside real-world robotic demonstrations, achieving significantly higher tracking survivability under rapid motion.
authors: Yongqing Liang, Yuzhong Chen, Sihang Li, Junsuk Kim, Chase Kidder, Hui-ping Wang, Yunzhi Xu, Raihan Haque, Yubiao Zhang, Chen Feng
bullets: Targets catastrophic divergence in conventional monocular pose trackers caused by rapid object motion.
Tracks object masks to remain robust under partial and severe occlusions.
Uses a kinematic factor graph for temporal regularization and forward pose prediction.
Employs parallel multi-hypothesis verification to avoid local minima.
Demonstrates higher tracking survivability on challenging benchmarks and in real-world robotic demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: An Overview of the RoPT pipeline. The system integrates a mask-guided visual perception frontend with a continuous kinematic factor graph that regularizes updates and generates multihypothesis pose forecasts. To ensure robustness against rapid dynamics, the pipeline routes refined candidates through a pose scoring module. If catastrophic tracking loss occurs, the failure-aware self-recovery module synthesizes a virtual CAD rendering and establishes 3D-2D correspondences with the incoming RGB frame, seamlessly healing the trajectory.

Existing open-loop methods output erratic, unreliable poses, whereas our tracker correctly signals a tracking failure. (d) Pose Recovery: Upon the object’s reappearance, our method successfully re-establishes and recovers the accurate 6-DoF pose.

papers.abstract: We present Register Anything Model (RAM), a unified model for generalizable 3D point cloud registration that robustly estimates 6-DoF transformations across diverse domains spanning sensors and environments. Existing registration methods are typically tailored to a single domain, with carefully tuned architectures and hyperparameters, and thus degrade markedly when applied to novel domains. We bridge this gap by training a single model on diverse data from indoor, outdoor, and object domains. A central challenge is the severe geometric discrepancy across domains, i.e., differences in scene scale, sensor noise, point density, and structural patterns, which hinders processing with a unified point-based model. To address this, we introduce a geometry-aware normalization strategy that jointly voxelizes and normalizes point clouds into a standardized geometric space, adaptively based on their geometric properties to preserve salient local structures while standardizing resolution. Built on this normalization, RAM follows a hierarchical coarse-to-fine paradigm, and employs an efficient geometric transformer that models local geometric consistency instead of globally over all points. This design mitigates discretization noise introduced by voxelization, and improves computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in terms of inlier ratio and registration recall. Notably, our method outperforms the counterparts trained on each separate domain, showing superior generalization capability.
authors: Zheng Qin, Junhua Xi, Yan Huang, Jiahong Lai, Anwen Huang, Qiong Li, Guangda Zhang, Kai Xu
bullets: Targets the poor cross-domain generalization of registration methods tuned to individual sensors or environments.

Trained on diverse indoor, outdoor, and object data, RAM achieves state-of-the-art inlier ratio and registration recall across 12 benchmarks.
Outperforms models trained separately for each domain, demonstrating stronger generalization across domains.

papers.abstract: Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of a reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while preserving scene geometry. Recent methods perform this transfer by optimizing the appearance representation of neural scene models including Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). These methods optimize an RGB appearance representation, in which a single per-point colour combines the effects of material reflectance, environment illumination, together with the shading it produces, and the viewing direction. When stylization modifies this combined colour, the illumination effects present during stylization are baked into the stored appearance, so the stylized scene cannot be rendered under different illumination. To address this limitation, we present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware 3D Gaussian representation. Rather than modifying a per-point RGB colour, RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field recovered by inverse rendering, while leaving roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and the estimated environment lighting unchanged. As a result, the stylized scene keeps all the components a physically-based renderer needs other than the edited albedo, and can therefore still be relit. RxGS optimizes the albedo field using a nearest-neighbour feature matching loss together with a spatial smoothness prior over Gaussian centres. We evaluate the method using a Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) based on optical-flow warping error. RxGS achieves the lowest GCC on all evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scenes and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while additionally supporting relightable stylization, which existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods do not provide.
bullets: Existing methods combine material, lighting, shading, and view effects into RGB, preventing relighting after stylization.
RxGS uses a BRDF-aware 3D Gaussian representation and keeps roughness, metallicity, normals, and estimated environment lighting unchanged.
Albedo optimization combines nearest-neighbour feature matching with a spatial smoothness prior over Gaussian centres.
It achieves the lowest geometry-consistency cost on all evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scenes and remains competitive on real-captured scenes.
The abstract does not specify limitations beyond performance variation between synthetic and real-captured scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of RxGS. Given posed multi-view images and a reference style image, a BRDFaware Gaussian scene representation is first reconstructed with GS-IR, which separates the scene into geometry, diffuse albedo, material attributes (roughness and metallicity), surface normals, and one global environment lighting. RxGS stylizes by optimizing only the diffuse albedo field, with a nearestneighbour feature matching (NNFM) loss and a spatial smoothness term, while leaving roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and the lighting unchanged. The stylized BRDF-aware representation therefore keeps its relightable property and can be rendered under novel illumination without further optimization.

Fig. 1 Comparison between stylization on an RGB appearance representation and stylization on a BRDF-aware scene representation. Existing methods transfer appearance onto a per-point RGB colour, which already combines material reflectance and illumination. The illumination present during stylization is therefore written into the stored colour, and the result no longer changes when the lighting changes. RxGS instead modifies only the diffuse albedo and leaves the estimated lighting representation unchanged, so the stylized albedo can be rendered under different illumination conditions, producing relightable stylized scenes without re-running the stylization.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.
authors: Noam Rotstein, Yoad Tewel, Chen Tessler, Haggai Maron, Gal Chechik, Or Litany, Yoni Kasten, Yuval Atzmon
bullets: Addresses the gap between realistic video generation and usable 3D animation for specific assets.
Separates an arbitrary-skeleton 3D motion model from a pretrained video model, linking them with lightweight cross-attention.
Predicts joint locations in video to recover the camera and register 3D motion in the scene.
Uses curated synthetic edits plus human and robot video to create nearly 200K training pairs.
Supports text-to-motion/video, video-to-rig motion, rig-motion-to-video, and keyframe control; evaluations report more faithful, scene-responsive animation than video-first pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview. Given a text prompt, a rig, and an optional reference image, the model jointly denoises video latents Zv and motion tokens Zm. A graph network encodes the rig into per-joint descriptors D, using the joints’ 2D locations in the reference image, and these condition the motion branch; a graph-attention layer inside each Motion DiT block propagates features along the rig edges. Zero-initialized cross-attention bridges exchange features in both directions at paired blocks, each branch querying the other’s intermediate features, so joint training begins from the two pretrained branches acting as they did in isolation. An auxiliary joint-localization head (right) attends from joint features to video patches and returns each joint’s image position as a weighted combination of patch coordinates, giving 2D–3D correspondences used to fit a camera.

Figure 3: Text-driven rig animation across diverse assets. Each row shows a text prompt, an input mesh, and sampled poses from animations generated by competing methods and JCA (ours). Our method more faithfully captures the requested actions while preserving the asset’s geometry.

Figure 5: Scene-aware rig animation and motion localization. Given a penguin rig, a rendered initial frame of a snowy 3D scene, and a text prompt, our model jointly generates video and 3D rig motion. Top: frames from the generated video, where the penguin moves forward and slides down the snowy slope. Middle: the raw 3D motion produced by the motion branch, rendered in the input scene before localization. The penguin’s motion is not aligned with the depicted scene geometry and, in later frames, appears beneath the snow surface. Bottom: the same generated motion after applying our joint-localization and camera-alignment scheme described in section 3.3. The estimated alignment correctly places the motion on the visible penguin and registers it with the generated video and scene.

Figure 6: Prompt-adherence evaluation of one animation with GPT-6 Astra. In the first turn, the judge is given the asset’s short description and 48 frames of the animation, 16 from each of the front, right, and left views, each frame labeled with its view; the figure shows two frames per view. It is asked to describe the motion it observes in chronological order. In the second turn, it scores the motion against the action prompt. The complete prompts and responses are given in section B.3.

papers.abstract: Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
authors: Rundong Luo, Yunong Liu, Di Cao, Matthew Tancik, Shyamal Buch, Colton Stearns, Wenqi Xian
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible reconstruction and physically correct object placement.
Combines geometric, visual, and physical tools with agent-driven edit-and-validate loops in a physics simulator.
Improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement across diverse inputs.
Produces physically stable scenes that better predict real-robot policy outcomes than the baseline.
Supports more reliable replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of SceneRig. From a single image, SceneRig recovers objects, supporting surfaces, and their relations, and initializes a gravity-aligned metric scene through physical settling. Geometry, material, and lighting agents construct the surrounding scene. Finally, a pose-refinement agent inspects paired reference/render crops and invokes geometry- and physics-grounded tools to correct object placement.

Figure 1 Single-image simulation-ready scene reconstruction for robotics. SceneRig combines vision tools, agentic reasoning, and physical simulation to create an editable, simulation-ready scene from a single image (top). Its reconstructions support real-to-sim policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay, reproducing real-world outcomes more faithfully than SimFoundry (bottom).

Figure 3 Qualitative scene reconstruction results. Compared with the baselines, SceneRig more consistently preserves object identity, scale, and relative placement while reconstructing the surrounding scene.

papers.abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
authors: Om Shivam Verma, Shaya Farahmand, Lingjun Zhao, Lu Gan
bullets: Addresses the limits of existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods, which require dense 3D voxel annotations and fixed semantic classes.
Represents scenes with sparse 3D Gaussians aligned to foundation models.
Uses Gaussians to communicate and fuse geometric and semantic information across agents.
Evaluated on Semantic-OPV2V, where it outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent methods.
Targets broader scene understanding for transportation safety and multi-robot efficiency.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview. CoGaussian starts with randomly initialized embeddings. A transformer layer uses multiscale features of images to update the embeddings, followed by a Head Layer that predicts Gaussians. During Joint Training, all agents predict ego Gaussians which are communicated with each other and aggregated. This set of Gaussians is used for training. In the Fusion pipeline, the neighbors predict and send Gaussian embeddings to the ego agent. Radius-gated Attention uses these neighbor Gaussian embeddings to update ego embeddings. The Fusion Head predicts ego Gaussians, and pre-trained Head from Joint Training predicts neighbor Gaussians. These are aggregated to form the final prediction used for both training and inference.

papers.abstract: Video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction typically use separate representations, requiring RGB decoding and visual re-encoding to recover geometry from generated latents. We propose Latent Bridge, which connects video generative latent spaces with geometric feature spaces to directly predict 3D geometry from video latents. We develop representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE, enabling feed-forward prediction of cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds without the intermediate RGB pathway. Each bridge is trained on RGB videos through feature distillation, while the video encoder and geometry model remain frozen. Training requires neither ground-truth geometry nor execution of the downstream geometric aggregator or prediction heads. At inference, the same video latents support both RGB decoding and geometry prediction. The same trained bridge can be reused for image-to-video and text-to-video generation within the same video latent space, without bridge retraining. Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D demonstrate competitive geometric reconstruction quality, efficient end-to-end generation and reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding, highlighting latent alignment as a practical and reusable interface between video generation and 3D reconstruction. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hustvl/Latent-Bridge.
authors: Shuai Zhang, Zhanpeng Ouyang, Zhengqing Chen, Ruohong Mei, Shaoyu Chen, Weiqiang Ren, Hui Sun, Qian Zhang, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang

papers.abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.
authors: Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras, Christos Davatzikos
bullets: Pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans pooled from multiple studies.
Supports both weight initialization for downstream fine-tuning and standalone feature extraction.
Improved brain-age prediction accuracy and convergence speed relative to random initialization.
Frozen embeddings outperformed anatomical volumetric features on four of five classification tasks and competed with a larger-data foundation model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Brain2Vec pre-training architecture and downstream applications. (Pre-training) Brain2Vec is a 3D Masked Autoencoder (MAE) pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans from the iSTAGING consortium. Input volumes are divided into 8× 8× 8 patches, with 75% randomly masked. A 12-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder processes only the visible patches to generate a 768-dimensional latent representation. Mask tokens are then introduced, and an 8-layer ViT decoder reconstructs the original scan. (Evaluation) The pre-trained encoder serves two complementary roles. First, it provides a robust weight initialization for end-to-end fine-tuning on a downstream task (brain age regression), accelerating convergence and improving accuracy relative to random initialization. Second, its frozen 768-dimensional embeddings serve as fixed features for lightweight downstream models, including a Support Vector Regressor (SVR) for brain age regression and SVMs for five binary classification tasks: CU vs. AD, elevated BMI, diabetes, smoking status, and hypertension. We additionally assess the quality and interpretability of these frozen embeddings via self-attention visualization, correlation with anatomically-defined Regions of Interest (ROIs), and latent-space manipulation, showing that Brain2Vec encodes spatially localized, neuroanatomically meaningful representations.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video requires inferring motion from noisy and intermittently visible observations. Long-range tracks provide valuable geometric constraints, but integrating their fragmented temporal coverage into shared, continuous motion remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{RayCo4D}, a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D reconstruction that explicitly separates visual measurements from latent 3D motion states. Each track is associated with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray, and its image and depth observations constrain shared latent motion nodes through local many-to-many associations. Each node maintains an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ pose and body-frame velocity at sparse support times. A white-noise-on-acceleration process prior couples neighboring states and defines continuous-time interpolation, allowing observations across visibility intervals to jointly constrain the same latent state sequence.The inferred shared motion is transferred to Gaussian primitives through dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ residuals capture fine-scale non-rigid deformation beyond the shared scaffold. Experiments on diverse monocular dynamic scenes show that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, improves structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering.
authors: Yuanxiang Ni, Xianliang Huang, Ruihan Hou, Feng Xie, Hao Zhang
bullets: Addresses noisy, intermittently visible observations and fragmented long-range tracks in monocular dynamic reconstruction.

Models each node with an SE(3) pose and body-frame velocity, coupled by a white-noise-on-acceleration prior for continuous-time interpolation.
Transfers shared motion to Gaussian primitives via dual-quaternion blending, with local SE(3) residuals for fine non-rigid deformation.
Reports competitive novel-view synthesis and improved structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, with continuous-time rendering support.

The inferred motion is propagated to Gaussians via dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local residuals capture fine-grained non-rigid deformation for dynamic rendering and optimization.

papers.abstract: Geometric Relative Positional Encoding has become the primary mechanism for injecting spatial inductive biases into multi-view transformers. Existing designs condition attention on camera-level frustums or ray-marched depth, associating cross-view tokens through the sensor geometry. Such sensor-centric formulations, however, describe only where a token is observed from, leaving the rich surface geometry of the scene region depicted by the token. In this paper, we advocate a shift toward surface-aware positional encoding that explicitly grounds patch tokens in the geometry of physical surfaces. We introduce HRoPE, which represents the local geometry of each patch as a slanted 3D plane, following the slanted support-window assumption of classical multi-view stereo. We inject token-level, plane-induced homographies into attention as relative transformations. This equips the transformer with a geometric prior for rectifying perspective distortions and aligning patch features across viewpoints. Our encoding requires no ground-truth geometry: the plane parameters can be predicted end-to-end under a view-synthesis objective alone, or derived from foundation models. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV show that our best variant of HRoPE consistently outperforms the evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis. Extensive ablations and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed encoding. Please refer to our project page at: https://gaohchen.github.io/HRoPE
authors: Huachen Gao, Yang Yang, Xiaoqian Liang, Xingyu Chen, Youjia Zhang, Qi Zhang, Baorui Ma, Anpei Chen, Wei Yang

Experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV report consistent gains over evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis.
Ablations and analysis support the effectiveness of the surface-aware encoding.

papers.abstract: Low-cost multi-zone single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) sensors provide compact time-of-flight measurements but are limited by sparse sampling and unreliable depth estimates near geometric discontinuities. This letter presents a reliability-aware reconstruction framework for V-shaped surfaces using two complementary TMF8821 acquisition configurations. Point-wise reliability is learned from sensor confidence, transient peak amplitude, and peak sharpness, and is incorporated into a graph-based depth optimization. The reconstructed geometry is evaluated by robust two-plane fitting and a perpendicular cross-section. Experiments on 60-degree, 90-degree, and 120-degree targets reduce the mean V-angle error from 11.21 degrees to 9.66 degrees (13.8%). For the representative 90-degree target, the combined point-to-plane RMSE decreases from 14.56 mm to 13.65 mm.
bullets: Addresses unreliable depth estimates near geometric discontinuities in low-cost SPAD time-of-flight sensing.
Combines two TMF8821 acquisition configurations for complementary measurements.
Learns point-wise reliability from sensor confidence, transient peak amplitude, and peak sharpness.
Uses reliability in graph-based depth optimization, evaluated through two-plane fitting and perpendicular cross-sections.
Across 60°, 90°, and 120° targets, mean V-angle error drops from 11.21° to 9.66%; the 90° target’s point-to-plane RMSE falls from 14.56 mm to 13.65 mm.

papers.abstract: This work presents SplatFlux, a feed-forward latent-to-4DGS framework for both video-based 4D reconstruction and conditional 4D generation. Our key observation is that observed videos and conditionally generated content can be represented in the same pretrained video latent space, allowing both tasks to be formulated as latent-to-4DGS decoding. To construct compact and temporally coherent 4D scenes, SplatFlux introduces a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation that explicitly predicts dynamic probabilities for Gaussian primitives. This representation separates static scene structures from moving regions, enabling complete 4D scene construction in a feed-forward manner through static aggregation and dynamic motion interpolation. To learn static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic Gaussian motion without costly annotations, we further develop an auxiliary distillation strategy that provides pseudo dynamic masks and optical-flow cues. Extensive experiments across 3D and 4D reconstruction and generation demonstrate that SplatFlux achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Runmin Zhang, Binglin Ren, Zhu Yu, Fudong Wang, Jiangke Lin, Yichun Shentu, Si-Yuan Cao, Yi Yuan, Hui-Liang Shen
bullets: Unifies observed-video reconstruction and conditional 4D generation through a shared pretrained video latent space.
Uses a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation with dynamic probabilities for each Gaussian primitive.
Builds scenes via static aggregation and dynamic motion interpolation.
Employs auxiliary distillation to obtain pseudo dynamic masks and optical-flow cues without costly annotations.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across 3D/4D reconstruction and generation tasks.

papers.abstract: Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) aims to bypass cumbersome Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by directly reconstructing scenes from unposed image sequences. In this work, we present CrossFit-GS, a deferred-commitment progressive framework that mitigates cumulative trajectory drift and breaks the self-reinforcing loop of distorted-map error propagation. Specifically, we partition the input sequence into interleaved subsets and maintain two complementary submaps. Each candidate pose is cross-refined against a frozen opposite submap that has never been optimized using the target frame, thereby providing an independent geometric reference for pose estimation. Checkerboard validation and spatial coverage safeguards further reject unreliable updates, and only verified poses are committed to their corresponding owner submap. Once the trajectory has been refined, the intermediate submaps are discarded and the final global representation is trained from scratch using the fixed refined poses. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that CrossFit-GS substantially reduces cumulative trajectory drift and consistently improves both camera pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods.
authors: Zijian Wu, Jinliang Wang, Mingfeng Jiang, Zidian Lin, Ying Song, Ziqian Lu
bullets: Targets pose-free 3DGS without relying on Structure-from-Motion.
Splits image sequences into interleaved subsets and maintains two complementary submaps.
Cross-refines candidate poses against an opposite submap that has not used the target frame.
Uses checkerboard validation and spatial-coverage checks to reject unreliable updates before commitment.
Evaluations on multiple benchmarks show improved pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CrossFit-GS. The input sequence is partitioned into two interleaved folds, each associated with a separate Gaussian map. For a frame in Fold B, its pose is refined against the frozen Map A, with visual-support checks and an accept-or-keep validation rule governing the update. The frame subsequently contributes only to Map B. The roles of the two folds alternate, ensuring that a frame does not train the map used to assess its pose. Finally, a unified Gaussian representation is trained from scratch using all training images and the fixed estimated poses.

papers.abstract: Existing feature lifting approaches for open-vocabulary segmentation rely on simple backprojection to assign features to primitives. In the case of 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction, the primitives overlap heavily, leading to suboptimal reconstructions, governed by many primitives per ray. Backprojection, however, reduces to a least-squares solvable problem, exactly when no two primitives share a ray. Motivated by this insight, we propose OV-Foam, which uses PowerFoam as the underlying representation. This representation uses a power-diagram to partition the scene, resulting in zero overlap between primitives and a substantial reduction in primitives per ray, which ultimately simplifies the lifting problem and allows for closer-to-optimal feature assignment. We show that the space partitioning primitives of OV-Foam reach near-optimal assignment, and our experiments demonstrate improved open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.
authors: Yousef Rajeh (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology), Alejandra Esparza Pelcastre (Universidad Panamericana), Ivan Viola (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology), Dominik Engel (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology)
bullets: Existing methods use backprojection, but overlapping Gaussian primitives make feature assignment difficult.
OV-Foam uses PowerFoam to partition scenes into non-overlapping primitives.
Fewer primitives per ray simplify lifting and bring it closer to the least-squares optimum.
The representation achieves near-optimal feature assignment and improves open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.

papers.abstract: Examining existing benchmarks for grounding in 3D VLMs reveals a pervasive "semantic leakage" in the evaluation and prompting protocols: a heavy reliance on bounding boxes as spatial prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes are highly informative of object categories, they introduce a shortcut for the models to neglect visual information during 3D VLM training. We demonstrate this with a "blind" LLM that, prompted only with the box coordinates, can perform surprisingly well. To further analyze this shortcut, we propose point-based grounding prompting - querying models with a single 3D point instead of a box. Under this protocol, the accuracy of the blind LLM drops from 36.4% to 18.0% on ScanNet's Nr3D, and similarly degrades for 3D VLMs (e.g. LL3DA). Building on this insight, we introduce P$^3$-VLM, a novel tri-pathway 3D VLM that supports point-based prompts and achieves 52.1% state-of-the-art accuracy on location-grounded captioning under this setting. To achieve this, we redesign the architecture while keeping it detector-free, scene-centric, and suitable for 3D GS inputs. P$^3$-VLM utilizes three complementary pathways (location-, task-, and context-aware), enabling strong reasoning about scenes without any bounding box dependencies. The key benefit of point-based learning is a consistent improvement across settings: P$^3$-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance under point-based grounding while also improving robustness, OOD generalization, and performance on ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA benchmarks, reflecting its reduced reliance on bounding-box shortcuts and resulting stronger visual-spatial reasoning.
authors: Anna-Maria Halacheva, Jan-Nico Zaech, Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Existing 3D VLM grounding benchmarks risk semantic leakage because bounding boxes reveal object-category information.
A blind LLM using only box coordinates reaches 36.4% on ScanNet Nr3D, but falls to 18.0% with a single 3D point, exposing the shortcut.
P$^3$-VLM is a detector-free, scene-centric, tri-pathway 3D VLM designed for point prompts and 3D Gaussian Splatting inputs.
Its location-, task-, and context-aware pathways achieve 52.1% accuracy on point-based location-grounded captioning.
Point-based learning also improves robustness, out-of-distribution generalization, and ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: P3-VLM architecture overview. Three complementary pathways process the voxelized 3D scene: the location-aware pathway extracts a single token at the queried point; the task-aware pathway produces prompt-guided scene tokens by first refining the task prompt tokens and subsequently utilizing them for visual refinement of the sparsified features; the context-aware pathway distills 8 global scene summary tokens via unconditional cross-attention. Notably, the context and task pathways operate on the sparsified features for efficiency gains.

papers.abstract: Camera design heavily influences perception task performance, yet cameras are typically designed by domain experts through costly experimentation, in isolation from the tasks they serve. Existing joint-design methods either rely on differentiable simulation limited to pre-captured 2D images, restricting them to optics or image-processing pipeline design, or use non-differentiable camera simulators optimised with derivative-free or reinforcement-learning methods that scale poorly with the number of design parameters. We present a differentiable framework for jointly designing complex camera systems and downstream perception tasks. We use it to design two coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras, a monocular and a stereo configuration, by jointly optimising the coded aperture mask, camera parameters, and a depth estimation network end-to-end. Our framework represents scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructed from real-world captures, providing a differentiable image formation process for gradient-based optimisation over design spaces intractable for prior differentiable approaches. Results demonstrate that our differentiable method improves over existing coded aperture design and non-differentiable camera design baselines, offering a step forward in automated and principled camera design for autonomous systems.
bullets: Addresses the costly, task-agnostic process of designing cameras through manual experimentation.
Jointly optimizes coded aperture masks, camera parameters, and a depth-estimation network end-to-end.
Uses 3D Gaussian Splatting from real-world captures to enable differentiable image formation and gradient-based design optimization.
Demonstrated on monocular and stereo coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras.
Improves over existing coded-aperture and non-differentiable camera-design baselines, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 7. The stereo depth-from-defocus method. Per-view AiF proxy images are synthesised by fusing the Tikhonov-deconvolved focal stack using a differentiable Laplacian sharpness measure and passed to a frozen RAPIDFlow [29] network to estimate dense disparity. The disparity is then used to warp the right-view into the left-view coordinate frame via bilinear grid sampling. The left-view focal stack, the warped right-view focal stack, and a depth map derived from the disparity estimate are concatenated and fed into the monocular U-Net backbone with frequency injection, yielding the reconstructed AiF image and depth map for the left view.

Figure 1. We introduce a differentiable method that jointly optimises camera parameters and perception tasks, using 3DGS scenes reconstructed from real-world captures and a coded aperture simulation modelling depth-dependent optical blur. Camera parameters and the perception network are jointly updated via gradientbased optimisation of the task loss (red arrows), spanning geometric parameters (FoV, pixel count, multi-camera configurations) and high-dimensional optical parameters (coded aperture mask).

Figure 6. The monocular depth-from-defocus method. The backbone follows the U-Net of Ikoma et al. [16], which takes a coded aperture image and its Tikhonov-deconvolved focal stack as input and jointly predicts the AiF image and depth map. We augment this backbone with a frequency injection module. In this module, the input image is divided into patches, a 2D Fourier transform is applied to each patch independently, and the log-magnitude spectrum is computed to capture local, spatially-varying defocus strength. The per-patch spectra are encoded by a lightweight 3-layer convolutional network, reassembled into a 2D feature map based on each patch’s location, and injected at the bottleneck of the U-Net.

Figure 8. Qualitative comparison for the monocular experiment under the Noise×200 scenario. Our jointly optimised camera, mask, and perception model again produce sharp AiF images and accurate depth, while the fixed-camera baseline (Ikoma et al. [16]) and the derivative-free joint optimiser (TaCOS [43]) produce images with more defocus blur and lower depth accuracy in these regions.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison for the monocular experiment. Our jointly optimised camera, mask, and perception model produce sharp AiF images and accurate depth, while the fixed-camera baseline (Ikoma et al. [16]) and the derivative-free joint optimiser (TaCOS [43]) degrade noticeably in blurry regions.

Figure 9. Qualitative comparison of the proposed stereo method with a coded aperture dual-pixel camera method (CADS [12]) and the monocular alternative. Our method achieves better AiF reconstruction by combining varying focus planes across the two views, and better depth estimation by exploiting disparity as an additional cue.

Figure 4. Our method fuses photometric cues from a foreground-focused and a background-focused view for higher AiF quality and improves depth accuracy by leveraging disparity. Full comparisons with baselines are presented in the supplementary material.

Figure 2. A camera captures the real-world scene (blue arrow), which 3DGS models as a 3D Gaussian representation. At each step, this representation is rendered with the current geometric camera parameters into pinhole RGB images and depth maps; the coded aperture simulation then convolves these RGB renders with depth-dependent PSFs computed from the coded mask, focus distance, and f-number via a physical optics model, followed by a physics-based noise model. The resulting renders are fed to the perception task network, and the task loss ltask is backpropagated through both stages (red arrows) to jointly update all learnable parameters (green text).
Figure 5. Prototype of the optical system used for real-world validation and the real-world stereo results.

Figure 10. (a) The optimised coded aperture masks in both monocular and stereo experiments, the manufcatured masks, and their measured PSFs. (b) The captured coded aperture image, reconstructed AiF image, and estimated depth map for the monocular setup. The AiF and depth recovery on real hardware show plausible outcomes but with modest accuracy gap attributable to the sim-to-real domain shift and manufacturing tolerances.

[16], tested with their original Phase mask and with an Amp. (amplitude) mask matched to our settings) and a derivative-free joint optimiser (TaCOS [43]). papers.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.
bullets: Vanilla NeRF geometry can be noisy because shape and radiance ambiguities explain the same images.
The method samples candidate surfaces from density and evaluates appearance consistency along virtual rays from multiple directions.
Visibility-weighted color consistency constrains geometry without ground-truth depth or normal labels.
Additional regularization penalizes opacity for inconsistent predictions and promotes local normal smoothness.
On eight Replica scenes, mean Chamfer distance decreases by 30.8% versus vanilla NeRF.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed framework. The shared NeRF renders training views for RGB reconstruction and supplies the density field for candidate surface sampling. The geometry-optimization branch generates virtual cross-rays through each candidate, renders their appearances, and estimates visibility weights to reduce the influence of occluded rays. Cross-ray consistency, occupancy suppression, and local normal smoothness jointly regularize the field.

Fig. 3. Details of candidate sampling and visibility-aware cross-ray construction. (a) Uniform proposals and rendered-depth anchors are filtered by an intermediate opacity band to obtain candidate points. The curved patch schematically represents the current density boundary. (b) For a candidate x𝑖 , the auxiliary sphere is centered at x𝑖 + 𝑙0n𝑖 with radius 𝑟 . papers.abstract: 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) is used in indoor environments, such as smart homes, to analyze human movement and monitor human states. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is suitable for this task because it is robust to lighting variations and does not capture images of human appearance. However, radar observations often provide insufficient information about certain body parts or contain overlapping reflections from multiple body parts, limiting accurate 3D joint localization. To address these limitations, we propose the Initialization-to-Refinement Pose Framework (I2R-Pose), comprising two stages: Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement. In the first stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations and human skeletal structure to compensate for insufficient joint information and estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the second stage, separately extracted radar observation features predict joint-wise positional corrections that refine the initial pose and generate the final pose sequence. The framework supports individual and fused inputs of time-Doppler/time-range (TD/TR) maps and radar point clouds (PCs). To evaluate performance across indoor activities, we construct the Radar Motion and Spatial Information for 3D Human Pose Estimation (RaMoS-Pose) dataset, providing synchronized TD/TR maps, radar PCs, and 3D joint ground truth (GT). Evaluations on RaMoS-Pose and the publicly available MVDoppler-Pose dataset show that I2R-Pose reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and by 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose with fused inputs, compared with the best-performing existing methods evaluated on each dataset.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.
authors: Injae Kim, Minseok Joo, Jihwan Park, Sehyung Kim, Minseong Bae, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Existing methods generate a dense Gaussian set before pruning, so inference cost remains nearly fixed regardless of the final budget.
RLSplat learns how to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians across local scene regions.
A resource-linear decoder refines Gaussians using efficient hierarchical neighbor search and local attention.
In zero-shot evaluation, it outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, including a stronger baseline with 4× fewer Gaussians.
At low budgets, RLSplat runs up to 4.1× faster and uses 9.6× less peak memory.

papers.abstract: Semantic occupancy mapping supports embodied perception during exploration and detailed scene understanding afterward, giving rise to two complementary requirements: online incremental mapping for maintaining an up-to-date global map under causal constraints, and offline global map refinement for improving the completed scene representation with additional computation. We present VEOcc++, a unified voxel-centric framework that connects both stages through a persistent sparse voxel feature map. During exploration, the map expands with newly observed regions and integrates aligned local features through reliability-guided updates, while context-aware decoding produces the current semantic occupancy map. After exploration, cached local features are consolidated as complementary evidence and combined with the completed online representation for multi-scale spatial refinement. On EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet, VEOcc++ achieves 67.12\% IoU and 58.40\% mIoU, establishing new state-of-the-art performance for online incremental mapping. With the local predictor fixed, our online mapping pipeline outperforms VEOcc fusion by 3.70 IoU and 3.74 mIoU points, demonstrating substantial gains from the proposed global mapping design. Offline global map refinement further improves the completed map to 67.79% IoU and 59.37% mIoU using only the observations acquired during exploration. Zero-shot deployment on a mobile robot further demonstrates transferability to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalability to large-scale indoor mapping. Project page: https://wryzju.github.io/VEOccpp/.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Jiahan Li, Yong Liu, Kexin Zhang

Demonstrates transfer to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalable indoor mapping on a mobile robot.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps. Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy by more than 50\% points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.

papers.abstract: Simulation-ready world reconstruction demands physical interactivity beyond visual realism, which existing black-box 3D generation fails to deliver. We present NeoWorld-3, a coding-agent framework that reconstructs interactive 3D worlds from visual observations via tunable, executable programs. At its core, NeoSDK provides the underlying computational engine for low-level geometries, part composition, differentiable parameter refinement, and physics validation. At the same time, NeoMCP exposes these capabilities as structured, tool-callable APIs for vision-language agents to visually inspect, edit code, and iteratively refine programs. Through a hierarchical coordinator-worker architecture, the framework scales seamlessly from standalone articulated objects to complex compositional scenes. Evaluations across object-level and scene-level reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that NeoWorld-3 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness. Crucially, manipulation trajectories planned within our reconstructed twins achieve successful zero-shot execution on a physical dual-arm robot, completing the Real-Sim-Real loop.
authors: Eachen Soong, Zijian Niu, Haoran Xu, Yihong Dong, Yunbo Wang, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually realistic 3D generation and simulation-ready physical interactivity.
Uses NeoSDK for geometry, composition, differentiable refinement, and physics validation.
Uses NeoMCP tool APIs with vision-language agents to inspect, edit, and iteratively refine reconstruction code.
A hierarchical coordinator-worker design scales from articulated objects to complex scenes.
Reports state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness, with successful Real-Sim-Real execution on a dual-arm robot.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D object detection is a core perception service for autonomous driving, but deployment requires robustness to point-cloud corruption while meeting latency and memory requirements. Existing approaches address robustness and resource efficiency separately, resulting in compact detectors that are fragile under corruption or robust detectors that remain costly to deploy. We therefore formulate LiDAR perception provisioning as constructing a detector that remains accurate under point-cloud corruptions while meeting constraints on inference latency and peak GPU memory. To achieve robustness, we first craft corrupted samples that mimic extreme weather conditions. Then we train candidate detectors offline by ordering clean and corrupted samples by perturbation sensitivity, through which detectors learn more from hard corrupted samples. We estimate perturbation sensitivity using an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors by tracking changes in confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections. To improve efficiency, we narrow the network and use offline neighborhood-density measurements to determine how many points and neighbors each sampling stage processes. We evaluate our method using AP (Average Precision) under clean and corrupted conditions, inference latency, and peak allocated GPU memory. On KITTI for Car detection with PointRCNN, our method improves Moderate AP under corruption by 3.32 points over the original detector while reducing mean latency by 19.8% and peak allocated GPU memory by 53.9%. Across two datasets, two detector architectures, and three object classes, our method improves AP under corruption by 4.03 points on average over the corresponding original detectors, while reducing mean inference latency and peak allocated GPU memory by 14.4% and 38.0%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/drunklibai/robust-efficient-lidar-perception.
authors: Tingxu Han, Zijie Shen, An Guo, Lyuke Wang, Chunrong Fang, Zhenyu Chen, Wei Song

Narrows the network and uses offline neighborhood-density measurements to reduce processed points and neighbors.
Across two datasets, two architectures, and three classes, corruption AP rises 4.03 points on average, while latency and peak GPU memory fall 14.4% and 38.0%.

papers.abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg
authors: Koushik Swarna, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Lam Ngo, Wenxuan Li, Jiancheng Yang, Alan Yuille, Zongwei Zhou
bullets: Addresses broken or fragmented anatomical segmentations, especially for difficult structures.
Learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities and anatomical descriptions, without using medical images during correction.
Scales from 50 to 377 anatomical classes using existing predictions, and transfers across CT and MRI without retraining.
Across 13 public benchmarks, reported Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder CT cases and 10% for individual prostate MRI cases.
Corrected labels improve downstream segmentation, including one model’s Dice increase from 57.1% to 67.5%, and support annotation of 45,000 CT scans.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of DART. Training (top): a segmentation probability map predicted by a segmentation model is cropped, resized to 128×128×128, and corrupted with Gaussian noise. A 3D U-Net learns to reverse the corruption. Conditioning (middle, blue): an anatomical description is encoded by a frozen text encoder, projected by a trainable MLP, added to the timestep embedding, and injected into every residual block. Inference (bottom): probabilities are thresholded at 0.5 only to locate the crop. Their original values within the crop are resized, noised up to t∗, and denoised under the same description. The final result is thresholded to obtain a segmentation mask. Blue components are contributed by this work.

Figure 3: On five hard structures, DART outperforms the two strongest baselines on every metric. Predictions from TotalSegmentator, AtlasNet and WholeBodySeg on the external benchmarks, averaged over the three models and over the benchmarks that annotate each structure. The mean curve passes the mean input Dice of 0.53 at about 40% of the training examples. (b) The same runs grouped by anatomy.

Figure 12: Architecture of DART-Seg (Rokuss et al., 2026).
