papers.title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
papers.tldr: DART uses text-guided diffusion to share anatomical shape knowledge across classes and imaging modalities, correcting implausible segmentation predictions without new voxel-level training annotations.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction from sparse posed monocular frames requires reasoning over observations that vary jointly in viewpoint and time. Existing methods either predict Gaussian primitives from observation-aligned features or aggregate multi-frame information through compact latent queries. However, the former tightly couples Gaussian allocation to individual frames, while the latter does not explicitly structure observed evidence according to its temporal relation to the requested timestamp. Consequently, evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps can be difficult to align and integrate. We present \textbf{HiQGS}, a query-based hierarchical framework for feed-forward Gaussian scene reconstruction from sparse monocular frames. HiQGS introduces a \textbf{Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder} that organizes multi-resolution geometry-appearance visual features according to image location, observation time, and camera pose, thereby preserving complementary appearance and structural cues. Our \textbf{Time-Adaptive Decoder} use target timestamp queries the resulting hierarchical representation to retrieve relevant spatiotemporal evidence and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state. Experiments on static and dynamic scene reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy, validating the effectiveness of hierarchical visual encoding and target-time-aware Gaussian querying.
authors: Qiaowei Miao, Qifeng Cheng, Yijing Guo, Yuru Xiao, Ziqian Ni, Sheng Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of aligning visual evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps in feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction.
Uses a Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder to organize multi-resolution geometry and appearance features by image location, observation time, and camera pose.
Employs a Time-Adaptive Decoder that queries the representation at the requested timestamp and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state.
Experiments on static and dynamic scene benchmarks show strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy.
The method is designed for sparse monocular observations and explicitly targets both temporal and viewpoint variation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HiQGS. Given sparse posed frames from a monocular video, the Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder (HSE) organizes complementary multi-level geometry features and fine-grained appearance features into a hierarchical context. TP-RoPE grounds the context tokens by patch location, observation timestamp, and camera pose. The Time-Adaptive Decoder (TAD) adapt a scene-level Gaussian queries on the requested timestamp and retrieves evidence from both feature streams to predict the corresponding Gaussian scene state G(t∗). The resulting Gaussians are rendered from the target camera, while the target-independent context representation can be reused to decode multiple timestamps.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10K under the interpolation setting. HiQGS reconstructs the scene and renders held-out intermediate viewpoints with coherent geometry and fine-grained appearance details.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on the Waymo dataset. The target at +0.4 s lies within the temporal range of the context frames and evaluates temporal interpolation, whereas the target at +1.2 s lies outside this range and evaluates temporal extrapolation.
Figure 4: Qualitative depth comparison under sparse depth supervision. HiQGS recovers object geometry and delineates object boundaries more accurately than the baselines.
Table 3: Quantitative comparison of RealEstate10K interpolation and extrapolation with two context views. For baseline methods, we use the published results reported in TokenGS.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison of Waymo original-view RGB synthesis with 4 context frames and 16 target frames per 20-frame clip. For baseline methods, we use the published results reported in StreetForward.
Table 4: Ablation study on the Waymo dataset. PSNR and SSIM are reported on full-image evaluation.
Table 2: Quantitative comparison of Waymo sparse-depth accuracy against projected LiDAR depth.

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical spatiotemporal querying for feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction; directly advances 3D dynamic scene reconstruction.
papers.title: HiQGS: Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Querying for Feed-Forward Gaussian Reconstruction
papers.tldr: HiQGS reconstructs static and dynamic 3D scenes from sparse posed monocular frames by hierarchically organizing spatiotemporal evidence and querying it at the target time to predict Gaussian representations.

papers.abstract: While feed-forward models excel in static 3D geometry estimation, extending them to dynamic 4D scenes requires modeling visual geometry as a causally evolving state. Current methods typically rely on unordered temporal aggregation, which lacks the directional structure of physical time. Furthermore, existing supervision often treats geometry and motion as disjoint objectives, failing to exploit their inherent physical coupling. Consequently, they lack a unified constraint to effectively supervise temporal state transitions, leading to inconsistent 4D scene representations. To address this, we propose a feed-forward framework for causal 4D visual geometry learning from monocular videos. At its core, Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba augments temporal aggregation with directional state propagation. Through complementary Temporal-Spatial and Spatial-Temporal Scans, CSM continuously propagates geometry-aware states across frames to model spatiotemporal evolution. To align this causal state evolution with observable dynamics, we introduce Unified Motion Supervision. Rather than treating motion as an independent objective, UMS leverages geometry-aware predictions from the camera and depth heads to construct a unified forward motion field that is consistent with the underlying 3D structure. This geometry-grounded supervision explicitly constrains inter-frame state transitions, enabling stable states propagation across frames. Extensive evaluations on dynamic benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across video depth, camera pose, and optical flow estimation. These results validate that the synergy between the directional state propagation of Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba and Unified Motion Supervision effectively captures continuous scene evolution, significantly reducing temporal drift and reinforcing spatial-temporal consistency in 4D representation learning.
authors: Qiaowei Miao, Yijing Guo, Lipei Zhang, Qifeng Cheng, Yuru Xiao, Ziqian Ni, Sheng Yang
bullets: Targets temporal inconsistency in dynamic 4D reconstruction caused by unordered frame aggregation and separate geometry–motion supervision.
Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba propagates geometry-aware states directionally across frames using complementary temporal-spatial and spatial-temporal scans.
Unified Motion Supervision derives a geometry-consistent forward motion field from camera and depth predictions to constrain state transitions.
Evaluations on dynamic benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance for video depth, camera pose, and optical flow, with reduced temporal drift and improved spatiotemporal consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our causal spatiotemporal state evolution framework. Given an ordered monocular video, the model first extracts geometry-aware tokens with global context, and then applies Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba (CSM) to propagate these tokens through causal spatiotemporal state evolution. Complementary Temporal-Spatial Scan (TS Scan) and Spatial-Temporal Scan (ST Scan) update geometry-aware states across temporal and spatial dimensions while preserving the temporal order of scene evolution. The updated spatiotemporal representations parameterize camera extrinsics, intrinsics, pixel-aligned 3D point maps, and forward optical flow. Unified Motion Supervision (UMS) constructs a unified forward motion field with geometry-grounded supervision mechanism, enforcing geometry-aligned inter-frame state transitions.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of dynamic geometry reconstruction. Our method produces more accurate and temporally coherent geometry in dynamic regions, with sharper structures and fewer artifacts than existing feed-forward 4D methods.

Figure 2: Comparison of 4D modeling paradigms. Attention-based methods [25, 37] aggregate context through pairwise token affinities, while Image/Video Mamba [15, 14] applies generic bidirectional scans for visual representation learning. In contrast, CSM introduces geometry-aware causal scans that propagate states along the temporal order of the video. The complementary TemporalSpatial Scan and Spatial-Temporal Scan jointly model temporal evolution and spatial structure, enabling ordered spatiotemporal state propagation for monocular 4D visual geometry.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of optical flow estimation. Benefiting from our unified motion supervision, our model yields highly accurate motion fields with sharp boundaries. Notably, in the middle columns where moving objects occupy a small proportion and share high visual similarity with the background, Flow3r struggles to effectively detect the foreground optical flow. In contrast, our approach successfully disentangles these challenging motions.

Table 1: Methodological comparison of feed-forward 3D/4D visual geometry representations. We compare spatiotemporal modeling paradigms and supervision mechanisms across feed-forward 4D methods. Our model combines temporally ordered state propagation with Unified Motion Supervision (UMS), which provides geometry-grounded supervision by coupling inter-frame motion with evolving 3D geometry, rather than treating motion cues as isolated auxiliary objectives.
Table 2: Camera pose estimation on dynamic benchmarks. Best results are in bold, second-best are underlined.
Table 5: Ablation study on architectural components and training strategies. Evaluation is performed on Sintel. Best results are shown in bold.

Table 3: Video depth estimation on dynamic benchmarks. Metric δ < 1.25 is reported in %. Best results are in bold, and second-best results are underlined. “OOM” denotes out-of-memory under the same single-pass feed-forward inference setting.
Table 4: Comparison results of optical flow estimation.

papers.selection_reason: Causal spatiotemporal state evolution for monocular 4D reconstruction; directly advances 3D dynamic scene perception.
papers.title: Causal Spatiotemporal State Evolution for Monocular 4D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: A feed-forward monocular 4D reconstruction framework models dynamic scenes through causal spatiotemporal state propagation and geometry-grounded motion supervision.

papers.abstract: Generating high-fidelity, city-scale 3D environments plays a crucial role in applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and urban digital twins. However, the scarcity of real-world city-scale 3D training data forces existing methods to either stitch independently generated assets or learn from synthetic urban corpora, often sacrificing realism and global consistency. In contrast, 2D image data and their corresponding generative models are abundant and encode rich visual priors. To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a novel framework that leverages 2D diffusion models to generate globally consistent city-scale 3D textures without relying on city-scale 3D training data. Specifically, CityPaint integrates geometric priors with the generative power of 2D diffusion models, introducing a robust top-$K$ camera baking strategy for iterative texture projection. To address the artifacts of 2D-to-3D projection, we further propose a decoupled refinement mechanism that separately optimizes terrain and building textures. Extensive experiments show that CityPaint produces globally coherent textures with fine local details and achieves favorable results against strong baselines in both visual quality and cross-view consistency.
authors: Yuchen Zou, Lihuang Fang, Siyu Zhu, Xiao Hu
bullets: Addresses the lack of real-world city-scale 3D data and the resulting realism and consistency issues.
Combines geometric priors with 2D diffusion models for iterative texture projection.
Introduces robust top-K camera baking to guide texture generation across views.
Uses decoupled refinement to separately optimize terrain and building textures, reducing projection artifacts.
Experiments show fine local detail, global coherence, and favorable visual quality and cross-view consistency versus strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the CityPaint Pipeline (Stages 1 & 2). In Stage 1, we construct a 3D city mesh from OpenStreetMap (OSM) data and establish heightfield-aware camera trajectories for stable observation. In Stage 2, a conditional diffusion model iteratively synthesizes the scene guided by rendered depth and semantic maps. The generated views are accumulated into a global UV atlas using a face-wise top-𝐾 camera baking strategy to suppress artifacts from grazing angles.
Figure 5: Qualitative comparison of different city generation methods (zoom-in recommended for details).
Figure 6: Effect of top-𝐾 camera baking. Without it (left), facade textures are blurred and inconsistent; our method (right) produces sharper, coherent details.

Figure 3: Texture Refinement (Stages 3 & 4). Top: tile-wise UV denoising restores terrain continuity and removes seams. Bottom: object-centric orbit rendering recovers fine-grained building facade details.

Figure 4: Visual comparison of reference distributions. Top: Google Earth imagery often suffers from 3D reconstruction artifacts, blurred textures, and compression defects. Bottom: Our proposed CityWeb benchmark provides a cleaner, highfidelity, and photorealistic reference distribution.
Table 2: Quantitative comparison on geometric consistency (CE, DE) and visual fidelity (FID, KID, NIQE, BRISQUE) using Google Earth and CityWeb.
Table 3: Ablation study of core components.

papers.title: CityPaint: A Free Lunch from 2D Diffusion for City-Scale 3D Texturing
papers.tldr: CityPaint uses 2D diffusion priors to create globally consistent, detailed textures for city-scale 3D environments without city-scale 3D training data.

papers.abstract: 4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding. We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity. In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Li Gao, Yu Liu, Pengzhan Zhou
bullets: Addresses identity recovery when objects disappear inside opaque carriers and later reappear as new detections.
Uses geometry-weighted target-to-carrier transfer, per-node GRU memory during transport, and a two-time compatibility readout.
Achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy in the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, versus 0.570 for both no-memory controls.
Correctly re-links 36/36 held-out real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed-binding control.
Generalizes to unseen longer gaps, but remains limited by shared-carrier ambiguity and lacks end-to-end raw-video re-identification.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CVG-SGM. (1) Identical targets disappear with separately trackable carriers and reappear without continuous target tracks. (2) Nodes from GT, SAM2, or 4DSG pass through a track-indexed encoder and masked intra-frame attention. (3) Geometry-weighted cross-node transfer lets target-specific evidence enter a carrier’s recurrent state, updated by a shared GRU that maintains it through the gap; an auxiliary relation head reads these states under relation supervision. (4) At reappearance, routing weights rkc from current detection–carrier geometry combine with identity compatibility Bci from end-of-carry memory as ski = ∑ c∈C rkcBci to recover the historical identity.

Figure 1: Cross-visibility-gap identity persistence through remembered carrier relations. (a) Controlled 2t2c diagnostic: two identical targets bind to carriers cA and cB , are occluded while the carriers swap, and reappear near their current carriers at locations that are uninformative with respect to their own pre-gap positions. (b) The bindings persist as memory through the gap, re-linking each fresh detection to its identity; on unseen long gaps, FULL improves re-link accuracy from 0.576 (NOMEM) to 1.000. (c) Complementary human-operated cup-shuffle videos provide offline carrier-recovery evidence, while full real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level 2t2c re-linking is reported in Table 4.

Table 4: Real-data full re-linking over 120 RGB-D/SAM2 episodes. “All” descriptively combines 240 train/validation/test decisions; the held-out test contains 36 decisions. Controls are deterministic, while Neural FULL is identical across five training seeds.
Table 3: Mechanism ablations on controlled 2t2c re-linking. “Explicit msg.” denotes the general geometry-weighted cross-node message in Eq. (5).
Table 5: Instance-level roster scaling and carrier collision. “Sym. Range” spans Hard-mean, Hard-max, and Hard-last; entries report mean ± sample SD over seeds 0–2.

papers.selection_reason: Memory mechanism for persistent object identity across visibility gaps in 4D scene graphs, combining spatiotemporal memory with 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Cross-Visibility-Gap Identity Persistence for 4D Scene Graphs
papers.tldr: CVG-SGM preserves object identities across visibility gaps by storing target–carrier relational bindings, achieving perfect re-linking in controlled and reported real-feature episodes.

papers.abstract: 3D point clouds generation requires capturing both part-level layout and surface detail while preserving permutation equivariance. Existing latent generative models often encode an entire shape into a single vector, which limits their ability to retain part-level structure. We propose TokenFlow, a hierarchical flow matching framework that represents each shape as a set of latent tokens and couples a rectified flow over these tokens with a conditional flow over points. A bottleneck of $M \ll N$ learnable tokens aggregates global context through cross-attention at $O(NM)$ cost. On ShapeNet, TokenFlow achieves the best MMD and coverage across airplane, car, and chair, while obtaining 1-NNA comparable to the strongest baselines. On ModelNet, its learned latent set reaches the best reported linear-evaluation accuracy on ModelNet10. These results show that representing a shape as a set of latent tokens, aggregated at $O(NM)$ cost, provides an effective representation for 3D point cloud generation.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of retaining part-level structure when encoding an entire point cloud into one latent vector.
Represents each shape with M ≪ N learnable latent tokens and uses cross-attention to aggregate global context at O(NM) cost.
Combines rectified flow matching over latent tokens with conditional flow matching over points.
On ShapeNet, achieves the best reported MMD and coverage across airplanes, cars, and chairs, with 1-NNA comparable to leading baselines.
On ModelNet, the learned latent set attains the best reported linear-evaluation accuracy on ModelNet10.

figures.caption: Figure 1. TokenFlow pipeline. The prior flow transports Gaussian noise to a set of latent tokens over a Transformer encoder with several layers whose output is rescaled by a time-conditioned γ. The conditional point flow then decodes those tokens into a point cloud. A shared per-point MLP embeds each point and feeds two separately projected branches that are added, a code path in which the pooled token set and the time embedding give the scale and shift of an adaptive layer normalization over the point features, and a token path that cross-attends from the points to the latent tokens.
Figure 2. Qualitative comparisons against previous state-of-the-art methods.
Figure 3. Interpolation and extrapolation in the latent space.
Figure 5. Multi-class results generated by TokenFlow.
Figure 4. Illustration of CBA block. ”TE” means token embeddings while ”PE” represents point embeddings.

Table 4. Generation results on Airplane, Car, and Chair compared with baselines using 1-NNA as the metric. Lower is better. For clarity, the table is divided into two splits: the bottom corresponds to results from the past three years while the top corresponds to the earlier methods.
Table 2. Generation results using MMD, COV and JSD (↑/↓ as marked). MMD-CD and MMD-EMD are scaled by 103 and 102; JSD by 102. “–” marks unreported entries.
Table 3. Classification results on ModelNet10 (MN10) and ModelNet40 (MN40) datasets. Missing entries are denoted as “–”.

papers.selection_reason: Latent token flow matching for 3D point cloud generation; relevant to 3D vision generation.
papers.title: TokenFlow: Latent Token Rectified Flow Matching for 3D Point Cloud Generation
papers.tldr: TokenFlow generates 3D point clouds with hierarchical flow matching over a compact set of latent tokens, preserving global part structure and fine surface detail.

papers.abstract: Although deep learning-based point cloud denoising methods have demonstrated impressive results in recent years, their effectiveness usually degrades substantially in real-world scenarios where the noise distribution of test point clouds deviates from that of the training set. To address this challenge, we propose a test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework that enables existing denoising approaches to adapt to unknown noise patterns at test time without relying on additional supervision or retraining from source data. Taking a pre-trained denoising model and a test noisy point cloud as input, TTAD first employs a residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module to estimate the sample-specific noise distribution through analyzing the deviation between the noisy input and its pseudo-clean version denoised by the initial model. Then, a noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module is designed to build sample-specific noisy-noisier test-time training pair from the denoised point cloud, and update the model parameters over a few adaptation steps per sample at test time through contrastive learning. Furthermore, TTAD naturally extends to a continual TTAD (CTTAD) setting, facilitating efficient progressive refinement across sequential test samples with consistent noise distributions, while reducing the computational cost per sample. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the generalization ability of existing denoising models under unseen noise, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.
authors: Kun Jiang, Shida Fu, Fanhao Yi, Weiqing Li, Zhiyong Su
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when test-time noise differs from training noise.
Uses residual-driven noise modeling to estimate each input’s sample-specific noise distribution.
Constructs noisy–noisier training pairs for noise-aware contrastive adaptation over a few test-time steps.
Extends to continual TTAD for efficient progressive refinement on sequential samples with consistent noise.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improved generalization across multiple metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed TTAD framework. (a) The input noisy point cloud Xt is first denoised by a pre-trained model fθ to produce a pseudo-clean output Ỹ . (b) The residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module utilizes the residual noise N̂t = Xt − Ỹ to estimate the test-time noise distribution p(n) of Xt via a lightweight Gaussian mixture model (GMM). (c) The noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module generates a sample-specific noisy-noisier pair (X̃(1) t , X̃ (2) t ) of Ỹ . Within each test-time adaptation step, we first use the reconstruction loss Lrecon, identity loss Lid, and consistency loss Lconsist to update the online model fθonline via gradient descent at each iteration step. After that, the target model’s parameters θtarget are updated as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online model’s parameters θonline. Finally, we can use the final θtarget to obtain the adapted denoised result Yc = fθtarget (Xt).

Figure 1: Illustration of existing point cloud denoising methods and the proposed test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework. The source model (PointFilter [13]) fθ is trained on synthetic datasets with Gaussian noise. fθ performs well on noisy point clouds with seen (Gaussian) noise (a), but fails under unseen noise (b). The proposed TTAD framework significantly enhances the denoising performance of fθ by adapting it to unseen noise distributions during test time (c).

Figure 9: Performance comparison of different parameter update strategies on point clouds under Gaussian and unseen (Pulse, Exponential) synthetic noise. Results are averaged over three selected baseline denoising methods. Each group compares three strategies: Baseline (blue), Fully Update (orange), and EMA (green), evaluated by Chamfer Distance (top row) and Point-to-Mesh Distance (bottom row). Across all noise types, the adaptation strategy with EMA consistently improves generalization to unseen noise while maintaining source-domain performance on Gaussian noise.

Figure 3: Visualization of denoising results on different unseen 2% noise conditions. All baseline models (Score [11], PF [13], IPFN [14], LaPDA [34], and PD-LTS [29]) are trained on Gaussian noise and tested on inputs corrupted by (a) Pulse noise and (b) Exponential noise.

Figure 4: Visualization of denoising results on additional unseen 2% noise conditions. All baseline models (Score [11], PF [13], IPFN [14], LaPDA [34], and PD-LTS [29]) are trained on Gaussian noise and tested on inputs corrupted by (a) Laplace noise, (b) Uniform noise, and (c) Mixed noise.

Figure 5: Qualitative results on the Paris-Rue-Madame dataset [41]. TTAD improves denoising quality under real-world noise, removing scattered outliers, suppressing LiDAR scan-line artifacts, and restoring smooth and coherent surface structures.

Figure 6: Average processing time comparison. The baseline model (blue) has a constant low runtime. Standard TTAD (green) incurs a constant high cost due to per-sample re-initialization. In contrast, CTTAD (orange) becomes increasingly efficient by reusing and incrementally updating parameters across samples.

Figure 7: Performance comparison under unseen 2% Pulse noise, showing the average error tracked over a sequence of point clouds. While TTAD (green) shows stable, strong performance, CTTAD (orange) initially trades a minor performance dip for long-term gain, ultimately outperforming both baselines.

Figure 8: Visualization of noise direction distributions using spherical-to-polar projection. Left: Ground-truth input noise shows a structured pattern. Middle: Our RDNM captures the dominant directional structures effectively. Right: Standard Gaussian noise appears spatially uniform and lacks structure. Each dot represents a normalized noise direction projected to 2D; the denser areas indicate dominant noise directions.
Figure 10: Effect of GMM component number M on the distribution fitting error (blue curve) and computational time (red curve) under complex mixed noise.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation for point cloud denoising under unseen noise; directly fits test-time learning and 3D perception.
papers.title: Test-time Adaptation for Point Cloud Denoising under Unseen Noise
papers.tldr: TTAD adapts pre-trained point cloud denoisers to unseen test-time noise without source data or additional supervision by modeling noise and performing per-sample contrastive updates.

papers.abstract: The Jetson AGX Orin is a common computer for robots and vehicles, yet measured accuracy, speed and energy of current depth estimators on it are hard to find. We benchmark nine model families as of October 2026: the monocular Depth Anything V2 and 3, Depth Pro, MoGe-2, Metric3D v2 and UniDepth V2, and the stereo methods libSGM, NVIDIA ESS and Fast-FoundationStereo. Every method runs on the Orin as a TensorRT FP16 engine or native CUDA code at up to three input sizes, up to the full 5.7 MP, and is scored for metric accuracy against Middlebury 2014 ground truth (non-occluded pixels of the 10 scenes whose disparity stays below 256 px), GPU time, energy and licence. Stereo is far more accurate. At 30 fps, NVIDIA's ESS reaches 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; with more compute, Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33%. The best monocular models reach 12% with the true focal length (Depth Anything 3 Metric-L in 33 ms, Depth Pro in 803 ms), and 3.8-4.0% only with an oracle per-image scale (MoGe-2-L, UniDepth V2-B, Metric3D v2-L). Stereo error falls as the input resolution grows; no monocular model improves, and the metric scale of most drifts away from the truth outside their training resolution. At depth discontinuities, which AbsRel barely registers, the monocular models scatter 17-46% of the edge points between foreground and background, learned stereo 2-9% and libSGM at full resolution 1%. We give recommendations per frame-rate budget and release all code, per-scene results and engine build scripts.
bullets: Benchmark covers nine monocular and stereo depth model families on Orin using TensorRT FP16 or native CUDA, across resolutions up to 5.7 MP.
At 30 fps, NVIDIA ESS achieves 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33% with more computation.
With true camera focal length, the best monocular models reach about 12% AbsRel; oracle per-image scaling improves selected models to 3.8–4.0%.
Increasing resolution improves stereo accuracy but not monocular accuracy, whose metric scale often drifts outside training resolution.
At depth edges, foreground/background assignment errors are 17–46% for monocular models, 2–9% for learned stereo, and 1% for full-resolution libSGM.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks monocular and stereo depth estimators, which are core 3D perception methods relevant to 3D vision and embodied platforms.
papers.title: Which Depth Estimator for Jetson AGX Orin? A 2026 Benchmark of Monocular and Stereo Methods
papers.tldr: On Jetson AGX Orin, stereo depth methods are substantially more accurate and more reliable than monocular models, while meeting real-time budgets more effectively.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.
authors: Marcel Rogge, Ren\'e Schuster, Didier Stricker
bullets: Frustum visibility can count fully occluded Gaussians, weakening gradient statistics and suppressing needed densification.
The method filters statistics to views where a Gaussian actually contributes and normalizes by average contribution rather than raw view count.
Integrated with StopThePop, it improves all reported image-quality metrics on occlusion-heavy scenes, with up to 6% lower LPIPS.
It uses less than half as many Gaussians as a view-count normalizer and keeps counts bounded during longer training schedules.
On smaller benchmarks, it remains competitive while using a fraction of competitors’ Gaussian counts.

papers.selection_reason: Occlusion-aware densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting improves 3D scene representation, a key component of 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: An occlusion-aware densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting improves image quality while using substantially fewer Gaussians in heavily occluded scenes.

papers.abstract: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.
authors: Yunpeng Zhao, Haoxiang Zhang, Chao Liu
bullets: Models thermal evolution using shared scene-level and Gaussian-specific local latent states.
Uses differentiable RK2 integration to infer continuous dynamics and extrapolate beyond observed times.
Works with both static 3D and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, including deforming targets.
Supports novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction.
Experiments on real infrared and synthetic dynamic data show improved reconstruction and stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines.

papers.abstract: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones. Complementing this, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) to enforce learning from high-confidence dense signals. On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ (1-/5-shot), UGA sets new state of the art with an average +3.08 HM IoU over the strongest prior baseline.
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Shengtang Wu, Han Zhang, Ruike Cao, Yinsheng Li
bullets: Problem: Low-quality few-shot support samples can cause models to learn spurious geometric patterns.
Method: UG-Update estimates episode reliability from intra-class dispersion and selectively gates residual gradient updates.
Method: UB-Filter retains high-confidence pseudo-labels to provide denser, more reliable supervision.
Result: On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ under 1-/5-shot settings, UGA reports a +3.08 HM IoU improvement over the strongest prior baseline.
Scope: The approach targets generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation with unreliable support and pseudo-labeled supervision.

papers.abstract: Creating photorealistic human heads typically involves trade-offs between representation power, efficiency, and generalizability. Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on 3DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. However, their efficiency nonetheless depends on the number of rasterized Gaussians, and the time needed to optimize and prepare the head (the enrollment time) is often high. In light of this, we propose EGGHead, which introduces a novel Gaussian allocation algorithm that efficiently assigns Gaussians to the head's semantic regions given a fixed Gaussian budget. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds.
authors: Pilseo Park, Andrew Hou, Michel Sarkis, Ning Bi, Yiying Tong, Xiaoming Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between Gaussian-splatting fidelity, rendering efficiency, and enrollment time.
Introduces semantic-region-aware Gaussian allocation under a fixed Gaussian budget.
Generates the head in a single forward pass, reducing preparation requirements.
Reports improved reconstruction quality, novel-view synthesis, and rendering speed over prior single-image face-modeling methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Training Pipeline. We propose a single-image, generalizable, and lightweight Gaussian head model that adaptively allocates M Gaussians with minimal impact on rendering quality. Secs. 3.1–3.4 constitute the main reconstruction pipeline: GAM first allocates M Gaussians from the source image, Voronoi tessellation provides sparse geometric priors, and image/depth features are used to predict Gaussian attributes for rendering and refinement. Sec. 3.5 is trained in parallel to predict a density map supervised by the GAM-derived density map. It is independent of the main reconstruction pipeline during training and is used at inference time for density-based Gaussian allocation.
Figure 3. Inference-time Pipeline. During inference, we replace GAM with density-based sampling to reduce computation, and incorporate a Face Symmetry Module to complete occluded regions.
Figure 9. Ablation on Mirroring Gaussians. We show the effect of mirroring Gaussians for handling occluded regions. Our method naturally fills in the occluded areas.

papers.abstract: Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.
bullets: Targets DTM generation from satellite imagery affected by camera errors, changing illumination, and limited image disparity.
Optimizes a textured height map together with broad trajectory corrections and high-frequency pointing jitter.
Uses surface-projected patch NCC, a reflectance model, and shadow rendering to enforce cross-image consistency across illumination conditions.
Requires calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses, but no ranging/depth data or structural terrain priors.
Evaluated on four planetary datasets, with aligned terrain RMSEs ranging from 0.43 m to 16.18 m.

papers.abstract: Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework. Project page: https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream-page/
authors: Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yu-Lun Liu, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited novelty and simplicity of VLM-generated 3D assets and the API constraints of existing procedural systems.
Uses Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation to combine existing procedural algorithms with novel, photorealistic, seed-diverse assets.
Introduces an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline with semantic scene planning and deterministic frustum-guided grid placement.
Supports precise object placement, procedural population, animation, editability, and large-scale world construction.
Evaluations across 100 object and 20 scene tasks show improvements on four perceptual metrics, supported by diversity, ablation, and human-preference analyses.

papers.abstract: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. Experiments on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2 achieve state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods. By grounding image-space alignment in 3D planes, PlanarCityLoc enables more accurate aerial localization with lightweight, textureless city maps.
authors: Oussema Dhaouadi, Shao Jie Hu-Chen, Jakob Gollreiter, Samir Jusufi, Nikolas Rieger, Caroline Wendlandt, Christian Wender, Jingfeng Mao, Guangming Wang, Zuria Bauer, Marc Pollefeys, Daniel Cremers, Olaf Wysocki
bullets: Targets urban drone localization when GNSS is degraded, using textureless LoD city models.
Addresses ambiguous silhouettes and errors caused by imperfect building segmentation.
Initializes geometry-aware alignment, matches facade and roof planar patches, then refines camera pose with PnP.
Uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning.
Achieves state-of-the-art recall among evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2.

figures.caption: Figure 1. PlanarCityLoc overview. (a) Silhouette-based localization compares predicted building masks with renderings of the LoD model. (c) A coarse pose ξf is obtained through altitude initialization, cost-volume search, and multi-scale particle filtering. (d) We iteratively match visible LoD planes to image patches and refine the pose using PnPRANSAC on the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences. (e) Equal-weight rank aggregation of complementary metrics selects the final pose.

papers.title: PlanarCityLoc: Breaking Silhouette Ambiguity in LoD Aerial Localization via 3D Planes

papers.abstract: Neural networks that respect the symmetries of point clouds commonly compute high-order representations of the rotation group to improve their expressivity. Such models are known to be universal, and thus able to separate any pair of point clouds, when using representations of sufficiently high order, yet no precise bound on this order, as a function of the number of points, was previously known. We establish the first quadratic lower and upper degree bounds for polynomials that separate point clouds of n points up to rotations and permutations. By showing Tensor Field Networks and MACE can express all invariant polynomials of a given degree with sufficient representation order, we additionally derive the first explicit, quadratic bound on the representation order sufficient for these architectures to be complete, replacing previous existence results with concrete guarantees. We further show that, under local regularity assumptions, point cloud separation can be achieved with a message-passing-based model using invariants whose degree depends only on the size of a local neighborhood, rather than on the size of the full point cloud. Finally, we provide counterexamples showing MACE must compute high order irreducible representations to separate locally regular point clouds.
authors: Snir Hordan, Harm Derksen, Mircea Petrache, Nadav Dym
bullets: Establishes the first quadratic lower and upper bounds on polynomial degree needed to separate n-point clouds up to rotations and permutations.
Shows Tensor Field Networks and MACE can represent all invariant polynomials of a given degree with sufficient representation order.
Derives the first explicit quadratic completeness bound for the required representation order in these architectures.
Under local regularity assumptions, message-passing models can use invariants whose degree depends on neighborhood size rather than total point-cloud size.
Constructs counterexamples showing MACE may still require high-order irreducible representations for locally regular point clouds.

As t goes from 0 to 0.1 the pentagon moves counterclockwise and the triangle moves clockwise. The point clouds of w(0) and w( 2π15 ) are isometric. The latter is obtained from the first by rotation over 8π 15 and applying the permutation (1 2 3 4 5)(8 7 6) to the columns of w.
Figure 2: A family of regular point clouds which cannot be separated by mace without high degree/correlation order. See Proposition 12 for details.

Table 1: Smallest number K of points per cutoff ball from which local MACE with the readout equation 6–equation 7, irreducible degree ℓmax (rows), correlation order νmax (columns) and T iterations is provably not (SE(3)×Sn,Rρ,K)-complete, by Corollary 43. Each cell lists the thresholds for T = 1 /T = 2 /T = 3, in this order. All entries equal to 4 come from Lemma 41: the invariant channels of the model are unchanged underX 7→ −X , so it cannot tell a chiral cloud from its mirror image; 4 is the least possible value, since Rρ,K contains only one-point clouds when K ≤ 3 (Remark 40). Entries marked 4† were known before this work: with T = 1 the invariant channels are functions of distances (νmax = 1) or three-body invariants (νmax = 2), which are classically inversion invariant. Entries marked 4∗ rest on the same known mechanism, but the observation that two iterations with νmax = 1 still produce no pseudoscalar is stated here. Entries in bold are new: they come from the two-ring family of Definition 34 and Theorem 37, apply to models that can produce pseudoscalars, and grow linearly in ℓmax and like νTmax in νmax.

papers.selection_reason: Provides expressivity and degree bounds for equivariant point-cloud networks such as Tensor Field Networks and MACE, directly relevant to 3D vision.
papers.title: Degree Bounds for Separating Polynomial and Neural Invariants for Point Clouds
papers.tldr: The paper gives quadratic degree and representation-order bounds for invariant models that separate point clouds under rotations and permutations, while showing local methods can suffice under regularity assumptions.

papers.abstract: Generating reusable driving environments requires both controllable future observations and an explicit representation that supports rendering from different viewpoints, yet existing methods still recover explicit scenes from generated RGB videos through optimization for each sequence. To overcome these limitations, we present Drive2Gauss, a feedforward framework that converts jointly generated RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow into dynamic 4D Gaussian scenes. A Multimodal Video Generator predicts the three modalities from reference multiview images and future control signals. Furthermore, we introduce a Gaussian Query Decoder that uses depth to initialize sparse 3D queries and flow to associate the queries across time, and integrates appearance information through spatiotemporal feature aggregation and iterative query refinement. The reconstruction stage operates in a single feedforward pass without optimization for each scene. Extensive results on nuScenes demonstrate that our approach attains an FID of 6.38 and an FVD of 12.43 for future RGB generation, a PSNR of 29.91 dB when reconstructing its generated observations, and supports both direct rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing. Code and more visualizations are available at https://zttt04. github.io/Drive2Gauss_page/.
authors: Tong Zhao, Zhiyuan Han, Lin Chen, Bowen Xie, Yunxi Qiao, Bohan Li, Weiqing Xiao, Gen Li, Shu Han, Xuyang Dai, Cheng Bi, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
bullets: Addresses the need for reusable, controllable driving environments with explicit novel-view rendering.
A multimodal video generator predicts future RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow from multiview references and control signals.
A Gaussian Query Decoder initializes 3D queries from depth, links them over time using flow, and refines them with spatiotemporal appearance features.
On nuScenes, it reports FID 6.38, FVD 12.43, and 29.91 dB PSNR for reconstructing generated observations.
Supports rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing; evaluation is demonstrated on nuScenes and generated observations.

Depth and flow initialize 3D queries, while RGB features from multiple views and context frames are aggregated by the Spatiotemporal Feature Aggregation module. The updated queries are decoded into dynamic Gaussian primitives for rendering.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of feedforward 4D Gaussian reconstruction. For each method, the upper row shows the generated RGB observation used as input, while the lower row shows the corresponding rendering from the reconstructed 4D Gaussian scene. papers.abstract: We present PnP-Transformer, a neural pose solver designed as an iterative-free, differentiable alternative to classical PnP-RANSAC algorithms. PnP-Transformer regresses the 6D object pose by processing predicted semi-dense 2D-3D correspondence fields alongside confidence scores, while mapping geometric inputs into a continuous latent space. To evaluate its practical utility, we integrate PnP-Transformer into a zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipeline, where the correspondence module and pose solver are trained separately. PnP-Transformer achieves a 41.2% mean AR score with low latency (0.46 s/obj) on seven core BOP benchmark datasets, surpassing all prior baselines (such as RayPose with 39.1% AR) but one (Co-op with 58.4% AR). When the pose solver is replaced with EPnP-RANSAC (similar to Co-op) while keeping the correspondence module unchanged, the RANSAC alternative outperforms PnP-Transformer on six of the seven datasets by reaching 52.2% mean AR at a cost of an additional 60 ms per object, revealing an accuracy-latency trade-off. Code and pretrained models are available: https://github.com/ebylmz/pnp-transformer
bullets: Processes semi-dense 2D–3D correspondence fields and confidence scores in a continuous latent space.
Regresses 6D pose without iterative optimization and can be integrated into a zero-shot pipeline with separately trained components.
Achieves 41.2% mean AR at 0.46 s/object across seven core BOP datasets, outperforming most prior baselines but not Co-op.
EPnP-RANSAC reaches 52.2% mean AR with the same correspondence module, at an additional 60 ms/object cost.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Proposed architecture. (a) Method Overview: During an offline onboarding stage, RGB-D templates are rendered from the 3D CAD model and processed through a ViT encoder to acquire the template features. At inference, a query image crop is similarly processed using the same encoder to obtain query features. A transformer decoder and following heads then predict the patch-level match matrix M and displacement offset O across all query-template pairs. The template with the highest overall match confidence is selected, and its corresponding 2D–3D correspondence field with associated point-wise confidences (u,X, c) is fed into PnP-Transformer to regress the relative transformation ∆ = (R, t) ∈ SE(3) while producing the latent representation z of the recovered transformation. (b) PnP-Transformer Module: PnP-Transformer consists of three primary sub-modules: PnP-Encoder that processes input correspondences into a geometric latent vector z, Pose-Encoder used during training to map ground-truth target poses (Rgt, tgt) into target embeddings z̄, and Pose-Decoder that regresses final relative 6D pose parameters from z.

Fig. 2: Representative pose estimation results on BOP datasets. Predicted (red) and ground-truth (green) object contours overlaid on the input images. Rows 1 and 2 represent success cases for PnP-Transformer and PnP-RANSAC, respectively, while Rows 3 and 4 show their corresponding failure cases.

Fig. 3: Visualization of the learned pose latent space. (a) Trajectory Tracing : Background points represent camera poses sampled across an icosphere, color-coded by azimuth angle. The mapped trajectory of a continuous 360◦ camera orbit around the world Y-axis forms a closed loop in the latent space. (b) Latent Additivity : A relative displacement vector ∆z = zB − zA extracted from a source pose pair (blue) is applied to neighboring starting points zstart. The resulting transferred shifts (red arrows) demonstrate similar displacements.

papers.title: PnP-Transformer: A Neural Pose Solver for 6D Object Pose Estimation

papers.abstract: Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation.

papers.abstract: Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4--1.8\% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Integrated with direct aperture optimization, the pipeline generated plans in 15.2 minutes; in a blinded review, senior clinicians rated 14 of 15 plans acceptable without editing.

Compresses volumetric dose maps with an autoencoder, enabling 3D diffusion on a single GPU while preserving prescription values as exact scalar inputs.

Evaluated on 900 head-and-neck VMAT plans from five centers, achieving a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy and no systematic reference-dose bias among six frameworks.
With direct aperture optimization, plans were generated in 15.2 minutes and 14 of 15 were judged acceptable without editing by senior clinicians.

papers.abstract: Thin cylindrical objects offer little space for planar markers. We propose a dual-colour-stripe marker that uses the known curvature of an object to improve pose measurement with a single camera. The boundary between two colours provides a long centre line, while dots and printed edges supply features at different depths. We analyse how this depth separation improves the estimation of rotation about the cylinder axis, or roll. For a camera-facing marker at 15 cm, the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound on roll standard deviation is 2.00{\deg}for a flat marker, 0.38{\deg}for a single curved marker and 0.21{\deg}for a wrap-around marker. Monte Carlo roll RMS errors are within about 10% of the corresponding standard-deviation bounds. A first-order relation connects the sagitta of the curved marker to the roll sensitivity provided by a stereo baseline. The analytical and simulation results explain how curvature improves monocular measurement and provide a basis for designing marker geometry.
bullets: The marker addresses the limited space available for planar markers on thin cylinders.
Its colour boundary provides a long centre line, while dots and printed edges offer features at different depths.
Analysis relates curvature-induced depth separation to improved rotation-about-axis (roll) sensitivity.
At 15 cm, the roll standard-deviation bound is 2.00° for a flat marker, 0.38° for a curved marker, and 0.21° for a wrap-around marker.
Monte Carlo errors closely match the analytical bounds, supporting marker-geometry design based on curvature.

papers.abstract: Joint 4D reconstruction of a human and object from a monocular video is essential for understanding how people interact with their environment. While recent methods have made noticeable progress, capturing such human-object interactions remains difficult due to two main challenges. First, a video typically contains composite semantic context spanning multiple interaction phases, making it difficult to track the temporal changes of the interaction in the reconstruction. Second, under human-object occlusion, a single-view observation contains incomplete visual information about the interaction, resulting in geometrically inconsistent reconstructions. To address these challenges, we introduce HORIA, built upon two core designs. First, we decompose the entire input video into temporally grounded and semantically distinct interaction phases with motion-aware captioning, obtaining a specific text description for each phase. Second, conditioned on these text descriptions of the interaction, we propose an interaction-aware re-rendering that compensates for the limited single-view observation. Specifically, we render the initially reconstructed 4D human and object from novel viewpoints and refine the renderings with a text-to-video diffusion prior, which provides auxiliary novel-view supervision beyond single-view cues. As a result, our framework produces temporally coherent and accurate 4D reconstructions under diverse interaction scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Hyeongjin Nam, Taeryung Lee, Daniel Sungho Jung, Kyoung Mu Lee
bullets: Addresses interaction-phase changes and incomplete geometry caused by human-object occlusion in single-view video.

Provides auxiliary supervision beyond the original monocular observations.
Reports accurate, temporally coherent reconstructions across diverse interactions with state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for AR/VR and real-time communication applications, yet remains challenging when reconstructing 3D scenes from limited viewpoints. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels in dense-view scenarios, it suffers from overfitting and geometry degradation under sparse inputs. Current approaches often tackle these problems from a local perspective, addressing either data quality or training regularization individually, lacking a unified and interpretable framework for systematic improvement. We introduce a new perspective that reframes sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning viewpoint, treating each Gaussian primitive as a neuron and leveraging deep learning regularization techniques. Under this unified framework, our approach generates more effective supervision from scarce observations through two strategies: (1) data-related supervision enrichment via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization; and (2) training-time regularization via motion-aware dropout and early stopping, which suppress overfitting while preserving dynamic-scene stability. Extensive experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward baselines. Our system won first place in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 challenge.
authors: Lejia Ye, Bin Wu, Jingjing Gao, Yiyang Wu, Xiaohu Zhang
bullets: Reframes each 3D Gaussian primitive as a neuron, providing a unified perspective on sparse-view reconstruction.
Enriches supervision with optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization.

Outperforms reported optimization-based and feed-forward baselines on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset.
Won first place in the challenge’s sparse-view track.

papers.abstract: Fine industrial robotic manipulation requires 6D pose, scale, and an operation-ready 3D model. Existing industrial pose estimation relies on CAD models, object-specific training data, or stable workcells, limiting use with unseen objects; zero-shot methods suffer from single-view occlusion, generative bias, and scale uncertainty. We present OV-PEAR, an observation-verified framework for 3D reconstruction and pose-scale estimation of unknown industrial objects. Its three-stage object-centric pipeline: (1) segments RGB-D instances and generates object-level 3D hypotheses; (2) anchors them to the robot frame via appearance-aware view retrieval, explicit scale search, and visibility-sensitive registration; (3) back-projects multi-view RGB-D evidence into the object-canonical frame to verify voxel occupancy, suppress hallucinations, and produce reusable trusted object models. On BOP-Industrial, OV-PEAR achieves 0.657 average AR and improves pose and voxel-level geometric consistency in real scenes; real-robot connector assembly reaches 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success. The model library and pose-scale log enable short-term object-level state maintenance at 0.02 ms/frame.
authors: Guoqin Tang, Qingxuan Jia, Yichen Tan, Zihang Lv, Ruiquan Wang, Zeyuan Huang, Gang Chen

Achieves 0.657 average AR on BOP-Industrial and reports 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success in real-robot connector assembly.
Maintains short-term object-level state at 0.02 ms/frame using a model library and pose-scale log.

papers.abstract: Robotic simulation, navigation, and inspection need photorealistic and geometrically accurate maps. Radiance fields achieve photorealism, but building them from robot data raises three challenges. A robot's trajectory serves its task, not reconstruction, so images from few viewpoints leave the geometry under-constrained. Residual errors in camera poses and intrinsics blur the map. The map's GPU memory grows with scene size, which limits its level of detail in large scenes. We present \textbf{SpaRV}, a \textbf{Spa}rse \textbf{R}adiance \textbf{V}oxel map rendered by differentiable ray marching, which lets irregular LiDAR scans supervise it alongside images. LiDAR depth and occupancy anchor the under-constrained geometry, and normal and smoothness regularizers keep it smooth between LiDAR points. To correct camera errors, SpaRV alternates map training with photometric optimization of the camera poses and focal lengths. To bound GPU memory in training and rendering, SpaRV holds one submap at a time at full resolution and the rest at coarser octree levels. Experiments show that SpaRV keeps the geometry consistent away from the captured trajectory and sharpens textures by optimizing the camera parameters. On one 24\,GB GPU, SpaRV reconstructs a university campus captured in 63{,}582 images and simulates other cameras and LiDARs. Our code will be released at \url{https://github.com/hku-mars/SpaRV}.
authors: Jianheng Liu, Yunfei Wan, Fangming Cheng, Xiangyu Hong, Zuhao Zou, Haotian Li, Longji Yin, Chunran Zheng, Jiarong Lin, Fu Zhang
bullets: Addresses under-constrained geometry from task-driven trajectories, camera calibration errors, and GPU-memory limits in large scenes.

Maintains one full-resolution submap while storing others at coarser octree levels, bounding memory during training and rendering.
Reconstructs a university campus from 63,582 images on one 24 GB GPU and supports novel-camera and novel-LiDAR simulation.

papers.title: SpaRV: Sparse Radiance Voxels for Scalable Geometrically Consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering

papers.abstract: Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy models can be trained without 3D labels by rendering their predictions into the images and supervising them with 2D pseudo labels. In sparse Gaussian representations trained this way, Gaussian positions are learned only through pixel-wise rendering losses, which we hypothesize give small foreground objects little weight. In trained GaussianFlowOcc models, the Gaussian density on foreground voxels is on average only 1.62 times that on background voxels. We propose a training-only foreground attraction loss that back-projects foreground pseudo-label pixels with pseudo depth and pulls nearby Gaussians toward these 3D points, favoring Gaussians that already predict the target class; the inference network is unchanged. On Occ3D-nuScenes, the loss raises this concentration to 2.40 over three seeds. Over three seeds, the mean foreground IoU increases from 6.29 to 6.96 and is higher for each seed, whereas the change in mean mIoU (13.53 to 13.82) is within the seed-to-seed variation of the baseline. Single-run ablations further indicate that pseudo-label targets outperform targets placed at ground-truth voxels and that acting on the Gaussian positions alone is not sufficient, and a single-seed test shows that the model degrades less when fewer Gaussians are kept at inference.
bullets: Weak 2D rendering supervision underweights foreground objects, leaving foreground Gaussian density only 1.62× that of background voxels.
The proposed loss back-projects foreground pseudo-label pixels using pseudo-depth and pulls nearby, class-compatible Gaussians toward them during training.
On Occ3D-nuScenes, foreground density rises to 2.40× background density, and mean foreground IoU improves from 6.29 to 6.96 across three seeds.
Mean mIoU increases only from 13.53 to 13.82, within baseline seed-to-seed variation.
Ablations favor pseudo-label targets over ground-truth voxel targets; the method also shows less degradation when fewer Gaussians are retained at inference.

papers.title: Where Do the Gaussians Go? Foreground Attraction for Camera-Based Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy

papers.abstract: We introduce ReDT, a feed-forward visual geometry transformer designed to scale multi-view reconstruction to high-definition (HD) inputs. Existing visual geometry transformers are typically trained at fixed, standard definition (SD) resolutions and exhibit degraded reconstruction quality and poor computational scaling to high input resolutions. While recent efficient architectures reduce the complexity of inter-frame attention, expensive intra-frame and encoder attention remain largely unaddressed, making HD reconstruction impractical with existing architectures. ReDT addresses both limitations with a resolution-aware architecture designed to scale to high-resolution inputs. The key idea of ReDT is to first map each view to a fixed-size set of basis tokens, compute correspondences in this compact constant-size basis space, and then project the outputs back to the original resolution for dense prediction. By decoupling the internal representation from input resolution during attention, ReDT substantially reduces the computational cost of high-resolution 3D reconstruction and improves model performance at all resolutions. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets spanning SD to FHD (2K) show that ReDT outperforms state-of-the-art visual geometry transformers in both reconstruction quality and computational efficiency. For instance, on the ETH3D (2K) dataset, ReDT achieves a $16\times$ speedup, a $34\%$ reduction in peak GPU memory usage, and a $33\%$ reduction in chamfer distance over VGGT-$\Omega$. \href{https://redt.github.io}{Project Website.}
authors: Abteen Arab, Guile Wu, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Existing visual geometry transformers scale poorly to HD inputs because intra-frame and encoder attention remain expensive.
ReDT maps each view to a fixed-size set of basis tokens, computes correspondences in this compact space, and projects results back for dense prediction.
Experiments across SD to FHD (2K) datasets show improved reconstruction quality and computational efficiency at all tested resolutions.
On ETH3D at 2K, ReDT reports 16× faster inference, 34% lower peak GPU memory, and 33% lower Chamfer distance than VGGT-Ω.

papers.abstract: To determine where computation is needed in volumetric segmentation networks, we analyze block-level redundancy and stage-wise token-mixer contribution. Centered Kernel Alignment reveals high input-output representational similarity within blocks of representative convolutional, hybrid, and Transformer-style segmentation networks. Similarity-guided pruning reduces their parameter counts by 39-75% while decreasing mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points. To examine token mixers within blocks, we introduce Anatomical Relation Distortion, which quantifies how bypassing a mixer distorts feature relations between labeled anatomical positions. Applied to an unpruned candidate architecture, Centered Kernel Alignment indicates high representational redundancy in intermediate encoder mixers, whereas Anatomical Relation Distortion shows that they contribute little and the bottleneck mixer most. These findings motivate SlimFormer++, which uses Selective Mixing blocks with windowed Mamba mixing in the first encoder stage and only residual channel MLPs in deeper stages. At the bottleneck, Augmented Mixing injects similarity-weighted sparse long-range context into the axial taps of a depthwise convolution at cost linear in voxel count. Evaluated against 12 baselines across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets (1,809 cases), SlimFormer++ achieves the highest mean Dice (87.84%) and lowest mean HD95 (6.50 mm) with the fewest parameters (5.98 million). These results support stage-aware token mixing as a design strategy for improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in volumetric segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/WHHHHHY822/SlimFormerPlusPlus
authors: Yang Hong, Lei Zhang, Zhihong Liu, Jianqing Mo, Xujiong Ye
bullets: Block-level redundancy analysis shows 39–75% parameter pruning can reduce mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points.
Anatomical Relation Distortion indicates early and intermediate encoder mixers contribute little, while bottleneck mixing is most important.
The model uses windowed Mamba mixing early, residual channel MLPs in deeper stages, and augmented sparse long-range mixing at the bottleneck.
Across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets, it reports 87.84% mean Dice and 6.50 mm mean HD95 with 5.98M parameters.
The findings support stage-aware token mixing as a strategy for efficient volumetric segmentation.

papers.abstract: Turning a moving-camera perspective video into a 360{\deg} video requires more than just generating content outside the input frame: observations revealed over time must be preserved, unseen regions completed, and the resulting scene kept consistent as the camera viewpoint changes. Existing methods assign these different requirements to a single conditional video model, requiring them to be jointly learned from panoramic video data. We instead present a modular, 3D-driven framework that distributes these three responsibilities across specialized components, all connected through a shared scene representation. Input observations are reconstructed explicitly in 3D, while a pretrained panoramic image model completes unobserved content from a selected panoramic render. This generated content is lifted into the shared 3D scene, where it remains spatially anchored across camera viewpoints. Without requiring any additional panoramic-video training, our framework achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on a static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set. These results support our decomposed, 3D-driven formulation as a promising alternative to direct video generation in this setting.
authors: Michael Wakeham, Mrinmoy Kumar Das, Wenqi Wang, Ayush Tewari, Boqing Gong, Deepti Ghadiyaram
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving observed content, completing unseen regions, and maintaining consistency as the camera moves.
Explicitly reconstructs input observations in 3D and uses a pretrained panoramic image model to generate missing content.
Lifts generated content into a shared 3D scene representation, spatially anchoring it across viewpoints.
Achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on the static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set.
Does not require additional panoramic-video training; evaluation is scoped to static scenes.
