To complete as much unobserved scene content as possible, we select the frame with the least observed coverage and complete missing regions using a panoramic image model (Sec. 3.2). After estimating and aligning its depth, the completed panorama is lifted into an unobserved-region 3DGS and combined with the observed-region 3DGS, allowing the completed scene to persist when rendered along the input camera trajectory. papers.title: A 3D-Driven Framework for Moving-Camera Perspective-to-360{\deg} Video Generation

papers.abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe interaction bottleneck. Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a small set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
authors: Mohammad Omama, Aeyan Ashraf, Sandeep Chinchali
bullets: Addresses the interaction bottleneck of deep feature matchers on edge devices, where each query must otherwise process every database image independently.
Defers inter-image interaction to the final layers, separating reusable intra-image Context Blocks from lightweight online Interaction Blocks.
Introduces E-SToRE, which reduces spatial tokens before cross-image interaction using entropy-guided token reduction and expansion.
Evaluated on HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen.
LateMatch achieves over 2× lower effective computation; E-SToRE adds 10–14% savings with negligible accuracy degradation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Rethinking visual localization with cacheable image matching via LateMatch. (A) Standard visual localization pipelines require matching a single query image against Top-K (e.g., K = 100) retrieved database images. (B) Traditional matching architectures interleave intra-image context building and interimage cross-attention across all layers, preventing any caching and causing a severe computational bottleneck. (C) Our proposed LateMatch architecture breaks this bottleneck by deferring cross-image interaction to the final layers, decoupling the network into offline-cacheable Context Blocks (CBs) and online Interaction Blocks (IBs), reducing the effective compute cost by over 2× without sacrificing much on performance.

papers.title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
papers.tldr: LateMatch makes visual localization more efficient by caching image-specific processing and limiting online cross-image matching, cutting computation by over 2× with minimal accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Driving-scene reconstruction via feed-forward Gaussian splatting from sparse multi-view images remains challenging due to two factors. First, cross-camera photometric inconsistency, caused by variations in exposure, ISP, and illumination, can be incorrectly absorbed into Gaussian geometry. Second, unreliable local geometric supervision arises from normal-based constraints near depth discontinuities. To address these issues, we present \textbf{MCSplat}, a multi-view consistent feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for driving scenes. MCSplat constructs a canonical appearance space from depth-guided multi-camera correspondences to decouple geometry learning from camera-specific appearance. A multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer restores raw camera appearance from canonical renderings, enabling photometric supervision without contaminating Gaussian geometry. To improve local geometric reliability, we estimate Fisher-information-based uncertainty from photometric sensitivity and use it to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and generalization across driving datasets. Geometry-oriented evaluations further reveal enhanced cross-view depth consistency and local surface-normal agreement, while qualitative results show fewer geometric artifacts and more coherent structures across overlapping views.
authors: Yifei Wang, Wei Tian, Wenhua Bao, Jia Zhou, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Jianhua Wu, Shuai Yuan, Zhipeng Zhang, Xingliang Liu, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Bingzhao Gao
bullets: Addresses photometric inconsistency across cameras and unreliable normal supervision near depth discontinuities.
Builds a canonical appearance space using depth-guided correspondences to decouple geometry from camera-specific appearance.
Uses a multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer to restore raw camera appearance for cleaner photometric supervision.
Estimates Fisher-information-based uncertainty to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision.
Reports better reconstruction quality, cross-view depth consistency, surface-normal agreement, and fewer geometric artifacts across driving datasets.

Compared with LiDAR depth, it also yields improved depth estimation in pedestrian regions. On the planar poster surface, our method avoids texture-induced depth ambiguity, producing a more reasonable depth prediction.

papers.abstract: Resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles need scene memories that localize a camera and render nearby views without a desktop GPU. Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and capacity-sensitive. We present LENS, an edge scene-memory acceleration system on the AMD KR260 that brings an ACEsplat-style workload to a low-power FPGA/ARM platform. Rather than proposing a new scene model, LENS co-designs the two dominant kernels with the board data path: an INT16 SCR accelerator that preserves pose accuracy, and a bit-exact fixed-point ordered 3DGS renderer that rewrites alpha transmittance as a log-sum-exp recurrence and removes provably useless streamed Gaussians. All LENS latency, power, and quality results are board-measured. The SCR engine preserves DSAC* localization accuracy at 25.42 ms, the on-board renderer reaches 34.11 dB on Cambridge against ACEsplat's 33.20, novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K reaches 27.84 dB against 26.11, and all ten Wayspots scenes reach the ACEsplat rendering target. LENS wins performance per watt over a Jetson Orin NX on every deployment task, by 1.9x to 5.7x at about a quarter of the power, and is faster in absolute latency on localization and Wayspots rendering. On-device training reaches ACEsplat-level quality but not the GPU's time or energy, marking the remaining boundary for a future training accelerator.
authors: Que Haohua, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
bullets: Targets GPU-dependent scene memories for resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles.
Co-designs an INT16 scene-coordinate regression accelerator and a fixed-point, bit-exact ordered 3DGS renderer for the AMD KR260.
Preserves DSAC* localization accuracy with 25.42 ms latency and achieves 34.11 dB on Cambridge and 27.84 dB on RealEstate10K.
Outperforms the Jetson Orin NX by 1.9×–5.7× in performance per watt at roughly one-quarter the power.
On-device training matches ACEsplat quality but remains slower and less energy-efficient than GPU training.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.
authors: Hyebin Kim, Hwasik Jeong, Joonhyuk Park, Gyeongjin Kang, Jungwoo Kim, Younghyun Kim, Eunbyung Park
bullets: Targets the difficulty of recovering fine-grained geometry and appearance in feed-forward 3DGS.
Uses view-wise grouping for efficient neighboring-view interaction and 3D spatial grouping to reconnect geometrically related tokens.
Uses rendering reconstruction error as explicit feedback to refine structures and appearance beyond one-pass prediction.
Generates a compact set of Gaussians to retain fine-detail benefits without unnecessarily increasing primitive counts.
Reports state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method Overview. Compact Gaussian generation predicts fewer Gaussians per token than existing pixel-aligned methods, maintaining a compact 3DGS representation. Finally, direct error feedback incorporates reconstruction errors obtained by rendering the input views to further refine token representations.

papers.abstract: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io
authors: Yizheng Xie, Yalda Foroutan, George Shramko, Daniel Rebain, Shrisudhan Govindarajan, Andrea Tagliasacchi
bullets: Addresses the failure of static 3D representations under object interactions and the sequence-replay limitation of time-conditioned dynamic methods.
Decomposes the scene into a shared static Gaussian base plus per-object slots representing two states, such as on/off.
Differentiably discovers which Gaussians belong to each object state without manual annotations.
Allows users to freely combine learned slot states and render the resulting scene from arbitrary viewpoints.
On a new casual-capture dataset, it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality.

papers.abstract: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.
authors: Yimeng Dou, Adam M. Saunders, Andre T. S. Hucke, Michael E. Kim, Adam W. Anderson, Eric R. Tkaczyk, Bennett A. Landman, Daniel Moyer
bullets: Targets active-light capture settings such as camera flashes, underwater vehicles, and endoscopy, where light direction changes with camera pose.
Separates per-point color into albedo and spherical-harmonic illumination within NeRF or other NVS pipelines.
Uses differentiable SH evaluation and closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion for joint optimization of lighting, albedo, and geometry.
Analytically generalizes illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining.
Achieves the best reported mean PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS across five held-out scenes among compared methods.

Capture), the method factors appearance into albedo and illumination before volumetric rendering. The albedo branch (IIa) samples a global coordinate position x through a scene MLP to predict per-sample albedo ρ(x), density σ(x), and a global normal n from the density gradient. The illumination branch (IIb) starts from a single trainable l=4 SH code Esh ∈ R25×3 shared across all frames, and rotates it analytically into each frame via the Wigner-D matrix D(l) derived from the known rotation Rt ∈ SO(3), so that the rotated coefficients become Ẽt. Albedo ρ(x) and illumination factor α(xc,nc) are multiplied into the factorized radiance ρ′ = α⊙ρ and composited through volumetric rendering, producing a full render C(r), a clean albedo render∑ i wi ρ (i.e., a render without illumination effects), and an illumination map α.

Fig. 1. (a) Robots that operate in dark environments, such as subterranean exploration (SubT challenge) [1], deep-water surveys by the remotely operated vehicle Hercules [2], and nighttime driving [3] rely on onboard lights that move with the platform. (b) In standard novel view synthesis (NVS, left), hundreds of images are captured while the camera moves around the scene under fixed illumination field L, and a radiance field is reconstructed with methods such as NeRF, 3DGS, or their derivatives. However, in co-located capture (right), the camera and a light source are rigidly attached, so the surface illumination changes with every pose, as the light source is moving as well. We model this moving illumination through the irradiance E(n), so the irradiance for a given normal is computed by analytically rotating the coefficients with a Wigner-D matrix of the known camera motion, where the residual spatial variation from the near-field source is absorbed by a learned per-sample MLP (see III for more details). papers.abstract: Recovering metric 3D geometry from images is fundamentally ill-posed due to perspective projection ambiguity. Current geometry models incorporate supplied or predicted intrinsics during inference, but do not use them to supervise model adaptation. To refine these predictions, test-time adaptation (TTA) typically relies on external depth measurements. In this paper, we instead use camera intrinsics as an output-side geometric verifier. Comparing the point cloud's viewing rays with those defined by the known intrinsics yields a direct measure of geometric inconsistency. We propose \textit{IntriAdapt}, a TTA framework that minimizes this closed-form geometric residual. By optimizing a lightweight LoRA adapter on a frozen geometry foundation model, our method aligns the prediction with the specific camera model without depth sensors or external priors. We further extend this approach to video sequences, demonstrating that adapting a short sequence generalizes to other sequences captured by the same camera. The adapted model processes held-out images in a feed-forward pass, without repeating optimization for each frame. Experiments on ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks across multiple base models show that \textit{IntriAdapt} consistently outperforms both unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.

bullets: Addresses perspective ambiguity in image-based metric 3D geometry estimation.

Optimizes a lightweight LoRA adapter while keeping the geometry foundation model frozen.
Sequence adaptation generalizes across images from the same camera, enabling feed-forward inference on held-out frames.
Across ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks, it outperforms unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is emerging as a practical way to build a representation for robotics applications. However, deploying it on real-world platforms exposes multiple challenges. Rapid maneuvers of a robot induce motion-blurred images, which corrupt the reconstructed geometry and cause camera pose drift. Furthermore, the number of Gaussians grows without bound during continuous online mapping. In this study, we present RoMo-GS, an online 3DGS system designed to address these challenges. Instead of averaging N discrete sub-frames as in prior motion blur-aware 3DGS, we analytically integrate each projected Gaussian over the exposure interval, yielding an O(1) complexity per Gaussian. Building on this, we bound the Gaussians' growth with a Hessian-based pruning score, while jointly refining pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam and an online LM step over the Gaussians. On multiple public datasets and a self-collected dataset, RoMo-GS matches or exceeds offline deblurring 3DGS methods in rendering quality while running 15--150x faster, and operates online at competitive quality with about 20% fewer Gaussians than the online 3DGS baseline.
authors: Sangwoo Jung, Di Deng, Jiahui Fu, Laura Herlant, Ayoung Kim, Yafei Hu
bullets: Addresses geometry corruption and camera-pose drift caused by rapid robot motion, plus unbounded Gaussian growth during continuous mapping.
Analytically integrates each projected Gaussian over the exposure interval, achieving O(1) complexity per Gaussian instead of averaging discrete sub-frames.
Uses Hessian-based pruning to limit Gaussian growth and jointly optimizes pose, velocity, and Gaussians.
On multiple public and self-collected datasets, matches or exceeds offline deblurring 3DGS rendering quality while running 15–150× faster.
Operates online with competitive quality using about 20% fewer Gaussians than an online 3DGS baseline.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation remains challenging due to the loss of fine-grained details and limited adaptability to varying scene structures. In this paper, we propose SAP-Depth, a novel architecture based on Scene-Adaptive Probabilistic. Unlike traditional methods, we introduce a Dynamic Bins mechanism powered by a Learnable Parameter Predictor, which adaptively estimates scene-specific depth distributions conditioned on the input image context. Furthermore, a Bin-wise Probability Distribution Decoder is designed to effectively fuse multi-scale representations to predict dense depth probability distributions, significantly enhancing boundary sharpness and structural recovery. Through the collaborative coupling of these proposed modules, our model achieves dynamic prediction of scene-specific depth distributions. Extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset show that SAP-Depth outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, particularly in its ability to better preserve complex edge details. Further, tests on the Make3D dataset validate the model's excellent generalization capability and robustness.
authors: Bowen He, Li Zhang, Yujie Chen, Chang Cheng
bullets: Addresses lost fine details and limited adaptability across varying scene structures.
Uses Dynamic Bins with a Learnable Parameter Predictor to estimate image-conditioned, scene-specific depth distributions.
Employs a Bin-wise Probability Distribution Decoder to fuse multi-scale features and predict dense depth probabilities.
Reports improved accuracy and complex-edge preservation on KITTI, with generalization and robustness validated on Make3D.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of our proposed SAP-Depth framework. The system consists of two main components: a depth network and a pose network. (a) The depth network utilizes a shared encoder to extract multi-scale features, which are then decoupled into two branches: the LP Predictor predicts global adaptive depth bins, while the HAP-FAM estimates pixel-wise bin probabilities. The final highquality depth map is generated by the linear combination of the predicted bins and probabilities. (b) During training, the pose network takes adjacent frames (It, It′ ) to estimate the 6-DoF relative pose Tt→t′ , enabling the photometric reconstruction loss for self-supervision. 3 Proposed Method

papers.abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Han Zhang, Yixuan Lin, Yuyang Hou, Bin Wu, Ruike Cao, Li Xiao, Yinsheng Li

Proposes HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method using task, obligation, and supervised control-replay rewards.
HORN achieves 75.1 ± 1.0% on challenges and 77.2 ± 0.8% overall, without degrading control accuracy.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.

papers.abstract: AI-based 3D generation models such as Hunyuan 3D and Meshy can produce visually appealing 3D shapes from an image or text prompt.However, they typically focus on an object's external appearance, often producing incomplete or implausible interior geometry. Consequently, the generated shapes are not guaranteed to be functionally valid, limiting their direct use in downstream applications such as simulation and fabrication. In this paper, we present a computational approach to functionalize AI-generated 3D shapes through interior geometry construction. Our key observations are that a part's functional role defines its interior geometry, and such geometry is often smooth, relatively simple, and closely related to the part's external shape. Inspired by these observations, we introduce an interior-aware part graph to encode information necessary for constructing interior geometry within an AI-generated 3D shape, and build the graph via VLM-based shape segmentation and graph attribute inference. Guided by the graph, we model the interior geometry of each part as a generalized cylinder and infer its parameters from the part's external geometry through an optimization. The resulting 3D shapes are functionally valid while preserving their AI-generated external appearance. We demonstrate our approach on a variety of AI-generated 3D shapes, including vessels, containers, and storage furniture, and fabricate selected examples for functional validation.
authors: Haoyu Tang, Fancheng Gao, Kan Chen, Peng Song
bullets: AI-generated meshes often look convincing externally but have incomplete or implausible interiors, limiting simulation and fabrication use.
An interior-aware part graph captures the information needed to construct functional interior geometry.
VLM-based segmentation and attribute inference build the graph from each generated shape.
Each part’s interior is modeled as a generalized cylinder, with parameters optimized from its exterior geometry.
Experiments on vessels, containers, and storage furniture—including fabricated examples—demonstrate functional validation.

(b) Segment the teapot into four parts using a learning-based method. (c) Assign each segmented part (rendered in red) to one or multiple functional components. (d) Refine the body–spout part by splitting it into two parts (i.e., a body and a spout), corresponding to the body and spout components. (e) Merge the knob part and lid base part into a single part, corresponding to the lid component. (f) The segmented teapot consists of four functional parts.

Guided by the graph, we (d) construct interior geometry for each identified part and compose the parts’ interior geometries together with the AI-generated exterior surface to form (e) the output shape.

papers.abstract: Collision detection for complex non-convex objects is a bottleneck in physics simulation, virtual reality, and robotics. Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer proximity and penetration queries efficiently, but their greedy leaf-sphere construction is sequential and computationally expensive, which limits both large-scale preprocessing and runtime use. In this work, we present ML-IST, a machine-learning-based method that reformulates leaf-sphere generation as a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback corrects the coarse prediction and fills residual gaps at finer scales, and a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Averaged over the test set, a single-GPU implementation of ML-IST reduces mean leaf-generation time by a factor of $2.0$--$2.6$ over single-core CPU construction across target capacities of 64--512 spheres, and qualitative results on complex models show multiscale sphere distributions that follow principal volumes and slender features. We further integrate ML-IST into the Jolt Physics and Bullet engines; in an alpha-puzzle benchmark it reaches 55.89~FPS, the highest among the compared representations (conventional IST, GImpact, and convex decomposition). These results support learned leaf generation as a practical component for fast, runtime construction of detailed collision representations.
bullets: Targets the sequential, expensive leaf-sphere construction bottleneck in inner sphere trees for non-convex collision detection.
Predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry in a single shot.
Uses differentiable coverage feedback to fill residual gaps across scales, followed by geometric projection for validity.
Reduces mean leaf-generation time by 2.0–2.6× versus single-core CPU construction across 64–512 target spheres.
Integrated into Jolt Physics and Bullet, achieving 55.89 FPS in the reported alpha-puzzle benchmark among compared representations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall ML-IST architecture. A seven-channel voxel representation is encoded into local and global geometric features for base-sphere prediction. A differentiable renderer generates five coverage-feedback maps, which are concatenated with the original input and processed by a second encoder. A correction head refines the base spheres, while medium- and detail-sphere heads predict additional candidates. The three groups are concatenated and geometrically projected to obtain IST leaves. Layer annotations give the output shape of each Conv3D stage as (channels, depth, height, width); for example, (24,96,96,96) denotes 24 channels at 96× 96× 96 resolution, and B is the batch size.

Figure 3: Mean per-model generation time of ML-IST and GT-IST at different target leaf counts K, averaged over 100 models from the held-out test set. GT-IST runs on a single core of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8368Q CPU with SIMD vectorization enabled, whereas ML-IST inference runs on one RTX 4090 GPU. Training used four RTX 4090 GPUs, and a separate ML-IST model was trained from GT-IST labels for each K.
Figure 2: ML-IST inner-sphere sets for complex nonconvex models. Each pair shows the input surface mesh and the corresponding ML-IST prediction.

Figure 7: Runtime frame rate of four collision representations in the alpha-puzzle benchmark. ML-IST reaches 55.89 FPS, compared with 31.33 FPS for GT-IST, 26.79 FPS for GImpact, and 2.57 FPS for convex hulls with convex decomposition.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing sub-millimeter detail of small objects underpins tasks such as circuit-board defect detection, specimen digitization, and archiving. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed images alone, but macro optics violate two conditions it depends on. The field of view (FOV) and the depth of field (DoF) shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error can take a sample out of frame, and only a thin focal plane is sharp in frame. Existing automated macro-capture rigs handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, but typically rely on classical photogrammetry and offline, human-in-the-loop processing. We present MicroSplat, which generates a 3DGS using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator arm. After a single up-front object-localization step, the system runs unattended. It performs calibration, plans collision-free viewpoints, captures and fuses a focal stack at each viewpoint, segments the object across all views, and optimizes a 3DGS model warm-started with the arm's own poses. We further compare against blur-aware 3DGS methods, which infer sharp scenes from defocused images, and find that measuring sharpness with a controlled focal sweep outperforms inferring it. We provide real and synthetic datasets (including robot and camera parameters) and the fitted 3DGS reconstructions.
authors: Roman Mineyev, Robert Azarcon, Suvrat Jain, Chuizheng Kong, Shreyas Kousik
bullets: Addresses macro-optics challenges: millimeter-scale field/depth of field and sensitivity to viewpoint error.
Runs unattended after one object-localization step, including calibration, collision-free viewpoint planning, capture, segmentation, and model optimization.
Fuses focal stacks at each viewpoint to obtain sharp imagery across the shallow focal range.
Uses arm poses to warm-start 3DGS optimization and compares controlled focal-sweep sharpness measurement with blur-aware alternatives.
Provides real and synthetic datasets with robot/camera parameters and fitted 3DGS reconstructions.

papers.abstract: We present RhinoNet, a simplicial complex-based point cloud neural network, that creates a geometry-preserving embedding of high-dimensional point clouds. RhinoNet takes collections of datasets, also called {\em data cohorts}, and processes each dataset (point cloud) within the cohort as a simplicial complex. These simplicial complexes have datapoints as vertices and edges learned by Vietoris-Rips filtration. Using simplicial wavelets and MLP layers, RhinoNet computes a vector representation of each dataset in a latent space produced by an autoencoder. The latent space is optimized such that an optimal transport distance between pairs of point clouds is preserved between the latent representations. We apply RhinoNet to single-cell datasets collected on patients---a common source of such high-dimensional data. RhinoNet creates a patient level representation, known in biological contexts as a phenoscape. We establish that RhinoNet generates organized phenoscapes, whereas other methods such as static maps do not. Next we show that we can generate entire point clouds by sampling and decoding this phenoscape. We show two modes of generation via 1) latent flow matching and 2) geodesic interpolation in latent space, followed by a decoding back into the point cloud space. RhinoNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-cell and spatial data cohorts relative to tested baselines. Overall, RhinoNet lifts the concepts of representation learning and generative modeling to the point cloud or population level and defines a neural model for phenoscaping.
authors: Siddharth Viswanath, Hiren Madhu, Eddie Cavallin, Benjamin Jones, Alistair Wilkinson, Christopher Tape, Michael Perlmutter, Rex Ying, Ian Adelstein, Smita Krishnaswamy
bullets: Processes each dataset as a Vietoris–Rips simplicial complex with datapoints as vertices and learned edges.
Uses simplicial wavelets, MLP layers, and an autoencoder to encode datasets into a latent phenoscape.
Optimizes latent representations to preserve optimal-transport distances between point clouds.
Generates point clouds through latent flow matching or geodesic interpolation followed by decoding.
Applied to single-cell and spatial data cohorts, achieving state-of-the-art performance against tested baselines and producing organized phenoscap es.

papers.abstract: A 3D asset admits multiple valid part decompositions, while semantics-aware segmentation should reflect both the desired granularity and the parts a user wants to extract. Ideally, a practical segmentation model should strive for a simple principle: what you ask for is what you get. However, realizing this goal is hindered by two core obstacles: the lack of multi-granularity training data and the absence of a holistic control mechanism. We propose FLEXPART, a unified framework for text-controlled 3D mesh segmentation. To establish flexible control, we introduce a holistic control prompt comprising semantic part names with location and shape clauses. To support this mechanism, we utilize an automated Vision-Language Model (VLM) pipeline to construct a large-scale dataset of multi-granularity partitions and their corresponding prompts. Driven by this data, FLEXPART generates a view-independent part-identity field in native 3D space, directly assigning discrete part IDs to mesh faces. To compel the model to respect semantic conditions rather than rely on geometric priors, we train the model using randomized background dropping. Furthermore, an inference-time VLM planner can automatically complete descriptive clauses from 2D renderings, allowing users to simply name the desired parts in ordinary words. FLEXPART with planner-completed prompts outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 15% in mIoU, even when that baseline receives ground-truth guidance. On our held-out FLEXPARTBENCH, FLEXPART leads at each granularity and improves average mIoU by 22% over the strongest baseline. With only the requested part names supplied by the user, it also improves IoU by 35% over the strongest click-driven baseline on selective segmentation.
authors: Yiqun Zhao, Jiachen Xu, Yihao Zhi, Yunfei Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses the lack of multi-granularity data and holistic control in semantics-aware 3D part segmentation.
Uses prompts containing part names plus location and shape descriptions to control segmentation.
Builds a large-scale multi-granularity dataset with an automated VLM pipeline.
Predicts discrete part IDs directly on mesh faces and uses randomized background dropping to emphasize semantic cues.

An inference-time VLM planner can complete descriptive clauses from renderings, enabling ordinary-word part requests; the method reports gains over evaluated baselines across granularities and selective segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Granularity control on FLEXPARTBENCH. For each method, panels show fine (large), coarse (top right), and medium (bottom right) granularities. While baselines receive their optimal inputs (e.g., GT part counts for PartField), only FLEXPART (driven by level-specific item lists) successfully adapts its semantic decomposition across all three levels. Conversely, PartField and SAMPart3D are biased toward geometric boundaries over the requested semantic groupings, and Find3D suffers from severe surface fragmentation. Meanwhile, SegviGen struggles to follow the ground truth, since relying on a single reference map fails to resolve occlusions.

Figure 7. Generalization to generated assets. Four Hunyuan3D 3.1 meshes. Although these AI-generated meshes lack well-defined geometric boundaries, our method generalizes robustly by following semantic instructions rather than relying on rigid geometric priors.

Figure 2. FLEXPART. Left: a part-aware VAE encodes a point cloud carrying position, normal, and part ID. Its decoder can be queried at any 3D coordinate, with two cross-attention modules for geometry (SDF) and a discrete, binary-encoded part ID. Face-centre queries produce the mesh labels. Right: a text-conditioned DiT generates the field’s latent representation from the geometry latent (green) and encoded text tokens. A full decomposition (blue) and a selective input (red) differ only in the control prompts, and in the selective case an explicit background item absorbs parts that belong to the background. Each part item is visualized in the color corresponding to the input prompts.

Figure 10. One annotation call. The images and the prompt a single Stage 2 request receives, for the left_arm group of a five-group coarse partition. The overlay places the group in the whole object, the solo render shows its shape without occlusion, and the full scene is the object it belongs to; four viewpoints of each cover the parts a single view hides. The call returns one JSON object, and the aggregation step maps PartName, SpatialRelation and Shape to the item’s three clauses.

Figure 12. Following the prompt on an existing mesh. Both methods receive the same watertight meshes and part names for coarse and fine decompositions. CubePart allocates and generates an independent latent geometry for each requested item, whereas our method retains the input surface and predicts its face labels. The displayed cases illustrate the resulting differences in partition and surface preservation. Top: At the fine level, CubePart fails to generate the waist, leaving the chest and pelvis disconnected; in contrast, our method continuously labels the original surface. Middle: The coarse prompt requests both arms and both legs as separate items, but CubePart erroneously merges them (purple). Our method correctly separates the arms (green) and legs (grey). At the fine level, CubePart generates the right hand as fragmented specks. Bottom: CubePart handles the coarse request successfully but its fine-grained output (armour plates, brackets, hoses) becomes a cloud of fragments. Our method instead assigns labels on the unchanged input surface, yielding a complete partition without post-processing.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on PartObjaverse-Tiny. Left of the divider, -GT denotes ground-truth conditions (our annotated prompt; SegviGen’s rendered guidance map), and -Auto denotes automatic conditions (our planner-completed names; SegviGen’s predicted map). Right of the divider, baselines use their native inputs. As shown, baselines suffer from missing occluded parts (SegviGen), over-segmenting along geometric seams (PartField, P3-SAM, SAMPart3D), or imprecise boundaries (Find3D). FLEXPART avoids these issues, effectively following the semantic intent from GT.

Figure 5. Selective part segmentation. The background parts become one brown region. Our two columns denote the same model, evaluated with either the ground-truth prompts or the planner-written descriptions. A click indicates the part the user wants to segment, which may lead to a region with ambiguous boundaries, as seen in P3-SAM and SegviGen.

Figure 9. What the grouping call sees, per view. Each component carries a numbered mark in both renders, so the returned groups are lists of IDs. The two renders disagree about where a boundary is only where a texture hides one, which is why both are given. Sixteen such pairs cover the object, and one call returns all three levels.
Figure 6. Ablation study of two design choices. The RGB palette fragments parts that part IDs keep whole (rectangles); w/o dropto-background training reduces accuracy.

Figure 11. What the visual planner is given. Four of the sixteen turntable views, 90◦ apart, of the bare mesh; these are its only visual input, alongside the user’s command. This object is also the first row of Fig. 7.
Figure 8. Failure cases with vague descriptions (location and shape).

FLEXPART significantly outperforms all baselines at every level, and even our -direct protocol (Tab. 1) exceeds all baselines on average. Although PartField performs reasonably well at the fine level by merely fitting the geometry, all baselines struggle at the coarse and medium levels where semantic understanding is required.

Table 3. Selective part segmentation. Query IoU averages over the named parts, and BG IoU covers the background region. FLEXPART outperforms all click-driven baselines, even when relying on planner-generated prompts from names only. While baseline methods using solely part names (Find3D) fail to extract user-intended parts, our control prompts successfully achieve accurate selective segmentation.

Conditioning denotes the input signals. -GT uses ground-truth annotations, while -Auto relies on automated inputs (e.g., predicted color maps or planner-completed lists). -direct evaluates our predictions without region-to-GT rematching, and still outperforms all baselines.
Table 7. Category distribution of FLEXPARTBENCH over its 364 objects, following the proportions of the source libraries.
Table 5. Multi-granularity training.

Table 8. Semantic conditioning beyond part count. Geometry and the requested number of regions K are fixed. The mismatched condition uses genuine same-K annotation text with semantics that do not match the target grouping. We report raw area-weighted mIoU without post-processing, following Sec. 4.1.

Table 4. Ablation. Full averages the three granularities on a human category subset from FLEXPARTBENCH; Selective is the accuracy on Selective-190. Using an RGB palette instead of part IDs fragments cohesive regions, resulting in lower accuracy across both tasks. Furthermore, drop-to-background training is vital; it facilitates semantics-aware understanding and strictly enables selective segmentation.

papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.
authors: Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone
bullets: Addresses the gap between foundation-model-based 3D mapping and complete robot autonomy pipelines.
Integrates FOUND-IT with a mobile manipulator using a single uncalibrated camera.
Supports object change detection, multiple mapping sessions, navigable-path reasoning, and grasping for scene rearrangement.
Reports rigorous on-robot experiments assessing the system’s effectiveness and limitations.
The scope is constrained by the limitations of monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction.

It demonstrates the integration of this memory system into a full autonomy pipeline for tasks like object grasping, path planning, and scene rearrangement, directly fitting 3D foundation models, robot manipulation, and embodied memory.
papers.title: Foundation-Model-Driven 3D Scene Graphs for Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: The paper integrates a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph system into a mobile manipulator and evaluates its usefulness for end-to-end spatially informed tasks.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes. The source code is publicly available at https://mias.group/MaSS.
authors: Mengtan Zhang, Yuchuan Cui, Yu Ma, Zizhan Guo, Wei Ye, Rui Fan
bullets: Self-supervised depth models can learn dataset-specific structural biases instead of transferable geometry, causing conflicts across domains.
MaSS separates structural representations from contextual features through a dedicated pathway for depth decoding.
A scene-structure discrimination objective encourages generalized, layout-aware structural features.
Across four datasets, MaSS benefits from joint mixed-domain training, unlike prior methods.
Zero-shot tests on eight additional datasets show strong generalization, including to out-of-distribution scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 3: The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.

Figure 2: Feature activation map comparison among a conventional self-supervised depth model, DINOv2, and the two representations learned by MaSS. (a) The conventional depth model tends to encode dataset-specific biases, whereas (b) DINOv2 lacks sufficient geometric cues. In contrast, MaSS decouples features into contextual and structural representations: (c) contextual ones capture fine-grained object details and foreground–background relations; (d) structural ones encode global scene layouts that are transferable across diverse datasets.

Mixed-dataset models (†) are evaluated for the image resolutions of 384×640. Supervised foundation models are reported at their pretrained resolutions (518×518 for [37] and 768×768 for [25, 26]). Results on the DIML [54] dataset are not reported for method [37] that was pretrained on this dataset. The best results for self-supervised and supervised models are marked in bold type, respectively. SSI* and LSQ* denote the predicted depth and its alignment with the ground-truth in the inverse depth domain.

papers.title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
papers.tldr: MaSS improves the scalability and cross-domain generalization of self-supervised monocular depth estimation by learning transferable scene-structure representations.

papers.abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.

papers.abstract: Panoptic occupancy unifies 3D geometry, semantics, and instance identities, but its development is limited by scarce instance-aware annotations. Existing benchmarks mainly provide semantic labels reconstructed from incomplete sensor observations, while panoptic datasets have limited domain coverage or annotation completeness. We introduce PanoBench, a camera-centric panoptic occupancy prediction benchmark spanning synthetic and real-world driving scenes. It combines PanoBench-CarlaOcc, PanoBench-nuScenes, and PanoBench-KITTI360 through canonical data interfaces and unified evaluation protocols, providing multi-resolution annotations with persistent instance identities. The synthetic branch derives complete panoptic geometry from simulated meshes. For real-world data, a new pipeline reconstructs backgrounds using geometric priors and topology constraints, generates foreground mesh assets from multi-frame multi-view images, and fuses them into sparse panoptic voxels. A unified valid-mask protocol evaluates complete thing instances supported by temporal observations while scoring stuff regions at the voxel level. Analyses of observation fidelity, geometric completeness, spatial continuity, and temporal consistency demonstrate the benefits of the resulting annotations over existing occupancy benchmarks. We benchmark representative methods on semantic occupancy prediction, panoptic occupancy prediction, and 4D occupancy forecasting, and study voxel resolution, synthetic-to-real transfer, and storage efficiency. These results reveal complementary strengths of volumetric and ray-based metrics and persistent challenges in real-world instance-aware prediction. PanoBench is available at https://mias.group/PanoBench.
authors: Yi Feng, Zizhan Guo, Junwu E, Yu Ma, Mengtan Zhang, Jin Wu, Wei Ye, Hanli Wang, Qijun Chen, Danwei Wang, Rui Fan
bullets: Addresses the lack of complete, instance-aware annotations combining 3D geometry, semantics, and persistent identities.
Integrates CarlaOcc, nuScenes, and KITTI-360 with canonical interfaces, multi-resolution annotations, and unified evaluation protocols.
Reconstructs real-world panoptic occupancy using geometric and topological priors, multi-view foreground assets, and sparse voxel fusion.
Evaluates semantic occupancy, panoptic occupancy, and 4D forecasting, including voxel resolution, synthetic-to-real transfer, and storage efficiency.
Findings highlight complementary volumetric and ray-based metrics and ongoing challenges in real-world instance-aware prediction.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing high-quality, renderable 3D scenes from long videos is essential for robotic perception and embodied intelligence. Many feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction methods rapidly predict 3D scenes from a small set of images, but extending them to longer sequences presents two bottlenecks: jointly processing all views increases GPU memory requirements, while accumulating pixel-aligned predictions redundantly represents the same surfaces and increases storage and rendering costs. We present LonGaussian, a streaming feed-forward framework that reconstructs compact, globally renderable Gaussian scenes from long image sequences with known intrinsics and unknown camera poses. Built on a pretrained streaming 3D reconstruction backbone, LonGaussian decodes long-context geometric features into dense Gaussians. Within each chunk, multi-frame point tracks link repeated observations of the same surface and guide a learned merger to consolidate the corresponding Gaussian predictions. Rendered-depth consistency filtering further suppresses Gaussians from other chunks that incorrectly occlude locally reconstructed surfaces. On DL3DV and RealEstate10K benchmarks, LonGaussian improves novel-view rendering quality while using substantially fewer Gaussians than the evaluated feed-forward baselines.

bullets: Addresses memory growth and redundant Gaussian storage in long-context feed-forward 3D reconstruction.
Uses a pretrained streaming reconstruction backbone to decode geometric features into dense Gaussians from images with known intrinsics and unknown poses.
Links repeated surface observations within each chunk using multi-frame point tracks to guide learned Gaussian merging.
Applies rendered-depth consistency filtering to remove Gaussians that incorrectly occlude locally reconstructed surfaces.
On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, improves novel-view rendering quality with substantially fewer Gaussians than evaluated feed-forward baselines.

papers.abstract: Jointly reconstructing RGB and X-ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real-world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross-modal insight discovery. We propose a unified representation in which all Gaussian primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, with only surface-proximal primitives additionally carrying appearance attributes. We perform cross-modal registration through clean multi-view stereo and X-ray geometric proxies instead of aligning two sets of optimized Gaussians, improving alignment stability. We then jointly optimize the unified representation via supervision from both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss derived from X-ray geometry to guide RGB reconstruction. Experiments on the InsideOut dataset and our Flower & Insect dataset show that our framework achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, higher RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and a more compact representation than maintaining two independent geometries.
authors: Wangze Xu, Chu Zhou, Mae Yamaguchi, Linrui Dai, I-Chao Shen, Takashi Ijiri, Imari Sato
bullets: Addresses redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and weak coupling in separate RGB/X-ray models.

Experiments on InsideOut and Flower & Insect show more robust alignment, better RGB rendering, preserved X-ray reconstruction, and compactness.

papers.abstract: Cage-based deformation (CBD) parametrises 3D geometry through a small set of control handles, effectively enabling a variety of tasks from animation and interactive modelling to tool-based co-design, neural deformation transfer, and aerodynamic shape optimization. Many optimization approaches relying on CBD employ regularisation strategies to reduce the distortion of the deformed mesh by encouraging smooth, regular cage deformations. These techniques offer soft guidance to an optimization algorithm towards desirable deformations, but compete with the task objective rather than changing the deformation parameterization itself. In this work we introduce Structural Affinity for CBD, an explicit regularisation method which enables smooth deformations through control cages by exploiting a two-cage structure to couple cage-handle motion directly. Structural Affinity precomputes an affinity matrix using mean-value coordinates, binding the inner control-cage to a coarser outer-cage. This matrix defines how much a cage handle displacement propagates to neighbouring handles which substantially decreases and often eliminates cage self-intersections, reduces mesh distortion, and adds linear overhead at deformation time. Across robotic control--morphology co-design, source-to-target neural deformation transfer, and aerodynamic wing shape optimization, Structural Affinity produces more regular deformations and substantially reduces reliance on hand-designed structural loss terms. We report consistent gains on three complementary diagnostics: the cotangent Laplacian, a proxy for surface smoothness; cage distortion, capturing whether control handles move coherently; and surface roughness, which measures undesirable oscillation in wing geometry.
authors: Aviraj Newatia, Shengan Yang, Hantao Zhong, Rika Antonova
bullets: Addresses self-intersections, irregular cage motion, and mesh distortion in cage-based deformation optimization.

Demonstrates consistent improvements in cotangent-Laplacian smoothness, cage distortion, and surface roughness across robotics, neural deformation transfer, and aerodynamic wing optimization.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in 3D generation has motivated growing interest in compact generative representations of complex 3D scenes. For native 3D Gaussian scenes, however, learning such representations remains challenging due to widely varying primitive counts, nonuniform spatial density, and differences in geometry and appearance even among spatially neighboring primitives. In this work, we introduce TriFold, a native 3D Gaussian VAE that encodes Gaussian scenes into a fixed-layout triplane latent and jointly reconstructs their geometry and appearance. The key insight is to impose structural regularity on the latent space while preserving the spatial adaptivity of the underlying Gaussians. During encoding, we use cell-wise learned queries to aggregate projected Gaussians into multiple slots per cell, reducing the information loss caused by single-feature pooling. During decoding, occupancy prediction identifies active regions, where query-based set prediction and candidate selection reconstruct local Gaussian sets with spatially varying primitive counts. Building on this representation, we train a latent flow-matching model for conditional scene-level 3DGS generation, enabling point-cloud-conditioned synthesis and single-image-conditioned amodal generation. Experiments demonstrate that TriFold achieves high-fidelity reconstruction and generation from a single image that provides only a partial observation of the scene, validating its effectiveness for native 3D Gaussian representation learning. https://fantasy-amap.github.io/TriFold
authors: Yun Wang, Chiyu Wang, Fan Jiang, Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Guangchi Fang, Mu Xu, Dapeng Wu
bullets: Addresses variable primitive counts, uneven spatial density, and heterogeneous geometry and appearance in native 3D Gaussian scenes.
Uses cell-wise learned queries with multiple slots to aggregate projected Gaussians while reducing information loss.
Decodes with occupancy prediction, query-based set prediction, and candidate selection to reconstruct spatially varying local Gaussian sets.
Trains a latent flow-matching model for point-cloud-conditioned synthesis and single-image-conditioned amodal generation.
Experiments show high-fidelity reconstruction and single-image-conditioned generation from partial scene observations.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian models have made novel view synthesis almost instantaneous. Feed-forward methods predict Gaussians directly, either in two stages or in a single merged pass. Using two separately trained models is attractive because each can specialize in its own objective: one for accurate pose estimation and the other for high-quality reconstruction, rather than forcing a single jointly trained network to compromise between the two. A natural instantiation pairs a frozen pose estimator, VGGT, with a frozen reconstruction backbone, TokenGS. Prior work, such as VGGT-X and 3R-GS, also adopts a two-stage design, but attributes the resulting quality degradation to noisy pose estimates and introduces learned refinement. We show that this is not the primary source of the problem. Through per-camera analysis across 107 scenes from two datasets, DL3DV and MipNeRF360, using COLMAP poses as the reference, we find that the rotation error after alignment is small (median 1.6 degrees), whereas the translation scale is offset by a large, dataset-consistent factor. Controlled ablations over 140 DL3DV scenes show that the primary obstacles are two integration failures rather than pose error: a coordinate-frame inconsistency and a translation-scale mismatch, both of which can be corrected deterministically. With these fixes, a frozen VGGT driving a frozen TokenGS achieves 22.47 PSNR, within 0.51 dB of the COLMAP reference, with no additional training, when poses are estimated from all scene views. In the sparse setting, where reconstruction uses only four context images under the standard pose-free protocol, the same pipeline matches this all-view quality, yielding a fully COLMAP-free pipeline without any refinement step.
bullets: Two-stage pipelines can suffer quality loss from integration failures, not primarily noisy pose rotations.
Analysis across 107 scenes finds small aligned rotation error but a large, dataset-consistent translation-scale offset.
Controlled ablations identify coordinate-frame inconsistency and translation-scale mismatch as the main obstacles.
Correcting both issues enables a fully COLMAP-free pipeline using four context images, matching its all-view reconstruction quality.
With all scene views, the corrected frozen pipeline reaches 22.47 PSNR, within 0.51 dB of the COLMAP-pose reference.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV. Naı̈ve integration collapses under the coordinate-frame mismatch; each deterministic fix progressively restores structure, and our full pipeline produces renderings visually indistinguishable from the COLMAP reference, using no ground-truth poses.

Figure 2. VGGT vs. COLMAP pose error decomposition. Left: rotation error after convention alignment is small (median 1.60◦ on DL3DV, 1.32◦ on MipNeRF360). Right: the translation scale ratio is large and consistent (median 7.0 on DL3DV), far from the ideal ratio of 1.0. For typical scenes, rotation error is small; the dominant systematic offset is scale.

Figure 1. Our training-free composition pipeline. A frozen VGGT estimates camera poses, and a frozen TokenGS reconstructs 3D Gaussians; the two are connected by three deterministic, training-free operations. All input views (the four context images and the target) pass through VGGT in a single forward pass so that every camera pose lies in one shared coordinate frame. The predicted poses are then corrected by convention conversion, frame-consistent inference, and scale correction before conditioning TokenGS. Reconstruction uses only the four context images (bottom path); the target image is included solely to estimate its pose in the shared frame. No component is trained or fine-tuned.

papers.abstract: Mainstream point cloud completion methods are unanimously based on deep learning architectures. On one hand, these methods tend to repetitively stacking attention modules to enhance network performance, which drifts away from the neat design of unified and interpret-able networks; on the other hand, nearly all existing architectures rely solely on feed-forward connections to propagate information, neglecting feedback from deeper layers. The recurrent neural architecture, formed by feedforward-feedback loops, have shown its ability to generate Illusory Contours (ICs) in the V1 brain region of mammals; and ICs are essentially a completion mechanism of the brain for visual information. Motivated by this, we design a Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder (BRICE) to "imagine" what is missing in the incomplete 3D point clouds. Building upon the foundation model of Predictive Coding (PC), the plug-and-play nature enables BRICE to be seamlessly integrated into mainstream point cloud completion baselines. Experimental results show that BRICE can enhance various completion baselines on different 3D datasets such as MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom. Our code: Https://github.com/wangyunlei-wyl/BRICE.
authors: Yunlei Wang, Dawei Li, Xue-song Tang
bullets: Addresses the reliance on stacked attention and purely feed-forward information propagation in existing completion networks.
Models illusory-contour formation in the visual cortex through feedforward-feedback recurrent connections.
Provides a plug-and-play encoder that can be integrated with mainstream point-cloud completion baselines.
Enhances multiple baselines across the MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom datasets.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.

papers.abstract: N-dimensional splatting extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with view direction and time to model view-dependent and dynamic effects. Each primitive is lifted into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables, then conditionally sliced at each rendering query. N-DGS and UBS share this step across Gaussian and Beta kernels: recovering the conditional mean, opacity, and covariance requires per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products in every forward pass. We introduce direct conditional parameterization, replacing this covariance-derived readout with explicit per-effect parameters: a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. Unrestricted conditional coordinates recover a valid joint covariance; our factorization adds spatial-scale and coupling priors. Applied to both kernels, the parameterization yields dGS (Gaussian) and dBS (Beta). Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, they match or exceed their covariance-derived counterparts on quality, with gains up to +1.26 dB in the main MCMC evaluation. Production slicing is 6.9-7.7 times faster than on-the-fly covariance-derived conditioning; complete-render profiling gives 1.25-1.91 times speedups on four trained scenes. Direct conditioning provides a structured, kernel-agnostic alternative for N-dimensional splatting. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/dgs/.
authors: Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Van Nguyen Nguyen, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Arun Innanje, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
bullets: N-dimensional splatting models view-dependent and dynamic effects by conditioning primitives on query variables.
The method replaces per-query covariance inversions and regression products with explicit Cholesky precision and factorized query-to-position parameters.
Applied to Gaussian and Beta kernels, it produces dGS and dBS with structured spatial-scale and coupling priors.
Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, quality matches or exceeds covariance-derived methods, with gains up to 1.26 dB.
Production slicing is 6.9–7.7× faster, while complete rendering is 1.25–1.91× faster on four trained scenes.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity 3D generative modeling underpins game asset creation, medical imaging, and VR/AR environmental design, where geometric structure directly influences perception and decision-making. Diffusion models represent a powerful paradigm for point cloud generation. However, existing approaches rely heavily on local voxel or patch features and often miss global structural organization, and much less work has studied how global conditioning can be used to improve generation quality. In this paper, we introduce HilbertGen-3D, a novel topology-aware conditional diffusion framework based on Hilbert-Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). HMC computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them via a 3D Hilbert curve to expose structured spatial dependencies, and estimates the generalized fractal dimensions from scale-dependent partition functions. We encode these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, and inject them into a diffusion denoiser through an efficient bottleneck fusion module. Across the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories of ShapeNet, our two conditioning variants reduce the absolute deviation of 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) from 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and increase coverage by up to 5.88 percentage points relative to TopoDiT-3D. This shows that combining local density cues with global Hilbert-multifractal structure provides a simple and effective recipe for high-fidelity and diverse 3D generation.
authors: Ziyi Zhang, Shixuan Li, Yorie Nakahira, Paul Bogdan, Guannan Qu
bullets: Addresses the inability of local voxel or patch features to capture global geometric organization in 3D generation.
Computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them with a 3D Hilbert curve, and estimates generalized fractal dimensions.
Encodes these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, fused into the diffusion denoiser through a bottleneck module.
On ShapeNet Chair, Airplane, and Car categories, it improves 1-NNA closeness to 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and coverage by up to 5.88 points versus TopoDiT-3D.
Scope is limited to the reported ShapeNet categories and two proposed conditioning variants.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HilbertGen-3D. Multi-scale voxel measures are serialized along 3D Hilbert curves to construct Hilbert-ordered sequences, while generalized fractal dimensions form the global descriptor D. Separate encoders produce HMC tokens C and a global HMC embedding gHMC, respectively. The noisy point cloud Xt is embedded into geometry tokens Ht, which are fused with the projected HMC tokens through bottleneck latents B. Successive DiT blocks update B, with adaptive layer normalization conditioned on the timestep embedding Etime(t) and the projected global embedding Pg(gHMC). The processed latents update the geometry tokens, and the output head unpatchifies and devoxelizes the predicted features to obtain the noise estimate εθ(Xt, t, C) for DDPM training and reverse-diffusion sampling.

papers.abstract: FOR-species20K is the largest public LiDAR benchmark for tree-species classification, pooling 25 independently collected terrestrial, mobile, and airborne laser-scanning datasets across 33 species. We introduce a multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves official hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at the time of submission. We then examine what this score measures. Because the hidden test is species-balanced, its overall accuracy is more comparable to a macro metric than to accuracy under the public set's long-tailed distribution. Moreover, the official random split places every source dataset in both training and evaluation. A logistic probe recovers source identity from out-of-fold model probabilities with 69% accuracy, while geometric features identify the source above 90% within two widely shared species; 18 of the 33 species occur in only one source. Under a source-species-cell holdout, evaluated on 5,566 trees from eight eligible species that retain the same LiDAR-type training support in other sources, the unweighted species mean falls from 82% to 36%, and tree-weighted accuracy falls from 95% to 60%. Count-matched retraining and experiments with two alternative backbones indicate that this gap is not explained by reduced training support alone, while an external PureForest experiment shows a smaller but consistent grouped-split effect. These results establish the 85% leaderboard score as strong in-distribution performance, but not as an estimate of source-disjoint generalization, motivating balanced metrics and source-aware evaluation. The code is available at: https://github.com/JaeLee18/FOR20K-lidar-tree-species
bullets: FOR-species20K combines 25 terrestrial, mobile, and airborne LiDAR datasets covering 33 tree species.
A multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model raises hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%.
The official random split mixes source datasets across training and evaluation, enabling substantial source-identity cues.
Under source-species-cell holdout, performance drops to 36% unweighted species mean and 60% tree-weighted accuracy.
The study recommends balanced metrics and source-aware splits for evaluating LiDAR tree-species recognition.
