papers.abstract: Internet-scale photo collections of real-world landmarks have driven progress in 3D computer vision yet remain highly challenging for modern 3D foundation models (3DFMs) that estimate scene structure in a single feed-forward pass. In this work, we introduce ArchWorld, a benchmark of 3D architectural landmarks with high geographic coverage and rich metadata. We use this benchmark to conduct a thorough error analysis of current 3DFMs to understand where they fall short and how they can be improved. We examine socially relevant disparities in model error and find that model performance varies by geographic region; however, unlike typical fairness regimes, the trends only partially match training data representation. Our investigation reveals that the observed geographic disparities reflect not only differences in data representation and scene size but also differences in region-specific architectural features and background distractors that make scenes from different regions inherently vary in difficulty. Leveraging insights from these model failings, we introduce an intervention scheme that improves 3DFM performance while simultaneously reducing geographic disparities.
authors: Nicky Kriplani, Yiwen Zhang, Angelina Wang, Hadar Averbuch-Elor
bullets: Introduces ArchWorld, a landmark benchmark with broad geographic coverage and rich metadata.
Analyzes errors in single-pass 3D foundation models and identifies region-dependent performance differences.
Finds that disparities reflect data representation, scene size, architectural features, and background distractors.
Shows that geographic error trends only partially align with training-data representation.
Develops an intervention scheme that improves model performance and reduces geographic disparities.

papers.abstract: Visually plausible articulated assets may still fail during contact interactions or exhibit inaccurate motion. We present FACT (Fidelity-Aware Construction of Articulated Twins), an agentic framework that progressively constructs articulated twins to improve geometry, contact, and dynamic fidelity. The agent drives an evidence--diagnosis--revision loop on a shared editable representation, selecting measurements and model edits using quantitative feedback, while numerical tools execute and validate the updates. It reconstructs editable articulated geometry from images through feature planning, targeted measurements, and diagnostic refinement. On this reference, it repairs collision proxies through task-aware local repartitioning before fidelity-constrained compression. Finally, it constructs response models from passive-response videos, using simulation residuals to guide model revision and constrained physical parameter fitting. Experiments show that FACT improves geometric reconstruction over baselines, enables more reliable interaction with simpler collision proxies, and better reproduces held-out physical responses than direct parameter inference.
bullets: Targets failures in visually plausible assets, including inaccurate motion and unreliable contact interactions.
Uses an evidence–diagnosis–revision loop on a shared editable representation, guided by quantitative feedback and numerical validation.
Reconstructs editable articulated geometry from images through feature planning, targeted measurements, and diagnostic refinement.
Repairs collision proxies with task-aware local repartitioning, then applies fidelity-constrained compression.

Learns response models from passive-response videos using simulation residuals and constrained physical parameter fitting; experiments report better reconstruction, interaction reliability, and held-out response reproduction than direct inference.

papers.abstract: Reducing radiation exposure in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is important for patient safety; however, ultra-low-dose imaging suffers from severe noise, which may affect diagnostic interpretation without appropriate image enhancement. While current 3D deep generative models, particularly diffusion models, have shown strong reconstruction fidelity, their practical use can be limited by long inference times. In contrast, faster 2D-based alternatives may have difficulty maintaining volumetric consistency, an important consideration for whole-body PET imaging analysis. To bridge this gap, we propose a one-pass conditional 3D rectified flow (3D Flow) framework for whole-body PET image denoising that incorporates a novel optimized non-uniform sampling strategy. The model is trained with a one-pass linear-interpolant velocity-matching objective. This approach reconstructs a full 3D volume in approximately 30 seconds in our implementation, compared with multi-hour inference for the evaluated 3D DDPM baseline. Evaluations including zero-shot transfer to an independent clinical dataset show that our model achieves favorable global image quality and lesion conspicuity compared with the evaluated 3D DDPM and DDIM baselines, including on challenging short-acquisition data. Furthermore, the proposed method shows promising zero-shot transfer performance across the evaluated datasets and unseen dose levels (down to 1/100 of the standard dose), with artifact-focused visual comparisons supporting the need for further lesion-level validation. By balancing reconstruction fidelity and computational efficiency, this work presents a candidate approach for ultra-low-dose whole-body PET image denoising.
bullets: Targets severe noise from ultra-low-dose PET to support safer imaging.
Uses conditional 3D rectified flow with a one-pass velocity-matching objective and optimized non-uniform sampling.
Reconstructs a full 3D volume in approximately 30 seconds in the reported implementation, versus multi-hour inference for the evaluated 3D DDPM.
Shows favorable global quality and lesion conspicuity against evaluated 3D DDPM and DDIM baselines, including short-acquisition data.
Demonstrates promising zero-shot transfer across evaluated datasets and unseen dose levels down to 1/100 of standard dose; lesion-level validation remains needed.

papers.abstract: Large-scale pre-training has transformed representation learning in 2D vision, yet its transferability to 3D single object tracking (SOT) remains insufficiently understood. Directly fine-tuning self-supervised 3D encoders, such as masked autoencoders (MAE), often leads to sub-optimal adaptation because the reconstruction objective is not fully aligned with the spatial-temporal matching requirements of tracking. In this paper, we observe that this difficulty can be interpreted as a layer-wise transfer mismatch: shallow layers tend to preserve transferable geometric cues, while deeper layers become increasingly specialized to the reconstruction pretext task and are less suitable for downstream tracking. Based on this observation, we propose MAETrack, a lightweight adaptation framework for transferring pre-training MAE representations to 3D SOT. MAETrack includes Layer-Selective Initialization (LSI), which initializes only the shallow stages of the tracking backbone from pre-trained weights while re-initializing deeper stages, and Geometric Residual Gating (GRG), which reinforces structurally salient regions in the search BEV features before template-search fusion through residual spatial modulation. Extensive experiments on standard 3D SOT benchmarks show that MAETrack consistently improves upon vanilla fine-tuning baselines with limited computational overhead. More broadly, our results suggest that effective transfer from 3D reconstruction pre-training to 3D tracking is not merely a matter of partial fine-tuning, but depends on a tracking-oriented transfer principle that preserves shallow geometry while adapting deeper representations to the downstream objective.
bullets: Identifies a layer-wise transfer mismatch: shallow MAE features retain useful geometry, while deeper features specialize in reconstruction.
Uses Layer-Selective Initialization to transfer only shallow pretrained stages and reinitialize deeper tracking stages.
Applies Geometric Residual Gating to emphasize structurally salient regions in search BEV features before template-search fusion.
Experiments on standard 3D SOT benchmarks show consistent gains over vanilla fine-tuning with limited computational overhead.
The approach focuses on transferring 3D reconstruction priors to tracking rather than relying on partial fine-tuning alone.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Framework of the proposed MAETrack. The pipeline takes a template point cloud and a search point cloud as inputs with an unified feature extraction. To inherit robust geometric priors, its shallow layers are initialized from MAE-pre-trained weights via Layer-Selective Initialization (LSI), while the deep layers are randomly re-initialized to adapt to the tracking task. Then, the search features are fed into the Geometric Residual Gating (GRG) module, which learns a spatial gating map through a spatial gate to selectively enhance informative geometric patterns via residual scaling. Finally, the template and refined search features are aggregated in the template-search fusion module and input the tracking head to predict the 3D bounding box.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising path for overcoming the limited visual capability of current medical imaging agents. Yet applying RSI to volumetric imaging remains difficult: failures can arise from acquisition, perception, training recipe, or downstream inference, while self-generated feedback and logged trajectories provide little guidance on which component should change. We introduce ReVision3D, an RSI system that leverages 3D volumes with spatially grounded annotations to determine where visual evidence is lost and recursively improve the corresponding visual capability. A frozen language-model designer proposes revisions to acquisition, perception, training, or inference, while the verifier and system-level objective remain fixed. Our key insight is that an annotated volume forms an exact replay world for view rendering and spatial verification: unvisited views can be rendered on demand, and localized predictions can be checked directly against reference masks. This grounded feedback directs targeted revision, while only changes that improve beyond measured seed noise are retained. Each accepted change triggers renewed attribution, allowing the dominant bottleneck to shift across rounds. On abdominal CT, attribution identifies perception as the dominant remaining limitation. Revising that level enables ReVision3D to achieve 79% liver recall and 83% kidney recall at under 0.4 false positives per patient, outperforming the evaluated frozen multimodal foundation models, with the largest gains on small lesions. Our framework is public available with interactive demo in this project page: \url{https://leeh43.github.io/ReVision3D/}
bullets: Targets failures across acquisition, perception, training, and inference rather than revising components blindly.
Uses annotated 3D volumes as replayable worlds for on-demand view rendering and direct spatial verification.
A frozen language-model designer proposes revisions; changes are retained only when they exceed measured seed noise.
On abdominal CT, perception was identified as the dominant bottleneck, yielding 79% liver recall and 83% kidney recall at under 0.4 false positives per patient.
Reported gains were largest for small lesions and exceeded those of the evaluated frozen multimodal foundation models.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) cooperative perception enhances autonomous driving by enabling vehicles to share information beyond their direct line of sight. However, existing V2V datasets are limited by a small number of participating agents, static collaborator selection strategies, and a significant domain gap between simulated and real-world environments. To overcome these challenges, we introduce SV2V-RSim, a large-scale, multi-modal, near-realistic simulation dataset engineered to elevate agent diversity and realism. Additionally, we present the Select Vehicles Adaptively (SVA) module, which optimizes collaborator selection to balance perception performance against communication bandwidth constraints. Our dataset is generated using the Unreal Engine 5-based simulator that integrates high-fidelity 3D assets, diverse environments, and intricate traffic scenarios. All vehicles within a specified range of the ego vehicle are equipped with sensor suites, enabling dynamic and adaptive collaborator selection. SV2V-RSim encompasses four maps, four weather conditions, six time periods from sunrise to night, 203K LiDAR frames, 402K RGB frames, and 788K annotated 3D bounding boxes across 17 object classes, supporting a range of cooperative perception tasks such as 3D object detection, segmentation, and depth estimation. Benchmarking on recent cooperative perception algorithms demonstrates that SVA achieves a superior performance-bandwidth trade-off, while sim-to-real experiments and No-Reference Image Quality Assessment validate the dataset's high realism and practical effectiveness. Our dataset and code will be publicly available.
bullets: Addresses limited agent diversity, static vehicle selection, and the simulation-to-real-world domain gap in existing V2V datasets.

Experiments report improved performance–bandwidth trade-offs, with sim-to-real and image-quality evaluations supporting dataset realism and practical utility.

papers.abstract: \textit{Gromov-Wasserstein Distances} (GWDs) provide quantitative ways of comparing probabilistic distributions defined on different metric spaces by applying techniques from the optimal transport theory. As such, GWD can be potentially useful in a large variety of applications ranging from graph matching problems to 3D object detection. However its practical use at scale is significantly limited by cubic time complexity computations involving dense intra-space distance matrices. Even though in the Euclidean metric spaces several techniques (e.g. involving scalable kernel methods) were proposed to address it, to the best of our knowledge, analogous techniques for general geodesic distances on manifolds, or shortest-path distance on graphs in their discretized variants, were not developed. In this paper, we present \textbf{E}fficient \textbf{G}eodesic \textbf{Gro}mov-\textbf{W}asserstein methods (EGGroW), a new class of efficient algorithms designed to calculate geodesic Gromov-Wasserstein distances with entropic Sinkhorn-like approaches, leveraging recently introduced \textit{GenusSink} methods \citep{genussink} and the theory of random features. We provide important downstream applications, namely: 3D pose estimation and 3D template detection. In the latter setting, we formulate a partial 3D template recovery as a staged problem: capacity-constrained scene selection is followed by semi-relaxed recovery of template visibility and correspondence. Our empirical findings show that EGGroW provides accurate solutions when standard Euclidean-based techniques fail and is characterized by light computational footprint, as our theoretical analysis predicts.
bullets: Addresses the cubic cost of dense intra-space distance matrices in Gromov-Wasserstein computations.
Introduces efficient entropic Sinkhorn-like algorithms for general geodesic distances on manifolds and discretized graphs.
Combines GenusSink methods with random-feature techniques to reduce computational demands.
Applies the approach to 3D pose estimation and partial 3D template recovery with visibility and correspondence estimation.
Experiments indicate accurate performance where Euclidean methods fail, with a lightweight computational footprint.

papers.abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.
authors: Yitong Xia, Zeren Jiang, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Processes clean video latents in one encoder pass, avoiding iterative denoising.

Demonstrates the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have expanded 3D understanding and synthesis. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. We make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.

papers.abstract: Single image 3D generation aims to dress a given 3D mesh with relightable materials while faithfully preserving the visual details of a reference image. Existing methods either introduce artifacts when fusing inconsistent multi-view predictions or struggle to preserve fine details through implicit image-feature conditioning. To resolve these challenges, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, built on the principle of decoupling visible-material estimation, surface alignment, and observation-guided 3D completion. This division of labor allows the 3D generator, trained on limited 3D data, to focus its capacity on preserving visible evidence and completing unobserved surfaces. Specifically, we first train an MLLM-based image editing model to predict lighting-separated PBR maps in the reference view. We then project these maps onto the visible surface and encode them with the pretrained material VAE encoder into native observation latents that share the generation target's latent space. An interleaved flow transformer holds these latents as fixed, read-only anchors while alternating unobserved-region and full-surface updates to generate complete material latents. This design achieves super-alignment with the reference, delivering What You See Is What You Get fidelity on visible regions and coherent completion on unobserved surfaces. Trained solely on public datasets, SUPRA-Tex achieves SOTA performance in both geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation, matching or even exceeding leading commercial systems on in-the-wild images. papers.abstract: Reconstructing human motion in 4D requires identifying the same surface points through articulation, deformation and changes in visibility. We introduce Dense4D, to our knowledge the first feed-forward model dedicated to dense 4D correspondence across the body, clothing and hair from a set of monocular RGB images, without a body template. Trained specifically for human geometry, Dense4D jointly processes person-centred crops with known image-to-crop transforms to predict Human Point Maps (HPMs) and depth for each image. An HPM assigns each person pixel the 3D position of its observed surface point at a common reference time. These maps support amodal correspondence: points hidden in the reference image can be localised from observations in other frames. Matching HPM coordinates across crops establishes correspondence without predicting camera poses or large scene displacements; per-image depth then lifts the matches into 3D tracks. Experiments on real people demonstrate substantially higher tracking accuracy and closer agreement with scanned surfaces than the evaluated baselines. Points from different frames assemble into coherent human geometry in the reference pose, providing visible evidence of consistent dense correspondence through articulation and clothing deformation. Additional qualitative results, videos, and an interactive viewer are available at https://alpguler.com/dense4d.
bullets: Handles articulation, deformation, and visibility changes, including amodal correspondence for surfaces hidden in the reference view.

This reveals inconsistency between their point-transfer and depth predictions, even when the target surface itself looks plausible. Dense4D instead matches target-image pixels and lifts them with their predicted depth, so transferred points lie on its target surface by construction. papers.abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have recently achieved strong performance in multi-view 3D reconstruction, but they still rely primarily on appearance-based attention and often struggle in dynamic scenes with weak geometric cues. In this work, we introduce a motion- and gravity-aware framework under the Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm. During training, residual optical flow and gravity direction are provided as privileged signals to guide geometric representation learning; during inference, the model uses standard visual inputs only. We integrate these priors into transformer backbones with lightweight architectural changes, preserving feed-forward efficiency. Experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent gains in reconstruction accuracy and robustness, especially in scenes with dynamic objects, ambiguous structure, and challenging camera motion. Our analysis further shows that the optimal injection stage is backbone-dependent: middle-layer integration is generally preferable for VGGT, while late-stage integration is more effective for {\pi}3. These results suggest that LUPI offers a practical way to inject motion and physical priors into feed-forward 3D reconstruction without increasing test-time complexity.
authors: Shiyao Qian, Yuan Ren, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Targets weak geometric cues and dynamic-scene challenges in appearance-driven multi-view reconstruction.
Uses residual optical flow and gravity direction as privileged training signals, while inference relies only on standard visual inputs.
Adds these priors to transformer backbones through lightweight architectural changes.
Standard-benchmark experiments report consistent gains, particularly with dynamic objects, ambiguous structure, and difficult camera motion.
Prior injection works best at different stages depending on the backbone: middle layers for VGGT and late layers for π3.

papers.abstract: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an answer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included. Commodity edge accelerators optimize the mean through dynamic scheduling, OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention, so their per-frame latency can be measured but not bounded. We build FALCON, a camera-based 3D occupancy front-end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embedded FPGA drawing 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under inference, and make the latency guarantee layered and explicit: programmable-logic (PL) compute is cycle-bounded analytically; inference is a measured envelope over 100k-frame traces; and a watchdog enforces output delivery, publishing the previous output flagged stale when a frame is late. The deadline runs use a fixed-work proxy of six ResNet-50 DPU inferences per frame, not the full occupancy network: across three 100k-frame enforced runs, all 300k proxy frames delivered an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms, the worst of the three runs. The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline composes to about 1.3 s per frame on the board and is not yet a 10 Hz system. The two operations the DPU cannot run, a view-transform gather and a bilinear resize, become fixed-trip-count PL IPs numerically matched to their software references. On the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set the board reaches mIoU 29.88, 92.8% of an FP32 baseline the DPU cannot run. On a ResNet-50 probe over 100k frames the KR260 tail stays within 1.5 times its median (2.0 times for the six-inference proxy), where Jetson Orin reaches 4.4 times and the worst datacenter GPU run (NVIDIA L4) 23.6 times. The deployment recipe, HLS sources, and raw timing traces are released.
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
bullets: Targets worst-case deadline compliance rather than average latency for autonomous-driving perception.
Implements unsupported view-transform gather and bilinear resize operations as numerically matched FPGA logic.
On three 100k-frame proxy runs, all 300,000 frames produced an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms.
Achieves 29.88 mIoU on the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set, or 92.8% of the FP32 baseline.
The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline takes about 1.3 s per frame and is not yet a 10 Hz system; deployment artifacts and timing traces are released.

papers.abstract: Splatting-based radiance-field representations have recently gained popularity in robotic perception, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis (NVS) through explicit scene primitives. However, existing splatting methods typically rely on iterative nonlinear optimization that jointly optimizes millions of coupled primitive parameters, resulting in substantial computation time, peak GPU memory consumption, and susceptibility to local minima. In this paper, we propose CF-Splat, a novel closed-form triangle-splatting framework for efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh either pre-existing or provided by upstream mapping or reconstruction pipelines. Our key insight is that, by properly formulating the problem over the given mesh geometry and calibrated cameras, the rendered pixel colors can be expressed linearly with respect to the per-vertex spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, allowing multi-view scene appearance estimation to be formulated as a global linear least-squares (LLS) problem without the need of iterative nonlinear optimization. To guarantee a well-posed solution under uneven multi-view observation coverage, we introduce adaptive SH regularization that constrains insufficiently supported high-order SH coefficients and yields a unique global minimizer. To ensure the scalability to large-scale scenes, we develop a triangle-structured matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that avoids explicitly constructing the large sparse normal system while producing the same LLS solution. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that CF-Splat achieves competitive or superior NVS quality compared with state-of-the-art splatting methods. While, CF-Splat requires approximately 27.5-378.0 times less computation time and 1.8 times lower peak GPU memory on average than 3DGS across scenes of different scales on a consumer-grade laptop.
bullets: Targets the high computation, memory use, and local-minima susceptibility of nonlinear splatting optimization.
Represents rendered colors linearly using per-vertex spherical-harmonics coefficients over calibrated cameras and mesh geometry.
Uses adaptive SH regularization to produce a unique solution despite uneven multi-view coverage.
Employs a matrix-free, preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver for large-scale scenes without forming the normal system.
Reports competitive or better NVS quality than state-of-the-art splatting, with substantially lower computation time and lower peak GPU memory than 3DGS.

papers.abstract: Language-guided 3D affordance grounding aims to localize functional regions on 3D objects according to interaction intents. However, existing methods exhibit poor generalization to unseen objects. One challenge is the query-target gap: a semantic discrepancy between query features encoding interaction intents and target-region features, leading to inaccurate grounding. End-to-end training favors query representations tailored to seen objects, limiting their compatibility with shifted target-region features on unseen objects. To address this issue, we propose BridgeAfford, a framework that reduces the query-target semantic gap from two complementary perspectives. First, Interaction Region Alignment (IRA) promotes cross-object alignment among geometrically similar interaction regions during training. This enables structures on unseen objects that resemble previously observed ones to produce representations similar to those learned during training, facilitating target-region recognition. Second, Visual Evidence Aggregation (VEA) leverages a 2D affordance model to refine the attention distribution and guide the query toward the correct region, yielding more target-aware queries. Extensive experiments on the LASO and PIAD datasets demonstrate that BridgeAfford outperforms existing methods, particularly on unseen objects, highlighting its robust generalization ability.
authors: Yijie Su, Yakun Zhu, Yi Bin, Pengpeng Zeng, Liang Chen, Guoqing Wang, Jingkuan Song, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets poor generalization caused by mismatched query and target-region representations.
Interaction Region Alignment aligns geometrically similar interaction regions across objects during training.
Visual Evidence Aggregation uses a 2D affordance model to refine attention and make queries more target-aware.
Experiments on LASO and PIAD show improved performance, especially for unseen objects.
Scope: focuses on generalization to shifted or previously unseen 3D objects.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of BridgeAfford. (a) BridgeAfford follows the LASO pipeline and improves generalization from two sides: IRA aligns geometrically similar interaction regions across objects, while VEA lifts multi-view 2D affordance predictions into 3D as an attention bias. (b) During initialization, new region features are directly inserted when empty slots are available; otherwise, the two most similar entries are merged to release a slot for the new entry. (c) Visual evidence is incorporated as an attention bias to guide query-to-point attention toward interaction regions.

Figure 1: Motivation for BridgeAfford. (a) Accurate prediction relies on high semantic similarity between the query and the target-region representation. However, shifted local representations on unseen objects may prevent the model from extracting the target region, resulting in query features with low similarity to it. (b) Unseen objects may contain interaction regions that are geometrically similar to those of seen objects. Aligning these regions with geometrically similar regions on training objects promotes consistent representations, helping the model recognize interaction regions and incorporate their semantic information into the query. (c) Objects may contain novel interaction structures that cannot be reliably aligned with those observed during training based on geometric similarity. We therefore use a more generalizable 2D affordance model to directly guide feature extraction, facilitating the generation of target-aware queries.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D assets with explicit parts requires two properties at once: geometric detail inside each part and structural coherence across the whole object. Recent image-conditioned 3D generation models adopt a structured 3D representation that anchors tokens to explicit spatial positions, capturing both properties, but their output remains a single fused mesh. We ask how a part-decomposed generation model can inherit both properties of these holistic priors, and answer with STRUCTPARTS, a framework whose core technical contribution is a dual-frame coordinate interleaving mechanism: each shape latent is interpreted under both a part-local and an object-global reference frame, and processed through a global-local inter-leaved transformer that simultaneously reuses the prior's geometric detail at the part scale and its structural coherence at the whole-object scale. As its structural input, STRUCTPARTS uses a segmented mesh scaffold, a coarse mesh paired with a face-level segmentation mask kept entirely within the prior's native 3D representation. With only lightweight finetuning, both intra-part detail and inter-part coherence emerge from the same pretrained weights. On PartObjaverse-Tiny, STRUCTPARTS matches or surpasses prior part-decomposed models at a fraction of their training cost, while naturally supporting part-mesh refinement and part-level editing.
authors: Yiqun Zhao, Binbin Huang, Haobin Duan, Zibo Zhao, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining fine intra-part geometry with whole-object structural coherence.
Uses dual-frame coordinate interleaving, interpreting latents in both part-local and object-global frames.
A global-local interleaved transformer transfers geometric detail and structural coherence from pretrained holistic priors.
Conditions generation on a segmented mesh scaffold represented in the prior’s native 3D format.
On PartObjaverse-Tiny, matches or exceeds prior part-decomposed models with substantially lower training cost and supports part refinement and editing.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of STRUCTPARTS’s pipeline. Given a single image, our method first constructs a 3D segmented scaffold using the structure generation model followed by a segmentation model. We then sample points from each part surface to construct the voxel indices in both the per-part normalized space and the shared global-shape space. These voxel indices serve as position embeddings to guide the diffusion model’s sampling process. The segmented scaffold and part meshes depicted here are dataset-provided ground truth (GT), used to illustrate the part-wise data flow. part k, we use local embeddings RoPEL(·) = RoPE(·, I(k)L ) and global embeddings RoPEG(·) = RoPE(·, I(k)G ), which are then injected into the shape latents described next.

Figure 3: Layout-conditioned part decomposition. Comparison among methods that accept an explicit layout (HoloPart, X-Part, FullPart, OmniPart): each row shows assembled shapes for part coherency and exploded views for per-part geometry. Baselines drop fine details, leave incomplete shapes, or introduce floaters; STRUCTPARTS preserves both by reusing the holistic prior.

Figure 5: Ablation on positional-embedding strategies. Three variants compared against STRUCTPARTS’ dual frame: LRoPE only loses global structure (parts treated identically in their own normalized frames); GRoPE only recovers global layout but degrades small or off-center parts under unnormalized coordinates; GRoPE + part embed. (as in prior work) still misses fine geometric detail. Only the dual-frame design recovers both global structure and per-part detail.

papers.abstract: Partial shape matching is a crucial yet underexplored problem in 3D vision, with significant relevance to real-world scenarios where shapes are often only partially observed. Existing feature descriptors face difficulties in this setting, as traditional representations either struggle with the boundaries of partial shapes or heavily depend on the shape's spatial position. While existing approaches have employed DINO features for partial shape matching, these features are not inherently suited for handling partial observations. In this work, we propose a method to refine DINO features using LoRA-based self-supervised learning, enabling the generation of feature descriptors that are robust to partiality. Our features substantially improve performance on partial shape matching compared to traditional or vision foundation features. Additionally, when integrated into existing partial shape matching pipelines, we achieve state-of-the-art results on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.
authors: Viktoria Ehm, Dongliang Cao, Riccardo Marin, Daniel Scholz, Weikang Wang, Florian Bernard, Daniel Cremers
bullets: Addresses partial 3D shape matching, where boundaries and spatial-position dependence challenge existing descriptors.
Refines DINO features through self-supervised learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA).
Produces geometry-aware descriptors designed to handle partial observations.
Improves partial shape matching over traditional and general vision-foundation features.
Achieves state-of-the-art results when integrated into existing pipelines on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Our Self-Supervised Training Pipeline: Given a full mesh X , we first generate a partial observation Y . After randomly rotating both shapes with different rotation matrices around the Y-axis, we render the partial and full shape from different perspectives with cameras C. For every camera ci ∈ C, we obtain an image IiX of the full shape, which is then passed through a frozen DINOv3 architecture with a LoRA module with rank r to extract pixel-wise features Qi X . These are then backprojected on the shape and averaged to get vertex-wise features FX . Similarly, we proceed for the partial shape Y . Finally, we use the Geodesic-Aware PointInfoNCE contrastive loss to align corresponding vertices of both shapes and separate all others based on geodesic distance. In our experiments we use 4 views for the partial and 9 views for the full shape.

papers.abstract: We introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D scene generation framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background and dynamic character representations. Recent advances in generative models have enabled text-driven dynamic scene synthesis, but editable 4D scene generation remains challenging due to the need to preserve spatial geometry and temporal dynamics. Existing approaches typically generate holistic scene videos, where the background and dynamic characters are coupled, making object-level editing and flexible camera control difficult. Edit4D addresses these limitations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and scene-character composition. Using these prompts, we synthesize multi-view scene images with text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors and reconstruct a background 3D Gaussian splatting representation. We then generate a character image, animate it with an image-conditioned video prior, reconstruct a 4D mesh, and bind Gaussian primitives to obtain a character representation. Finally, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization. A global scene refinement is then performed to improve harmonization and rendering consistency. By integrating stage-specific components, Edit4D enables controllable camera motion, flexible object-level editing, and the practical construction of editable 4D scenes. Project page: https://chanwo0kim.github.io/Edit4D/
authors: Chanwoo Kim, Tackgeun You, Hwasup Lim
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving geometry and temporal dynamics during editable 4D scene generation.
Decomposes user instructions into background, character, and composition prompts.
Reconstructs backgrounds with 3D Gaussian splatting and characters as animated 4D meshes with bound Gaussians.
Uses text-guided segmentation, contact-aware optimization, and global refinement for consistent scene composition.
Enables controllable camera motion and object-level editing, though the abstract reports no quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Detailed Generation Pipeline of Edit4D. It then constructs a dynamic 3D character via video-guided mesh reconstruction and Gaussian binding. In the third stage, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization to obtain an editable 4D scene. Finally, we perform a global scene refinement to improve appearance harmonization and rendering consistency.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have enabled effective multi-view 3D reconstruction by predicting Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.
authors: Sheng Ye, Jiangke Lin, Fudong Wang, Yi Yuan, Zhen-Hui Dong, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussians in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas.
Uses entropy-guided 3D anchors to concentrate representation where visual complexity is higher while preserving scene coverage.
Anchors aggregate multi-view features with occlusion awareness, exchange information, and decode into local Gaussian sets.
A lightweight enhancement module refines Gaussian-splatting RGB outputs for improved rendering fidelity.
Experiments on diverse benchmarks report state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality with an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Anchor3DGS. Given uncalibrated multi-view images, (1) a VGGT-based [28] geometry backbone first predicts the scene’s geometric scaffold. (2) A fixed budget of 3D anchors is then sampled from the scaffold, combining uniform sampling with entropy-guided sampling. (3) Each anchor is projected back into all input views to gather features via occlusion-aware aggregation, and then interacts with other anchors through self-attention. (4) Finally, each anchor is decoded into a set of local Gaussians, which are rasterized and refined to yield the final RGB output.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of novel view synthesis. Our method recovers sharper textures and finer details while mitigating artifacts in poorly observed regions.
Figure 5: Rendering metrics under varying anchor count N and decoded Gaussians K (left), and qualitative comparisons of removing the enhancement module and entropy-guided sampling (right).

Figure 1: Anchor3DGS reconstructs 3D scenes from uncalibrated multi-view images. Our anchorbased representation achieves better rendering quality with fewer Gaussians, and avoids the empty holes that pixel-aligned methods (e.g., AnySplat [11]) commonly leave in poorly observed regions.

Figure 3: Uniform sampling ensures broad spatial coverage but wastes anchors (red dots) on uninformative regions (e.g., textureless sky). In contrast, our entropy-guided sampling allocates more anchors to visually complex regions while still maintaining coverage of the scene.

papers.abstract: Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
authors: Sibaek Lee, Kyeongsu Kang, Seongbo Ha, Yewon Jeon, Joonyeol Choi, Daegeol Ko, Jaehyuk Hur, Taemin Choi, Minsu Kim, Hyungjoo Ahn, Wonsok Yoo, Hyeonwoo Yu
bullets: Addresses missed user-specified targets in distilled 3D language maps without sacrificing other-word queryability.
Uses a text-promptable segmenter to blend target-region visual embeddings with target text embeddings, leaving non-target regions unchanged.
Computes the smallest effective blending coefficient in closed form, avoiding tuning hyperparameters.
Centers the read-out to remove query-agnostic effects caused by shared components in text embeddings.
Improves open-vocabulary segmentation across three benchmarks, roughly doubling base mIoU on Replica, and transfers to other language maps and real-world robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Real-to-sim conversion aims to turn a captured video of a real environment into an editable 3D scene while preserving the geometry and layout of what was observed. Existing methods often follow a one-pass, loosely coupled paradigm: each stage receives only limited feedback from previous stages, allowing errors to propagate without reliable correction and leaving the final scene inconsistent. We present GRASE, an agentic framework that closes this loop by treating the captured multi-view video observations as a standing reference throughout scene modeling. Instead of committing to intermediate estimates, GRASE revises its current hypothesis whenever rendered evidence disagrees with the capture, overcoming the fixed intermediate assumptions of conventional pipelines. Specifically, GRASE first fits the architectural shell and its openings from depth and multi-view cues. An agent then places generated assets in a shared coordinate frame while checking their spatial relationships. Finally, each asset's geometry and placement are refined iteratively to improve agreement across the observed views. By coupling these steps through feedback, GRASE localizes structural discrepancies and revises only the responsible components, while preserving cross-view consistency. The resulting 3D scenes are faithful to the input, consistent across views, and suitable for simulations. In our experiments, GRASE substantially outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, including a direct real-to-sim conversion using GPT6-Astra.
authors: Zhaorui Lin, Haohan Liu, Zhen Chen, Xiangru Huang

Produces faithful, cross-view-consistent scenes and substantially outperforms prior methods in experiments, including a GPT6-Astra-based baseline.

papers.abstract: Traditional keypoint descriptors, such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), are computed from local image patches. They may be unreliable in scenes with repetitive patterns or weak textures, where patches at different locations can look similar. We propose the Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor (CLAD), a keypoint matching method that addresses this problem by using global geometric context from line correspondences. CLAD represents each keypoint with a vector whose elements indicate its proximity to matched lines. It can therefore use the keypoint's spatial relationships to the lines in the scene. We use HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema) to detect both clear and weak linear structures and to establish enough line-to-keypoint associations to represent this context. Evaluations on the TUM RGB-D SLAM dataset and outdoor video sequences show that CLAD provides geometrically consistent matches that complement those obtained with traditional local descriptors. In repetitive scenes, where local descriptors may not distinguish similar patches, CLAD uses global structure to improve matching reliability. The method is computationally lightweight and practical to implement.
bullets: Targets ambiguities in local descriptors such as SIFT and ORB when patches look similar.
Builds keypoint vectors from spatial relationships to matched lines, capturing global geometric context.
Uses HOME to detect clear and weak linear structures and create line–keypoint associations.
Evaluations on TUM RGB-D SLAM and outdoor video sequences show geometrically consistent matches that complement local descriptors.
Designed to be computationally lightweight and practical to implement.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Examples of keypoint matches obtained with ORB (top) and CLAD (bottom). Each pair of corresponding keypoints and its connecting line are shown in the same color. These examples illustrate a limitation of descriptors based only on local image information: in challenging scenes, many local patches may look alike, causing methods such as ORB to confuse different keypoints. In contrast, CLAD uses the global geometric context provided by line correspondences, which helps it find more reliable matches in these cases.

papers.abstract: Point-cloud streams are central to autonomous driving and robotics, yet existing segmentation networks process every frame from scratch, although consecutive frames largely overlap. We observe that the intermediate features of point-cloud transformers remain semantically consistent across frames for the same spatial region, especially in deep stages. Building on this, we present SpaceCache, a training-free feature cache that reuses these features across frames. Tokens of previously observed regions skip a sequence of transformer blocks and take their cached features, only the remaining tokens are computed, and the full token layout is restored for dense prediction. Lightweight cache management keeps reused features reliable by limiting each entry's age and evicting low-confidence entries. Unlike token merging, SpaceCache selects tokens at negligible cost and runs its cache operations once per encoder stage. On both outdoor and indoor benchmarks, such as nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet, with two transformer backbones of Utonia and LitePT-B, SpaceCache achieves up to 1.65x speedup with less than 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.

bullets: Addresses redundant frame-by-frame processing caused by substantial overlap in consecutive point-cloud streams.
Uses a training-free cache to let previously observed tokens skip transformer blocks while computing only new or changed tokens.
Maintains reliability by limiting cache-entry age and evicting low-confidence features; cache operations run once per encoder stage.
Evaluated on nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet with Utonia and LitePT-B backbones.
Achieves up to 1.65× speedup with less than a 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.

papers.abstract: Geometric light detection and ranging (LiDAR)--inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) provides efficient state estimation but lacks the continuous map representation and global refinement capabilities of neural implicit SLAM, while neural implicit methods remain computationally expensive. We propose Lightweight LiDAR--Inertial Neural SLAM (LIN-SLAM), a hybrid method that couples high-rate geometric LiDAR--inertial estimation with neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement for accurate real-time onboard SLAM. Experiments on twelve representative sequences from three datasets spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) among the evaluated state-of-the-art geometric and neural implicit methods, while substantially reducing runtime compared with existing neural implicit SLAM methods. On a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a 16-channel LiDAR, LIN-SLAM sustains real-time localization and neural mapping over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory through challenging repetitive corridor environments, with an endpoint closure error of only 0.141~m. To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR--inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a mobile robotic platform while maintaining state-of-the-art localization accuracy. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Shiqi Che, Yijie Liu, Shuo Wang, Wenxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between efficient geometric SLAM and computationally costly neural implicit SLAM.
Uses high-rate geometric estimation alongside neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement.
Evaluated across twelve sequences from three datasets and multiple LiDAR configurations.
Reports the lowest overall mean ATE among evaluated geometric and neural implicit methods, with reduced runtime versus neural implicit baselines.
Runs online on a Unitree Go2 with a Jetson Orin NX over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory, achieving 0.141 m endpoint closure error.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the lightweight LIN-SLAM pipeline. A geometric generalized iterative closest point (GICP)–IESKF frontend processes LiDAR sub-sweeps and IMU measurements to provide local poses and motion-compensated scans. Full-sweep keyframe candidates associate geometry with source intervals, terminal poses, and covariances for asynchronous transfer. The neural implicit backend uses optimized C++/CUDA computation to reduce processing overhead, fixed-capacity replay storage and local neural windows to control stored data, and preallocated workspaces to reduce repeated allocation. Frontend relative motion initializes neural tracking; continual mapping and loop-based global optimization update the neural map. Backend corrections provide globally corrected poses at the frontend rate.

papers.abstract: Point cloud upsampling is essential for 3D applications but remains challenging due to sparse, under-constrained observations. Multi-view images can resolve geometric ambiguity, but existing multi-modal methods do not fully exploit visual cues. We propose ControlFlow3D, a framework that distills knowledge from pretrained foundation models into a lightweight generation network during training, enabling strong performance without multi-view images available at test time. Specifically, our method performs conditional flow matching in a structured latent space defined by a frozen 3D encoder. Multi-view image tokens and 3D latent tokens are jointly clustered into shared prototypes via unsupervised soft KMeans; the resulting prototypes guide the flow trajectory through velocity control and are aligned by a consistency loss that progressively transfers image knowledge into the base network. A Mamba-based geometry decoder then maps latent features to dense coordinates with linear complexity. We also construct ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark that is 31 times larger than prior datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its strong generalization capability.
authors: Yuang Liu, Zhi Zuo, Zhengkai Zhao, Lirui Zhang, Pan Gao, Hao Feng, Zhengzhe Liu
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity from sparse point clouds by leveraging multi-view information during training.
Uses conditional flow matching in a structured latent space from a frozen 3D encoder.
Aligns clustered image and 3D latent prototypes to control flow trajectories and transfer visual knowledge.
Employs a Mamba-based decoder to generate dense coordinates with linear complexity.
Introduces ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark, and reports strong cross-benchmark generalization.

To distill multi-view knowledge into this network, we introduce an unsupervised prototype-guided velocity controller that jointly clusters image Fimg and 3D tokens F3D into shared prototypes. During inference, the model takes only the sparse point cloud as input and produces the final dense point cloud.

papers.abstract: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.
authors: Haoran Liu, Di Wu, Wang Luo, Hengyuan Na, Miao Hu, Guocong Quan

On complex full-scene videos, improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB and reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5% versus a controlled V$^3$-style baseline.
Reaches 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

papers.abstract: We identify a theoretical incompatibility between 3D point cloud masked autoencoding and SE(3)-equivariant networks. We prove that standard masking triggers a topological collapse, effectively forcing the model to hallucinate orientation without a reference frame. To resolve this, we introduce SIEVE (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance), an SE(3)-equivariant self-supervised framework that compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings. At its core is the spherical projection mask, which preserves global pose while obfuscating local semantics, sidestepping the obstruction by construction. Experiments confirm that SIEVE circumvents the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail. On downstream point cloud tasks, the resulting embeddings improve over coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors, with the largest gains on generalization to unseen shape categories.
authors: Jongann Lee, Sun Woo Park, Yun Young Choi
bullets: Standard masking is theoretically incompatible with SE(3)-equivariant networks because it removes the reference needed to infer orientation.
SIEVE extracts geometry into SE(3)-invariant scalar embeddings.
Its spherical projection mask preserves global pose while hiding local semantics.
Experiments show SIEVE avoids the collapse observed with constant and noise masks.
The embeddings outperform coordinate-based and hand-crafted geometric baselines, especially on unseen shape categories.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SIEVE Framework. SIEVE extracts SE(3)-invariant embeddings using self-supervised reconstruction on an equivariant bottleneck. The equivariant encoder compresses raw point coordinates into an invariant scalar encoding, while the vector pipeline is blocked. The spherical projection mask is applied to the input point cloud and supplied as the new vector embedding. It and the semantic details from the scalar embedding are used by the equivariant decoder to reconstruct the point cloud on a node-level.

Figure 1: Random masking causes representational collapse; spherical projection masking does not. Random masking functions ignore subtle geometric data inherent in point clouds. This imposes topological obstructions in reconstructing the desired non-trivial vector bundles characterizing the underlying geometry of point clouds, as demonstrated in Theorem 2.6. As a result, representational collapse can occur as shown in Section 4.2. SIEVE utilizes a spherical projection mask, thereby possessing capabilities in reconstructing a class of pullbacks of vector bundles defined over a wide variety of 2 and 3-dimensional manifolds as demonstrated in Theorem 3.1.

Figure 5: Reconstruction Comparison and Representational Collapse. We evaluate the reconstruction (blue) of the input point cloud (red) under different masking strategies. Using our spherical projection mask, the model achieves near-perfect reconstruction. Reconstructing with a constant vector mask or the ellipsoid noise mask results in a catastrophic representational collapse. We refer to Appendix A.3 for further discussions.
Figure 3: Pre-trained SIEVE Encoder Embeddings. We visualize the PCA components of the pre-trained SIEVE embeddings. These embedding are invariant to point cloud rotation and translation.
Figure 4: Validation Loss of SIEVE on two baselines: GATr and SE(3)-Transformer. Trained on the synthetic dataset.

In addition, the cumulative percentage is also plotted. From the top left, we plot the analysis results for SIEVE with no noise, ‘simple noise’ strategy, ‘curv and norm’ strategy, and ‘nearest neighbor attention mask’ strategy.

papers.abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app
authors: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Zhiwei Fang, Rulin Zhou, Quanlu Zhang, Changjing Liu, Beilei Cui, Yiming Huang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses projection ambiguity, distal-joint error accumulation, and imbalanced joint learning in monocular robot pose estimation.

Introduces bone-length and ray-depth losses with joint-wise weighting for topological consistency and scale stability.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across robot types and cameras, including zero-shot cross-scene evaluation on a new benchmark.

papers.abstract: Spatial agents have access to reconstruction and segmentation tools, yet inconsistent predictions and fragmented object identities can prevent their outputs from becoming reliable 3D scene information. A simple oracle experiment exposes this perception bottleneck: replacing tool-predicted perception with ground-truth 3D bounding boxes raises an agent to nearly full score across five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, while retaining the same reasoning tools. Motivated by this finding, we believe the devil of spatial reasoning lies in 3D itself, and introduce DeSpatial(Devil of Spatial), which explicitly decomposes spatial understanding into perception and reasoning. DeSpatial has a shared 3D perception tool to reconcile independent perception outputs into a unified, metric, gravity-aligned 3D scene. This perception tool has two core components: a) a joint segmentation--depth co-refinement module that consolidates masks of the same object and removes projection artifacts caused by inconsistent segmentation and depth within a single frame; b) a cross-view instance fusion module that consolidate voxel-overlapping instances but not allowed to merge same-frame instances. This fusion module additionally fuses spatially disjoint fragments caused by insufficient multi-view observations, by checking their 3D structure and source mask appearance. After receiving the complete and unified 3D scene information, the agent chooses reasoning or computational tools to solve the spatial problem. DeSpatial achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video results on VSI-SUPER, revealing the bottleneck of spatial understanding lies in a precise 3D perception itself.
authors: Yifei Liu, Xiaolong Zhou, Ziyang Gong, Yifan Zhou, Yuanyuan Gao, Yuning Gong, Yuchen Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Xiao Sun, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: An oracle experiment finds that ground-truth 3D boxes nearly solve five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, exposing perception as the main bottleneck.
DeSpatial explicitly separates 3D perception from downstream reasoning and computation.
Its shared perception tool builds a metric, gravity-aligned scene using joint segmentation–depth refinement and cross-view instance fusion.
The system prevents erroneous merges while reconnecting fragmented instances using 3D structure and mask appearance.
It achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video evaluation on VSI-SUPER.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of DeSpatial. The VLM receives the video and question and calls our shared perception tool. Joint segmentation–depth co-refinement cleans per-frame observations; cross-view instance fusion associates them into distinguished individual objects. Colors identify individual masks before fusion and persistent instances afterward. Gravity estimation establishes a common vertical direction. The VLM then reasons and answers using reasoning and computational tools.

Figure 3: Cross-view instance fusion. (a) Voxel overlap links partial observations, while sameframe exclusions prevent distinct objects from merging, including through indirect connections. (b) Visual fragment association handles observations without shared voxels. Multiple source views and a common 3D view provide complementary appearance and structural evidence to an identity judge. A positive decision combines the observed fragments and their provenance.

Component selection then removes residual detached points that distort the bounding box, retaining the top-k components for k confirmed object parts, usually one.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic spatial reasoning decomposed into unified 3D perception and reasoning; directly relevant to spatial intelligence and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: DeSpatial: The devil of Agentic Spatial Reasoning Lies in 3D Itself
papers.tldr: DeSpatial shows that reliable agentic spatial reasoning depends primarily on accurate, unified 3D perception rather than reasoning alone.

papers.abstract: Cultural heritage documentation increasingly relies on image-based 3D surface reconstruction, with photogrammetry software making such workflows accessible to archaeologists, conservators, and heritage technicians. These tools have been successful for conventional multi-view acquisition, but they do not routinely exploit richer multi-view, multi-light data, despite its potential for improving fine-scale surface reconstruction. This limitation is particularly relevant in heritage contexts, where controlled-light acquisition devices such as RTI domes are already used to capture illumination-varying image sets. The challenge is therefore to connect these existing acquisition practices with recent computer vision methods in a form that can be used within operational heritage workflows. In this work, we address this need by integrating state-of-the-art components from computer vision for multi-view, multi-light surface reconstruction into Meshroom, an open-source photogrammetry framework. Rather than proposing a new reconstruction algorithm, our contribution is to assemble and expose existing advanced methods, namely a complete photometric stereo ecosystem (calibrated, self-calibrated and universal), automatic object masking, and multi-view normal-and-reflectance integration, within a usable heritage-oriented workflow. The proposed system thus provides an intermediate software layer between computer vision research code and practical cultural heritage applications, making recent techniques easier to use and evaluate.
bullets: Addresses the limited use of illumination-varying image sets in conventional photogrammetry-based heritage documentation.
Builds on existing tools rather than introducing a new reconstruction algorithm.
Integrates calibrated, self-calibrated, and universal photometric stereo, automatic object masking, and multi-view normal-and-reflectance integration.
Provides a practical software layer connecting computer vision research methods with heritage acquisition practices such as RTI dome imaging.
Supports easier application and evaluation of fine-scale surface reconstruction techniques in operational workflows.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Our contribution: integrating a user-friendly multi-view, multi-light surface reconstruction pipeline into Meshroom [20] for cultural heritage practitioners. Top: reconstructing a lithic biface; the multi-view, multi-light inputs in the gallery (left), a per-view normal map from photometric stereo in the image viewer (centre), the final surface in the 3D viewer (right), and the processing graph (bottom; see Fig. 3). Bottom: the photometric stereo methods integrated as interchangeable Meshroom nodes [37,38, 40].

Fig. 3: End-to-end data flow of the proposed pipeline. SAM 3 segments the multiview, multi-light images, restricting the rest of the pipeline to the object of interest. Structure-from-motion recovers the camera parameters, optionally guided by the masks (e.g . discard turntable-induced multiple motions), and an optional coarse geometry proxy that may be subsequently used by self-calibrated photometric stereo methods. Photometric stereo (calibrated, self-calibrated, or universal) turns the masked images into per-view normal maps, and optionally reflectance maps. Multi-view normal integration then fuses the per-view normals and reflectance with the camera parameters into a single mesh textured with the recovered reflectance.

Fig. 7: Engraved bone from the Gourdan cave, rendered under grazing light: a reference photograph, the UniMS-PS [22] per-view normals, three photogrammetric reconstructions (RealityScan [19], Metashape [30] and COLMAP [60, 61]), and the surface integrated from these normals by RNb-NeuS2 [6]. The engravings are barely visible with photogrammetry but recovered by the proposed pipeline.

Fig. 9: Woman with a calathos (ceramic, 4th century BC), with columns in correspondence. Top: shading renders of the reconstructed geometry, next to a reference photograph. Bottom: the same surfaces relit under a single grazing light matched to the reference, so that fine relief is revealed by the cast shadows; the black box magnifies the right corner of the mouth (inset, top left of each panel). Columns: reference, RealityScan [19], the proposed pipeline (PS [13], 8 views under 35 illuminations each) and a structured-light scan [3]; photogrammetry uses 48 views. Among the shown modalities, the proposed pipeline best brings out the fine granularity of the ceramic micro-relief, including next to the structured-light scan at this resolution, and the grazing relighting matches the relief seen on the reference.

Fig. 8: Lithic biface, from left to right: a reference photograph, RealityScan [19], the proposed pipeline, and an Artec Micro 2 scan [2]. For each method, a diagonal splits the relit texture (upper left) from the geometry alone (lower right); the circular inset magnifies the fine flake-scar relief of the boxed region.

Fig. 5: Calibrated photometric stereo in Meshroom. (a) A calibration sphere placed in the scene, here beside the Cypriot warrior head, is detected automatically (green circle) by the SphereDetection node. (b) The calibrated sub-pipeline, SphereDetection→ LightingCalibration→ PhotometricStereo, recovers the perimage light directions from the sphere and then the per-pixel normals and reflectance.

Fig. 6: Head of a Cypriot warrior (terracotta, 6th century BC), under a matched viewpoint. From left to right: a reference photograph, three photogrammetric reconstructions from 121 views, namely Metashape [30], COLMAP [60, 61] and the Meshroom photogrammetry pipeline [20], and the proposed pipeline with self-calibrated near-light PS [13], integrated by RNb-NeuS2 [6] (13 views under 12 illuminations each, namely 156 images). The black insets magnify the eye (top) and the braided beard (bottom). The reference is consistent with the recovered relief, supporting that it is genuine rather than hallucinated; the proposed pipeline restores sharper relief, notably the separated strands of the beard, at a comparable image budget.

Fig. 2: Texture from Meshroom’s standard photogrammetry pipeline bakes in the acquisition lighting: lit more at the front, this Socrates bust reconstructs darker at the back despite an identical material.

Fig. 4: Multi-light acquisition with an RTI dome (here a Mercurio Imaging dome [36]). Left : the dome seen from the front, its 105 LEDs distributed over a hemisphere around a central camera; firing the LEDs one at a time yields one image per light direction. Right : such a dome in use on the Panneau des Chevaux in the Chauvet cave.

papers.abstract: Generating novel views from limited observations requires preserving both the appearance and spatial structure of a scene. Although recent approaches exploit fine-grained geometric cues, they do not explicitly model high-level semantic and spatial properties such as object identity, attributes, and inter-object relationships. In this work, we investigate whether 3D language understanding can provide complementary supervision for novel-view generation. We introduce Ask4NV, built on a pretrained unified multimodal model with a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture. Our model incorporates camera geometry into both VAE and ViT representations and leverages understanding features during generation through joint self-attention with a modality-aware attention masking strategy. Experiments demonstrate strong image quality and geometric consistency in novel-view generation, alongside competitive 3D language understanding. Further analysis shows that joint training improves cross-view correspondence in VAE representations and similarity in a 3D-aware feature space.
authors: Jahyeok Koo, Hyeonseo Yu, Seungho Jang, Jaewoo Jung, Jiwon Kang, Seokju Cho, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Targets the challenge of preserving both scene appearance and spatial structure from limited observations.
Introduces Ask4NV, built on a pretrained unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers model.
Encodes camera geometry in VAE and ViT representations and integrates understanding features via masked joint self-attention.
Achieves strong image quality and geometric consistency while maintaining competitive 3D language understanding.
Joint training improves cross-view correspondence and 3D-aware feature similarity.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall architecture of Ask4NV. Given source images and camera parameters of the source and target views, (a) for novel-view generation, the images are first encoded into VAE and ViT features by their respective visual encoders, and camera geometry is incorporated into these representations before they are passed to the transformers. (b) The generation transformer processes the camera-aware VAE tokens, while the understanding transformer processes the camera-aware ViT tokens together with text tokens for 3D language understanding. (c) During novel-view generation, these modality-specific tokens interact through joint self-attention under a unified modality-aware attention mask.
