papers.abstract: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an efficient framework for dynamic scene reconstruction. Most existing approaches model scene dynamics with deterministic deformation fields, assuming each Gaussian follows a distinct geometric trajectory over time. This assumption breaks down underwater, where light scattering, refraction, marine snow and low visibility create substantial physical ambiguity in captured images. We present PUGS, a physics-guided uncertainty model for underwater dynamic 3DGS. PUGS learns inherent uncertainty induced by underwater image formation and leverages it as a physical signal for dynamic scene modeling. Rather than estimating a single deterministic displacement, it parameterizes each Gaussian's motion as a probability distribution with expected deformation and physical uncertainty. We adopt stochastic deformation optimization to sample Gaussian trajectories via local reparameterization, exploring multiple physically plausible solutions during training. We further propose uncertainty stochastic annealing and a dual-path self-consistency distillation objective, converting stochastic exploration to deterministic reconstruction while preserving temporal coherence. Extensive experiments on underwater dynamic datasets and physics-aware benchmarks demonstrate superior rendering quality, temporal consistency and reconstruction robustness. Our method achieves 1.16 dB PSNR gain over the strongest baseline on UVEB and 3.99 dB on DRUVA.
authors: Tingjun Li, Yuxi Wang, Guoqiang Zhong, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Targets ambiguity in underwater imagery caused by scattering, refraction, marine snow, and low visibility.
Represents each Gaussian’s motion with expected deformation plus physical uncertainty.
Uses stochastic deformation optimization to explore multiple plausible trajectories during training.
Applies uncertainty stochastic annealing and dual-path self-consistency distillation for deterministic, temporally coherent reconstruction.
Reports PSNR gains of 1.16 dB on UVEB and 3.99 dB on DRUVA over the strongest baseline, with improved rendering quality and robustness.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the PUGS Pipeline for Underwater Dynamic Scene Reconstruction. Given a monocular video, SfM initializes a set of canonical Gaussians. To address the observational ambiguities caused by underwater physical disturbances, our deformation field predicts not only the displacement mean ∆µ but also the positional uncertainty ∆σ, yielding a complete characterization of the motion distribution. A deterministic rendering path (clean path) and an uncertainty-aware rendering path (uncertainty path) are then constructed in parallel and jointly optimized via a self-consistency distillation constraint. Meanwhile, Gaussians with high uncertainty are adaptively split to enhance local representation capacity, thereby improving the robustness of underwater reconstruction. In this way, underwater dynamics modeling addresses the failure of deterministic deformation fields under ambiguous observations, while uncertainty-guided optimization leverages the learned uncertainty to allocate representation capacity and stabilize training.

Fig. 1. We present PUGS, a method that explicitly models physical uncertainty in dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting. On the challenging underwater sequence, a deterministic deformation-based method (Row 1) entangles structural motion with optical interference, producing floaters, blur, distortion, and ghosting artifacts. In contrast, PUGS (Row 2) learns a per-pixel physical uncertainty signal ∆σ (visualized as heatmaps) that captures where and when the optical medium degrades observation reliability. This uncertainty is annealed over time β(t) : 1 → 0, enabling the model to progressively resolve physical ambiguity and produce clean, artifact-free renderings that closely match the ground-truth reference.

Fig. 3. Qualitative Comparison on UVEB dataset. We conduct comparisons across nine scenes and provide zoomed-in views for each scene to examine the rendered reconstruction details, with a particular focus on dynamic content and complex scene regions. Our method consistently produces higher-quality results in both dynamic and static regions.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly supervised with local object and predicate classification losses. Although effective for slot-wise label prediction, this formulation does not provide a graph-level semantic distance between a predicted scene graph and its ground truth: semantically mild label errors and structurally disruptive relational errors can be treated similarly, and subject-predicate-object facts are not compared as scene-level units. We propose Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry, a graph-level supervision objective that measures the semantic and structural discrepancy between 3D scene graphs. Our key idea is to reinterpret the conventional classifier outputs of a 3D scene graph predictor as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field, where object and predicate predictions jointly define contextual subject-predicate-object facts. This formulation yields a differentiable metric-based training objective with an efficient factorized implementation and can be applied to existing 3D scene graph prediction architectures without modifying their network design. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate that our supervision improves downstream graph-conditioned 3D scene generation, while ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of the proposed graph-level terms and user studies show better graph descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.
authors: U-Chae Jun, Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiwoo Kang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of local object and predicate classification losses, which do not compare complete scene-level relations.
Recasts classifier outputs as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field over contextual subject–predicate–object facts.
Introduces a differentiable, factorized graph-level metric that can be integrated into existing 3D scene graph architectures without redesigning them.
Experiments on 3DSSG show improved downstream scene generation, with ablations supporting complementary graph-level terms.
User studies report better graph descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.

Figure 1: Reference 3D scene graph and two example graphs with identical object and predicate classification error counts but different graph-level semantic similarity to the reference. EchoScene [44] reconstructions visualize this difference at the 3D scene level.

Figure 5: Qualitative graph prediction examples from generator-limited scene domains. Because the 3D-FRONT-based graph-conditioned generators support a restricted set of room types and object categories, laundry- and bathroom-like scenes are difficult to include in the generation-based FID/KID evaluation. We therefore compare the predicted graphs directly, before graph-to-generator conversion. OCRL often produces locally plausible but domain-inconsistent graphs, such as replacing laundry appliances with generic furniture or replacing shower-related components with unrelated objects. In contrast, our method better preserves domain-compatible object semantics and the relational scaffold of the scene.

Figure X: Web interface example for the pairwise user study. Participants compare anonymized predictions and reconstructions under scene-level descriptiveness, plausibility of object relations, inputscene faithfulness, and structural preservation criteria.

(b)–(e) For each backbone, we compare the original predictor on the left with the corresponding “+ Ours” variant on the right, followed by the scenes generated from each reconstructed graph by CommonScenes and EchoScene. Red annotations in the reconstructed graphs highlight predicted object or relation labels that differ from the reference graph, and blue titles indicate variants trained with our graph-level supervision. Our supervision yields more coherent graph reconstructions, leading to generated scenes that better preserve the reference object composition and spatial layout across both downstream generators.

Figure 6: Failure case of the proposed graph-level supervision. The input point cloud depicts a kitchen-like scene, and the reference 3D scene graph contains a contextually atypical object label, commode, together with fine-grained directional predicates such as front and right. Our method preserves the overall relational scaffold of the scene, including standing on, build in, attached to, and higher than, but predicts the atypical commode as a contextually plausible kitchen cabinet and relaxes some directional predicates into the broader proximity relation close by. This case illustrates that the contextual semantic prior improves global graph coherence in general, but can occasionally favor common scene-compatible labels over rare or fine-grained annotations.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly optimized with object-node and relation-edge classification losses. These objectives encourage exact object and relation label recovery, but they do not directly optimize semantic proximity to the ground-truth scene graph: two wrong graphs can receive comparable penalties even when one is much closer in object roles and relation contexts. A direct graph-distance loss is difficult in general, since graph matching and graph edit distance require correspondence search and edit-cost design. Our key observation is that prior supervised 3D scene graph prediction protocols are conducted on fixed object-node indices and supervised edge slots. This can turn a scene graph comparison into a well-defined aligned graph-distance problem. To this end, we propose SWORD, a Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance that builds block-normalized object and relation ground distance metrics from training scene graph annotations through a deterministic base-to-context order, without external semantic priors. SWORD lifts these metrics to Wasserstein distances over aligned node and null-augmented edge marginals, providing semantic graph-distance supervision beyond exact-label penalties while preserving the ground-truth graph as the unique zero-distance solution in aligned marginal probability space. We prove that SWORD is a strict metric on aligned marginal probabilistic scene graphs, preserves scene-graph-grounded substitution ordering, controls additive graph-grounded semantic observables, and yields a surrogate upper-bounding decoded semantic error.
authors: U-Chae Jun, Jaeeun Ko, Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiwoo Kang
bullets: Problem: Exact-label losses do not distinguish between wrong graphs that are semantically closer or farther from the ground truth.
Method: Exploit fixed object indices and supervised edge slots to define aligned graph comparisons without correspondence search.

Method: Learn block-normalized object and relation ground metrics from training annotations using a deterministic base-to-context ordering, then lift them to Wasserstein distances over nodes and null-augmented edges.
Contribution: SWORD is proven to be a strict metric on aligned probabilistic scene graphs, preserve substitution ordering, control semantic observables, and upper-bound decoded semantic error.
Scope: The approach relies on aligned node and edge supervision protocols.

papers.abstract: Recently, the integration of generative priors has revolutionized Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkably high data efficiency. However, although methods based on Text-to-Image (T2I) models excel in general scenes, their efficacy degrades sharply when confronted with open-world environmental perturbations, such as illumination variations and adverse weather. Since T2I priors are optimized for semantic synthesis rather than preserving pixel-level structure, they struggle to decouple geometry from appearance under severe visual shifts, easily triggering structural hallucinations. Therefore, our core insight is to model open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, fully leveraging the powerful structure-preserving editing priors of Image-to-Image (I2I) models. Based on this, we propose OpenDepth, a robust open-world MDE framework that introduces "Intra-Domain Awareness" -- the capability to map diverse stylistic inputs sharing identical geometry into a unified latent space. To achieve this, we first align shallow features within the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to unified geometric representations. Additionally, we introduce a joint RGB latent reconstruction task, requiring the model to recover clean RGB information from degraded inputs. This multi-stage strategy effectively decouples environmental style interference, compelling the model to focus strictly on underlying geometric recovery. Extensive evaluations show that OpenDepth sets new SOTA records for robust zero-shot depth estimation across standard and extreme weather benchmarks, demonstrating exceptional structural integrity and adaptability.
authors: Mengke Zhang, Tianyi Yang, Xinzhuo Li, Anlong Ming
bullets: T2I-based depth methods can hallucinate structure when environmental appearance shifts severely.
OpenDepth treats depth estimation as geometry-consistent inference across differently styled versions of the same scene.
It aligns shallow DiT features to unify degraded observations with shared geometric representations.
A joint RGB latent reconstruction task helps separate environmental style from underlying geometry.
Experiments report state-of-the-art robust zero-shot performance on standard and extreme-weather benchmarks, with strong structural integrity and adaptability.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the OpenDepth framework. To harness editing priors for robust open-world depth estimation, we introduce Latent Feature Alignment (L𝑓 𝑒𝑎𝑡 ) and Unified RGB Reconstruction (L𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜𝑛). This dual-constraint strategy projects diverse degraded inputs into a unified latent domain, strictly decoupling environmental styles from geometric structures.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on zero-shot depth estimation. OpenDepth demonstrates superior detail preservation and structural consistency over Lotus-D [21], FE2E [58], and DepthAnything-AC [50] across both general and open-world conditions, as highlighted by white arrows.

In a separate controlled experiment, bothmodels are trained on the same 59K samples from Hypersim [42] and Virtual KITTI [6]. The T2I model (LotusD [21]) suffers from severe structural hallucinations under visual degradations, while the I2I baseline better preserves scene geometry, suggesting stronger inherent robustness for depth estimation.

The I2I baseline exhibits significantly higher and more stable similarity than the T2I model, demonstrating inherent intra-domain awareness. (Right) Effect of our Latent Feature Alignment.

(Right) Our RGB Reconstruction perfectly aligns these diverse perturbation clusters into a unified latent domain, demonstrating true style-invariance for consistent geometric perception.

papers.tldr: OpenDepth repurposes image-to-image editing priors to improve zero-shot monocular depth estimation under illumination changes and adverse weather.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.
authors: Jiaqi Tang, Yu Wang, Yang Liu, Jing Tao, Fandong Zhang, Zhou Zhen, Xiahai Zhuang, Qingchao Chen, Yining Yang, Yizhou Yu
bullets: Models were evaluated consistently across 14 segmentation, classification, and regression tasks covering multiple anatomies and modalities.
No model ranked among the top three across all tasks; architecture advantages varied by task.
Transferability estimators agreed with fine-tuned rankings differently for segmentation versus image-level prediction tasks.
InsightRank uses task-specific frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware comparisons to rank models before fine-tuning.
A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks, but shortlist effectiveness varied by target type.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Study overview: benchmarking and transferability estimation for 3D medical imaging. a, Two complementary workflows use the same pool of 21 pretrained encoders and two scratch controls. Frozen features provide voxel-level evidence for segmentation and patient-level evidence for classification and regression, from which InsightRank produces pairwise rankings and a three-model shortlist. Separately, downstream fine-tuning of all 23 candidates across 14 tasks yields 322 three-fold mean outcomes and the reference rankings used to evaluate model selection. The reference benchmark covers the full candidate pool, not only shortlisted models. b, Indicator assignments depend on the target and encoder pair: segmentation uses class-balanced nearest-centroid accuracy (G), activation amplitude (N) and centroid margin (B); classification and regression use effective dimensionality (C) and neighbour-outcome agreement (R). Arrows indicate the preferred direction. Pairwise wins, ties and losses are aggregated with equal weight. c, Evaluation compares predicted and fine-tuned rankings, measures performance loss at a fixed shortlist size, and compares recorded extraction-plus-training time with exhaustive fine-tuning where timing data are available. Images, outcome curves, matrix colours, example shortlists and charts are schematic; they do not show measured predictions, survival-curve estimates or numerical results. Task-specific evaluation and timing coverage are detailed in Methods.

Fig. 4 Comparison-dependent evidence for spatial targets. a, Three feature statistics assigned to model-pair types, followed by the shared net-win aggregation. b, Weighted Kendall correlations for the complete pool and within-architecture rankings across nine tasks. c, Pairwise concordance of each statistic, averaged across tasks; outlines mark fixed assignments. Predicted ties count as half agreement and 0.5 denotes chance-direction agreement. d, Top 1 and Top 3 regret in Dice percentage points. All candidates use the same task-specific probe and three-fold reference. Both coronary annotation qualifications are detailed in Methods.

Fig. 3 Cross-task benchmark of 3D medical model candidates. a, Ranks of three-fold mean downstream outcomes for 23 candidates across nine segmentation and five classification or regression tasks. Numbers show within-task ranks; colour shows (r − 1)/(M − 1), with rank r and candidate count M = 23. Outlines identify winners. Scratch models are non-pretrained controls. b,c, Maximum task coverage of any single fixed model at rank threshold k. The maximizing model may change with k, so each curve is an optimistic envelope rather than one model’s performance. Dagger and double dagger mark the coronary annotation qualifications detailed in Methods.

Fig. 5 Selection loss at a matched training budget. a, Mean regret versus shortlist size in the predefined four-task comparison. The random curve is an exact expectation over uniformly sampled subsets. The fixed recommendation uses ranks from other tasks only, as specified in Methods. b, Task-level Top 3 regret. All methods use the same downstream reference; no additional models were trained. Both coronary tasks retain their annotation qualifications.

Fig. 2 Pretraining provenance and downstream task atlas. a, The registered model pool contains 17 OpenMind-derived checkpoints (14 trained with the full collection, two using T1-weighted or image-quality-filtered subsets, and one DINO-derived), four external pretrained-weight models and two randomly initialized controls. ViT-VoCo inherits weights from the VoCo GitHub repository rather than OpenMind; the exact upstream checkpoint variant used here was not independently verified. Counts denote model candidates, not pretraining images. b, The 14 downstream datasets are grouped by anatomical target: nine brain, one head-and-neck, three heart or coronary, and one kidney task. TopCoW is assigned to the brain group because it segments the intracranial Circle of Willis. Card colour denotes segmentation (teal), classification (ochre) or regression (violet); each card identifies its target and imaging input. The coronary-plaque and coronary bridge-vessel CTA datasets are private, hospital-curated in-house datasets, as indicated on their cards. Plaque annotations remain under quality review (†). For the provisional bridge-vessel task (‡), 44 of 546 series lacked matched masks and were encoded as all-background labels in training and evaluation rather than excluded. c, All 23 candidates have three-fold downstream references on all 14 tasks (322 model–task means), and frozen-feature scoring covers the same candidates on nine segmentation and five image-level tasks.

papers.title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
papers.tldr: A benchmark of 23 self-supervised 3D medical vision models shows that transferability is highly task-dependent, while InsightRank can reduce fine-tuning costs by prioritizing candidates.

papers.abstract: Modeling 3D hair strands is challenging due to complex hairstyle geometry, scarce high-quality training data, and incomplete or noisy input observations. Foundation models offer broader hairstyle priors, but their outputs are not directly usable for strand-based rendering and simulation. Existing approaches require costly per-instance optimization to fit hair priors to meshes from foundation models and 2D orientations from specialized predictors trained on limited hair data, restricting efficiency and generalization. We present HairFlow, a multimodal conditioned diffusion framework for efficient and controllable hair strands modeling. HairFlow conditions strand generation on two complementary representations: a coarse mesh that constrains global shape and multi-view sketches that specify local strand flow. HairFlow combines an Orientation VAE with a conditioned diffusion transformer to generate volumetric fields that are traced into explicit strands. To overcome the lack of paired sketch-strand training data, we introduce an automatic synthesis pipeline that generates geometrically aligned multi-view sketches with diverse styles representative of inference-time inputs. Experiments show that HairFlow generates plausible 3D strands that faithfully follow the input conditions across diverse hairstyles, substantially reduces inference time, and supports flexible multimodal control.
authors: Yating Wang, Kui Wu, Ran Yi, Zixuan Lu, Tongtong Wang, Zhongtian Zheng, Lizhuang Ma, Yuefan Shen
bullets: Addresses complex hair geometry, limited training data, and noisy or incomplete observations.
Uses a coarse mesh for global hairstyle shape and multi-view sketches for local strand flow.
Combines an Orientation VAE with a conditioned diffusion transformer to produce volumetric fields traced into explicit strands.
Introduces automatic synthesis of aligned, stylistically diverse sketch–strand training pairs.
Experiments show plausible strands that follow inputs across diverse hairstyles, with reduced inference time and flexible multimodal control.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HairFlow. HairFlow takes two geometric inputs—a coarse hair mesh and multi-view sketches—to specify global shape and local strand flow. These conditions can be obtained from images or text using foundation models, or provided by artists. Mesh and camera-aware sketch encoders produce tokens that condition a diffusion transformer through cross-attention. The transformer generates latents in the space of a pretrained Orientation VAE, which decodes them into an orientation field for explicit strand extraction.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of single-view 3D hair reconstruction. HairLRM and HairFlow share the same input mesh, supplemented by HairStep orientation maps or sketches from image generation models, respectively. Inputs appear to the left of the corresponding strands. The color wheel below HairLRM illustrates the direction-to-color mapping.

Figure 6: Flexible Sketch Guidance: (a) Sketches with different stroke widths and styles yield similar strand geometry. (b) Joint conditioning on sketches from two viewpoints produces a single hairstyle consistent with both views. (c) Two sets of artist-drawn 3D strokes on the same mesh are projected into multi-view sketches, guiding the generated strands to follow different flow patterns.

Figure 5: Effect of the sketch condition. From left: input image, mesh, mesh-only result, sketch, and mesh+sketch result. Results within each row share the same mesh and random seed. Colors encode 3D tangent directions.

Figure 3: Hair sketch synthesis pipeline. (a) Input strands and template head mesh. (b) Multiview orientation maps; colors encode directed 2D tangents as shown in the circular legend. (c) Bidirectional tracing from sampled seeds; arrows show local directions, and the inset details tracing from the highlighted seed. (d) Sketch variations through stroke density, line width, and localized seed sampling.
Figure 7: Qualitative comparisons with HairGPT (Luo et al., 2026) and Hao et al. (2026). Their input images and reconstruction results are taken from the respective papers, as code is unavailable.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison. Silhouette IoU (↑) is evaluated on 30 real images. Angular error (◦, ↓) is measured between 3D orientation fields derived from reconstructed and ground-truth strands on 326 validation hairstyles.

Table 2: Additional quantitative comparisons with HairLRM. We report mean angular errors (◦, lower is better) for VAE reconstruction on the training and test sets, and for strand generation conditioned on meshes alone or with additional 2D cues.

papers.title: HairFlow: Modeling 3D Hair Strands with Multi-Modal Conditioned Diffusion
papers.tldr: HairFlow efficiently generates controllable 3D hair strands from coarse meshes and multi-view sketches using conditioned diffusion.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal fusion for 3D object detection assumes that cameras and LiDAR are broadly complementary. In practice, how much each modality is trusted at a given location is decided by learned weights that are neither characterized nor auditable. We label every ground-truth object by which modalities detected it, then mine the resulting 0.4M-object database across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Because the patterns shift with distance from the ego vehicle, we read the mined model through Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution (SSFA), which conditions Shapley attribution on distance zones and exposes structure that global attribution averages away. Three assumptions built into the current fusion design do not hold. The modality-preference boundary tracks the object itself: a traffic cone is nearly six times as likely as a truck to be seen by the camera alone (16.8% vs. 2.9%), regardless of range. Camera-only detections peak at 10-30 m, inside the band usually ceded to LiDAR, and fall away on either side. The drivers of failure are not additive either: the distance - density interaction alone outweighs the entire main effect of viewing direction. We further find that modality dominance is directionally non-stationary, with objects behind the vehicle being markedly more LiDAR-dominant than those in front. We compile the mined structure into a Modality Reliability Map and inject it into four pretrained fusion detectors through a lightweight attention layer. This improves performance by up to 1.3 mean Average Precision (mAP) while fine-tuning under 4% of their parameters in 2-3 GPU-hours. Our work lifts reliability out of the weights and treats it as a quantity that can be examined before deployment. That is what a safety measure for multi-modal perception must rest on.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Mona Jaber, Shanxin Yuan, Ahmed Sayed
bullets: Mines modality detections for 0.4M objects across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo to characterize when cameras and LiDAR disagree.
Introduces Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution to reveal distance-dependent structure hidden by global attribution.
Finds that modality preference depends on object type and location: cameras favor some objects and peak at 10–30 m, while rear-facing objects are more LiDAR-dominant.
Shows failure drivers are interactive rather than purely additive, with distance–density effects outweighing viewing-direction main effects.
Injecting a Modality Reliability Map into four pretrained fusion detectors improves performance by up to 1.3 mAP while fine-tuning under 4% of parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and corrects camera-LiDAR perception reliability for autonomous driving 3D detection; relevant to embodied perception and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Mining Cross-Modal Perception Gaps in Autonomous Driving: When Camera and LiDAR Disagree
papers.tldr: A large-scale analysis shows that camera–LiDAR reliability varies by object type, distance, interaction effects, and direction, enabling a lightweight reliability map that improves fusion detection with minimal fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.

papers.abstract: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/octree-nn/octmole and https://huggingface.co/Disembo/octmole, respectively.
authors: Yu-Tong Jin, Yi-Yang Tian, Qiwei Ye, Peng-Shuai Wang
bullets: Models sparse molecular structure from coarse global shape to fine local geometry.
Uses a hierarchical occupancy flow plus a joint atom flow for atom identities and in-cell offsets.
Cell corruption improves robustness to generated molecular support.
Shows strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality on QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, with efficiency gains over dense 3D generation.
Enables spatial conditioning for shape control, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation without task-specific retraining.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. The hierarchical spatial flow approach is a transferable technique for 3D generation tasks.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph generation requires understanding both object semantics and metric spatial relations. However, existing open-vocabulary methods often struggle with spatial predicates because language similarity reflects semantic co-occurrence rather than explicit geometry. We propose GHOST, a Geometry-constrained Hybrid diffusion framework for Open-vocabulary 3D Scene graph generaTion. GHOST jointly models continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates, following a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to ensure geometrically consistent relation prediction. It introduces language-grounded constraint induction, which maps predicate embeddings to differentiable geometric constraints that guide both layout refinement and predicate reweighting. A Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser further couples node and edge reasoning through noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both closed-set and open-vocabulary settings, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.
authors: Changqun Feng, Wangxiandi Yin, Xin Hu, Ruiting Dai, Feiyang Yang, Jielei Wang, Tao He
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language similarity and explicit 3D spatial geometry in open-vocabulary relation prediction.
Uses a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to jointly model continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates.
Induces differentiable geometric constraints from predicate embeddings to refine layouts and reweight relation predictions.
Employs a Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser with noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 3DSSG, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GHOST. GHOST jointly denoises object geometry and relation predicates through a hybrid reverse diffusion process. At each step, the Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser (GTCD) first refines object geometry, then applies language-grounded constraint guidance to enforce geometric consistency, and finally decodes predicate tokens conditioned on the corrected layout. This denoise→ project→ decode ordering ensures that the recovered scene graph is both spatially coherent and open-vocabulary capable.

Figure 1: VLM-based open-vocabulary 3DSGG methods perform about 30 points worse on spatial predicates than on nonspatial ones (a), because they rely on language co-occurrence priors rather than true 3D layout, e.g., a model may predict “pillow on sofa” simply because the relation is common, while ignoring the actual scene layout (b). GHOST replaces such priors with explicit geometric constraints, substantially narrowing this gap (c).
Figure 5: Geometric Oracle Experiments. Even a perfect geometric oracle applied post-hoc yields only modest spatial gains over the one-shot baseline.

Figure 4: Qualitative OV scene graph predictions on 3DSSG [43]. Top: comparison between RelationField and GHOST. Bottom: a GHOST failure case caused by an object recognition error from the upstream detector. Green = correct; red = error.

Figure 3: Accuracy–efficiency trade-off (predicate R@5). All GHOST variants share the same weights and environment and differ only in reverse-step count 𝑇 . ReLaGS is excluded due to the unavailable source code.

papers.abstract: Repetitive structures can give an incorrect pose candidate more inlier support than an accurate one, causing visual localization to select it. History-Guided Pose Reselection (HPR) uses coarse position forecasts from up to five past localization outputs to distinguish well-separated current-query candidates. The best-fitting forecast proposes an alternative; HPR accepts it only if every well-fitting forecast is much closer to it than to the localizer's pose. HPR needs no odometry and returns the selected candidate unchanged, using prediction for selection rather than pose refinement. With one development-set threshold, HPR improves recall within 5 meters and 10 degrees in all 12 main configurations of Hierarchical Localization (HLoc), MASt3R-based pose generation, and JIST-based retrieval, losing successes on fewer than 0.4 percent of queries. On NAVER Gangnam B1, HPR corrects 97 HLoc failures and loses six successes; gains persist within 0.25 meters and 2 degrees on all three HLoc test sets. Median HPR runtime on HLoc candidates is below one millisecond, excluding pose generation. Recovery weakens under less frequent localization.
authors: Jaehyun Kim, Wonseok Kang, Tae-Wan Kim
bullets: Repetitive structures can make an incorrect pose candidate appear more supported than the correct one.

papers.abstract: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used to encode relative positions in Transformers. In multi-view settings, however, patch coordinates are defined independently in each image: the same 3D point can therefore have different coordinates across views, making them insufficient for establishing cross-view correspondences. We introduce WorldRoPE, a probabilistic world-centric RoPE for multi-view attention. At each layer, WorldRoPE back-projects each patch token into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame. These primitives represent multiple plausible 3D supports for a token, jointly capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite spatial extent of its patch frustum. When a key token's support is projected into a query view, it induces a distribution over where that key may appear in the query image. WorldRoPE integrates the rotary operator over this distribution in closed form, combining rotations at the projected primitive centers according to their mixture weights with covariance-dependent attenuation. This makes attention less sensitive to uncertain key locations in the query view, without rasterizing or warping token features. The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Kyujin Lim, Bohyung Han
bullets: Per-image patch coordinates cannot reliably establish correspondences for the same 3D point across views.
Each token is back-projected into volumetric Gaussian primitives capturing alternative depths, uncertainty, and patch-frustum extent.
The method integrates RoPE over the induced projected-location distribution using mixture weights and covariance-based attenuation.
It guides cross-view attention with predicted geometry while allowing updated features to refine geometry across layers.
Experiments show effectiveness for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have driven remarkable progress in 3D vision,yet their quadratic complexity renders them impractical for long video sequences. Streaming 3D reconstruction addresses this bottleneck by processing frames sequen?tially with constant memory. However, existing recurrent architectures inevitably suffer from progressive degradation over long sequences, as they fail to account for the intrinsic reliability of observations and the accumulated confidence of the historical state, leading to severe error accumulation. To address these issues, we introduce BAT3R, a training-free Bayesian adaptation framework comprising two synergistic modules: State Innovation Gating (SIG) and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU). SIG acts as a distributional regularizer that anchors state evolution to its geometric initialization, effectively arresting representational drift during long-term inference. Building on this, BASU reformulates state update as a recursive Bayesian inference process within a Kalman filtering framework. By jointly modeling the temporal reliability of observations via information-theoretic gain and spatial relevance via cross-attention maps, BASU achieves an asymmetric spatio-temporal state fusion: well-consolidated historical regions are protected from redundant updates, while genuinely novel scene content is aggressively incor?porated. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (7-Scenes, TUM, ScanNet, KITTI, etc.) demonstrate that BAT3R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online 3D reconstruction methods, with the most significant gains observed on long sequences and complex scenes.
authors: Lijian Li, Yuanpeng He, Yudian Zheng, Chung-ju Huang, Linyu Li, Dongming Jin, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Chi-Man Pun
bullets: Streaming reconstruction uses constant memory but recurrent methods accumulate errors over long videos.
State Innovation Gating anchors evolving representations to their geometric initialization, reducing drift.
Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating models observation reliability and spatial relevance for asymmetric state fusion.
Historical regions are protected from redundant updates, while novel content is incorporated more strongly.
Experiments across standard benchmarks show consistent gains over existing online 3D reconstruction methods, especially on long and complex sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the BAT3R framework consisting of two modules State Innovation Gating (SIG) and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU). SIG prevents representational drift by anchoring updates to the initial geometric state, while BASU optimizes observation fusion through a recursive Kalman filtering framework. By balancing observation reliability with historical confidence, the framework achieves robust, uncertainty-aware 3D scene reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Garment manipulation requires inferring both garment identity and complete configuration from partial, self-occluded observations. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: completing a partial observation requires a garment-specific deformation prior, while identifying the garment requires a configuration that explains the observation. We introduce ClothAtlas, which jointly identifies garments and estimates their complete configurations from partial point clouds and a library of canonical meshes. A shared graph-conditioned flow-matching model samples configurations for each candidate mesh and ranks candidates by observation fit. The model accommodates different mesh shapes, vertex counts, and connectivities, allowing new garments to be added from canonical meshes alone without retraining. On held-out DexGarmentLab garments, ClothAtlas ranks the correct mesh first among 221 candidates for all 22 test garments from a single flat observation. From a single self-occluded observation, it identifies 15/22 garments, compared with 8/22 for a deterministic graph estimator. Persistent vertex identities support grasp-target localization on real garments, reducing mean error from 15.4 to 6.4 cm overall and from 17.0 to 8.3 cm on occluded targets compared with dense descriptor matching. Project page: https://clothatlas.github.io/
authors: Jens Lundell, Alberta Longhini, Lei Shu, Hemal Arora, Evan Robert, Carlota Par\'es-Morlans, Marcel B\"usching, M{\aa}rten Bj\"orkman, Jeannette Bohg

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has been becoming a promising 3D reconstruction technique because of its advantage of high-fidelity rendering effect with high efficiency. However, it still suffers from coarse density control and semantically blind loss functions when reconstructing the fine-grained structures in complex urban scenes. Thus, this study proposes SG-GS, a semantic-guided 3DGS method for fine-grained structure reconstruction. It takes the semantic segmentation deduced by the Segment Anything Model (SAM) as a constraint and systematically integrates it into both Gaussian density control and loss function design. On the one hand, a semantic-constrained adaptive density control mechanism is constructed, which dynamically allocates gradient thresholds to different semantic regions of the scene and introduces an additional boundary-enhanced densification strategy, so that new Gaussians are directed to structurally critical regions. On the other hand, a multi-feature guided loss function is designed, and fine-grained supervision signals are gradually introduced through a phased progressive training strategy, alleviating the artifacts caused by the lack of semantic constraints in the basic loss. Experiments on three datasets show that the proposed method consistently improves reconstruction accuracy. Compared with the original 3DGS, the PSNR increases by approximately 2.7% to 5.2%, while artifacts on linear structures and boundary blurring are effectively mitigated. The method can serve the fine-grained 3D reconstruction of urban scenes.
authors: Yueling Liao, San Jiang, Xing Zhang, Zhongwen Hu
bullets: Addresses coarse density control and semantically blind losses in 3D Gaussian Splatting for complex urban scenes.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward reconstruction recovers camera poses and dense geometry from image sets whose views are assumed to come from a single scene. In practice, uncurated image collections often contain views from disjoint scenes, and reconstructing these views jointly can corrupt camera poses and geometry. Existing pipelines typically resolve view associations in separate stages before final reconstruction, leaving view graph initialization and reconstruction inference only loosely coupled. We introduce Graph3R, which unifies view graph initialization with feed-forward reconstruction through a shared geometric representation. A lightweight verification head predicts pairwise covisibility from the multi-view features of $\pi^3$ to construct a view graph. This graph classifies the input views into scene groups. For each group, we mask the shared features before decoding camera poses and dense geometry. Reusing the multi-view features allows Graph3R to reconstruct disjoint scenes separately with a single backbone pass. Across three benchmarks, Graph3R improves average maximum recall at 100% precision by upto 8.99 percentage points over the baseline, while improving reconstruction quality on mixed-scene inputs. Regarding the multi-session mapping task, Graph3R improves cross-session localization and achieves competitive pose estimation accuracy, while delivering a runtime speedup of approximately $35.9\times$ over the baseline when reconstructing the query group. By integrating learned view association with geometric inference, our approach takes a step toward end-to-end reconstruction from uncurated image collections.
authors: Jingwen Yu, Hengli Wang, Jianhao Jiao, Zhonghang Liu, Ping Tan, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses pose and geometry corruption when uncurated image collections mix disjoint scenes.
Uses a lightweight covisibility-verification head over multi-view features to build a view graph and group images by scene.
Masks shared features per group, then decodes poses and dense geometry while reusing a single backbone pass.
Improves average maximum recall at 100% precision by up to 8.99 percentage points across three benchmarks and improves mixed-scene reconstruction quality.
For multi-session mapping, improves cross-session localization, maintains competitive pose accuracy, and reports an approximately 35.9× query-group reconstruction speedup over the baseline.

Graph3R proposes a unified paradigm that jointly predicts the view graph and scene structure with a single backbone inference as detailed illustrated in Fig. 3.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian segmentation typically binds semantic features to the per-Gaussian state via per-scene gradient training (1-4 h) or the more recent closed-form distillation. Both commit each primitive to a single feature; therefore, boundary Gaussians spanning multiple 2D instances are forced into a hard decision that degrades retrieval accuracy and yields unstable mask boundaries at render time. We present DIGS, a training-free framework with two stages, class-agnostic mapping and multi-modal encoding, that decouples instance discovery from linguistic naming. At the Gaussian level, our distribution-informed representation maintains an explicit top-$M$ label distribution per primitive, updated by a tempered Dirichlet rule; preservation of multi-peaked label distributions at boundary primitives allows a late-argmax renderer to recover clean instance boundaries. A bidirectional state machine aggregates these distributions into a persistent class-agnostic instance ontology. The instance-level encoding stage then fuses the CLIP visual embedding of each instance's isolated 3D footprint with the CLIP-text embedding of an LLM-generated attribute description, disambiguating visually similar instances. On a single A100, DIGS completes mapping and instance encoding on LERF-OVS in 1.0-3.2 min per scene, depending on whether LLM fusion is enabled, and serves native 3D queries in 5.4 ms. It reaches 71.95% mean mIoU on LERF-OVS, outperforming both the training-free SFS and training-based LaGa baselines. DIGS also achieves the highest mean mIoU on LERF-Mask and 3D-OVS and surpasses Gaga and ObjectGS on Replica under their respective evaluation protocols. Code is available at https://github.com/ZephyrZos/DIGS.
authors: Zhifan Zeng, Wenbo Xiao, Arcot Sowmya, Changming Sun
bullets: Addresses boundary artifacts caused by assigning each Gaussian a single semantic feature.
Uses a tempered Dirichlet rule to maintain top-M label distributions and a late-argmax renderer for cleaner boundaries.
Builds a persistent, class-agnostic instance ontology with a bidirectional state machine.
Fuses CLIP visual embeddings of isolated 3D instances with CLIP-text embeddings from LLM-generated descriptions.
Runs in 1.0–3.2 minutes per scene, serves queries in 5.4 ms, and reports 71.95% mean mIoU on LERF-OVS; it also achieves the highest mean mIoU on LERF-Mask and 3D-OVS.

papers.abstract: We present Unravel, a training-free framework that turns a single image into an interactive 3D scene, where every object is an independent and movable asset. Existing generators either produce one entangled geometry in which no object can be moved, or predict all objects in one feed-forward pass, where a wrong guess cannot be detected or repaired. Unravel instead takes a different approach: it first takes the scene apart, and then puts it back together. Starting from the input image, an agentic harness that iteratively peels the image layer by layer, and adopts point cloud as major modality for spatial relationship recovery. Specifically, a vision-language model plans which objects are fully visible, an image editor removes them and restores the occluded regions. Every edit is verified before being incorporated into the reconstruction. This process gradually turns occluded parts of the scene into direct observation, allowing objects to be reconstructed when they are best exposed rather than hallucinated from the original image alone. The scene is then rebuilt in reverse removal order, so that the supporting objects are naturally placed before the objects they support. Since a single-view image only reveals part of an object, we treat the observed points as a lower bound on its size: an asset may grow to cover its points, but can not shrink away from them. Finally, we physically settle the reconstructed scene to remove floating objects and interpenetrations, followed by an agentic audit that corrects remaining placement errors. Extensive experiments on diverse indoor scenes show that Unravel recovers more objects, places them more faithfully, and produces scenes that are more physically-plausible than existing methods.
authors: Hui Shan, Keyang Luo, Binjia Zhou, Ming Li, Kai Li, Xin Wang, Zhenyang Li, Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Runze Zhang, Xin Wang, Yanwei Fu, Zhen Chen, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Targets the limitations of entangled scene generators and one-shot object prediction, where objects cannot be moved or errors are difficult to fix.
Uses a training-free agentic process: a vision-language model selects visible objects, an image editor removes them and restores occlusions, and each edit is verified.
Represents spatial relationships with point clouds and reconstructs objects in reverse removal order to preserve support relationships.
Treats visible points as a minimum object extent, then physically settles the scene and audits placements to reduce floating and intersecting objects.
Experiments on diverse indoor scenes report more complete object recovery, more faithful placement, and greater physical plausibility than existing methods.

papers.abstract: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a core technology in autonomous systems that enables them to estimate their own position and build a map of unknown environments simultaneously. SLAM systems in dynamic environments are of great practical importance. However, existing dynamic SLAM approaches still have several limitations like over-removal and high computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose a real-time RGB Dynamic SLAM framework that precisely removes moving objects at the pixel level without relying on predefined labels or segmentation models. Our system combines pixel motion predicted by ego-motion using DUSt3R with point tracking from All-Tracker, removing only actually moving pixels by analyzing discrepancies between the two motion sources. Unlike object-level masking methods, our approach eliminates only currently moving regions, allowing temporarily static parts to be utilized for tracking. Operating at approximately 10 FPS, the system achieves real-time performance on standard 30 FPS video streams by subsampling every 3 frames. Relying solely on RGB inputs, this significantly improves upon state-of-the-art dense dynamic SLAM approaches (0.5-3 FPS), presenting a highly practical solution.
authors: Yewon Kim, Paul Hongsuck Seo, Sang Chul Ahn
bullets: Addresses over-removal and high computational cost in existing dynamic SLAM systems.
Compares ego-motion-based pixel motion from DUSt3R with All-Tracker point tracking to identify moving pixels without labels or segmentation models.
Uses pixel-wise rather than object-level masking, retaining temporarily static regions for tracking.
Runs at approximately 10 FPS on subsampled 30 FPS video, using RGB input alone.
The reported scope is dense dynamic SLAM, with performance positioned against methods running at 0.5–3 FPS.

papers.abstract: 3D instance segmentation requires representations that are both geometrically structured and semantically discriminative. Pure 3D encoders model spatial structure well but often lack strong appearance semantics, while directly lifting 2D priors into 3D by concatenation injects rich semantics without ensuring that they align well with the underlying 3D structure. In this paper, we address this problem by formulating 2D-to-3D semantic transfer as a \textbf{masked semantic reconstruction} task. Specifically, we mask a subset of background lifted 2D priors and train the 3D encoder to recover the missing semantic priors, providing explicit supervision for distilling rich 2D semantics into the 3D backbone. We further propose \textbf{geometry-modulated semantic injection}, which uses raw 3D geometry to modulate lifted 2D priors before sparse encoding, so that geometry explicitly controls semantic injection and alleviates the distribution gap between 2D semantic features and 3D geometric features. Experiments on two baseline frameworks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results in both full-data and few-shot settings on ScanNetV2 and ScanNet200. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/yharoldsu0627/Geometry_Guided_Semantic_Reconstruction
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between geometrically strong 3D encoders and semantically rich but potentially misaligned lifted 2D features.
Masks background 2D semantic priors and trains the 3D encoder to reconstruct them, explicitly distilling 2D semantics.
Uses raw 3D geometry to modulate semantic features before sparse encoding, improving geometry–semantic alignment.
Achieves state-of-the-art results across two baseline frameworks in full-data and few-shot settings on ScanNetV2 and ScanNet200.

During training, a subset of background superpoints is masked in the lifted 2D stream and reconstructed from geometry-modulated encoder features. The aggregated superpoint features are finally decoded into instance masks.

papers.abstract: Grounded spatial reasoning about indoor scenes rests on a geometric reconstruction that the multimodal system does not itself produce. Feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models operate under a fixed view budget, making frame selection a critical upstream decision. We show that under this setting the conventional preference for sharp frames can be actively harmful. Across nine handheld room scans, selecting the sharpest 16 of 200 candidate frames is the worst strategy we test, reaching 48\% room dimension error where uniform temporal sampling reaches 3\%. We trace this failure to a coupling between image quality and camera motion: sharp frames tend to occur during slow motion and therefore concentrate the selection in a narrow angular region, leaving $192^\circ$ of the room unobserved in the case we illustrate and over $300^\circ$ in the worst cells. A $2\times2$ factorial experiment that independently manipulates viewpoint spread and per-frame sharpness shows that spread has roughly three times the main effect of quality, and that blurry but well spread selections outperform sharp but clustered selections in 8 of 9 captures. The advantage also diminishes as the frame budget increases and angular coverage saturates, consistent with this mechanism. Finally, we ask whether the failure is detectable at inference: the reconstruction model's multi-view consistency score increases with reconstruction error, while a vision-language model given the same frames reports confidence unrelated to its own spatial estimation error. Under small view budgets, viewpoint coverage is a more important constraint than per-frame image quality, and neither uncertainty signal available at inference reveals this upstream failure.
bullets: Selecting the sharpest 16 of 200 frames produced the worst reconstruction, whereas uniform temporal sampling greatly reduced room-dimension error.
Sharp frames often cluster during slow camera motion, leaving large portions of the room unseen.
A factorial experiment found viewpoint spread had about three times the effect of image quality; blurry but well-spread frames beat sharp clustered frames in 8 of 9 scans.
Coverage benefits shrink as the frame budget grows and angular coverage saturates.
Neither reconstruction consistency scores nor vision-language-model confidence reliably revealed the upstream coverage failure.

Note also that these three captures have the best self-consistency in the set (0.3 to 1.1%, Section 3.3) while showing 8 to 12% accuracy error, so internal agreement between dense reconstructions does not predict agreement with reality.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes viewpoint coverage vs image quality in feed-forward 3D reconstruction and spatial reasoning; relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Sharper Frames, Worse Rooms: Viewpoint Coverage Dominates Image Quality in Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: For feed-forward 3D room reconstruction with few frames, broad viewpoint coverage matters far more than selecting the sharpest images, while common confidence signals fail to detect poor coverage.

papers.abstract: Multimodal 3D occupancy prediction underpins safe autonomous driving through comprehensive scene understanding. However, existing methods have largely pursued higher accuracy through sophisticated fusion, leaving resilience to missing sensors underexplored. In this paper, we investigate spiking neural networks (SNNs) as a means of building more resilient multimodal perception. Still, the discrete nature of spiking neurons makes optimization challenging. To overcome this difficulty, SpikeOcc is introduced with two complementary components, a Spiking Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) and Sensor Availability Learning (SAL). Specifically, SMoE organizes RGB, LiDAR, and joint fusion into specialized pathways, enabling full-width unimodal representations while retaining the original multimodal features via a bounded residual. Beyond sensor dropout, SAL employs a staged curriculum with explicit routing supervision, progressively improving robustness under severe sensing conditions. Remarkably, SAL also yields notable gains for conventional models, highlighting its broader potential for resilient multimodal learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpikeOcc maintains competitive full-sensor accuracy while markedly raising the performance floor under sensor outages. SpikeOcc illustrates the promise of neuromorphic computing, pointing toward more reliable and energy-efficient autonomous driving.
authors: Yiding Sun, Zijie Xu, Hongqiang Lin, Jiajun Cao, Dongxu Zhang, Kai Tang, Jihua Zhu, Wenxuan Liu, Zhaofei Yu, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of maintaining reliable perception when RGB or LiDAR sensors are missing.
Uses a Spiking Mixture-of-Experts to specialize RGB, LiDAR, and joint-fusion pathways while preserving multimodal features through a bounded residual.
Introduces Sensor Availability Learning with staged curriculum training and explicit routing supervision for severe sensing conditions.
Maintains competitive accuracy with all sensors and substantially improves the performance floor during sensor outages.
Suggests broader potential for resilient multimodal learning and energy-efficient autonomous driving; the abstract does not specify quantitative results or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: We present ScenePlacer, a framework for scene-level pose estimation of objects generated by state-of-the-art native shape generation models, placing generated 3D objects into scenes given a partial geometric observation without modifying the underlying generative pipeline. Existing scene generation approaches either generate objects directly in scene coordinates, compromising their canonical-space priors, or regress poses from complete generated shapes in the shape generation process - the latter being a poorly conditioned problem that is sensitive to scale ambiguity and partial observations. ScenePlacer decouples object generation from pose estimation by reformulating alignment as conditional visibility-field learning. Given an observed partial point cloud from reconstruction and a generated mesh, it predicts a visibility field defined in object space, then estimates the rigid transformation by aligning the partial observation to visible parts on the mesh. We propose a pretrained 3D shape VAE as our backbone, preserving its mesh prior while conditioning it on a separately encoded observation. We further introduce visibility-aware, radius-constrained supervision and synthesize training pairs using only object-level meshes and rendered views, eliminating the need for scene-level pose annotations. On 3D-FUTURE, ScenePlacer consistently outperforms existing placement and pose-refinement baselines under both ground-truth and monocular depth estimation. With generated objects, it achieves a Chamfer distance of 0.0077 and an F-score of 92.40 under estimated depth and improves to 0.0023 and 98.27, respectively, under ground-truth geometry.
authors: Ken Deng, Jiarui Liu, Guibiao Liao, Kunming Luo, Mochu Xiang, Hongyu Yan, Yebin Liu, Shenghua Gao, Yizhou Yu, Ping Tan
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and partial-observation challenges in scene-level placement of generated 3D objects.

Introduces visibility-aware, radius-constrained supervision and generates training pairs from object meshes and rendered views, avoiding scene-level pose annotations.
On 3D-FUTURE, reports Chamfer distance/F-score of 0.0077/92.40 with estimated depth and 0.0023/98.27 with ground-truth geometry, outperforming cited baselines.

papers.abstract: 3D editing aims to modify an existing 3D asset according to user intent while preserving geometry and appearance outside the intended edit region. Existing methods often rely on task-specific training, source-3D inversion, or external 3D masks, and lack a unified framework for diverse editing conditions and tasks. We propose UMAS3D, a unified 3D editing framework that is training-free, inversion-free, and free from external 3D masks. UMAS3D converts text, bounding boxes, reference images, and their combinations into common target-view guidance, after which addition, deletion, modification, appearance, and pose editing share the same downstream 3D generation process. Our key insight is to couple online edit-region estimation with region-aware source preservation. Mask-Free Adaptive Region Modeling (MARM) initializes an Edit/Keep prior from source-target visual differences and progressively refines it as the target structure evolves, while Source-Guided Preservation Steering (SGPS) constrains the current Keep-region states to retain source geometry and appearance without suppressing target-driven changes. Experiments show that UMAS3D supports addition, deletion, modification, appearance, and pose editing while effectively preserving unedited source content. These advances make UMAS3D a unified framework for flexible and source-preserving 3D editing across diverse editing conditions.

papers.abstract: Camera-based occupancy prediction provides geometric and semantic scene understanding for robot perception and has been adopted in autonomous vehicle and UAV perception systems. Gaussian primitives offer a promising alternative by potentially representing only occupied regions, thereby concentrating computation and representational capacity where needed and reducing wasted computation and memory in empty space. However, existing Gaussian-based methods suffer from poor primitive utilization, as ineffective training objectives leave some Gaussians in empty space, while the limited expressiveness of Gaussian functions restricts their ability to model complex shapes. To address these limitations, we propose a novel 3D representation, Gaussian Neural Field (GNF), which can accurately map voxel positions to semantic occupancies. In GNF, Gaussians and a neural network jointly parameterize the field, where the Gaussians define its spatial support and provide features for neural decoding, while the neural network enables more expressive occupancy modeling than Gaussian functions alone. We further develop the Gaussian Neural Field Transformer (GNFormer), a streamlined and flexible method that predicts GNFs for camera-based occupancy prediction. Across Occ-ScanNet, SSCBench-KITTI-360, and nuScenes-SurroundOcc benchmarks, GNFormer achieves the highest IoU and mIoU and the fastest inference among the compared single-frame methods. In the experiments, GNFormer can represent indoor and outdoor scenes with only 256 and 1024 Gaussians, respectively, substantially fewer primitives than prior Gaussian-based methods. The code will be released.
authors: Guangcheng Chen, Li He, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses poor Gaussian utilization and limited shape expressiveness in existing Gaussian-based occupancy methods.

papers.abstract: Generating complete 3D assets from sparse, unposed images requires preserving observed geometry while completing unseen regions. Joint reconstruction and generation offers a way to address both goals: reconstruction recovers the geometry observed in the input images, while generation contributes learned shape priors. However, combining camera-relative reconstruction with canonical-space generation introduces a coordinate mismatch that makes direct geometric interaction more difficult. Moreover, conditioning each 3D location on all views without accounting for their relevance may mix useful geometric evidence with unrelated image content, hindering local detail recovery. We present UniForge3D, which jointly models reconstruction and generation in a shared anchor-guided space, resolving their coordinate mismatch. This space follows the anchor view's azimuth while keeping the object upright. The two branches exchange features bidirectionally to predict per-view point maps and a complete sparse voxel structure. We further condition point-map prediction on the generated structure to establish pixel-to-voxel correspondences and select the most informative input view for each voxel. Features from the selected views then guide detailed shape generation, helping preserve observed geometric details. Our method achieves state-of-the-art appearance and geometry results on Toys4K and GSO, generating complete 3D assets with improved fidelity. Project webpage: https://xishuxishu.github.io/uniforge3d-project/
authors: Wenjue Chen, Wenyue Chen, Heliang Zheng, Rongfei Jia, Yuan Liu, Meng Li

Uses generated structure to establish pixel-to-voxel correspondences and select informative views for each voxel.
Reports state-of-the-art appearance and geometry results on Toys4K and GSO, with improved asset fidelity.

papers.abstract: Recent native 3D generators achieve high-quality asset creation by modeling structured 3D latents with flow-based transformers, but their high-resolution generation remains computationally expensive due to costly iterative sampling. In this work, we introduce a few-step distillation framework for native 3D generation, enabled by continuous self-consistency training with a custom JVP FlashAttention kernel and an analytic velocity regression objective for sparse structured 3D latents. To stabilize joint optimization, we further introduce an adaptive loss weighting strategy that automatically balances them without manual tuning. Beyond acceleration, we reveal a previously overlooked failure mode of few-step native 3D generation: sampling-induced latent distribution drift preserves geometric correctness but disrupts downstream PBR texture synthesis, causing texture artifacts on geometrically valid assets. To address this issue, we propose Channel Match, a training-free adaptive per-channel latent calibration method that restores the latent distribution without modifying either generator. We validate our approach on TRELLIS.2 at the $1024^3$ resolution setting. Our two-step model achieves $4.5\times$ faster geometry sampling while maintaining geometry quality comparable to the many-step teacher, and Channel Match further improves rendering quality by recovering the latent interface between geometry and appearance generation.
authors: Di Yang, Zhihao Li, Yanhai Xiong, Yufei Wang
bullets: Few-step sampling reduces the computational cost of high-resolution 3D generation.
The framework uses continuous self-consistency training, analytic velocity regression, and adaptive loss weighting for sparse 3D latents.
Channel Match is a training-free, per-channel latent calibration method that restores compatibility between geometry and PBR texture synthesis.
On TRELLIS.2 at 1024³ resolution, the two-step model provides 4.5× faster geometry sampling with comparable geometry quality to its many-step teacher.
Calibration improves rendering quality by mitigating texture artifacts on geometrically valid assets.

This controlled setting isolates the effect of latent distribution shift rather than geometry reconstruction errors, showing that the shift is a general issue of few-step sampling and can be effectively corrected by CM.)

papers.abstract: Category-level 6D pose and shape estimation requires recovering an object's pose and geometry from partial observations without an exact instance model. We present ASM-6D, which couples generative complete-geometry prediction with explicit category-level pose-shape inference through shared correspondences. Given an RGB-D image, ASM-6D generates alternative complete 3D correspondence hypotheses whose point identities are shared with a category-level Active Shape Model (ASM), including occluded points. Each hypothesis is fitted directly for rotation, translation, metric scale, and instance shape without a separate correspondence-assignment stage. We analytically eliminate translation and shape coefficients, reducing fitting to a nine-variable scaled-rotation optimization problem that enables efficient batched evaluation of multiple hypotheses in real time. ASM-6D achieves state-of-the-art performance on ROPE and HouseCat6D benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate the importance of generative correspondence prediction and active shape variation. The representation also supports shape completion, shape-dependent pose ambiguity, tracking, and robotic grasping at 6-38 Hz, depending on the inference budget.

papers.abstract: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.
authors: Rui Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Ran Cheng
bullets: Addresses the limitation of searching primitive configurations while keeping decoder transformation organization fixed.
Searches residual, sequential, and parallel stage-internal compositions while preserving fixed multi-scale interfaces.

A single source search takes about 12 GPU hours; the selected GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted baselines and reaches 27.11 dB PSNR for Gaussian novel-view synthesis.
