papers.abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.
authors: Daniel Sanchez, Djordje Mihajlovic, Federica Valeau, Luka Beni\'c, Raghuwansh Raj, Soutrik Sarangi, Snir Hordan
bullets: Addresses ambiguity and discontinuity problems in existing molecular point-cloud canonicalizations.
Selects a unique geometric representative with provable invariance under either O(3) or SO(3).
Achieves approximately 10⁻⁶ Å rotational invariance on QM9 and QM-sym, while mitigating discontinuity jumps on QM-sym.
Runs orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization.
Improves non-invariant model performance on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification relative to that method.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving increasingly relies on dense multi-view 3D reconstruction. While recent feed-forward geometric foundation models have revolutionized per-scene optimization, applying them to continuous, long-horizon driving sequences is computationally intractable due to GPU memory limits and the quadratic complexity of global attention. Existing scaling strategies are fundamentally limited, as causal streaming suffers from compounding scale drift and trajectory deviation, while rigid "chunk-then-align" heuristics fragment global context and produce trajectory discontinuities. To address these limitations, we introduce Drive3R, a block-wise streaming geometric foundation model. Its block-wise causal attention resolves the scalability bottleneck of fully bidirectional attention while avoiding the loss of local future context in purely causal streaming. Its confidence-aware re-anchoring further mitigates long-range drift by detecting unreliable streaming states, re-initializing the KV cache, and stitching refreshed segments through SE(3) alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Drive3R establishes a new state-of-the-art on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Specifically, on nuScenes, it improves over the recent DVGT-2 baseline from 0.1806 to 0.1081 in AbsRel, from 0.6750 to 0.5344 in point-cloud Accuracy, and from 1.5812 to 0.9092 in ATE.
authors: Tianyi Yang, Haojun Yang, Jipeng Xiao, Xuesong Chen, Shaoshuai Shi, Li Jiang, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses GPU-memory and quadratic-attention limits in continuous multi-view 3D reconstruction.
Uses block-wise causal attention to retain local future context while scaling beyond full bidirectional attention.
Detects unreliable streaming states, re-initializes the KV cache, and stitches refreshed segments with SE(3) alignment to reduce drift and trajectory discontinuities.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo; on nuScenes, it improves AbsRel, point-cloud Accuracy, and ATE over DVGT-2.

papers.abstract: Can a volume that reproduces every external RGB view still have an incorrect density? We study this question in emission-absorption rendering with an independently parameterized, physically bounded effective source. Appearance compensates a density change by replacing the radiance that it removes from the rest of each ray. We characterize the surviving density information with a shared spatial appearance field. Our first result is an optimal density-only gain after finite-degree spherical-harmonic source refitting. A coupled tensor gauge and physical localized packets identify the sharp limiting nonlinear inverse coefficient as its reciprocal. Our second result realizes positive gain at every fixed finite degree for a residual set of isotropic spatial sources at one fixed density. At the same references, growing angular capacity hides a fixed nonzero density error while retaining physicality and any prescribed finite set of smoothness bounds. Local identifiability and the absence of a capacity-uniform recovery modulus therefore coexist. Our third result constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity: central density doubles and relative density $L^2$ error exceeds $14.52\%$, yet every external RGB ray is unchanged. We connect these continuum results to shared finite representations, continuous pixel measurements and density-sensitive acquisition. Complete-class certificates separate SH0, SH1 and SH2 fits at one learned density. Finite-camera results expose the distinct role of spatial capacity, and transmission measurements separate otherwise identical RGB fields. Controlled training tests and captured-smoke profiles supply mechanism evidence with explicit observation scopes. The results show why rendering accuracy alone cannot certify density: recovery also depends on appearance capacity, spatial resolution and measurement design.
bullets: Studies density identifiability in emission–absorption volume rendering with physically bounded, independently parameterized sources.
Characterizes how finite spherical-harmonic appearance capacity limits density recovery, while increasing angular or spatial capacity can hide fixed density errors.
Constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity where central density doubles and relative density error exceeds 14.52% without changing any external RGB ray.
Shows that local identifiability can coexist with no capacity-uniform recovery guarantee.

Finds that transmission measurements and density-sensitive acquisition can distinguish cases that RGB rendering alone cannot; conclusions depend on appearance capacity, spatial resolution, and measurement design.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction is essential for reducing radiation dose and scan effort, but remains underconstrained due to limited projection information. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based CBCT reconstruction methods rely on gradient-driven densification, which becomes unstable under sparse acquisition and often leads to over-smoothed structures. We propose AD-GS, an Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that formulates Gaussian densification as an attenuation-aware Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process. By interpreting Gaussians as samples from an underlying anatomical attenuation distribution, AD-GS adaptively concentrates representation capacity in high-attenuation regions, enabling sharper structural boundaries under sparse projections. To further constrain reconstruction, we incorporate a semantic regularization based on zero-shot features from Segment Anything in Medical Images, enforcing multi-view consistency through semantic priors. Experiments on the ToothFairy3 dental CBCT dataset demonstrate that AD-GS achieves superior structural fidelity and boundary preservation compared with existing 3DGS-based approaches under sparse-view settings within the dental and maxillofacial setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yulinjiaxue/AD-GS-BMVC2026.

On the ToothFairy3 dataset, it improves structural fidelity and boundary preservation over existing 3DGS-based methods.
Scope: sparse-view dental and maxillofacial CBCT reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models (GFMs) directly predict dense geometry and camera poses from batches of images. Emerging visual SLAM methods chain together consecutive GFM batches to form dense point cloud maps. A core challenge is how to address the ambiguous geometric scale of GFM predictions: independent predictions are locally consistent up-to-scale but not constrained by any direct physical measurements. Models trained on data with known scale improve the consistency of GFM reconstructions but again do not directly measure it. Consequently, trajectories and 3D reconstructions from GFM-enabled SLAM methods inherit this issue. Motivated by parallels with classical visual-inertial odometry, we introduce FoundationVIO which integrates inertial sensing with GFM predictions to recover metric scale reconstruction using a factor-graph based approach. We demonstrate odometry estimates competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO methods and accurate dense reconstructions that outperform GFM-enabled SLAM methods. We also add a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism to create a full Visual-Inertial SLAM system capable of creating globally accurate reconstructions and pose estimates. We evaluate our method on three datasets with well known sensor systems and demonstrate its compatibility on ubiquitous camera and IMU sensors. The method runs at approximately real-time on a consumer-grade laptop GPU. Code: https://github.com/ori-drs/FoundationVIO.
authors: Jin Rhee, Yuhao Zhang, Frank Dellaert, Maurice Fallon
bullets: Addresses the scale ambiguity inherited by feed-forward geometric foundation models and GFM-based SLAM.
Uses a factor-graph approach to integrate inertial sensing with GFM geometry and camera-pose predictions.
Achieves odometry competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO and denser reconstructions than GFM-based SLAM methods.
Adds a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism for globally accurate visual-inertial SLAM.
Evaluated on three datasets with common camera/IMU systems and runs approximately in real time on a consumer laptop GPU.

papers.abstract: Visual localization enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to maintain absolute positioning in GNSS-denied environments. A common approach matches UAV images with geo-tagged orthographic maps and estimates camera pose using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) with elevations from Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, accurate and up-to-date DSMs are often unavailable in practice. Orthographic-perspective geometry (OPG) enables DSM-free localization in scenes with varying elevations, yet existing methods typically estimate pose indirectly through intermediate matrix estimation and decomposition. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-Depth Variable Projection (LDVP), which treats the unknown scales along perspective viewing rays as latent depths. By analytically eliminating these depths and solving for the horizontal camera center in closed form given the rotation, LDVP reduces nonlinear estimation to a rotation-only problem, enabling direct recovery of metric horizontal position without assuming a planar scene. To improve localization robustness across different scene structures, we further introduce Structure-Adaptive Coupling (SAC), which uses relative scene structure inferred from monocular depth estimation to select LDVP when the matched points are not dominated by a single plane, and Planar-PnP otherwise. Our local observability analysis reveals how scene elevation variation affects the geometric constraints of OPG, providing a basis for this adaptive strategy. Extensive experiments show that LDVP consistently outperforms existing OPG-based DSM-free methods, while SAC further improves robustness across diverse scenes and substantially narrows the gap to DSM-based localization. Code will be released at https://github.com/UAV-AVL/LDVP-SAC.
authors: Yibin Ye, Xichao Teng, Shuo Chen, Xiaokai Song, Yuli Sun, Qifeng Yu, Zhang Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of accurate, up-to-date Digital Surface Models (DSMs) for UAV localization in GNSS-denied environments.
LDVP treats perspective-ray scales as latent depths, eliminates them analytically, and reduces estimation to rotation-only optimization with closed-form horizontal position recovery.
SAC uses monocular depth-derived scene structure to choose LDVP for varied-elevation scenes and Planar-PnP for predominantly planar matches.
Experiments report consistent improvement over existing DSM-free OPG methods, with SAC narrowing the gap to DSM-based localization.
Scope: performance depends on matched scene structure and the quality of inferred relative depth.

papers.abstract: Set-based variational autoencoders (VecSet VAEs) represent 3D shapes as compact sets of latent tokens. Although each token originates from a query at a sampled surface location, whether these latents truly align with geometry remains unclear. We investigate this alignment and identify four issues: (i) attention-sink-like tokens that attract queries from across the shape; (ii) spatially periodic repetitions in decoder attention responses; (iii) mismatched normal information in encoder and decoder query features; and (iv) missing supervision of the intrinsic relation between signed distance fields and surface normals. To address these issues, we introduce Align-VAE with four corresponding modifications: (i) a shared bank of learnable decoder tokens provides a workspace for global computation; (ii) distance-biased cross-attention guides retrieval toward nearby predicted spatial anchors; (iii) normal-free encoder queries align the two stages' access to normal information while retaining normals in the encoder keys and values; and (iv) a screened Poisson-inspired regularizer supervises surface values and normal-direction derivatives. These changes align latent retrieval and field prediction with geometry without enlarging the per-shape code. On the ABO dataset, Align-VAE reduces Chamfer distance by 26.6% compared to the standard VecSet VAE.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.
authors: Hanxin Zhu, Jianqi Ma, Cong Wang, Zhihao Hu, Junyao Gao, Tianyu He, Junyan Lin, Jiayin Xiao, Jiateng Shou, Sen Liang, Weidong Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhang

Handles large-parallax motion, including 180° rotations without input-view overlap.

papers.abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40x compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.
authors: Chengzhen Wu, Kelei Liu, Sicheng Li, Lu Yu, Yiyi Liao
bullets: Addresses 4DGS storage overhead and the slow, scene-specific nature of prior compression methods.
Uses importance-based adaptive quantization to allocate bitrate according to Gaussian importance.
Introduces motion- and importance-aware packing that reorganizes attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps.
Leverages existing image and video codecs for post-training compression without per-scene optimization.
Compresses 4DGS in seconds while maintaining high quality, supporting practical deployment.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed 4DGS generalized post-training compression framework. For encoding, a per-point importance score is first derived from the input 4DGS through the importance estimator, based on which Gaussian attributes are adaptively scaled and quantized. Attributes are then packed to 2D maps according to their importance level and motion property, making them amendable for subsequent image and video coding. During decoding, attributes are obtained from the bitstreams and rescaled to their original value, restoring the 4DGS data for further rendering.

Fig. 1: Targeting the 4DGS representation which balances model compactness and rendering efficiency, we exploit the unequal importance and spatial-temporal properties of 4D Gaussians and propose a post-training compression method for 4DGS that fully leverages existing image and video codecs.

We further report the encoding time for our methods and other post-training approaches, represented by the size of the outer circle.

papers.title: TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: TETRIS-4DGS enables fast, generalized compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting with over 40× storage reduction while preserving high rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. Building on MOIS, we propose Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (MvFFN), which jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.
authors: Yuguang Li, Yichuan Deng, Zixuan Liu, Ivaylo Boyadzhiev, Xiuyuan Wu, Xinyu Zou, Linda Shapiro, Alex Colburn
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenges of camera pose, geometry, semantics, and global structure in multi-room reconstruction.
MOIS predicts each panorama column’s observed wall and its next two clockwise adjacent walls, keeping predictions local.
MvFFN jointly estimates coarse poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantics.
Layout Chaining aggregates overlapping local predictions into globally coordinated, connected floor plans.
Experiments report improved wall and junction accuracy over prior methods; the work also introduces the ZInD-CrossView dataset.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post-training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. To address this challenge, we propose GeoFix, a unified framework that improves geometric consistency and visual quality with a single geometric reward, applicable to both training and inference-time reward alignment. Our reward measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap-dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.
authors: Yeobin Hong, Hyojun Go, Dohun Lee, Jeongjae Lee, Sunghwan Hong, Federico Tombari, Zhaochong An, Jong Chul Ye, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses geometric inconsistency in video-diffusion-based 4D generation.
Uses one reward for both training-time and inference-time alignment, avoiding appearance-reward balancing.
Measures depth agreement in static scene regions while preserving valid object motion and appearance.
Calibrates for camera field-of-view overlap, which can otherwise make smaller camera movements appear geometrically better.
Reports a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.

papers.abstract: Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests. Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT-report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734-0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645-0.736 for the next-best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759-0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703-0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets. Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology-enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state-of-the-art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining. We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR
authors: S\'el\'ena Jean-Mactoux, Sophie Loizillon, Ghina Jardali, Amandine Cromb\'e, Nathalie Lassau, Alexandre B\^one
bullets: Uses contrastive vision-language pretraining on multicenter oncologic CAP CT-report pairs, including single- and multiple-series acquisitions.
Evaluated for disease detection, survival prediction, and image retrieval across internal and public test sets.
Achieved the best classification performance on CAP and oncologic subsets, and ranked first on three of four prognostic benchmarks.
Showed superior image retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets.
Preprocessing, training, inference code, and model weights are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Image-level MRI harmonization is often evaluated with a frozen site probe, a site classifier trained on raw scans and applied unchanged to harmonized ones: a drop in its accuracy is read as removal of site effects. We audit this practice on ABIDE I (1,112 T1-weighted scans, 17 sites) with ten output sets from seven harmonization methods and controls for chance, head shape, intensity, preprocessing and target alignment. We find that this verdict depends on how the probe is trained, even among probes that classify raw scans well: across random seeds, its balanced accuracy on the same CycleGAN outputs ranges from 0.13 to 0.59 (chance: 0.06). Low frozen-probe accuracy can also arise without harmonization: a Gaussian blur, which increases the intensity distance to the target site, lowers this accuracy to chance. Moreover, where the frozen probe fails, probes trained on the harmonized scans still recover the site, even from intensity histograms alone: on HACA3 outputs, the frozen probe scores 0.25, a probe trained on those outputs 0.75, and one using only their intensity histograms 0.71. Low frozen-probe accuracy therefore does not show that site information has been removed. We recommend reporting several probes trained to convergence, probes trained on harmonized scans, and target alignment.
authors: Muhammad Muqsit Islam, Gloria Garc\'ia Cuenco, Jos\'e M. Mart\'inez, Pierrick Coup\'e
bullets: The audit examines ten harmonized output sets from seven methods on ABIDE I MRI scans, with controls for chance, image properties, preprocessing, and target alignment.
Frozen-probe balanced accuracy varies widely across random seeds on identical outputs, despite strong raw-scan classification performance.
Non-harmonizing changes such as Gaussian blur can reduce frozen-probe accuracy to chance while increasing mismatch with the target site.
Site information can remain recoverable from harmonized scans, including from intensity histograms, even when the frozen probe performs poorly.
The authors recommend multiple converged probes, probes retrained on harmonized outputs, and explicit target-alignment reporting.

papers.selection_reason: Audits evaluation practices for multi-site MRI harmonization, highlighting the limitations of frozen site probes and proposing better metrics for adaptation across sites.
papers.title: Frozen Site-Probe Accuracy Is Not a Standalone Harmonization Score: An Audit of Evaluation Practice for Multi-Site MRI
papers.tldr: Frozen site-probe accuracy is an unreliable standalone measure of MRI harmonization because low scores can reflect probe instability or image degradation rather than removal of site information.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is severely under-constrained by limited X-ray projections. Learned reconstruction can provide complementary anatomical information, but using it as a prior in patient-specific Gaussian reconstruction introduces two challenges. First, the discrepancy between the learned prior and current reconstruction is spatially non-uniform: some local differences contain useful missing 3D information, whereas others reflect prior bias. Second, even a volumetrically beneficial correction can conflict with the observed X-ray measurements. Since X-ray measurements are line integrals, spatially separated corrections may affect overlapping rays, with their signed projection responses reinforcing or partially canceling in the measurement residual, so their feasibility cannot always be assessed independently. In this paper, we introduce RePrior, a multi-stage progressive prior-correction framework that addresses correction actionability, measurement feasibility, and representation expressivity. Selective Correction Proposal (SCP) first identifies actionable signed local corrections from prior--reconstruction discrepancies. Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation (MCR) then jointly enforces their consistency with patient-specific X-ray measurements, while Hybrid Residual Enhancement (HRE) recovers additional correction capacity through complementary voxel- and Gaussian-domain degrees of freedom around the reconciled anchor. RePrior requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning. RePrior gains approximately 2.6~dB in 3D PSNR over R$^2$-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN. Beyond prior-assisted reconstruction, it delivers additional gains in volumetric quality and observed-view projection fidelity, with consistent gains in held-out-view fidelity in the backbone-matched evaluation.
authors: Mengrui Yin, Tianxingjian Ding, Wufan Zhao, Ziyang Yan, Yu Tian
bullets: Addresses spatially varying prior bias and conflicts between volumetric corrections and overlapping-ray measurements.
Uses three stages: Selective Correction Proposal, Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation, and Hybrid Residual Enhancement.
Requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning.
Reports approximately 2.6 dB higher 3D PSNR than R²-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN.
Also improves volumetric quality, observed-view projection fidelity, and—under backbone-matched evaluation—held-out-view fidelity.

papers.title: RePrior: Measurement-Reconciled Prior Correction for Sparse-View CBCT Reconstruction

papers.abstract: Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing: it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure, not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting
authors: Senthil Palanisamy, Azwad Sabik, Alan Dolhasz, Mira Slavcheva
bullets: Dense, sequential, GPS-tagged drone imagery with many loop closures motivates pose-only optimization instead of joint bundle adjustment.
The evaluated system is specialized for real-estate Gaussian-splat capture and outperforms COLMAP in speed, but not reconstruction quality.
Failure sources include hand-tuned weights, greedy merging, and noisy GPS measurements.
Intrinsic limitations include scale drift when merging submaps with SE(3) edges and weaker coupling than constraints from shared 3D points.
The abstract proposes Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting as requirements for a viable design.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System overview. The image stream is split into per-sequence chunks that are optimized independently as dense SE(3) pose graphs, then merged pairwise into a single graph. Every chunk-level solve is independent, which is what the design intended to parallelize across the cloud.

Fig. 4: Qualitative output of the pose-only pipeline on a self-captured house: (a) the camera poses it estimates and (b) the resulting Gaussian-splat reconstruction. The poses are close to COLMAP and the splat is recognizable; the failures analyzed below are quality and consistency gaps, not gross breakage.

Fig. 1: The pose-only intuition. Bundle adjustment (left) couples the camera poses to a large landmark cloud through observation edges. Because the landmark block C is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, BA marginalizes the landmarks via the Schur complement into a much smaller, pose-only reduced system S = B−EC−1E⊤ (right), solves it for the poses, and only then back-substitutes for the points. Since BA’s expensive core is already this pose-only system, a pose-only formulation tries to assemble S directly from inter-pose relative-pose constraints (dashed), skipping the landmark detour. Both routes target the same S; this paper asks whether the shortcut recovers bundle-adjustment-grade poses.

Fig. 5: Camera centers, PGO versus COLMAP, both aligned to the GPS metric frame (house 2, 741 images, a 148m scene with 104m of vertical ascent). Left: the two sets of centers overlaid. Right: every frame that disagrees by more than 1m is highlighted in color, the rest green. The disagreement is pervasive, 90% of frames exceed 1m (median 1.2m), and worst on the vertical-ascent frames, up to 29m. The two regimes fail differently: the near-linear ascent trajectories suffer nadir degeneracies, while the rest of the scene inherits scaling error from noisy GPS, either way enough to soften the PGO splat relative to COLMAP.

Fig. 3: Splat quality. On house 1 the pose graph places cameras close to COLMAP (0.5◦, 2m), yet the PGO reconstruction (b) is visibly softer than COLMAP’s (a), the seam blur left by scale drift across chunk merges (Sec. 5.2) that a shared point cloud would have prevented. Row (c) shows the same on a second scene (house 2): in the zoomed roof crops the PGO splat (center) smears the shingle texture, while the COLMAP splat (right) resolves individual shingles, matching ground truth (left).

papers.title: When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting
papers.tldr: A specialized pose-graph optimizer is faster than COLMAP for Gaussian-splat drone captures but fails to match its reconstruction quality because pose-only constraints cannot fully resolve scale, multi-view coupling, and noisy weighting issues.

papers.abstract: Prior-free 6D object pose tracking seeks to recover the trajectory of an unseen object from a single RGB video without object-specific CAD models, posed reference images, or pose annotations. Geometric foundation models provide complementary object-centric and scene-centric cues, yet SAM3D CAD is indexed by an arbitrary object-local surface parameterization, whereas reconstructed evidence is expressed in a sequence-specific world frame with partial surface coverage. To exploit this complementarity, we formulate tracking as generation-reconstruction correspondence and introduce GRC-Pose, a correspondence-based framework that combines learned correspondence prediction with robust pose estimation. Concretely, GeoCorr-Matcher estimates weighted object-scene correspondences and per-match uncertainty for each pose candidate. FGH-Solver integrates these matches through multiple robust geometric estimators and sequence-level posterior inference, while a posterior-gated memory retains only inlier-supported observations through occlusion and viewpoint change. Extensive evaluation shows that with SAM3D CAD, GRC-Pose achieves state-of-the-art Average Recall and motion retention on HOT3D, improving the latter by 58% over prior art. On classical benchmarks including YCBInEOAT and LINEMOD, it remains highly competitive.
bullets: Addresses prior-free 6D pose tracking without CAD models, posed references, or pose annotations.
Predicts weighted object–scene correspondences and per-match uncertainty for candidate poses.
Combines robust geometric estimators with sequence-level posterior inference for pose estimation.
Uses posterior-gated memory to retain inlier-supported observations during occlusion and viewpoint changes.
Achieves state-of-the-art Average Recall and motion retention on HOT3D, with 58% higher motion retention than prior work; remains competitive on YCBInEOAT and LINEMOD.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.
authors: Joseph Lee, Yanjing Li, Bo Qiang, Gregory Lau, Allyson Ettinger, Noah A. Smith, Rory Donovan-Maiye, David Baker, Hanna Hajishirzi, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the limited range of objectives supported by protein design models requiring property-specific input representations.
Introduces Prompteina, an all-atom structure generator conditioned on natural-language descriptions of global and residue-specific properties.
Trains on Prompteina-Data, containing 1.8M protein structures and over 50M paired captions, with text–residue alignment.
Outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and leads on at least 13 of 20 binder-design targets; iterative feedback further improves performance.
Experimental validation against GM2A identified nine binders, with the strongest showing an apparent KD of 107 nM.

papers.abstract: 6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model-free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model-based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model-free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household-object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model-based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model-free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model-based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat-Lite, an inference variant that is $3.1\times$ faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at \href{https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat}{https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat}.
authors: Georgios Floros, Evangelos Sartinas, Orestis Vangelis, Maria Pateraki
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating poses for unseen objects without CAD models.
Uses an onboarding video to train a 3DGS model for detection, coarse pose estimation, and differentiable refinement.
Refines object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses and a continuous, nonsingular rotation representation.
Outperforms model-based methods on a household-object benchmark and model-free methods on a challenging industrial benchmark.
NovaSplat-Lite achieves 3.1× faster inference with negligible accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.
authors: Yingbo Ma, Kuangshi Ai, Gordon Dai, Chenglong Yu, Chaoli Wang, Hua Shen
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from final renders by identifying which symbolic edits persist, vanish, or interfere during execution.
Maintains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and compiles state changes into constrained alternative programs.
Validates repaired programs against runtime endpoints and preservation conditions, then uses visual verification for goal relevance.
Evaluated on BlenderGym and BlenderBench with two language models; consistently outperforms prior refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA.
Ablations examine execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction limits.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Conceptual overview of VETR. VETR refines scenes through execution-grounded evidence, bridging a scene program, its execution trace, and the realized 3D scene. Given a start and goal image, the system performs iterative updates guided by observed writes and realized bindings. This evidence-supported refinement targets viewpoint alignment, appearance (lighting/material) editing, and geometry and placement adjustments. Runtime checks test supported effects, while visual feedback guides subsequent proposals toward the goal.

Figure 2: Execution-evidence refinement before visual assessment. Each complete program executes from B. The private refiner constructs alternatives, compiles supported changes and compatible bindings, and checks their realization relative to the candidate’s reference record. For the numerical channel, Wh contains selected cells, Ch \ Wh contains captured cells to preserve, and properties outside Ch are not covered by that contract. Goal-image comparison occurs only in the ordinary visual verifier. Delivery, shortcuts, and the six-execution cap are specified in Algorithm 1. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of visual editing. Columns display the goal, start, VIGA final output, and VETR final output across three editing categories: light (color), geometry (chair position & orientation), and shape (facial expression). Red arrows and boxes highlight local regions of comparison. Reported values denote PL ×100 (lower is better). VETR achieves near-zero PL in the displayed light and geometry tasks and lower error in the displayed shape task. These output comparisons illustrate visual fidelity, not an independent verification of the refiner’s runtime mechanism.

Figure 4: Editing strategy and execution outcome on the same task. (a) The supplied procedural program. (b) Under the One-Shot prompt, GPT-5.6-luna rewrites the scene and accesses a socket absent in Blender 3.6, so this attempt yields no render. papers.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
authors: Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Addresses high inference cost from repeated cross-view observations and processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer.
GeoSemZip builds compact 3D voxel-token representations using semantic saliency and spatial coverage, while retaining discarded information in contextual anchors.
GroupRoute uses late entry, early exit, and recoverable group-wise skipping to adapt visual computation to token relevance.
Using a 67K-sample compression-aware post-training set, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of dense-model performance on two 7B 3D VLMs.
It accelerates LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×, demonstrating applicability to models with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GeoGR. (1) Projector-level Compression: GeoSemZip consolidates crossview observations into 3D voxel tokens using depth and camera poses. The compressed visual tokens are combined with text tokens to form the LLM input. (2) LLM-level Compression: GroupRoute confines visual computation to an intermediate-layer window through Late Entry and Early Exit. Within this window, Recoverable Group-wise Skipping routes query-conditioned token groups through or around complete LLM layers. Skipped tokens retain their hidden states and can resume computation after regrouping at subsequent anchor layers. Text tokens remain active throughout the LLM.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct scenes from unposed images, but the quadratic cost of global attention limits their scalability to large view sets. We present Zebra3D, a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework that improves the efficiency of pretrained 3D foundation models without training from scratch. Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and $\pi^3$, we observe a broadly consistent depth-wise pattern: early stages are relatively tolerant to linear replacement, while sensitive middle-to-late stages tend to exhibit more concentrated attention. Zebra3D exploits this structure by assigning linear-centered attention to tolerant stages and tile-sparse attention to sensitive stages, using landmark summaries to preserve unselected context. Closed-form affine fitting enables training-free conversion, while optional post-conversion training combines task supervision with output and relational feature distillation. Across all three backbones, Zebra3D achieves strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity, with training-free variants remaining close to their dense counterparts. End-to-end speedups increase with input view count, reaching up to $7.1\times$ at 1,024 views. After post-conversion training, Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5\% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94\% mean attention sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense VGGT fine-tuned on the same data and schedule.
authors: Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Akash Haridas, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of global attention in feed-forward 3D foundation models for unposed-image reconstruction.
Assigns linear-centered attention to tolerant early stages and tile-sparse attention with landmark summaries to sensitive middle-to-late stages.
Converts models without training from scratch using closed-form affine fitting; optional distillation-based post-conversion training further improves performance.
Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and π³, maintains strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity.
Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94% mean sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense fine-tuned VGGT; speedup reaches 7.1× at 1,024 views.

papers.abstract: Boundary-value problems for the Laplace equation develop singular behaviour near corners, edges and junctions that smooth approximators resolve poorly. We combine holomorphic neural networks with singular functions derived from the local geometry and boundary conditions. The representation is harmonic by construction, so no interior residual is needed: the network fits the smooth remainder from boundary data alone, and the enrichment terms capture the singular behaviour. Singular exponents are trainable, so the construction also applies when the local expansion is not known in advance. We extend the approach to three dimensions using independent networks evaluated along complex null directions. The enriched model is the most accurate tested method on every problem. Its margin is several orders of magnitude where the enrichment captures the singularity exactly, and a factor of about 1.7-2.1 over the next-best method on a CdZnTe radiation detector with many singular sites, in both two and three dimensions.
authors: Kalp Shah, Andrei Vlad Nicula, Mihnea Andrei B\^arsan, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jel\'inek, Alejandro Valverde Mahou
bullets: Targets the poor performance of smooth approximators near geometric and boundary-induced singularities.
Combines holomorphic neural networks with geometry- and boundary-informed singular functions.
Produces harmonic solutions by construction, avoiding interior residual evaluation and fitting only the smooth remainder at the boundary.
Trains singular exponents when the local expansion is unknown and extends the method to 3D via complex null directions.
Achieves the best tested accuracy on all problems, with especially large gains for exactly captured singularities and about 1.7–2.1× improvement on a CdZnTe detector problem.

papers.abstract: Deep learning on cortical surfaces faces a dilemma: capturing the complex topology of over 60 nomenclature-dependent sulci per hemisphere requires high-capacity models, yet the extreme scarcity of expert annotations ($N=62$ subjects) inevitably causes overfitting. Standard supervised approaches fail to generalize in this data-scarce regime, particularly for variable and small sulci where topological ambiguity is high. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a Geometric-to-Semantic Spherical Transfer Learning framework. First, we leverage massive unlabeled data (UK Biobank, $\approx$30,000 subjects) to pre-train a spherical encoder using a locally-optimized strategy. By relying solely on continuous surface features (curvature and depth), the relevance of this pre-training is confirmed by the model's ability to detect localized and rare topological traits, such as sulcal interruptions. The downstream labeling task, however, introduces extracted sulcal fundi (lines) as an explicit semantic input. To bridge this dimensional domain gap (from purely geometric to semantic) without causing catastrophic forgetting, these anatomical lines are integrated into the pre-trained backbone via a soft-initialized Topological Prior Injector. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms fully supervised baselines trained from scratch, achieving a mean Dice of 0.77. Crucially, a local analysis reveals that the self-supervised geometric priors yield the largest performance gains on variable and tertiary sulci (up to 14.8%), confirming that learning the cortex shape is highly beneficial for identifying its rarest parts.
bullets: Addresses overfitting from labeling more than 60 nomenclature-dependent sulci using only 62 annotated subjects.
Pre-trains a spherical encoder on curvature and depth from approximately 30,000 unlabeled UK Biobank subjects.
Injects extracted sulcal fundi as semantic inputs through a soft-initialized Topological Prior Injector while preserving geometric knowledge.
Achieves a mean Dice of 0.77 and gains up to 14.8% on variable and tertiary sulci.
Shows the strongest benefits for rare sulci and localized topological traits such as sulcal interruptions.

papers.tldr: A spherical transfer-learning framework uses large-scale unlabeled cortical geometry to improve labeling of rare and variable sulci when expert annotations are scarce.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D world models generate photorealistic, explorable scenes that remain frozen in time. OuroWorld is a mask-free framework that turns any static 3D Gaussian Splatting scene into a 3D cinemagraph: a dynamic scene with vivid, diverse motion looping seamlessly from any viewpoint. A vision-language model infers plausible dynamics and guides a video model to synthesize a reference video, which we lift and complete into multi-view videos. To learn from this imperfect supervision, we propose Inconsistency-Robust Periodic 4DGS: a Fourier-series deformation field guarantees looping by construction, while a Grounded Drift Field anchored at the reference view absorbs cross-view inconsistency. Unlike prior Eulerian methods limited to fluid-like motion, we capture general deformation, object motion, and illumination change. We introduce a ground-truth-free evaluation covering vividness, naturalness, loop seam coherence, and scene quality. On 39 reconstructed and generated scenes, OuroWorld outperforms all baselines and wins 70.8%-99.0% of user-study comparisons. Project page: https://ouroworld.userwei.com
authors: You-Zhe Xie, Ting-Wei Chou, Yu-Hsuan Li, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang, Yu-Lun Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that photorealistic 3D world models are typically static.
Uses a vision-language model and video model to infer and synthesize plausible motion, then lifts it into multi-view videos.
Introduces Inconsistency-Robust Periodic 4DGS, combining Fourier deformation fields for guaranteed loops with a reference-anchored drift field for cross-view inconsistencies.
Supports object deformation, object motion, and illumination changes beyond fluid-like motion.
Evaluated on 39 scenes with a ground-truth-free metric suite; the abstract reports outperforming all baselines and winning 70.8%–99.0% of user-study comparisons.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of OuroWorld. (a) Looping video generation. A VLM selects a reference view rendered from the input 3DGS, infers plausible scene dynamics, and prompts a video generation model to synthesize an approximately looping reference video. (b) Multi-view video generation. A 3D foundation model (VGGT-Ω) lifts the reference video into a dynamic point cloud, using static multi-view renders to improve depth. The point cloud is rendered from N surrounding viewpoints into incomplete videos with disoccluded holes, which a video inpainting model (TrajectoryCrafter) completes into multi-view videos. (c) Inconsistency-Robust Periodic 4DGS. The 3D cinemagraph is represented as a canonical 3DGS deformed by a Fourier-parameterized Periodic Deformation Field, which loops by construction. A Grounded Drift Field absorbs cross-view inconsistency of the generated videos during training and is discarded at inference.

Figure 7 Effect of drift. Without drift, fine details degrade over time: the clouds in Iceland Canyon blur and fade away (top row), the galaxy in World becomes blurry (middle row), and the rocks on the ground vanish (bottom row). In contrast, our full model preserves these details while maintaining vivid and coherent motion. The first column shows the full frame at t1 with the zoomed region outlined; the remaining columns zoom into that region at t1, and at t2 and t3 for each method.

Figure 5 Qualitative comparison under the orbit camera, one scene per source. The leftmost column shows the input 3DGS at t1; the others show each method at later time steps t2 and t3. 3D Cinemagraphy and 3D-MOM produce disocclusion holes and color artifacts, while Gaussians-to-Life and LoopGaussian remain nearly static. OuroWorld produces vivid, view-consistent dynamics such as changing illumination, rippling water, drifting fog, and curtains swaying in the wind. See the supplementary videos for full loops.

Figure 2 Motivation. Left: 3D world models generate frozen worlds; 3D cinemagraphs bring them alive. Middle: Existing 3D cinemagraph methods rely on Eulerian flow and are limited to fluid-like motion. Right: We turn any static 3D scene into a 3D cinemagraph, which requires (1) seamless looping and (2) vivid, diverse dynamics.

Figure 1 OuroWorld brings static 3Dworlds alive. Left : Given a static 3DGS scene from any source, e.g., the 3D world models HY-World 2.0, Marble, and Lyra 2.0, OuroWorld converts it into a 3D cinemagraph: a dynamic scene with vivid, diverse motion that loops endlessly. Right : free-viewpoint renders along a moving camera, with green boxes highlighting regions with noticeable dynamics. Smoke billows in the volcano (top), the galaxy scatters stardust (middle), and the ships bob up and down on the water (bottom). Motion stays consistent across viewpoints, and the scene at t=T returns to t=0, so the loop is seamless. See the supplementary videos for full results.
Figure A.1 Instruction given to GPT-5.5 together with the reference image to write the dynamics prompt.
Figure A.2 Motionmasks. (a) The 2D motion mask obtained by segmenting the moving entities in the reference image with SAM 3. (b) The corresponding 3D motion mask.

Figure 4 Learning deformation from inconsistent multi-view videos. Rows: canonical geometry, deformed scene at inference, per-view training renders, and generated training views. (a) w/o Drift Field: conflicting views are averaged, causing blur and erratic motion. (b) w/ Drift Field: drift on every view absorbs too much of the dynamics and is discarded at inference, reducing motion. (c) w/ Grounded Drift Field (ours): with no drift at the reference view, the deformation field must reproduce the reference dynamics, yielding a sharp scene with consistent motion.
Figure A.3 User study interface. Two videos of the same scene are shown side by side in random order (top), and participants choose one for each of the four criteria (bottom).

Figure 6 User study. In a two-alternative forced-choice study, participants compare OuroWorld with each baseline under four criteria. Bars show the percentage of votes preferring ours (left) versus the baseline (right). Ours is preferred in 70.8%–99.0% of comparisons across all baselines and criteria, with the largest margins in Vividness. 30 participants took part; see Appendix A.6 for details.

Table 2 Quantitative result. Vividness Degree measures motion, illumination, and appearance change. KVD measures the distance to the natural video distribution. MALF measures whether the scene loops while it actually moves, and Seam SSIM measures the similarity at the seam of consecutive cycles; Aesthetic Quality and Overall Consistency follow VBench to assess scene quality. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best results. Ours achieves the best Vividness, Naturalness, and Aesthetic Quality. Near-static methods (LoopGaussian, 3D Cinemagraphy) trivially reach a high Seam SSIM but near-zero MALF, whereas ours achieves the best MALF with a high Seam SSIM.

Table 1 Capability comparison. Mask-free: no user-provided 2D/3D motion mask. True 3D : free-viewpoint rendering, not pseudo-3D. Mathematical looping : the 4D output is guaranteed to loop. Diverse motion: not limited to one motion type. Illumination: time-varying lighting. Ours is the only method that satisfies all five properties.
Table A.1 Hyperparameters of OuroWorld.

Table 3 Ablation on consistency components. As illustrated in Fig. 4, removing the drift field blurs the scene (low VoL) and lowers both subject and background consistency; removing grounding lets drift absorb the dynamics, reducing the scene motion (lowest Vividness); removing scene-view consistent optimization breaks scene-view consistency and blurs the scene most severely (lowest subject consistency, VoL −22% under orbit). Our full model is best on all orbit-camera metrics.
Table A.2 Inputs and native loop periods of all methods. For Gaussians-to-Life, which does not loop, the period is the length of its generated motion.
Table A.4 Vividness breakdown of the ablation. SVCO denotes scene-view consistent optimization. Bold denotes the best result.
Table A.3 Vividness breakdown against baselines. MV, IV, and VV denote Motion, Illumination, and Visual Variation; Vividness is their average. Bold denotes the best result.

papers.abstract: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch
authors: Peter Kulits, Yiqing Xu, R. Kenny Jones, Cordelia Schmid, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Agents select parts from a discrete library while jointly reasoning about local and global constraints.
The benchmark scores validity, prompt alignment, and design quality across three scales and part-availability settings.
BrickAgent provides an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate designs.
Leading agents generally meet verifiable physical and semantic requirements but underperform human designs.
The benchmark and environment are publicly released at brickben.ch.

figures.caption: Figure 5: ELO. (a) We plot ELO against mean assembly cost. (b) To validate our model-based Design ELO computation, we perform a perceptual study where participants are tasked with judging design quality between a pair of assemblies for a given prompt. The prompt isn’t given to the judge, and they make their decision based only on the images. We find that the rankings agree on 34/36 agent pairs (Kendall 𝜏 = 0.89), suggesting the metric is an effective proxy for human judgment. The study covers the nine reference agents; Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol were evaluated after it.

Figure 2: BrickNet validation. We evaluate GPT-5.6 Luna on the BrickNet text-to-assembly validation set (Kulits & Schmid, 2026). While it was not specialized for this dataset, we find it exceeds task-specific baselines including BrickGPT (Pun et al., 2025) across metrics and nears the alignment of the ground-truth objects. (a) Sample inputs and model outputs. (b) Caption alignment following BrickNet’s evaluation protocol. PE (Bolya et al., 2025) and SigLIP 2 (Tschannen et al., 2025) score the similarity between the embeddings of the renders and of the caption, and VQAScore (Lin et al., 2024) the probability that a VQA model answers yes when asked whether the renders show the caption. See Kulits & Schmid (2026) for details on metric computation.

Figure 6: Human-design evaluation. We perform a perceptual study comparing agent designs with human designs. For each assembly in the Model and Set settings, we select a random assembly from the BrickNet dataset with a comparable number of parts and ask a human rater to identify the one made by a person. We find that raters are able to distinguish between the agent-designed and human-designed assemblies (a); the study covers the nine reference agents and the two baselines. While agent-designed assemblies often satisfy the prompt criteria, there is a clear gap in fine-grained design to those produced by humans (b).

Figure 4: BrickBench samples. We show one assembly from each of the eleven agents for three prompts in each setting. We observe the agents vary in their interpretation of the prompts. One assembly is missing for Muse because it did not deliver one within the turn budget.
Figure 3: BrickBench summary. We report summary metrics averaged across the three evaluation settings. See Tab. 1 for disaggregated results. The ELO-plot lines represent 95% intervals.

Table 1: BrickBench. We report metrics for each of the three evaluation settings and in the aggregate (Overall). Valid requires that the assembly satisfies the part requirement of the setting and is both collision-free and stable. VQA is the proportion of VQA questions satisfied (Sec. 4.4). ELO, Align ELO, and Design ELO are ratings estimated from pairwise VLM judgments (Sec. 4.4). Cost is the API cost in US dollars, or its equivalent for BrickGPT (Pun et al., 2025), of producing one assembly. *The Valid metric of BrickNet-14B (Kulits & Schmid, 2026) doesn’t include stability as the model doesn’t produce assemblies in a canonical frame and the direction of gravity is undefined.

Table 2: Environment ablation. We ablate the effect of the BrickAgent environment, pooled over the three evaluation settings (Overall; 300 prompts). While both agents consistently produce valid assemblies when given tools, they struggle without them to varying degrees: GPT-6 Astra is somewhat robust but its assemblies drop to being valid only 40% of the time while GPT-5.6 Luna’s fall to less than a percent. The environment improves the VQA of Astra but lowers its ELO within noise. Without it, Luna improves on both, suggesting the buildability constraint limits expressivity.

papers.tldr: BrickBench evaluates whether agents can generate semantically aligned, aesthetically designed, and physically buildable LEGO assemblies from text prompts.

papers.abstract: Generating an egocentric video from a single exocentric recording is a challenging case of novel view synthesis, as the two cameras share little overlap and much of the target view is unobserved. Current state-of-the-art methods reconstruct the scene explicitly by estimating depth, lifting the video into a point cloud, and re-rendering it from the egocentric camera to condition a video diffusion model. This deterministic mapping assigns each pixel to a single reprojected location, which preserves texture but translates depth errors into misplaced content. We ask what a video diffusion model should receive as its condition and propose a lifting-free answer: a learned view synthesizer, an LVSM-style transformer fine-tuned to render the egocentric view directly without depth, point clouds, or reprojection, resolving cross-view correspondence internally. In contrast, its probabilistic mapping averages each region over candidate source locations according to a learned correspondence distribution, preserving structure while fine texture is averaged away. We argue that this trade-off suits a diffusion generator, whose denoising training excels at restoring detail, so an effective condition should prioritize structural alignment over sharpness. This distribution's concentration also yields a per-region confidence, used both to mask low-confidence regions and to guide the generator toward high-confidence areas during early layout-forming denoising steps. Our approach consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art explicit pipeline and generalizes to other datasets without retraining. The synthesizer thus supplies view structure, and the diffusion model its detail.
authors: Suhwan Cho, Yonwoo Choi, Soongjin Kim, Jicheol Park, Taegyu Lim
bullets: Addresses exocentric-to-egocentric synthesis when the target view has little camera overlap and substantial unobserved content.
Uses an LVSM-style transformer to render the target view directly, avoiding depth estimation, point clouds, and reprojection.
Models cross-view correspondence probabilistically, favoring structural alignment over potentially misplaced sharp details.
Uses correspondence confidence to mask uncertain regions and guide early diffusion denoising.
Outperforms the prior explicit pipeline and transfers to other datasets without retraining, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: We present Pumpire, a unified benchmark for evaluating metric point-pair distance estimation capability of both image- and video-level 3D foundation models, with or without depth priors. In contrast to previous approaches that normally evaluate depth and camera intrinsics separately or evaluate point-clouds with geometric similarity metrics, which cannot directly reflect models' point-to-point distance estimation capability, Pumpire directly assesses point-to-point distances from the reconstructed geometry. To this end, we collect a large-scale and diverse dataset (pumpire-6k) comprising 100 real-world scenes, each annotated with physically measured point-pair distances and containing 64 frames, for a total of 6,400 frames. Building on this dataset, we establish a holistic evaluation protocol that covers both image- and video-level 3D foundation models and enables direct assessment of point-pair distance errors and cross-setting comparison. We conduct extensive experiments across 29 baseline configurations of representative 3D foundation models and provide a comprehensive analysis of the results. By offering this benchmark, we target the more fundamental ability to perceive and estimate physical scale in the reconstructed 3D space, which prior evaluation protocols have largely overlooked. The project page can be found at https://pumpire.github.io/
authors: Siyu Chen, Zehan Wang, Jiayang Xu, Yihan Wu, Jialei Wang, Junming Chen, Ziang Zhang, Yutong Ying, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Addresses a gap in evaluations that separately assess depth, camera intrinsics, or geometric similarity rather than physical distance estimation.
Introduces pumpire-6k: 100 diverse real-world scenes with measured point-pair distances across 6,400 frames.
Provides a unified protocol for comparing image- and video-level 3D foundation models, with or without depth priors.
Evaluates 29 representative baseline configurations and analyzes their distance-estimation performance.
Focuses on physical-scale perception in reconstructed 3D space, which prior protocols largely overlook.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Left: Overview of our data acquisition pipeline, including scene preparation, multi-view RGB-D capture, and the generation of raw data for subsequent annotation. Valid frames are first sub-sampled from the raw image sequence, followed by anchor-frame annotation, automatic keypoint tracking, deviation-based reannotation, and frame-by-frame verification to produce the final annotated sequence.

Figure 1: Overview of the Pumpire evaluation protocol. Pumpire provides a unified evaluation of image- and video-level 3D foundation models under geometry estimation and completion settings. Estimation models recover geometry from RGB inputs, whereas completion models additionally condition on depth priors. Pumpire back-projects depth maps predicted by 3D foundation models with their associated camera intrinsics and quantifies the results with the proposed metrics. Their predicted distance is compared with the physically measured ground truth using the proposed metrics as introduced in Section 4.
